artigo.texto: COMPWIRE vence pregão de R$ 161,8 milhões do Proderj para data center Licitação conduzida pela Prod do Rio de Janeiro reúne demandas de nove órgãos e entidades estaduais. Tempo de contrato é de 60 meses. O Centro de Tecnologia de Informação e Comunicação do Estado do Rio de Janeiro (Proderj) homologou o resultado de uma licitação que prevê até R$ 161,8 milhões para a contratação de equipamentos e soluções de armazenamento e proteção de dados da administração estadual. A expectativa do governo é que a modernização da infraestrutura tecnológica contribua para oferecer serviços públicos digitais mais eficientes e estáveis. O despacho foi publicado nesta quarta-feira (11), no Diário Oficial. A COMPWIRE Informática Ltda. foi declarada vencedora dos dois lotes da licitação. O primeiro, no valor de R$ 151,48 milhões, contempla soluções de armazenamento de alta disponibilidade, incluindo equipamentos com tecnologia flash e sistemas para grandes volumes de dados. O segundo lote, de R$ 10,317 milhões, prevê a contratação de equipamentos e soluções para a infraestrutura de datacenter. O pacote inclui hardware, software, treinamento, manutenção e atualização tecnológica pelo período de 60 meses. Segundo informações divulgadas pelo próprio governo, a iniciativa reúne demandas de nove órgãos e entidades estaduais, com o objetivo de centralizar contratações de tecnologia e evitar licitações individuais para serviços semelhantes. Os R$ 161,797 milhões não serão liberados de uma vez só. Os órgãos estaduais poderão aderir à ata de acordo com suas necessidades e disponibilidade orçamentária, pagando pelos serviços e equipamentos que efetivamente contratarem.

artigo.texto: A fabricante de chips holandesa Nexperia está com a demanda “totalmente acima da capacidade de oferta”, uma vez que fornecedores estão redirecionando sua capacidade produtiva para data centers de inteligência artificial (IA) em detrimento dos chips de tecnologias maduras, utilizados em automóveis e equipamentos industriais, advertiu o CEO interino, Stefan Tilger, durante a feira comercial Electronica, em Munique. Tilger afirmou que alguns concorrentes realocaram sua capacidade produtiva, afastando-se dos semicondutores de uso geral (commodities) fornecidos pela Nexperia, o que gerou gargalos em partes da cadeia de suprimentos automotiva. “A indústria automotiva está sofrendo bastante neste momento”, disse. Posição endossada pelo CEO da STMicroelectronics, Jean-Marc Chery. “Observamos muitos gargalos e muitas fábricas de chips estão se afastando das tecnologias convencionais”, advertiu. A demanda vinda dos data centers de IA e da robótica está absorvendo a capacidade produtiva, enquanto, por outro lado, os investimentos em tecnologias maduras — usadas para fabricar diodos, transistores e outros componentes básicos — ficaram estagnados por anos, advertem os especialistas. A Nexperia é especializada em semicondutores de baixo custo e alto volume, utilizados principalmente em veículos e equipamentos industriais. Ao contrário de concorrentes maiores, como a STMicroelectronics, a empresa possui um portfólio mais restrito, focado em componentes de tecnologias maduras. Chery mencionou que a estrutura fabril da própria STMicroelectronics oferece uma certa proteção contra restrições no fornecimento. “Controlamos parte do nosso futuro por meio de nossos investimentos em capital (CapEx) e de nossa própria capacidade de fabricação”, disse ele.

artigo.texto: São Paulo lança fundo de R$ 70 milhões para ISPs e data centers de pequeno porte Iniciativa quer ampliar o acesso a crédito em regiões ainda subatendidas por data centers e redes de conectividade, sobretudo no interior paulista. Operações de fusão e aquisição (M&A) também estão contempladas. A Desenvolve SP e a gestora Möbius Capital lançaram um Fundo de Investimento em Direitos Creditórios (FIDC) de R$ 70 milhões para provedores de serviços de Internet (ISPs) e data centers de pequeno porte. O objetivo é ampliar o acesso a crédito e apoiar investimentos em infraestrutura digital no Estado de São Paulo. Com apoio do fundo, os provedores, em linhas gerais, poderão antecipar os recebíveis de seus clientes, tanto pessoas físicas como jurídicas, e investir em operações de crédito destinadas a financiar a compra de equipamentos de infraestrutura e projetos de expansão de redes. O FIDC também visa a ampliar o acesso a crédito em regiões ainda subatendidas por data centers e redes de conectividade, sobretudo no interior paulista. Operações de fusão e aquisição (M&A) também estão contempladas. O fundo é composto por R$ 50 milhões da Desenvolve SP, nas cotas seniores, e R$ 20 milhões da Möbius Capital, nas cotas subordinadas. “Nossa meta é ampliar o acesso ao crédito e facilitar recursos para negócios inovadores. Por meio do blended finance, conseguimos atrair investimento privado, potencializar o impacto do recurso público e alcançar mais empreendedores”, afirmou o diretor-presidente da Desenvolve SP, Ricardo Brito, em nota. Já a Möbius Capital foi selecionada por meio de uma chamada pública. Além de sua experiência no setor de infraestrutura digital, a gestora apresentou tese, estrutura, estratégia, governança, equipe, histórico e valor pleiteado para o desenho da linha de crédito. “Temos um histórico de realizar financiamento para aquisições de provedores de Internet, operações via mercado de capitais para fomentar o crescimento de empresas do setor, além de dar apoio no avanço da profissionalização e governança dessas companhias”, destacou Roberto Savaris, sócio e fundador da Möbius.

artigo.texto: Huang Resigns: Nvidia's AI Infrastructure Roadmap in Question The departure of Jensen Huang without a clear long-term successor could mean turmoil at the data center economy bellwether, analysts say. This article was originally published on TechTarget.com. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned, the company announced Thursday morning. Executive vice president and CFO Colette Kress will serve as Interim CEO while the board considers both internal and external candidates for a long-term replacement, according to a company press release. The choice of Kress as interim CEO is an obvious one, given that the company reports earnings next week and that she would already be involved in established partnerships, according to analysts. ″[Huang] has already set up the technology path that she can lean on other executives to lead,” said Larry Carvalho, principal consultant at RobustCloud. “Nvidia does not need a showman right now but just solid execution without any distractions.” This change without a preselected long-term successor raises questions about the tech supplier’s future ability to execute and innovate, analysts said. The stakes are high for Nvidia, which has an overwhelming share of an exploding AI infrastructure market. The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that the Nvidia board was preparing to oust founding CEO Jensen Huang following a New York Times report earlier in the day that Huang had an extramarital affair with an Nvidia employee who reported to him. This news came three days after Huang confirmed an extramarital affair with a person outside the company suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset, raising potential national security and economic concerns. Huang’s future was already clouded as the Nvidia board conducted an investigation into the first affair, but an affair with an internal employee “makes this a conduct issue,” said Patrick Moorhead, an analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy. In the near-term, not much would change for IT buyers should Huang be forced out, but trouble could lie 12 to 24 months out, Moorhead said. “Nvidia is built around one person with no named successor,” he said. “The risk is that the future roadmap hasn’t been defined and that executing the current roadmap requires many command and control decisions that Jensen provides.” Nvidia is among the world’s most valuable publicly traded companies, with a $4.08 trillion market capitalization, according to Yahoo Finance. It held nearly 90% of the overall GPU market share across consumer and data center markets as of February, and 80% of the data center AI accelerator market share as of April, according to Silicon Analysts reports. In June, it also reached No. 1 in market share for data center Ethernet switching. The Question of Succession Huang, who founded Nvidia in 1993, has been an iconic public face for the company as it set the pace for AI infrastructure over the past four years. His two children also hold leadership roles at the company; his wife is a co-trustee to more than 500 million of Huang’s Nvidia shares. “It would be very tough to replace him … I’d be surprised if they could find someone internal,” said Rob Strechay, an analyst at VB Intelligence. ”[With] the web he has woven internally, there is a ton of loyalty [and] a lot of autonomy.” With no obvious successor, “that limits flexibility [for Nvidia] if this develops the wrong way,” said Steven Dickens, founder and CEO at HyperFrame Research. “From a corporate governance perspective, that is something the board needs to address in short order.” That said, while difficult, replacing Huang isn’t impossible, according to Strechay. “I’m not sure … that someone [else] couldn’t build the relationships across the ecosystem that Jensen has.” A company as large as Nvidia “probably has a deep bench who are unknown at this time,” RobustCloud’s Carvalho said. “At worst, they could go outside and find somebody to replace him. The main thing is, like Larry Ellison, he was the face of the company, but he’s not irreplaceable.” An Opportunity for Competitors Nvidia’s nearly unchallenged dominance in GPUs had likely already peaked, according to Silicon Analysts’ February report. In addition, this year has seen a strong trend toward chip diversification as AI inference and agentic orchestration, which have different infrastructure requirements, supersede model training, the report said. “My feeling is with [OpenAI’s] Jalapeno coming out on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and [Google] TPUs by next year in Q3, Nvidia could be in a tough spot,” Strechay said. Potentially, the effect of a less effective successor to Huang at Nvidia could echo Steve Ballmer’s succession of Bill Gates at Microsoft in 2000, which resulted in lost ground to competitors in consumer devices and falling stock prices despite strong revenue growth, according to Strechay. “If it is a Ballmer situation, things become tough for Nvidia as they are going from fighting the GPU wars to the CPU wars,” Strechay said. “It could also hasten consolidation in AI-specialized neoclouds.” Ideally, a healthy market should have multiple strong competitors, but “the reality is that Nvidia has locked in a tremendous amount of capacity, so even if people wanted to switch, they couldn’t,” Moorhead said.

artigo.texto: Labor Shortages Threaten Data Center Schedules Labor shortages and rising costs are making data center schedules more fragile, especially in Southern markets where specialized crews are already stretched. Data center developers face higher construction bids and intensifying competition for specialized workers in 2027, as demand for facilities and power infrastructure concentrates in Southern US markets where workforce capacity is already strained, according to JLL. In its 2027 US Construction Perspective, JLL forecasts national tender prices – what contractors bid for projects – will rise 4.2% in 2027, up from 3.1% in 2026 and above the pre-2020 norm of 2% to 3%. The projection applies to the broader construction market rather than data centers alone. The South is expected to contribute more to nonresidential construction growth than any other US region and to carry the heaviest workload per worker by 2028, driven by data centers, power projects, and public civil works. Matthew Giddings, JLL’s executive director of technical services, told Data Center Knowledge that developers risk underestimating the cost of assembling qualified crews. “The challenge isn't just finding workers. It's finding qualified workers in the right location at the right time,” he said. “The budget impact extends well beyond wage rates.” Developers are paying overtime and covering travel, lodging, and relocation premiums to bring specialists into markets without sufficient local labor. But adding crews can also increase costs without improving productivity if designs, materials, and construction sequencing are not well coordinated, Giddings noted. Labor Planning Must Start with Site and Power Strategy JLL said emerging data center markets may lack the workforce capacity to support multiple hyperscale developments simultaneously. Campuses increasingly include substations, utility infrastructure, and dedicated generation, requiring thousands of workers over multiyear construction programs. “You can't assume that labor will simply be available once a project is ready to break ground,” Giddings said. “Workforce planning needs to happen alongside site selection, permitting, and utility strategy.” He added that early relationships with trade schools, community colleges, and apprenticeship programs can help build local capacity, while waiting until construction is near leaves developers competing for workers already committed elsewhere. Power delivery presents a related staffing challenge. Utilities need crews for transmission lines and substations, while developers need electrical trades to build and energize facilities. Those labor pools are not interchangeable, Giddings said. “We've seen situations where facilities were substantially complete with power available but remained months away from operation because qualified commissioning personnel weren’t available,” he said. To reduce that risk, Giddings urged developers to coordinate utility work, equipment procurement, construction, and commissioning within a single schedule. Project Uncertainty Is Driving Bids Higher JLL’s outlook identifies metals, energy-intensive products, and related building packages as sources of cost pressure. Tender prices typically trail input costs by three to six months, meaning increases through late 2026 will continue to affect bids in early 2027. Giddings said contractors also price in risks they cannot confidently assess. “When a contractor is asked to commit to a guaranteed price or delivery date before design is fully developed or procurement risks are understood, they're going to account for that uncertainty in their pricing,” he explained. Early contractor involvement, clearer procurement plans, and an experienced owner’s team can improve pricing predictability. Established data center contractors with substantial backlogs can also afford to be selective, making it harder for owners to pass unresolved project risks downstream at low cost. Prefabricated electrical assemblies and standardized cooling infrastructure can reduce on-site labor requirements, but manufacturers still face staffing and capacity constraints. Giddings said repeatable designs deployed across campuses tend to add more value than isolated prefabrication decisions. Spending More Only Helps If It Removes the Bottleneck For AI-focused campuses, earlier operation can justify substantial additional spending. Developers should weigh acceleration against financing costs, customer commitments, equipment deployment, and revenue lost through delayed occupancy, Giddings said. That calculation depends on whether the additional spending actually changes the opening date. More construction labor offers little benefit if equipment delivery or commissioning still determines when the facility can operate. “Adding overtime or manpower doesn't help if the true constraint is transformer delivery, utility energization, or commissioning,” Giddings said. “Successful acceleration strategies target the actual bottlenecks rather than simply increasing construction spend.”

artigo.texto: Insight and analysis on the data center space from industry thought leaders. Winning Data Center Bids Starts with the Investment Tax Credit Contractors can win more data center bids by planning for the Investment Tax Credit early and helping owners capture more value. Picture two proposals for a data center bid. The pricing is similar. The timelines are similar. One covers the construction scope. The other shows how the project can be structured not just on a blueprint but on a tax return to unlock additional financial value. For an owner weighing the full economics of a data center investment, the difference can be compelling. For years, apart from the largest industry players, few other contractors could submit bids at that scale, much less win them. They couldn't compete with the giants on labor availability, balance sheet strength, or track record. Today, that landscape is changing. AI demand and an unprecedented wave of data center developments are stretching even the largest players. More firms are getting a chance to compete. The question for contractors is how to stand out once they are at the table. One of the most overlooked advantages is the availability of tax incentives, particularly the federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC). In projects that include eligible energy property, the ITC can materially improve project economics. In an industry where margins are tight, and bids are often won by fractions of a percentage point, that matters. Where the Value Comes From Power now sits at the center of every data center project. Developers are under pressure to meet rising energy demand while keeping long-term costs under control. As a result, more projects are investing in on-site solar, battery storage, microgrids, and other systems built for resilience. These assets may qualify for federal incentives, including the ITC. One of us spent years inside the IRS helping shape how the agency administered the ITC. The detail that surprises many contractors is that the credit is not simply a fixed rate applied at the end of a project. It is designed to stack, and its value can change substantially based on decisions made throughout development and construction. Where materials are sourced, how labor is structured, whether prevailing wage and apprenticeship requirements are satisfied, and how compliance is documented can all affect the size of the credit. Many of those decisions sit with the contractor. Why Timing Matters When contractors hear the word "tax" or "credit," many assume it is a matter for the owner's finance team or tax advisors to figure out long after construction is completed. That assumption leaves value on the table. Here's the thing most advisors don't tell you: by the time construction is finished, the best opportunities have usually passed. If sourcing is locked, labor plans are set, and the schedule was built without compliance in mind, the opportunity to maximize the ITC may be sharply reduced. Contractors who plan for the credit from the start can flag sourcing and labor choices that affect eligibility and size. They can build prevailing wage and apprenticeship requirements into the budget and set up documentation early, so the record will stand up to review. In doing so, the value they can deliver to a client can climb from 6% to as much as 60%. How the ITC Can Help Contractors Win a Bid Submitting a bid with an ITC strategy takes less tax expertise than many contractors expect. Contractors do not need to become tax experts. They need enough working knowledge to spot opportunities, ask good questions, and invite the right specialists at the right time. That is a realistic goal for a mid-sized firm, and it starts with the first planning conversation. Many of your competitors can build. Fewer can show an owner how to capture more value from the same project by aligning construction planning with the economics of eligible energy investments. For contractors looking to break into or move up in the data center sector, the Investment Tax Credit may be one of the smartest ways to win.

artigo.texto: The Rural Shift in Data Center Development As pressure on power, land, and permitting intensifies, more data centers are moving to rural areas, making remote sites a growing part of future development. Traditionally, key considerations when selecting a data center site have included access to power, proximity to end-user concentrations, and the availability of high-performance network infrastructure. Those factors help explain why data centers have historically been built in or near urban areas rather than in remote regions. Recent developments, however, suggest that this pattern is changing. Two-thirds of new US data center projects are targeting rural locations, marking a shift away from the longstanding concentration of facilities in major hubs such as Northern Virginia, Texas, and California. The change is not limited to the United States. Hyperscalers are also evaluating remote parts of South America as potential locations for the next generation of data centers. That shift raises two questions: Why are remote regions gaining prominence as data center sites, and does this represent a lasting change in site-selection strategy? Why Rural Sites Are Gaining Appeal Rural areas present distinct challenges as data center sites. They are often farther from end users, which can increase latency, and power and network infrastructure may be less developed or located farther away. At the same time, rural settings can offer advantages that may outweigh those drawbacks for some operators. One of the biggest is land availability. Securing enough land for a data center in or near an urban area can be difficult and expensive because undeveloped parcels are limited. In many rural markets, that constraint is less severe. Community opposition may also be more limited in less densely developed areas. Permitting can be simpler, too, because lower levels of surrounding development often mean fewer barriers to new construction. Power Constraints Are Reshaping Site Selection Another factor behind the shift toward less developed areas is the growing importance of on-site power generation. In a market where public power grids, including those in wealthy, highly developed regions, cannot always meet the capacity needs of new data centers, operators are increasingly exploring self-generated power. That can include dedicated generation assets or on-site plants. From that perspective, limited access to existing grid infrastructure in remote regions becomes less of a constraint. Fiber Is Still a Challenge, but a Manageable One On-site power does not solve every problem. Data centers still need access to high-performance network infrastructure, which, in most cases, means fiber-optic cables. Many rural areas currently have limited fiber access. Still, networking may be easier to address than power. Extending fiber is typically less expensive and less complex than building long-distance power infrastructure or developing major on-site generation capacity. In many cases, if existing fiber is available within a few hundred miles of a proposed site, connecting to it can be economically viable. Rural Data Centers Are Not New, but the Scale Is Although nearly nine-tenths of existing data centers remain concentrated in developed areas, the idea of placing facilities in rural regions is not new. Amazon, for example, explored the feasibility of data centers in Chile and Argentina more than eight years ago, and the discussion of rural data center development dates back at least a decade. What is different now is the level of execution. Over the past few years, operators have begun breaking ground on rural projects on a greater scale, driven by changing dynamics around power sourcing, land availability, and community response. Why the Shift to Rural Data Centers May Continue The factors that make rural locations more attractive are unlikely to disappear soon, suggesting that the industry will continue to expand into less-developed areas. That does not mean every new data center will be built far from cities. Urban sites will remain important for facilities that require ultra-low latency or whose scale does not justify the infrastructure investment needed to support a remote site. Even so, rural development appears to be shifting from exception to mainstream strategy. If constraints on power, land, and local opposition persist, a larger share of the industry’s next wave of large-scale projects is likely to be sited outside traditional metro hubs.

artigo.texto: New Approaches to Data Center Power Procurement As grid limits tighten, data centers may need to diversify power strategies to secure reliable capacity, control costs, and support faster growth. Data centers are consuming more power than ever, and many operators are adopting new strategies to secure the energy they need. Indeed, the era when a data center could simply connect to the public grid and call it a day may be coming to an end. Instead, data center operators are increasingly pursuing more creative strategies, from partnering with utilities to expand grid capacity to building dedicated power plants for their own use or installing generators that can both power a facility and feed electricity back to the grid. Here’s a look at these and other trends shaping data center power procurement. 1. Power Purchase Agreements In a world where public power grids are increasingly struggling to supply enough electricity to data centers, operators are keen to guarantee access to power. One way to do that is through power purchase agreements (PPAs), which are contracts that allow a data center to buy electricity at a fixed price from a utility or power producer. PPAs can help improve price predictability and, in some situations, support faster access to new power capacity. PPAs can also serve a separate purpose. In some cases, they provide data centers with access to electricity from renewable energy generation. This allows operators to reduce reliance on fossil fuels without having to build and operate their own solar, wind, or geothermal plants. That said, most grids cannot guarantee that the electricity delivered to a specific facility comes exclusively from renewable sources. For that reason, renewable energy PPAs are often better understood as a way for data centers to financially support the expansion of clean energy generation on the grid rather than as a direct source of fully renewable energy. 2. Behind-the-Meter Power Rather than relying primarily on utilities, some data center operators are choosing to generate their own electricity through a behind-the-meter approach. This strategy involves installing on-site generators capable of meeting all, or most, of a facility’s energy needs. This approach is expensive, but it gives operators greater control over their energy sources. It can also help them avoid delays associated with grid interconnection. And while fluctuations in fuel prices mean that behind-the-meter power costs aren’t entirely predictable, operators that run their own power generation assets typically have more direct control over energy planning than those that depend solely on utility-supplied power. 3. Microgrids Microgrids are another emerging strategy that some data center operators are using to procure power. A data center supported by a microgrid relies on a network of generators or small-scale power resources to supply electricity. These resources may be located on-site or in a nearby location connected directly to the facility. Microgrids are similar to behind-the-meter power, and in some cases the terms are used interchangeably. However, microgrids usually imply a more distributed system with multiple energy sources, which can improve resilience. They may also include energy storage infrastructure that data centers can use for backup power or load shifting. For example, a microgrid could capture and store solar power during the day, then deliver it to the data center at night. 4. Phased Energization In a growing number of cases, the public energy grid cannot supply enough electricity to meet a data center’s full power requirements on day one. The grid must expand its own capacity first. To address this challenge, some data centers are turning to phased energization. Although the term sounds technical, the idea is simple: instead of waiting until the grid can support a facility’s full electricity demand, a data center begins operations incrementally as power becomes available. The downside is that facilities using phased energization cannot support their full capacity from the moment they open. The upside is that they can begin partial deployment sooner, which is often preferable to waiting years for full grid capacity to come online. 5. Front-of-the-Meter Power Although the primary goal of most data center operators is securing enough electricity for their own needs, some, especially large hyperscalers, are experimenting with supplying power back to the grid. In other words, they are using on-site generation assets not only to support their own facilities but also to supply electricity to the broader grid. This strategy, known as front-of-the-meter power, may prove beneficial to the data center industry as it seeks to address concerns from regulators and the public that data centers are placing excessive strain on the grid and contributing to rising electricity costs. It may also help operators make better use of backup generators, which have traditionally been reserved for emergencies but could serve as supplementary grid resources during peak-demand periods, such as hot summer days when air conditioning places additional pressure on electricity networks. The New Reality of Data Center Power Procurement As power demand continues to rise, operators will need to look beyond traditional grid connections and tap into a wider mix of energy procurement strategies. Whether through PPAs, on-site generation, microgrids, or phased energization, the future of data center growth will depend largely on how effectively data centers secure reliable, flexible power.

artigo.texto: The hidden environmental cost of AI data centers September 4, 2026 Every question sent to AI models provides an instant reply that seems to appear out of nowhere, but answering queries requires physical infrastructure that consumes real energy, water and land. Somewhere around the world — maybe in Virginia, Sao Paulo or Hong Kong — a massive warehouse filled with fiber-optic cables and seemingly endless rows of humming servers is working to provide the processing power for the more than 2.5 billion questions ChatGPT alone fields daily. AI models, along with cloud storage, streaming, web hosting and social media, all have a very real physical footprint. If data centers were a country, their level of electricity use would make them the 11th largest electricity consumer in the world, according to researchers from the United Nations University. From energy to water to land, here's the real toll data centers take on the environment. An insatiable appetite for power Data centers are becoming some of the world's fastest-growing consumers of electricity. These warehouses of servers, routers and internet-connected devices run 24/7, while cooling systems operate continuously to keep the tech from overheating. In Frankfurt, Germany, the grid is currently so saturated that no new connections will be available until at least the 2030s. There, data centers consume about 41% of the city's electricity. In Dublin, it's double that. And data center electricity consumption is growing rapidly — it's expected to double by 2030 to about 945 terawatt-hours, around what Japan consumes annually, according to the International Energy Agency. How the AI boom could slow climate progress All that energy has to come from somewhere, increasing reliance on fossil fuels. One 2024 study found that more than half of the United States' data centers are powered by fossil fuels, emitting in excess of 105 million tons of CO2. Offsetting that would take more than 31,000 wind turbines running continuously for a year. The build-out is also keeping old coal plants alive. Utilities in the US have delayed the retirement of 15 coal-fired plants nationwide to meet surging demand, plants that together emitted nearly 65 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2023 alone. And utilities are also constructing new gas-fired power plants, with more than 100 GW of additional facilities across the country already announced. That would lead to more carbon emissions than burning 111 million pounds (50.4 million kilograms) of coal. Of course, data centers can also be powered by renewable energy. Pairing a facility with on-site renewables can ease pressure on the local power supply, and any surplus energy can even be sold back to the grid, making it more stable. However, using green electricity for data centers means there is less available for electrifying transport or decarbonizing other emissions-heavy industries. Hidden water demand Many data centers consume millions of gallons of water to stay cool. Servers generate constant heat, and water is one of the most effective ways to absorb and carry that heat away through evaporation. A single large facility can use up to 5 million gallons a day, roughly the same as a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people. About 80% of the water withdrawn for cooling simply evaporates; the rest becomes wastewater that can overwhelm local treatment systems never designed to handle that volume. In northern Virginia, the almost 300 data centers clustered in one region of the US state supply about a third of the world's online traffic. There, in what is known as the world's data center capital, facilities collectively used nearly 2 billion gallons of water in 2023. There are several more efficient ways to cool data centers. These include immersion cooling, where devices are bathed in a coolant, and closed-loop cooling systems which recycle water and can reduce freshwater use by up to 70%. Data centers are making cities hotter Cooling a data center doesn't get rid of the heat, it just moves it outside. That can exacerbate the urban heat island effect, which is when cities experience higher temperatures than rural areas. Researchers in Phoenix, Arizona, found a single large data center can emit as much waste heat as tens or even hundreds of thousands of households, raising nearby land surface temperatures by up to 9 degrees Celsius (16 Fahrenheit) and air temperatures by up to 2 degrees Celsius. Those effects can be felt as far as half a kilometer away. Since cities are already 0.5–4 degrees Celsius warmer than their surroundings, these higher temperatures can increase heat stress risks for nearby residents and push up air conditioning demand, requiring still yet more energy. Not all of that heat goes to waste: a growing number of data centers are capturing and piping it into nearby homes and businesses. This process, called thermal energy networks, can reduce data center power demand by up to 30%. Coal, gas and diesel all contribute to dirty air Powering and running data centers pollutes the air on two fronts. First, coal and gas plants release toxic particulate matter, which can lead to respiratory disease, heart disease, asthma and more health conditions for nearby communities. On-site diesel generators, used as backup power when the grid fails, also release harmful air pollutants. These generators pump out 200 to 600 times more nitrogen oxides than natural gas plants. One estimate found that when backup generators for all of Virginia's data centers were emitting at just 10% of their permitted level, they could contribute to 14,000 cases of asthma symptoms, more than a dozen deaths and up to $300 million in public health costs a year. Data centers take over large swaths of land Data center construction requires large plots of land to build on. Repurposing natural and agricultural areas into industrial zones can threaten biodiversity and disrupt local ecosystems. In Hattersheim, Germany, for example, an 18-acre (7-hectare) parc

artigo.texto: A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) autorizou o acesso de 645 MW de demanda à Rede Básica de transmissão para de projeto da Casa dos Ventos no Complexo Industrial e Portuário do Pecém, em Caucaia, no Ceará. A conexão está prevista para ocorrer por meio da futura subestação Pecém III a partir de 1° de dezembro de 2028, mas depende da conclusão de obras de transmissão e de adequações técnicas no sistema elétrico regional. O empreendimento está vinculado à empresa Pecém VDB 1, cuja participação integral foi adquirida pela Casa dos Ventos junto à Voltalia. A operação, submetida e aprovada pelo Conselho Administrativo de Defesa Econômica (Cade), envolveu os direitos de acesso à infraestrutura de transmissão necessários ao desenvolvimento de projetos de data centers no complexo cearense. O pedido de acesso do Pecém VDB 1 foi originalmente apresentado pela Voltalia Energia do Brasil ao Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS), em fevereiro de 2026, sendo que o ativo fazia parte do Complexo Industrial Projeto Amônia Verde de Pecém. Posteriormente, a Casa dos Ventos adquiriu a participação integral na empresa Pecém VDB 1, com o objetivo de aproveitar os direitos de conexão para desenvolver projetos de data centers. Conexão depende de obras na transmissão O parecer do ONS aponta que a conexão do data center à Rede Básica será feita por meio de dois circuitos na linha de transmissão de 500 kV entre Pecém II e Pacatuba, na futura Subestação Pecém III. A ligação envolve instalações de duas transmissoras, a STN e a Axia, antiga Chesf, e depende de uma intervenção na subestação Pacatuba, com prazo contratual para entrar em operação até 30 de junho de 2029. O ONS condicionou a viabilidade da conexão à entrada em operação de um conjunto de obras de transmissão na região Nordeste. Entre elas estão a Subestação Morada Nova, Teresina IV e Cratéus, além de obras associadas, contratadas no leilão de transmissão de 2024 e com prazo de conclusão até junho de 2029. A lista inclui ainda oito compensadores síncronos, equipamentos que ajudam a controlar a tensão da rede. Três foram contratados no leilão de transmissão de 2025 e outros cinco estão previstos no planejamento do setor. Estrutura de conexão compartilhada Para viabilizar a conexão, serão implantados quatro trechos de linha de transmissão em 500 kV, com aproximadamente 3,35 quilômetros de extensão, para conectar a futura subestação Pecém III à linha entre Pecém II e Pacatuba. A estrutura compartilhada também atenderá outras quatro unidades consumidoras, data centers demominados Pecém VDB 2, Pecém VDB 3, Pecém VDB 4 e Pecém VDB 5.

artigo.texto: O Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) solicitou uma avaliação sobre a regulamentação do Regime Especial de Incentivos para o Desenvolvimento da Infraestrutura (Reidi) ao Ministério da Fazenda, envolvendo projetos de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS). artigo.texto: A fabricante de pás eólicas Aeris Energy busca ampliar a adesão de credores ao plano de recuperação extrajudicial protocolado na última semana, enquanto aposta na expansão da demanda por energia eólica, especialmente com o avanço dos projetos de data centers no Brasil. A fabricante já conta com a adesão de credores que representam 42% dos créditos abrangidos pelo plano, que contempla aproximadamente R$ 1,5 bilhão em obrigações financeiras não correntes. O percentual foi suficiente para que o pedido fosse ajuizado, e agora a empresa tem 90 dias, contados da data do pedido, para concentrar esforços na obtenção das adesões necessárias à homologação do plano e na conclusão das negociações com os credores financeiros. Entre as alternativas em discussão estão a redução da dívida e a readequação dos prazos e das condições de pagamento das obrigações, de forma a compatibilizar o serviço do endividamento com a capacidade de geração de caixa da empresa. Durante teleconferência de resultados do terceiro trimestre de 2026, o diretor-presidente e de Relações com Investidores da Aeris, Alexandre Negrão, afirmou que as operações seguem normalmente, com manutenção das linhas de fornecimento e da capacidade de atendimento aos clientes. A companhia busca conciliar a reestruturação financeira com a recuperação da eficiência operacional. Mercado eólico ainda enfrenta desafios Na avaliação de Negrão, o setor eólico continua enfrentando dificuldades relacionadas ao ambiente regulatório, às condições macroeconômicas e às limitações de infraestrutura, fatores que afetam o ritmo de contratação de novos projetos. No Brasil, a companhia vê avanços em iniciativas que podem contribuir para a melhora gradual das condições do mercado. Entre elas, ele citou o leilão de transmissão realizado em outubro, que contratou aproximadamente R$ 8,8 bilhões em investimentos e contemplou cerca de 2 mil quilômetros de novas linhas. Outro destaque foi o mecanismo conhecido como Dia do Perdão, voltado à liberação de capacidade de transmissão anteriormente comprometida por projetos que não avançaram. Segundo Negrão, a Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) determinou recentemente a revogação de autorizações de 178 empreendimentos, que representam aproximadamente 7,8 GW de potência. A empresa também acompanha os leilões de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS), previstos para dezembro de 2026. Na avaliação do executivo, a tecnologia poderá ampliar a flexibilidade do sistema elétrico, facilitar a integração das fontes renováveis e contribuir para enfrentar os desafios relacionados à variabilidade da geração. Embora reconheça que os efeitos dessas iniciativas dependem de sua implementação e não serão imediatos, a Aeris considera que os movimentos representam avanços para a infraestrutura e a segurança energética brasileira. Data centers podem adicionar 13,2 GW à demanda até 2035 A expansão dos data centers é apontada pela fabricante como um dos principais vetores de crescimento da demanda por energia elétrica no Brasil. Levantamento apresentando pela companhia com base em dados do Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) identificou pedidos de conexão de empreendimentos que, caso integralmente viabilizados, poderiam representar uma demanda adicional de 13,2 GW até 2035. “Os data centers são hoje o principal vetor de crescimento da demanda por energia. Embora existam projetos de parques eólicos que já estavam previstos e seguem em desenvolvimento, eles representam uma parcela menor desse movimento. Com a regulamentação do Redata, a tendência é de aceleração ainda maior. Há muitos projetos previstos para os próximos cinco a seis anos, e vemos a energia eólica muito bem posicionada para atender a essa demanda”, afirmou Negrão. Números de pedidos da Aeris A companhia tem aproximadamente 1,6 GW em fornecimentos de pás eólicas previstos para 2026 e 2027, além de um pipeline de 0,8 GW em novos contratos em diferentes estágios de negociação. Atualmente, das seis linhas de produção da companhia, duas estão estágio maduro e quatro em estágio não maduro. A expectativa é que as unidades reativadas atinjam a maturidade operacional ao longo do primeiro trimestre de 2027. Nos nove primeiros meses do ano, a companhia entregou 83 sets de pás eólicas, equivalentes a aproximadamente 376 MW. Somente no terceiro trimestre foram 50 sets, ante 17 no trimestre anterior. Segundo Negrão, a demanda norte-americana para 2026 e 2027 continua sustentando oportunidades comerciais, embora as perspectivas para os anos seguintes permaneçam condicionadas ao cenário político e regulatório. O executivo também mencionou as restrições da capacidade produtiva interna dos Estados Unidos, que mantêm a necessidade de importação de equipamentos. Sobre as eleições de meio de mandato no país, afirmou que eventuais mudanças poderão facilitar a obtenção de licenças ambientais e de construção de novos empreendimentos, mas ainda não alteram significativamente as projeções da companhia. Resultados do terceiro trimestre No último trimestre, a fabricante apresentou uma receita operacional líquida de R$ 269,1 milhões, representando um crescimento de 50,3% em comparação ao terceiro trimestre de 2025, quando alcançou R$ 179, milhões. O desempenho é justificado pelo aumento do volume de produção e faturamento, impulsionado pela contribuição das novas linhas em fase de ramp-up, que passaram a contribuir para a receita do período. Já o prejuízo líquido ficou em R$ 109,2 milhões, redução de 38,1% em relação à perda de R$ 176,4 milhões do mesmo período do ano anterior. artigo.texto: A Engie Brasil Energia está avaliando oportunidades de aquisição de ativos renováveis em operação e vê no armazenamento de energia por baterias uma alternativa para o desenvolvimento de novos projetos. A companhia considera difícil ampliar sua atuação em geração renovável por meio de novos empreendimentos, mas mantém interesse na compra de ativos existentes. “A gente acha que renováveis está muito difícil de crescer em greenfield, exceto em baterias”, afirmou o gerente de Relações com Investidores da Engie, Leonardo Depiné, durante teleconferência de resultados realizada nesta quarta-feira, 11 de novembro. Segundo o executivo, a empresa tem analisado oportunidades de aquisição de ativos brownfield, mas ainda não há nenhuma operação concreta. No desenvolvimento de novos projetos, classificados como greenfield, a companhia considera os sistemas de armazenamento por baterias entre as possibilidades de expansão. A Engie também pretende participar do leilão de baterias previsto para dezembro, caso o certame seja realizado, levando em consideração as condições macroeconômicas e a rentabilidade dos investimentos. A companhia seguirá avaliando oportunidades nos próximos leilões de transmissão. No certame realizado em outubro, disputou lotes, mas não apresentou propostas vencedoras. Segundo Depiné, a empresa chegou perto de conquistar dois lotes, mas manteve os limites de retorno estabelecidos para seus investimentos. Curtailment e ressarcimento Na mesma apresentação, a Engie informou que ainda não reconheceu contabilmente os valores que poderá receber pela compensação dos cortes de geração de energia eólica e solar ocorridos entre setembro de 2023 e novembro de 2025. Segundo Depiné, a companhia ainda não tomou uma decisão definitiva sobre a adesão ao mecanismo de compensação. A expectativa é de que o eventual ressarcimento ocorra em 2027, quando os valores também poderão ser reconhecidos no balanço, caso a empresa decida aderir. A compensação foi estabelecida pela Lei 15.269/2025 e regulamentada pela Portaria Normativa 140/2026 do Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME). O mecanismo contempla cortes provocados por restrições de confiabilidade elétrica e indisponibilidade de instalações externas às usinas, mas não inclui aqueles decorrentes de excesso de oferta de energia no sistema. O procedimento prevê uma manifestação prévia de interesse das geradoras, cujo prazo foi encerrado em agosto, com participação da Engie. Para que a adesão seja vinculante, será necessário assinar um termo de compromisso que prevê a renúncia a determinadas reivindicações relacionadas aos cortes, como ações judiciais. A Câmara de Comercialização de Energia Elétrica (CCEE) será responsável por operacionalizar os cálculos e os pagamentos, após a apuração dos dados pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS). Depois disso é que as empresas vão decidir se assinam ou não o acordo vinculante. No terceiro trimestre de 2026, o curtailment atingiu 26% do potencial de geração eólica e solar das usinas operadas pela Engie, ante 23% no mesmo período de 2025. O percentual foi igual ao registrado no Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). Entre as eólicas da companhia, os cortes passaram de 19% para 22%, enquanto nas solares recuaram de 37% para 36%. No conjunto eólico Santo Agostinho, no Rio Grande do Norte, o curtailment alcançou 59%, ante 35% um ano antes. Revisão tarifária da TAG A Engie também comentou os efeitos da revisão tarifária do transporte de gás natural sobre os resultados da Transportadora Associada de Gás (TAG), da qual detém participação direta de 17,5%. A contribuição da TAG ao resultado da Engie Brasil Energia caiu de R$ 166 milhões para R$ 144 milhões no terceiro trimestre, redução de 13,3%, ou R$ 22 milhões. Segundo o balanço, a diminuição decorreu principalmente da menor receita da Malha Nordeste, que ainda depende da conclusão da revisão tarifária para o ciclo de 2026 a 2030. Durante a teleconferência, Depiné explicou que a TAG vem contabilizando provisoriamente uma redução de aproximadamente 50% na receita da malha sujeita à revisão, que representa cerca de 23% da receita da transportadora. Os valores serão ajustados após a conclusão do processo regulatório. A discussão envolve a metodologia utilizada pela Agência Nacional do Petróleo, Gás Natural e Biocombustíveis (ANP) para calcular a Base Regulatória de Ativos (BRA), considerada na definição da remuneração dos investimentos por meio das tarifas de transporte. Em outubro, a diretoria da ANP adotou o Método do Capital Recuperado e estabeleceu uma base regulatória de abertura de R$ 0 para a Malha Nordeste da TAG, por considerar que não há capital prudente ainda não recuperado nesses ativos. A decisão diverge da metodologia defendida pelas transportadoras. A TAG ainda acompanha o processo e avalia as medidas cabíveis para buscar o reconhecimento da metodologia que considera mais adequada à remuneração de seus ativos. Na segunda-feira, 9 de novembro, a ANP decidiu suspender por 15 dias a terceira etapa da revisão tarifária, após receber informações do MME sobre possíveis negociações entre a Petrobras e a Nova Transportadora do Sudeste (NTS) para reduzir os custos de transporte. A agência também determinou a avaliação da possibilidade de soluções negociadas com outras transportadoras e seus contratantes. Depiné afirmou que a Engie aguardará a conclusão do processo para avaliar seus desdobramentos, ressaltando que eventuais medidas relacionadas à revisão cabem à TAG. O executivo também disse não esperar que a metodologia adotada neste ciclo seja necessariamente aplicada às próximas revisões, uma vez que, segundo ele, a ANP indicou que cada processo poderá ter sua própria metodologia. Questionado sobre uma eventual indenização relacionada à TAG, o executivo afirmou que o contrato de compra da transportadora prevê mecanismos de proteção contratual, mas disse não ter detalhes sobre como eles poderiam ser aplicados em relação à Petrobras. artigo.texto: A Petrobras ampliou de dois para quatro os seus fornecedores de turbinas, diante da maior concorrência pelo equipamento em função do aquecimento do setor de data centers. “Todos sabem que o data center é um grande concorrente da indústria de petróleo, principalmente por causa das turbinas a gás. Esse é um gargalo que a gente tem”, disse a diretora de Engenharia, Tecnologia e Inovação da Petrobras, Renata Baruzzi. A Petrobras aumentou a projeção de Capex total para 2026, de US$ 19,4 bilhões para uma faixa entre US$ 24 bilhões a US$ 25,5 bilhões. Segundo a empresa, o ajuste se deve a mudanças no preço do brent, que registrou preços mais altos que o previsto no início do ano em função da guerra no Irã. Também contribuiu para o maior investimento o efeito cambial ao longo do ano. Assim, a empresa optou por intensificar investimentos com ganhos na produção. Com isso, de janeiro a setembro, a Petrobras investiu US$ 16,8 bilhões, sendo US$ 308 milhões na divisão de gás e energias de baixo carbono. As maiores divisas foram para o segmento de exploração e produção, que recebeu US$ 14,1 bilhões até setembro, o equivalente a 84% do Capex total. A concorrência com data centers para a aquisição de turbinas foi o único gargalo mencionado por Baruzzi neste contexto de aceleração dos projetos. “Não estamos vendo nenhuma questão do mercado, por enquanto. O que a gente tem feito, junto com a área de suprimentos, é tentar manter a resiliência dos nossos fornecedores. Tem fornecedores que já estão no Brasil e estão aumentando sua capacidade produtiva para nos atender”, disse a executiva, que reforçou que os projetos estão sendo cumpridos dentro do orçamento planejado. Aumento na projeção de produção Além da aceleração de projetos, a eficiência operacional da companhia levou a ganhos operacionais. “Já são 11 plataformas aptas a operar acima da capacidade nominal e estamos falando na ordem de 280 mil barris por dia adicionais já aprovados. Considerando o fechamento até outubro deste ano, o ganho médio de produção dessas plataformas foi da ordem de 90 mil barris adicionais por dia, mas estamos trabalhando para ampliar esses ganhos”, disse o diretor Financeiro e de Relações com Investidores, Fernando Melgarejo. “Se fosse adotado um Capex equivalente, estaríamos falando da ordem de 10 a 12 bilhões de dólares adicionais com novos sistemas de produção, o que foi possível sem esse Capex adicional, quando aumentamos a capacidade nominal”, complementou. Assim, a empresa elevou sua expectativa de produção para o ano, passando de 3,1 milhões de barris de óleo equivalente por dia para uma faixa entre 3,3 milhões e 3,4 milhões de barris de óleo equivalente por dia. Continuidade na liderança Em sua fala inicial, a presidente da Petrobras, Magda Chambriard, comentou brevemente a possibilidade de mudanças no comando da empresa. “Muitas vezes eu fui perguntada sobre quantas vezes se muda um presidente da Petrobras, quantas vezes há instabilidade interna do país. E o que a gente vem dizendo para todos é que estamos gerindo a companhia com serenidade, com tranquilidade, com continuidade. E esses resultados vêm sendo decorrentes de toda essa pacificação interna que nós estamos vivendo na companhia, com diretorias se ajudando, trabalhando em conjunto”, disse Chambriard. Resultados No terceiro trimestre de 2026, a Petrobras registrou lucro líquido de R$ 39,7 bilhões, com avanço de 21,5% em um ano. O Ebitda (“lucro antes de juros, impostos, depreciação e amortização”, na sigla em inglês) ajustado foi de R$ 85,8 bilhões, montante 34,3% superior do que o registrado no mesmo período de 2025. A divisão de gás e energias de baixo carbono registrou prejuízo de R$ 1 bilhão, revertendo lucro de R$ 127 milhões reportado um ano antes. A receita de vendas, entretanto, subiu 6,1% na comparação anual, fechando o 3T26 a R$ 13,1 bilhões. A receita fixa de leilões fechou o trimestre a R$ 789 milhões, contra R$ 314 milhões no 3T25. O preço médio de venda de energia elétrica teve queda de 23,7% em um ano, encerrando setembro de 2026 a R$ 177,36/MWh. A Petrobras antecipou a vigência do contrato de três térmicas (Termomacaé, Três Lagoas e Termoceará) contratadas no Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade na forma de Potência (LRCap) de março, que inicialmente operariam a partir de agosto de 2027, mas foram antecipadas para setembro de 2026. A Petrobras reportou um preço médio de venda de gás de US$ 9,68 por milhão de BTU, com aumento de 6% em um ano.

artigo.texto:
O presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), assinou nesta quarta-feira, 11, a prorrogação por mais 60 dias da medida provisória que proíbe as bets no Brasil. O ato está no Diário Oficial da União.
Com isso, a MP que revogou a autorização para exploração das bets no país continua valendo até que o Congresso Nacional vote seu texto.
A MP foi assinada pelo presidente da República, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, em 25 de setembro. Em seguida, associações judicializaram o caso para suspender a medida provisória, de modo que as apostas de alíquota fixa voltassem a operar no Brasil.
Enquanto isso, a AGU (Advocacia-Geral da União) entrou com uma ação na Justiça Federal de Pernambuco por impactos de 17 bets ao SUS (Sistema Único de Saúde) e à população brasileira. Ao todo, o órgão pedia R$ 1 bilhão por danos morais coletivos. O valor é baseado nos gastos que a saúde brasileira está tendo pelo avanço das bets e de doenças correlatas, como a ludopatia (vício em jogos ou gaming disorder), e supera os R$ 50 milhões que as plataformas de apostas repassaram aos cofres públicos.
A AGU também pediu ao STF a inconstitucionalidade da regulamentação que instituiu e viabilizou a exploração das bets no país. A Advocacia-Geral sustenta que as leis acatadas geraram um quadro de proteção normativa insuficiente a direitos fundamentais, demonstrando que a “liberdade regulatória” do modelo não foi contida nem mesmo pelas medidas infralegais tomadas pelo Executivo.
Dias depois, a mesma AGU apresentou pedido de manutenção da Medida Provisória (MP) nº 1.394/2026, que proíbe serviços de apostas online, também ao STF. Em solicitação enviada ao ministro Luiz Fux, relator do tema na Corte, o advogado-geral da União, Jorge Messias, apontou que a regulamentação até então vigente era falha e não foi capaz de conter prejuízos sociais, além do avanço de plataformas irregulares.

O valor é baseado nos gastos que a saúde brasileira está tendo pelo avanço das bets e de doenças correlatas, como a ludopatia (vício em jogos ou gaming disorder), e supera os R$ 50 milhões que as plataformas de apostas repassaram aos cofres públicos.
A AGU também pediu ao STF a inconstitucionalidade da regulamentação que instituiu e viabilizou a exploração das bets no país. A Advocacia-Geral sustenta que as leis acatadas geraram um quadro de proteção normativa insuficiente a direitos fundamentais, demonstrando que a “liberdade regulatória” do modelo não foi contida nem mesmo pelas medidas infralegais tomadas pelo Executivo.
Dias depois, a mesma AGU apresentou pedido de manutenção da Medida Provisória (MP) nº 1.394/2026, que proíbe serviços de apostas online, também ao STF. Em solicitação enviada ao ministro Luiz Fux, relator do tema na Corte, o advogado-geral da União, Jorge Messias, apontou que a regulamentação até então vigente era falha e não foi capaz de conter prejuízos sociais, além do avanço de plataformas irregulares.

artigo.texto: CATL Ties Battery-Swap Rollout to Sodium-Ion Push as Ya'an Lithium Permit and RMB 5.36 Billion Buyback Round Out the Story Published on 11/10/2026 at 13:51 | Editorial boerse-global.de CATL is betting that infrastructure can do more than move vehicles — it can move a chemistry. The battery giant said its expanding swap-station network will help spread its sodium-ion batteries, a link that matters more to the investment case than any single product launch. The network now spans roughly 200 Chinese cities, and CATL is targeting more than 3,000 swap stations for passenger cars by year-end. That reach is the point. A battery needs somewhere to go, and a swap network can supply the use cases — provided vehicles and packs actually meet there. Management's own framing is telling: CATL expects the buildout to support adoption of its sodium-ion line. Whether more stations translate into durable demand is the test the strategy has to pass. Trucks Join the Swap Equation The swap concept is not confined to passenger cars. On October 20, CATL unveiled an electric range-extender system for heavy trucks that pairs a swappable main battery with a 77 kWh auxiliary pack. Agreements covering 13,000 units were signed at the event. Those signatures give the truck push more weight than a technical showcase would. For investors, the appeal sharpens if the agreements turn into firm execution — CATL will have to prove the swap hardware against real-world duty cycles. The combination of a replaceable main pack and extra storage is the kind of product-and-application pairing that could reinforce the broader swap strategy, with the contracts as a concrete starting point. Ya'an Permit Becomes the Next Hurdle On the materials side, attention shifts to Sichuan. According to media reports, Ya'an's environmental authority published a notice on Friday proposing to approve the environmental impact assessment for a CATL lithium-chemicals project at the site. The plan calls for roughly 40,000 tonnes per year of battery-grade lithium carbonate and 30,000 tonnes of battery-grade lithium dihydrogen phosphate. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying CATL? The proposed approval is the relevant procedural stage — not a final green light. Additional growth headroom could open up if the announced intent is followed by an actual permit and then by construction. Until then, the project sits alongside the swap network and sodium-ion technology as an industrial building block rather than a booked contributor. Overseas Share Gains Underpin the Bull Case The demand backdrop is supportive. CATL's share of battery usage outside China rose to 33.7% in the first nine months of 2026, up from 28.6% a year earlier, according to media reports. That expansion beyond the home market strengthens the economic argument for further development steps — as long as the company defends the stronger position. New applications could reinforce the buildout. On October 28 at All-Energy Australia, CATL gave the TENER+ energy storage system with 9 MWh its global debut, signing letters of intent with Hitachi Energy, the EPEC Group and the University of New South Wales. A day later came a strategic cooperation with Dongfeng Motor to develop an integrated ecosystem of batteries, vehicles and energy services. Each could broaden the revenue base if the partners convert intent into working business. Buyback Executed, but Execution Still Rules Capital returns are already in motion. CATL said on November 2 that it had repurchased A-shares for RMB 5.36 billion under its previously announced program through the end of October — a completed deployment of capital that warrants its own assessment, separate from the operating story. The counterargument rests on the length of the implementation chain. The Ya'an approval intent, the storage letters of intent and the Dongfeng cooperation carry differing degrees of binding force. The optimistic scenario requires every one of them to produce an economically viable contribution; delays or weaker results would undercut that. Investors who have already priced in a hefty contribution would need to scale back expectations if execution stalls — a risk that would bite hardest if overseas share gains also lost momentum. For now, the combination of a firmer market position and steady project and partnership progress keeps a further growth scenario plausible. The next concrete catalyst is the environmental authority's actual decision on the Ya'an review; a permit would solidify the site's outlook. Anything beyond that requires execution and commercial development to deliver. That is where the latest procedural step either becomes more than a long-term option — or stays one. artigo.texto: Key Points - FSU chemist Justin Kennemur is part of a multi-institutional team funded by the U.S. Department of Energy that is investigating how specific ions are transported in polymer membranes. - The research could lead to improved electrolyzers, which are store excess electricity produced by power grids, and fuel cells that generate electricity for electric vehicles. A Florida State University polymer chemist is part of a multi-institutional team working to improve energy storage and production in technologies like fuel cells and electrolyzers through the synthesis of novel polymer membranes. Professor of Chemistry and Biochemistry Justin Kennemur and his collaborators have earned a $2.64 million grant from the U.S. Department of Energy’s Basic Energy Sciences program, one of the country’s largest sponsors of research in the physical sciences, to explore how specific ions are transported in polymer membranes, to develop new fluorine-free alternatives based on the underlying mechanisms and to apply this science to energy-related technologies. Nearly $800,000 of the grant will come to FSU. “Society’s need for abundant and accessible energy is a frontline challenge in scientific research,” Kennemur said. “It’s critical that this research is supported so we can continue exploring this area and prepare for the ever-growing demand for energy.” Heavily fluorinated polymers are frontrunners in the energy industry for their versatile properties and high performance when transporting ions. They’re used in energy-related applications like electrolyzers, which are used to store excess electricity produced by power grids for later use, and fuel cells that generate electricity for electric vehicles and spacecrafts. They’re also used in solar panels, wind turbines, heat generators, and other energy-storage and -production technologies. By breaking down the architectural design of fluoropolymers and investigating how structure correlates to dynamics, the research team aims to understand why they perform so well and whether fluorine is necessary for a polymer to transport materials efficiently. “We plan to reveal fundamental principles promoting fast proton, hydroxide, or salt transport in fluorinated membranes, such as Nafion, which are industry standards for conducting specific ions through the membrane,” Kennemur said. “Understanding these principles and ion-transport mechanisms will accelerate the development of new materials, in this case, analogous non-fluorinated polymers, that can optimize energy storage and production.” Based on these findings, Kennemur will develop fluorine-free hydrated polymers that exceed current performance levels by increasing ion transportation speeds, making them more capable of storing or producing large amounts of energy. “Rising concerns and regulations over ‘forever chemicals,’ which are potential by-products of fluoropolymer production that don’t break down naturally and have negative effects on human health and the environment, have revived interest in developing fluorine-free alternatives,” Kennemur said. The Basic Energy Sciences program supports fundamental scientific research that lays the foundation for new technologies and innovation in energy, environmental science and national security. This grant supports Kennemur and his collaborators — Karen Winey, the Harold Pender Professor of Engineering and Applied Science at the University of Pennsylvania; principal investigator Amalie Frischknecht, a physicist at Sandia National Laboratories; and Michael Hickner, the Craig A. Rogerson Endowed Professor of Chemical Engineering and Materials Science at Michigan State University — as well as student research assistants and postdoctoral scholars across the team’s labs. “This is a collaborative project connecting my chemistry research team with experts in chemical engineering, materials science and computation related to polymer science,” Kennemur said. “In addition to supporting our scientific discoveries in the laboratory, this grant is helping train future STEM leaders.” Kennemur received his doctorate in chemistry from North Carolina State University in 2010 and completed postdoctoral research at the University of Minnesota, Twin Cities, before joining FSU’s faculty in the Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry in 2014. During his time at FSU, he has earned the National Science Foundation’s Faculty Early Career Development Program (CAREER) Award, the Distinguished Service Award from the American Chemical Society’s Division of Polymer Chemistry, or POLY and the William R. Jones Outstanding Mentor Award from the Florida Education Fund. “Dr. Kennemur is a thoughtful, conscientious faculty member who has brought visibility to FSU through both his research re-energizing the field of low strain monomers to effectively expand its range of applications and his professional service,” said Wei Yang, chair of the Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry. “He’s not only an emerging leader in the field of polymer chemistry but also a committed, effective and skillful mentor.” To learn more about Kennemur’s work and research conducted in FSU’s Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry, visit chem.fsu.edu.

artigo.texto: Gasgoo Munich- At the 17th International Conference on Advanced Automotive Lithium Batteries (ABAA-17), Gotion High-Tech laid out its latest advances in all-solid-state batteries, lithium manganese iron phosphate (LMFP), and global manufacturing capacity. Yet it was Chairman Li Zhen who, in his opening remarks, pulled the conversation back to the industry's broader cycle. During the keynote, three of the company's technical experts walked through a systematic showcase of collaborative innovation spanning the entire value chain — from base materials to finished cells. With market demand barreling toward 5 TWh by 2030, the company has already built eight global R&D hubs and 20 production bases, said Zhou Fu, president of the General Research Institute. Gotion continues to deepen its work on key materials like high-compaction LFP and high-voltage single-crystal NCM, while building a flagship product matrix — spanning G-Cycle ultra-fast charging batteries, G-Edge smart batteries, and all-solid-state cells — to underpin electrification across every usage scenario. Image source: Gotion High-Tech Zeroing in on the frontier of all-solid-state tech, Dr. Pan Ruijun, who heads the solid-state project, said Gotion has cracked the full-chain process and equipment system — from materials to electrodes to cells — along the sulfide route. A semi-dry mixing method and a novel solvent system have sharply improved slurry stability. Warm isostatic pressing (WIP) trims electrolyte membrane thickness to 35 microns, boosts cell densification by more than 20%, slashes interfacial impedance by over 99%, and pushes cell yields past 90%. At the pack level, the system is racing toward lower stacking pressure and lighter weight. Cells from Gotion’s all-solid-state pilot line are now rolling off in batches, giving the company a firm foundation for mass production. On the LMFP front, Dr. Fang Yaoguo, vice president of the International Engineering Research Institute, detailed how Gotion conquered the chemistry’s inherent flaws — low conductivity, lattice instability, and manganese dissolution — along with the engineering hurdles. The fixes rely on proprietary techniques: particle nanocrystallization, dual-ion doping, particle-size gradation, and surface structuring. The third-generation Qichen LMFP cell now hits an energy density above 205 Wh/kg and can recharge to 70% in just 10 minutes, while delivering strong cold-weather performance and lower costs. In passenger vehicles, it delivers superior power; in commercial trucks, it shines as a weight-saver. By precisely bridging the performance gaps between LFP and NCM, the cell is rapidly expanding into a wider range of applications. Li Zhen, Image source: Gotion High-Tech Li Zhen didn’t dwell on technology alone. He laid out four guiding paradoxes: the fiercer the upheaval, the greater the need to revere science and seek truth; the faster the innovation, the tighter the loop between production and research must become; the more tangled the competition, the more vital openness and symbiosis grow; and the quicker the iteration, the higher we must climb to scout the next frontier. Innovation, he stressed, must bridge the “0-to-1” breakthrough with the “1-to-100” grind of real-world refinement — turning lab advances into safe, reliable products. Gotion, he added, will stay true to its mission of making green energy serve humanity, working alongside global peers toward the shared promise of the energy transition.

artigo.texto: Appear Inc. Begins Pre-Production of Solid-State Battery, Targets Mid-2027 Launch Field trials complete across motorcycles, e-bikes and scooters. Pre-production underway. Limited production on track for mid-2027, with full-scale production in 2028. SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Appear Inc., a San Francisco-based developer of next-generation solid-state battery technology, today announced that it has moved from proving its technology to producing it. The company has completed field trials on three types of electric vehicle: motorcycles, e-bikes and scooters. It has also completed advanced manufacturing trials and started pre-production manufacturing with a manufacturing partner. Alongside this technical progress, Appear has added new distributors and strategic partners in selective established and emerging markets. The company remains on track to begin limited commercial production in mid-2027, followed by full-scale production in 2028. The technology Most electric vehicles today run on lithium-ion batteries, which use a liquid electrolyte to move charge between the electrodes. Solid-state batteries replace that liquid with a solid material. This is widely seen as a path to safer batteries, with no flammable liquid to leak or ignite, and to more energy in a smaller, lighter cell. Watch the video: https://youtu.be/W2H44vFPjXY Appear's solid-state technology is built around three priorities: safety, performance and manufacturability. For motorcycles, e-bikes and scooters, where weight, range and safety matter on every ride, that combination is especially valuable. From the lab to the production line Following its advanced manufacturing trials, Appear has moved into pre-production with its manufacturing partner and is refining its processes for volume manufacturing. Building a route to market New distributors and strategic partners in selective established and emerging markets are expected to give Appear regional market access and distribution channels at launch. Partner details remain confidential. "We are moving beyond development and validation and into commercialization," said Prashant Rurs, Founder & CEO of Appear Inc. "We remain on track to begin limited production in mid-2027 and to scale up to full production in 2028." About Appear Inc. Appear Inc. is a San Francisco-based company developing next-generation solid-state battery technology for electric mobility and other energy storage applications. Media Contact: Isabella Smith +1 415 967 8207 SOURCE Appear Inc

artigo.texto: A judge has thrown out a key energy requirement and some legislative checks on a data center planned for Midtown St. Louis. TerraWatt, the company behind a planned $3.1 billion, 120-megawatt data center in the old Famous-Barr warehouse on Market Street as part of a planned technology district, filed suit against St. Louis in September. In his suit against the city’s Board of Adjustment, TerraWatt partner David Lambiaso argues that two conditions imposed as requirements on the construction of the data center are illegal and would be “practically impossible” for the planned project. The two requirements revolved around renewable energy and a measure that requires the Board of Aldermen to approve a community benefits agreement, which “exceed the scope of authority” of the board and the city's Board of Adjustment, the suit says. Lambiaso complained the provisions from the Board of Adjustment are “practically impossible on the 11-acre site,” the complaint read. The city’s renewable energy requirements, included in the site's conditional use permit, require the data center to use 2.4 megawatts of renewable energy. During a hearing held Thursday, 22nd District Judge Christopher McGraugh granted Lambiaso’s motion to remove a power supply mandate that required the petitioner to supply a minimum of 2.4 megawatts of their own power through renewable energy sources. Additionally, the judge removed a requirement that the project's community benefit agreement be approved by the Board of Aldermen. In his order, McGraugh said the Board of Adjustment exceeded its authority and ruled its actions “illegal and void.” He also ruled that the Board of Adjustment's functions are strictly administrative and cannot make policy. The city’s Land Clearance for Redevelopment Authority approved the community benefits agreement in September, but it still required approval from the Board of Aldermen. Lambiaso and the City of St. Louis are also being sued over the project by the Missouri Coalition for the Environment and several other plaintiffs who argue that the city illegally granted a use permit for the project. This story will be updated.
