artigo.texto: Cabot Corporation Major producer of coal-based activated carbon According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Coal Based Activated Carbon market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture. The global coal based activated carbon market is entering a phase of steady, regulation-driven expansion, with the forecast horizon to 2035 pointing to sustained demand across water treatment, air purification, and industrial process applications. Coal-based activated carbon remains the workhorse adsorbent of environmental infrastructure, valued for its hardness, high surface area, and cost-effectiveness relative to alternative precursors. As of 2026, the market is shaped by increasingly stringent discharge and emission standards, particularly in Asia-Pacific, where rapid urbanization and industrial expansion are outpacing legacy treatment capacity. At the same time, mature markets in North America and Europe are investing in upgrades and reactivation infrastructure, creating a two-speed demand profile. The competitive landscape is fragmented, with multinational chemical firms and specialized regional producers competing on product grade, impregnation technology, and supply reliability. While bio-based and coconut-shell carbons pose substitution pressure in select niches, coal-based grades retain a dominant position in high-volume water and air applications. This report provides a data-driven view of market size, structure, and the strategic dynamics that will define the industry through 2035. The baseline scenario for the world coal based activated carbon market through 2035 assumes continued regulatory tightening as the primary demand engine, with global consumption growing at a moderate pace. Water treatment remains the anchor segment, supported by municipal infrastructure investment and industrial wastewater compliance, particularly in Asia-Pacific. Air purification demand is expected to accelerate as emission control standards tighten across emerging economies, while gold recovery offers cyclical upside tied to mining activity. Supply-side dynamics are shaped by coal feedstock availability, energy costs, and environmental compliance at production facilities, which are pushing some capacity toward higher-value specialty grades. The market is also seeing gradual consolidation as smaller producers face capital and compliance burdens. Substitution risk from coconut-shell and bio-based carbons is real but concentrated in specific applications, leaving coal-based products dominant in large-scale water and air treatment. Overall, the market index is projected to rise from 100 in 2025 to approximately 142 by 2035, reflecting a compound annual growth rate of around 3.6%, with upside potential from faster infrastructure spending in emerging markets. Water treatment is the largest and most resilient outlet for coal-based activated carbon, spanning municipal drinking water, wastewater, and industrial process water. Demand is driven by the need to remove organic contaminants, taste and odor compounds, and emerging pollutants such as PFAS, which are increasingly regulated. Powdered activated carbon is widely used in batch treatment and seasonal taste-and-odor control, while granular and extruded forms dominate fixed-bed systems. Through 2035, demand-side indicators to watch include municipal capital expenditure on treatment upgrades, industrial discharge permit stringency, and the adoption of advanced oxidation processes that rely on carbon adsorption. Asia-Pacific is the key growth region, where urbanization and industrial expansion are outpacing legacy infrastructure. In mature markets, replacement demand and system upgrades sustain volumes. The segment is also seeing growing interest in reactivation services, which can extend carbon life and reduce waste, though this does not eliminate primary demand for fresh coal-based product. Current trend: Steady growth driven by regulation. Major trends: Increasing regulation of PFAS and emerging contaminants, Shift toward granular and extruded carbons for fixed-bed systems, Growth in reactivation and carbon recovery services, and Municipal infrastructure investment in Asia-Pacific. Representative participants: Calgon Carbon Corporation (Kuraray), Jacobi Carbons, Cabot Corporation, Haycarb PLC, and Donau Carbon GmbH. Air purification applications for coal-based activated carbon include flue gas treatment, volatile organic compound (VOC) abatement, and industrial odor control. Demand is closely tied to emission regulations, particularly in the power, cement, and waste incineration sectors. Activated carbon injection is a mature but growing technology for mercury and dioxin removal, especially in regions tightening air quality standards. Through 2035, the segment will be shaped by the adoption of best available techniques in emerging economies, where industrial expansion is increasing emissions. Demand-side indicators include the number of new incineration and industrial facilities, regulatory timelines for mercury control, and the adoption of carbon capture and storage pre-treatment. Coal-based carbons are favored for their cost-effectiveness and high adsorption capacity in high-volume applications. However, competition from impregnated specialty grades and alternative adsorbents is intensifying, pushing producers toward higher-value product formulations. Major trends: Tightening mercury and dioxin emission standards, Growth in activated carbon injection for flue gas treatment, Expansion of VOC abatement in industrial facilities, and Development of impregnated carbons for specific gas streams. artigo.texto: Política Acre avança em negociações na Turquia para certificação internacional de créditos de carbono O Acre deu mais um passo nas articulações para obter a certificação internacional de seus créditos de carbono. Durante agenda na Turquia, representantes do governo estadual se reuniram com a diretora associada da Art Trees, Lucia Madrid, para discutir o avanço do processo de certificação. O encontro contou ainda com a participação da presidente do IMC, Neidinha Lima, e do consultor internacional de mercados de carbono, Victor Hugo Rondon. A iniciativa busca ampliar as oportunidades de investimentos para o estado, fortalecendo a política de preservação ambiental e criando possibilidades de geração de renda e desenvolvimento econômico. A expectativa é que a certificação internacional valorize os resultados das ações de conservação da floresta amazônica e garanta benefícios às comunidades que contribuem diretamente para a proteção do meio ambiente. A proposta é transformar a preservação da Amazônia em oportunidades concretas, promovendo mais qualidade de vida para a população acreana.

artigo.texto: O governador Otaviano Pivetta (Republicanos) participa, hoje, na Turquia, do primeiro dia da conferência mundial do clima com presidentes de diversos países e delegações, cientistas, pesquisadores que encaminham decisões sobre proteção ambiental e reduções dos impactos no meio ambiente. A cúpula dos líderes políticos é hoje e amanhã, com temas centrais no financiamento climático para países em desenvolvimento e planos de adaptação climática, transição energética e redução de combustíveis fósseis e eletrificação. “Estamos na COP 31 com uma missão importante: apresentar o trabalho de Mato Grosso na redução do desmatamento e buscar reconhecimento internacional para nossos créditos de carbono. Também vamos conversar com investidores e mostrar que é possível unir conservação ambiental, desenvolvimento e novas oportunidades para o nosso Estado”, disse Pivetta, há pouco. “Uma agenda de muito trabalho e diálogo”, acrescentou. O tema de mercados de carbono: do potencial brasileiro aos investimentos em escala será debatido amanhã. Dia 13, será a implementação do mercado de carbono no Brasil: avanços e próximos passos’ A delegação de Mato Grosso tem a secretária de Meio Ambiente, Mauren Lazaretti e o deputado estadual Beto Dois a Um. O presidente Lula e ministros também estão na conferência. O governo instalou o Pavilhão Brasil que tem debatido inúmeros temas ambientais desde o último dia 9. Na programação de hoje também estarão sendo debatidas ‘energias da floresta: inovação aberta para transformar o acesso à energia’. Amanhã, o INPE abordará o ‘mapeamento de risco climático como base para soluções de adaptação’, o Ibama apresentará o tema ‘Brasil rumo ao desmatamento zero em 2030: resultados e desafios’. artigo.texto: Struggling marijuana farmers pivot to becoming AI data center sites to escape falling weed revenue — existing water and power infrastructure makes cultivation sites ideal for decentralized ‘mini data center nodes’ Let's get high... on AI. The AI data center boom is bringing hope to struggling cannabis farmers as they face increased competition, costs, and taxes amid reduced demand for marijuana. According to Arizona Public Media, the cannabis industry is in decline, with sales peaking in 2024 and oversupply driving prices down. And now, several growers are considering selling their cultivation facilities or converting them into “mini data center nodes.” These facilities already have many of the ingredients needed for AI data centers, such as the increasingly hard-to-get supply of electricity and water infrastructure. "For some reason, there's a lot more cannabis grown in Arizona than Arizonans use. And so, a lot of folks are getting out of that business, like myself, at least on the cultivation side. But these facilities can potentially be repurposed to be mini data center nodes," Moe Asnani, the former owner of two Tucson D2 Dispensaries, told the public broadcaster. He also added, "The whole idea is if you create these smaller nodes where people control their own data, where they're not at the mercy of other people's updates and things like that — that's kind of where the idea came in, because I believe in decentralization." Cannabis farming is both power- and water-intensive. Forbes looked at a 32,850-square-foot cannabis facility in Kalamazoo, Michigan, which is currently wired for 1.5 megawatts, which can be expanded to 2.5 megawatts in under a year and 15 megawatts in the long term. It's also provisioned for fiber internet and equipped with a state-of-the-art HVAC system for climate control, which should make it a tempting property for anyone wanting to put up a small data center — something that even OpenAI and Anthropic are interested in as massive hyperscale sites face opposition from the community. This concept is dubbed "adaptive reuse," with Tucson City Council member Paul Cunningham saying that it’s a more palatable alternative to massive, purpose-built sites sitting on the outskirts of town. "Data centers are dirty words, and everybody knows that. And no one wants to build a brand-new data center anywhere," the politician said. "But if we have buildings that were using that amount of water and that amount of energy already in their previous function and [it] can be done without being invasive, I'm OK with exploring that option." There is massive demand for data centers, but it’s not a guaranteed payoff for struggling cash-strapped growers looking to unload their unprofitable properties. Niki Krear, vice president of acquisitions of real estate investment trust New Lake Capital Partners, said that there’s a sweet spot between connectivity, costs, and regulation that data center operators look for in a site. "It’s a combination of finding affordable power, dense fiber networks, and favorable tax policies," Krear told MJBizDaily. Even though many cultivation facilities already boast higher-than-average power capacity for lighting and climate control, data centers often demand twice to thrice more, with upgrades possibly taking up to five years. Data center operators looking for smaller sites may also have to contend with NIMBY — not in my backyard — fights from neighbors. Additionally, there may be zoning restrictions, moratoriums, and regulatory hurdles, and the lack of economies of scale could end up costing operators more. As these new AI GPUs become available, data centers will need to sell their existing equipment and buy new hardware to remain competitive. Because suppliers usually offer favorable pricing for larger orders, upgrading these smaller sites will likely end up being more expensive on a per-unit basis. That said, growing opposition toward large new projects could make these former cannabis farms suitable alternatives for operators desperate to get more compute online quickly, provided they check all (or most of) the boxes they need. artigo.texto: 10 de novembro de 2026, às 07:34 O SoftBank Group registrou prejuízo líquido trimestral, pressionado por perdas em investimentos e por perdas extraordinárias ligadas a mudanças no plano de compras de equipamentos para geração de energia em projetos de data centers nos EUA. A holding japonesa de investimentos em tecnologia divulgou nesta terça-feira (10) prejuízo líquido de 1,115 trilhão de ienes (US$ 7,06 bilhões) no trimestre encerrado em setembro. O resultado contrariou a estimativa de lucro de 53,5 bilhões de ienes em pesquisa com analistas do Visible Alpha. No mesmo período do ano passado, o SoftBank havia registrado lucro líquido de 2,502 trilhões de ienes, impulsionado por ganhos de bilhões de dólares com o investimento na OpenAI. A empresa informou uma perda de 597,2 bilhões de ienes relacionada a alterações no plano de aquisição de equipamentos vinculados à geração de energia para data centers de inteligência artificial nos EUA. Segundo o SoftBank, uma de suas unidades revisou a estratégia de compras diante da evolução das exigências dos projetos em andamento e planejados. O resultado fraco se soma a contratempos recentes. A China bloqueou a aquisição de US$ 5,4 bilhões do negócio de robótica da ABB, anunciada em outubro de 2025, que buscava combinar IA e robótica. O SoftBank pretendia usar a unidade – fabricante de braços robóticos e outros dispositivos empregados em manufatura e logística – como vitrine de uma ofensiva mais ampla em aplicações físicas de IA. Nos EUA, a SB Energy, empresa de data centers apoiada pelo SoftBank, adiou o IPO após enfrentar resistência do mercado em relação à avaliação. A rival da OpenAI, Anthropic, pretende manter o plano de abrir capital ainda neste mês, apesar da volatilidade recente ligada a investimentos em IA, segundo o The Wall Street Journal. A OpenAI, por sua vez, levantou menos da metade do valor inicialmente pretendido em sua rodada mais recente, e a avaliação ficou abaixo do alvo, em US$ 1,25 trilhão. O SoftBank tem ampliado suas apostas em IA nos últimos anos, deixando para trás a estratégia anterior de investir em um portfólio diversificado de startups. Em outubro, a holding informou que aportou mais US$ 10 bilhões na OpenAI, elevando o total investido na dona do ChatGPT para US$ 64,6 bilhões e a participação para cerca de 13%. Na semana passada, a Arm Holdings, empresa britânica de design de chips controlada pelo SoftBank, informou lucro trimestral acima do esperado, com a demanda por IA sustentando o crescimento. artigo.texto: The city of Fort Worth held the first of two public hearings Nov. 10 in regards to a possible moratorium on accepting, processing and approving data center applications. Council voted to initiate a moratorium process at the Aug. 11 meeting, but the earliest it could be approved is Feb. 23, 2027, according to the presentation. What they’re saying The public hearing lasted more than one hour with each speaker in favor of implementing a moratorium on data centers. Before the public hearing, city council received a 156-page report from the Fort Worth Data Center & Infrastructure Commission. Resident Letitia Wilburn questioned holding the public hearing just an hour after the report from the commission. “The public hasn’t really had enough time to go through it,” she said. Other speakers voiced concerns about approving local rules that do not meet state regulations that could be passed or crafted by a new state legislature in 2027. “I think it’s really incumbent upon us academics to work with our elected officials, not to lecture at them, but to sit down together and say what do we know and what do we need to find out before we make real long-term decisions [about data centers],” said Michael Slattery during the presentation on the findings of the commission. Zooming out Of the four existing data centers in Fort Worth, three are in council District 10, according to previous reporting. Another is under construction in council District 7, and there are four proposed data centers in Districts 3, 6, 7 and 8. The Fort Worth Zoning Commission voted July 8 to deny a proposed ordinance that would restrict where data centers could be located in Fort Worth, according to previous reporting. On Sept. 21, Gov. Greg Abbott said Texas environmental regulators must stop issuing new permits for data centers, according to previous reporting. His order expands an existing pause on data center development in the state and stops new data center permits while the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, which operates the state power grid, conducts an audit of proposed data center projects. Despite the existing pause, a permit for a $430 million data center in the Alliance area of Fort Worth was filed Sept. 22 with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation, according to previous reporting. Looking ahead The second public hearing is slated for Jan. 12, a week later than planned earlier this summer. The moratorium on development and permitting could start if passed following a second reading Feb. 23. If approved in February, a 90-day moratorium would run through May 24, 2027. The city could approve a second 90-day window, but 180 days is the most allowed under state law, Assistant City Manager Jessica McEachern said. She added the moratorium does not apply to planned or approved projects or projects with zoning applications already submitted. McEachern said that under state law, data centers already in the works can choose to develop under the current standards or they could voluntarily develop to meet the higher standards. Hannah Norton contributed to this report.

artigo.texto: The growing adoption of renewable energy changes the energy infrastructure in many ways. In particular, solar photovoltaic (PV) systems become one of the main elements of such infrastructure providing a flexible source of clean energy at utility, commercial, industrial scales and even at remote infrastructures. Nevertheless, solar energy alone does not guarantee continuous power supply because of its generation dependency on weather conditions, daylight and seasonality. With the rising share of renewables, the ability to store the energy becomes crucial. One of the technologies designed to address this issue is battery energy storage systems (BESS). Meanwhile, the industries requiring a continuous power supply, including telecom facilities, consider solar and storage systems as a promising way to increase the reliability and decrease dependency on conventional energy sources. Thus, a combination of solar PV, battery storage and energy management turns out to be a promising solution to improve the resilience of energy infrastructure. Why Solar PV Requires Energy Storage As was mentioned, energy production using solar energy is highly variable. During daytime hours PV systems are able to produce more electricity than necessary. During nighttime or periods of insufficient solar irradiance, the production falls sharply or even stops. Thus, without efficient means to store electricity, a company is forced either to export surplus generation or even to curtail the generation depending on electricity market conditions and system design. Battery storage becomes a solution helping to store extra solar generation and consume it later. A typical hybrid solar-plus-storage system is composed of PV modules, battery modules, power conversion system (PCS), battery management system (BMS) and energy management system (EMS). These elements allow coordinating the generation, charging, discharging and consumption processes. For commercial and industrial applications, such system allows achieving the following objectives: - Energy shifting - Peak shaving - Provision of backup power - Integration of renewable energy - Implementation of microgrid operation The required storage capacity will depend on the specific load profile, generation of solar energy, backup time and operating strategy. Particularly, modular and containerized solutions turn out to be very helpful for flexible scaling of projects' capacity. The Growing Role of Containerized Battery Energy Storage Systems As energy storage projects grow larger and become more complex, integrated solutions for battery storage become of increasing interest. Containerized BESS combines battery modules, power conversion equipment, thermal management, fire protection and monitoring into a compact solution. Such system architecture can facilitate transportation, installation and system commissioning process. Compared to assembly of separate equipment at construction site, pre-assembled solutions can reduce on-site integration efforts and provide unified equipment configuration. Another advantage of this solution is scalability: depending on the specific of the project, multiple storage modules can be combined to achieve required power and energy capacities. It makes the technology applicable for renewables power plants, industrial applications, microgrids and grid services. However, there are many parameters to be considered when choosing a solution including: - Battery chemistry and cycle life - Rated power and usable energy capacity - Round trip efficiency - Cooling and temperature management - Fire detection and suppression - Battery management and energy management functionalities - Ability to work in grid-connected and off-grid mode Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries are extensively used in stationary energy storage applications owing to high level of thermal stability and positive cycle-life characteristics. Thus, for the project developers and system integrators, containerized battery energy storage systems can be viewed as a practical reference allowing to evaluate BESS architecture, capacity options and renewable energy applications. Solar and Battery Storage for Telecommunication Facilities Telecommunication facilities represent another type of application where power supply becomes very important. Cellular base stations, microwave transmission towers, wireless repeaters and remote communication facilities operate 24/7 and any interruption in power supply will have negative consequences for the network availability and quality of service. In urban environments, the telecom sites usually have access to power grid although some issues such as blackouts and voltage variations can become a problem. However, remote facilities face additional challenges in terms of limited access to power grid, difficulties with transportations and high expenses for diesel generator operations. Solar energy generation combined with battery storage turns out to be a good solution in this case. A typical hybrid telecom power system may include: - Solar photovoltaic modules; - Lithium battery storage; - Hybrid power controllers; - AC/DC power conversion equipment; - Backup from grid or diesel generator; - Remote monitoring and energy management. This system can use solar generation first of all to power the equipment and charge batteries from surplus energy. In case of shortage of solar energy, the stored energy can be used to power the equipment. Backup power from the grid or diesel generator can be used to supplement the lack of renewable energy and stored energy. Such approach allows reducing operating time of generator, expenses for fuel and maintenance costs as well as maintaining continuous power supply. However, the design of telecom power system requires thorough analysis of specific conditions. artigo.texto: Moura investe R$ 200 milhões para ampliar fábrica de armazenamento de energia em Pernambuco Com a chinesa CATL na comercialização, empresa mira o primeiro leilão de baterias do País, em dezembro, e projeta capacidade acima de 8 GWh por ano Clique aqui e escute a matéria O Grupo Moura vai investir R$ 200 milhões na expansão da fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia (Bess, na sigla em inglês) instalada em Belo Jardim, no Agreste pernambucano. O aporte busca colocar a empresa entre os principais fornecedores nacionais do segmento no primeiro leilão de baterias do País, marcado para dezembro. Com a expansão, a companhia projeta produzir mais de 8 GWh por ano. A iniciativa conta com a chinesa CATL, parceira da Moura. A informação é da Broadcast e foi publicada pelo jornal Estadão. A aliança com a CATL não começa agora e se estende a outras áreas, como a eletrificação de veículos, contou à Broadcast o diretor de operações de lítio do grupo, Spartacus Pedrosa. No caso das baterias, a Moura banca sozinha a fábrica e a CATL assume a venda dos sistemas, já que tem mais bagagem em disputas de leilões em diversos países, incluindo a América Latina. Cabem à brasileira a fabricação, a industrialização e o controle local. Novo mercado O leilão pode dar fôlego ao armazenamento no portfólio do grupo, hoje centrado em baterias para veículos. Perguntado se o Bess poderia virar um dos maiores negócios da empresa no País, Pedrosa afirma que o potencial existe. O executivo vê no certame um ponto de inflexão para a indústria nacional e para a segurança energética, num cenário de avanço da geração eólica e solar e de mais episódios de cortes na geração, conhecidos como curtailment. Há cerca de 10 anos no armazenamento, a Moura trabalhou até agora com projetos menores para comércio e indústria. O leilão abre a porta para o chamado utility scale, de grandes empreendimentos, com sistemas maiores e requisitos mais rígidos. A empresa já tem produtos de 30 MWh e agora mira projetos a partir de 120 MWh. Valor flexível Os R$ 200 milhões anunciados podem crescer, avisa Pedrosa. O número final depende das regras do edital, de quantos projetos forem contratados e de novas etapas de nacionalização e ampliação da produção. Em alguns cenários analisados pela empresa, o aporte total para atingir 8 GWh ultrapassa essa cifra. Em Belo Jardim, a Moura vai receber os módulos e montar o equipamento final, um contêiner de 20 pés equipado com refrigeração e sistema contra incêndio. A empresa trabalha com parceiros nacionais nessa etapa, o que também ajuda a reduzir a dependência de fornecedores chineses. Conteúdo local A exigência de conteúdo local ligada ao financiamento do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) é central na estratégia. Montar as baterias no País é o caminho escolhido para cumprir os índices do banco, com nacionalização entre 50% e 60%. Pedrosa explica que essa rota faz a bateria, item de maior peso no investimento, contar como conteúdo local. Por isso, a empresa diz ultrapassar sem dificuldade o patamar de 50% a 60%. A ampliação inclui ainda a compra de equipamentos adicionais encomendados na China, com chegada prevista para 2027. A produção da fábrica deve começar a partir do fim do primeiro semestre, para atender os projetos do leilão em que a Moura espera fornecer os sistemas.

artigo.texto: Base Power, a US-based energy company, is to expand its residential battery program with Denton County Electric Cooperative (CoServ) to 450 MW in North Texas, United States. Since the program was launched in March, Base Power has installed 75 MW of batteries in the homes of CoServ members, at a pace of about 10 MW a month. Each battery supplies the whole home with backup power during an outage, and it also forms part of a fleet that CoServ dispatches at peak demand. Base Power installs and maintains the batteries, whereas the cooperative decides when the fleet is charged and discharged. CoServ, the third-largest electric cooperative in the United States, serves more than 300,000 members in a fast-growing area of Denton, Collin and surrounding counties. Outside Texas, the company has signed its first utility partnership, with Central Georgia Electric Membership Corporation, for 50 MW of residential battery storage. Base Power to expand CoServ home battery program to 450 MW A residential battery fleet of 75 MW in North Texas is to be expanded to 450 MW under a program that Base Power runs with the electric cooperative CoServ. artigo.texto: A Microsoft vem pressionando o governo do presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, a suspender os planos de proibir as importações chinesas de um componente essencial utilizado em data centers de inteligência artificial, segundo três pessoas a par da situação. A Reuters noticiou em agosto que o governo Trump pretende proibir a importação para os EUA de novos modelos de transceptores ópticos chineses, que permitem que os dados trafeguem por cabos de fibra óptica à velocidade da luz dentro dos data centers. A preocupação é que eles possam ser usados por Pequim para roubar dados, instalar malware ou interromper o serviço nos data centers dos Estados Unidos. A Microsoft tem 35 data centers em construção nos Estados Unidos e outros 134 planejados, de acordo com a Cleanview, uma empresa de inteligência de mercado que acompanha o desenvolvimento de data centers. A startup faz parte de um grupo de empresas e associações setoriais que argumentam junto ao governo Trump que tal proibição poderia prejudicar irreparavelmente a vantagem dos EUA sobre a China na corrida pela IA, ao retardar ainda mais a implantação dos data centers, disseram as fontes. A empresa de nuvem e software foi uma das poucas que se reuniu com autoridades do Escritório de Política Científica e Tecnológica da Casa Branca e do Conselho de Segurança Nacional em setembro para alertar sobre os desafios na cadeia de suprimentos que tal proibição representaria, disseram duas das fontes. “Isso realmente ameaça, sem dúvida, paralisar (a implantação dos data centers)”, disse John Miller, consultor jurídico geral do Conselho da Indústria de Tecnologia da Informação (ITI), um grupo de lobby do setor de tecnologia, que instou publicamente o governo a não seguir adiante com a proibição. Ele disse que muitas empresas de nuvem já adquiriram os chips de IA necessários para a implantação. “Esses chips, sem transceptores ópticos, poderiam literalmente ficar parados lá, sem uso, até que você realmente tenha os transceptores para conectá-los”, acrescentou. Alguns data centers precisam de milhões de transceptores ópticos para conectar servidores, roteadores e switches. A Comissão Federal de Comunicações dos EUA (FCC), que supervisiona o setor de telecomunicações do país, está trabalhando na proibição. Os esforços da Microsoft e de outras empresas, que não haviam sido divulgados anteriormente, mostram como as deliberações da agência despertaram preocupações em um setor que se esforça para atender à crescente demanda por serviços de nuvem e IA, apesar da crescente reação negativa dos consumidores em relação ao aumento dos custos de energia e do consumo de água. A Microsoft se recusou a comentar. A Casa Branca, a FCC e a embaixada da China em Washington não responderam imediatamente aos pedidos de comentário. artigo.texto: Alberta's Gigawatt Play: Why Building Data Centers Means Building an Industry Key Highlights - Alberta's transition from data center planning to execution is testing whether its workforce, infrastructure and supply chains can scale alongside gigawatt-class projects. - Industry self-awareness and voluntary commitments on water, emissions and community benefits are becoming more prominent, even as public opposition intensifies. - Unrealistic development proposals can undermine legitimate projects, making credible power, appropriate siting and early-stage development discipline increasingly important. - Alberta's experience raises broader questions about regulatory fairness, community trust and the growing association between AI and the physical infrastructure supporting it. For Alberta's emerging data center industry, the difference between a roadmap and an excavator has become increasingly consequential. A few years ago, Western Canada's data center conversation revolved around the possibilities: abundant energy resources, available land, a favorable climate and the prospect of attracting hyperscale investment to a region better known for oil, gas and other industrial development. Today, earthmoving equipment is preparing the ground for what is expected to become Canada's largest data center, and the questions facing the province have changed accordingly. The shift was on display at Data Centre West 2026, held in Calgary in September, where some 500 industry and government leaders gathered to examine the infrastructure and policy requirements of Alberta's rapidly expanding digital economy. But for conference founder Vlad Oujegov, the most revealing development wasn't simply the appearance of projects measured in gigawatts. It was the growing recognition that building those projects will require Alberta to develop an entire supporting industry, while confronting the environmental, political and community questions that increasingly accompany large-scale AI infrastructure. "The theme last year was the data center roadmap," Oujegov told Data Center Frontier Editor in Chief Matt Vincent during a new episode of the Data Center Frontier Show podcast. "This year's theme really to me was about execution and actually getting things done, actually seeing projects materialize and construction beginning." Oujegov is president and founder of the Western Canada Data Centre Alliance, which organizes Data Centre West, and serves as National Data Center Power Systems Lead at Schneider Electric. His perspective draws on both Alberta's emerging development pipeline and the wider industrial ecosystem now being assembled around it. In DCF's earlier reporting from Data Centre West 2026, the central question was how quickly Alberta could convert growing hyperscale demand into deliverable capacity. The latest podcast conversation takes that question further, examining what happens when a relatively small digital infrastructure market begins preparing for growth on a scale that can transform its regional economy. The resulting challenges extend beyond power availability and construction schedules. They encompass skilled labor, service networks, development credibility, public accountability and the increasingly complicated relationship between the data center industry and the communities being asked to accommodate it. From Roadmap to Earthworks The clearest example of Alberta's transition is Meta's newly announced data center campus in Sturgeon County, northeast of Edmonton. Announced in July 2026, the planned 1-gigawatt, AI-optimized campus represents an investment of more than CAD $13 billion and will become Meta's first data center in Canada. The company anticipates approximately 3,000 construction workers at peak activity and more than 300 permanent operational jobs, along with approximately CAD $60 million in local road and water infrastructure improvements. The campus is located in Alberta's Industrial Heartland, an established industrial region supporting energy production, petrochemicals and related infrastructure. The provincial government's major projects registry identifies the development as under construction, with site grading having begun under a permit issued earlier in 2026. Its supporting energy infrastructure represents another substantial undertaking. The development is paired with the planned 932-MW Greenlight Electricity Centre, a dedicated natural gas generation project intended to help supply the campus. While construction activity has begun at the data center site, full delivery of its associated power infrastructure remains a longer-term proposition. That distinction matters. Breaking ground is an important step toward execution, but it is not the same as delivering a fully commissioned gigawatt of computing capacity. Nevertheless, the physical progress is striking for a market that Oujegov estimates had less than 100 MW of total data center load only a few years ago. A single development now under construction is larger than the province's earlier installed base by an order of magnitude, illustrating both the scale of the opportunity and the challenge of accommodating it. For Oujegov, satellite images showing the site's developing earthworks provide a tangible illustration of how far Alberta has moved from theoretical discussions. "It's really cool for me to see," he said, pointing to visible construction activity following years of preparation. The project also illustrates a broader change in the province's industrial positioning. Alberta is no longer simply attempting to persuade global operators that it belongs on the data center map. It must now demonstrate that its utilities, suppliers, construction industry and local institutions can support developments of a size and complexity previously uncommon in the region. artigo.texto: The Ministry of Power, an India-based federal ministry in charge of the electricity sector, has proposed to bring standalone energy storage providers under the Late Payment Surcharge Rules, 2022. The draft would create a category of energy storage service provider, which would cover operators that no generator, transmission company, distribution company (DISCOM) or consumer owns. Such a provider would have to be paid by the date in its power purchase agreement, or within 45 days if no date has been set. A bill that remains unpaid would carry a surcharge of the one-year lending rate of the State Bank of India plus 5 percentage points. That surcharge would rise by 0.5 percentage point for each month of delay. The ministry has said that investors and banks will fund such projects only if they are confident that the payments will be made on time. Ministry of Power proposes 45-day payment cover for standalone BESS A surcharge of the State Bank of India lending rate plus 5 percentage points would apply to late bills of standalone BESS providers under a Ministry of Power draft. artigo.texto: By Shereen Siewert | Wausau Pilot & Review Weston residents can weigh in Thursday on draft goals for the village’s next comprehensive plan, including a proposal to restrict hyperscale data centers. The “Shaping Weston’s Tomorrow” workshop runs from 5 to 7 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 12, in the board room of the Weston Municipal Center, 4747 Camp Phillips Road. The session is open to the public. “It’ll only be as good as the people that are here,” a village staff member told the Plan Commission on Monday. The draft economic development initiatives propose supporting industrial growth while restricting hyperscale data center projects, according to a Nov. 4 report from Planning and Development Director Jennifer Higgins. Staff has begun researching zoning rules for large data centers, and the topic came up at a meeting of the steering committee guiding the plan update. Marathon County is weighing a countywide data center ordinance, and Weston staff completed a county survey on data center planning last week, the report says. Staff also flagged the need to coordinate with the Town of Weston in the shared extraterritorial zoning area. No formal policy recommendation has been made, and any future ordinance would go through the Plan Commission and Village Board. At a state planning conference in October, Higgins attended a session recommending that communities define data centers as a land use and regulate their effects through measurable standards, including noise, lighting, heat, stormwater, landscaping and demand on utilities. Those lessons will inform the village’s ongoing rewrite of the zoning code, her report says. Thursday’s workshop will open with a short presentation from consultant MDRoffers Consulting, similar to one the steering committee heard earlier. Residents will then split into small groups by topic, such as transportation and land use, to discuss draft goals and objectives and report back to the full room. Staff hopes to record the session and is considering an online option for people who cannot attend. The draft goals draw on community surveys and steering committee work. An initial 2026 community survey drew 681 responses, and a separate questionnaire for young adults closed Sept. 18. Steering committee members showed strong support for an alternative draft vision statement, according to the report. Plan commissioners are not required to attend. Staff said they want the room filled with residents, since commissioners have already had their say through the steering committee. Input from Thursday will be compiled, and a joint committee will review a draft of the plan’s Vision and Directions volume this winter.

artigo.texto: FAIRFIELD — The City Council on Tuesday night unanimously placed a 45-day moratorium on a type of project that does not yet exist in the city. And by the tone of the council members' comments, and that of the majority of speakers at the special meeting – time to study the issues surrounding data centers is exactly what is needed for Fairfield. There was even a hint that an extension is a foregone conclusion. "We need a moratorium, there is no debate about that," Councilman Manveer Sandhu said, though not specifically about an extension. City Attorney David Lim cautioned the council about getting too far ahead of itself, and clarified that the moratorium applies to the entire city and not just the possibility that a data center could be built within the 300-acre Planning Area 6 of the Fairfield Train Station Specific Plan. That site had most of the focus because the city went to NorthPoint Development to test its interest in developing a data center. The initial answer, City Manager David Gassaway said, was NorthPoint was not interested. However, that position has changed. Gassaway made the presentation to the council, seeking direction on the kind of information it would want to see if such a project did go out to Area 6. He asked about location, buffers from urban development, water use, noise, environmental impacts, density – perhaps using just 100 of the 300 acres – the type of buildings, community benefits and utility taxes. But that brought at least one public comment that the staff should not be asking the council about helping to develop regulations for a project that the speaker – and many others – do not want near the One Lake community, and more than a handful do not want in Fairfield at all. The primary issues raised by the public were about water use, power use, noise, fire risk and response, pollution and to no small degree, the proximity to the One Lake community. A buffer of 3,000 feet that Gassaway suggested was viewed by many as not nearly enough. Ed Fischer said the city Fire Department is not equipped to deal with the kind of fires that data centers can generate, and Alicia Minyen added that substations with lithium battery technology would only heighten that risk. There were voices against the moratorium, primarily from representatives of the trade unions that believe the data center would create jobs – maybe not the center itself, but the other businesses that would be attracted to having a data center nearby and the energy infrastructure that would come with it. "The idea of opposing data centers (completely) is like walking around with blinders," said Dave Harrison, with Operating Engineers Local Union No. 3. He said the U.S. is already trailing China in the development of data centers, and that by simply wishing them away will not stop them from coming. Planning was needed, but through the land use standards not a moratorium. The economic promise is a big reason city staff approached NorthPoint in the first place, that and what Gassaway suggested would be a benefit to Travis Air Force Base. However, Councilman Doug Carr said he would want to hear from Travis AFB officials directly about whether they support a data center in the area. Clearly, more power capacity is a big issue for the base. Gassaway said the city has already lost a $400 million project because the energy infrastructure needed to support the company could not be developed in time to meet the deadline. Mayor-elect Pam Bertani said in a recent interview that economic development is at the top of the city's agenda. "We have been talking about economic development for years ... and this is what economic development looks like," Councilman Scott Tonnesen said. But he too had a laundry list of concerns he said would have to be addressed in the staff report on potential impacts. "It's not saying no to economic development," George Kennedy, chairman of the Planning Commission, said about the moratorium. He was speaking as a citizen. "It's talking about planning for it." At the end of the 45 days, which would be Dec. 25, the council could extend the moratorium another 22 months and 15 days. That decision would likely be made on Dec. 15, the last scheduled meeting of the council this year.

artigo.texto: The Cromwell Board of Education was asked for its stance on a proposed data center that would be situated near a middle school. A formal application for the data center developed by Global Common has not been submitted yet, according to the town. Still, concerned residents and parents sent inquiries to the board for their input. Stream Connecticut News for free, 24/7, wherever you are. The board agreed to issue a public statement in the near future laying out its priorities, which are the safety, education, and health of students. “I think we can continue to say that and continue to hold to those values and participate in the dialog representing what is so important to our students, to our families, and to our public schools," Alyssa Goduti, the Cromwell Board of Education Chair, said during Tuesday's board meeting. Cromwell Middle School is about half a mile away from the proposed site on Geer Street. Julie Burland, a parent, brought up her concerns about data centers at the meeting. “They operate 24/7, generating continuous equipment noise, including low-frequency humming that can travel beyond property lines and potentially affect nearby homes, schools and outdoor spaces," she said. Local The developer, Global Common CEO Bob Foxen, has said the data center would use little water and be powered by fuel cells, which he said are quiet. The town’s planning and zoning commission is considering a six- month moratorium on data centers. They’re holding a public hearing on Dec. 3. The board did not say whether it's in support, or against, the data center, but all at the meeting tonight agreed students are the priority. "We don't know what the health effects would be on our children," Susan Vanveldhuisen, a resident, said. "And they should come first."

artigo.texto: SAN JOSE, Calif. — November 11, 2026 — QuantumScape Corporation (NASDAQ: QS), a global leader in solid-state lithium-metal battery technology, today announced Osprey: its next-generation open platform for all-solid-state batteries. Osprey cells have delivered the world’s first public data demonstrating a sulfide-based cathode cycling 1,000 times under just one atmosphere of pressure – an unmatched capability that is necessary for automotive solid-state batteries. Osprey pairs the QS proprietary ceramic separator and anode-free lithium-metal design with a solid cathode, creating an all-solid-state cell. Osprey builds on the company’s QSE platform, and opens new licensing and co-development options for current QS customers and expanding its offering to developers of sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries. QS technology has demonstrated an enhanced safety profile compared to conventional lithium-ion cells, along with low operating pressure and excellent energy retention. Osprey’s all-solid cathode, paired with the proprietary QS ceramic separator, enables additional performance benefits, including faster charging, operation across a wider range of temperatures, and projected energy densities up to ~1,100 Wh/L. In early testing, Osprey cells have demonstrated: More information, including test results and conditions, can be found in a new white paper. The battery industry has long pursued all-solid-state batteries using sulfide-based electrolytes, but this has yet to result in a commercially viable technology. Sulfides can react with lithium metal, which shortens battery life, and they typically need to be held under high pressure to operate, which is impractical for vehicles and many other applications. Osprey is conceived as an open platform capable of working with a range of cathode chemistries. QS has tested Osprey with all-solid cathodes developed both in-house and by its automotive customers, laying the groundwork for multiple technology pathways for solid-state battery development. “Osprey is the result of years of frontier R&D efforts, and we’re excited to share it publicly for the first time,” said Dr. Siva Sivaram, president and CEO of QS. “The industry has invested heavily in sulfide-based batteries but keeps hitting the same fundamental limits. As the data shows, Osprey can address these limitations. We believe Osprey can unlock the full potential of all-solid-state batteries, and our goal is to make it the leading platform for solid-state battery development.” QS is already working with partners across the automotive industry on development using the Osprey platform. Cells based on the company’s QSE platform are shipping to customers today, and Osprey represents its long-term technology solution for all-solid-state battery development. ### About QuantumScape Corporation QuantumScape is on a mission to revolutionize energy storage to enable a sustainable future. The company’s next-generation solid-state lithium-metal battery technology is designed to enable greater energy density, faster charging and enhanced safety to support the transition away from legacy energy sources toward a lower carbon future. artigo.texto: Pylontech and SOLATECH Address Energy Management Needs in Iraq with Energy Storage Solutions BAGHDAD, IRAQ, November 12, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- Pylontech and its local partner SOLATECH held Pylontech Moving Studio - Iraq in Baghdad, presenting energy storage solutions for residential, commercial and industrial, and large-scale applications in response to household and business electricity needs. The event also shared practices in system safety, smart monitoring and installation support. The partners introduced a training and certification initiative for local installers to support the deployment of energy storage solutions in Iraq. For households and businesses facing unreliable electricity supply and the need to coordinate multiple power sources, energy management has a direct impact on daily life and business continuity. Making effective use of solar power during daylight hours, keeping essential loads running at night or during grid outages, and managing backup power more effectively are practical challenges that energy storage systems need to address The solutions presented by Pylontech start with these needs, incorporating the coordinated operation of solar PV, batteries, the grid and generators into system design to offer energy management options for users of different scales. For residential applications, Fidus Plus and Fidus Max offer nominal energy capacities of 16.08 kWh and 20.07 kWh respectively, allowing users to select a solution according to their loads and backup duration requirements. When paired with compatible inverters, the systems can store solar generation for use when needed, adding a controllable energy reserve for the home. Local status displays also make it easier to check battery operation. For shops and commercial and industrial sites, energy storage also supports electricity supply for essential business operations. Pylontech presented hybrid storage solutions including L260-HY, which coordinate solar generation, battery storage and backup power within an operating strategy. Equipped with a 125 kW hybrid inverter and 261 kWh of battery capacity, L260-HY can support solar energy use, energy shifting and backup supply for essential loads, depending on site conditions. System design considers loads, solar resources, grid conditions and available space to help businesses select configurations suited to their operational needs. As energy equipment becomes part of homes and businesses, users are increasingly concerned with long-term operation and maintenance. At the event, Pylontech introduced battery management, operational monitoring and fault diagnosis tools. Battery status monitoring, alerts and remote management functions, where applicable, help users and installation and service personnel understand system operation. Site surveys, technical solution design and after-sales diagnostic procedures also support equipment selection and ongoing maintenance. Founded in 2009, Pylontech has maintained a long-term focus on energy storage, with research and development capabilities in electrochemistry, power electronics and system integration. By combining its technical expertise from cells to complete storage systems with application needs in Iraq, the company aims to make energy storage more useful for household electricity supply and business operations. Building local installation capabilities was another focus of the collaboration. Pylontech and SOLATECH introduced a pathway for online learning, examinations and certification through Pylontech Hub, together with a verification process for inclusion on the installer map on Pylontech's official website. The initiative helps users find nearby installation partners while providing installers with ongoing learning opportunities and product resources. Through the continued development of products, technical support and local partnerships, Pylontech aims to work with SOLATECH and installer partners to improve the delivery and servicing of energy storage applications, helping users benefit from a more reliable and manageable energy experience after their equipment is installed. artigo.texto: Large data centers are now restricted by location, utility usage and hazardous waste practices in the city of Cuyahoga Falls following a 10-1 vote by city council Monday. The legislation requires data centers to be smaller than 5,000 square feet, and can only be located in areas zoned as manufacturing or employment districts. Since Cuyahoga Falls owns its electric and water utilities, Mayor Don Walters said the city was in a unique position to set its own limits for data centers' water and electricity usage. "We would be the ones that would have to approve that," he said. "When we put a strict limit on it, we know that we're capable of providing that and it won't affect our customers." Data centers are not permitted to use more than five megawatts of electricity, and the water consumption on the property is subject to approval by the city's water department. "Even if one of these small ones popped up and they wanted to build, we would have to review their water usage," Walters said. "We already have the cap on their electric usage, so it won't be detrimental to our residents, which is our main concern." Noise pollution produced by data centers can't exceed 70 decibels, which is about as loud as a washing machine. Air and water pollution discharges from data centers must meet standards set by the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency. Data centers within the city are also banned from releasing toxic and hazardous materials on their property, according to the legislation. If those materials are managed on site, it must be reported to the local fire department and meet OEPA requirements. A balance instead of a ban Rather than pursuing an outright ban on data centers, Walters said the city looked to create legislation that considers both industry and community. "We wanted to do something that was right-sized, so we didn't prohibit industry, but also protect everyone. And this is a good balance," Walters said. "A lot of communities are just doing outright bans. We think that is extreme. Might be great for their community, but we want the best of both worlds here." Cuyahoga Falls is already home to several small data centers that meet standards, Walters said, so they won't be affected by the new legislation. The city hasn't been approached for a large data center project, Walters noted, but the legislation serves as a proactive measure ahead of any future development. "We really don't have the land for a mega data center here, so we were never fearful of that, to come in like they do," he said. "We don't have the space for that in our city. However, we still want to have some guardrails to make sure that we're protected."

artigo.texto: MPPE convoca audiência pública sobre a potencial instalação de Data Centers em Pernambuco 03/11/2026* - O Ministério Público de Pernambuco (MPPE) convoca audiência pública, em Garanhuns, para promover o debate técnico, transparente e participativo acerca da possível instalação de centros de processamento de dados de grande porte (Data Centers) em Pernambuco e os impactos hídricos, energéticos e socioambientais, no próximo dia 11 de novembro, às 9 horas, no auditório da Universidade de Pernambuco, campus Garanhuns (Rua Capitão Pedro Rodrigues, 105). Link da transmissão para quem quiser acompanhar remotamente: https://meet.google.com/aun-tcpt-ucb A audiência é aberta a quem interessar e não precisa de inscrição prévia. Para quem desejar se manifestar oralmente na audiência, no dia e local haverá uma lista de inscrição apenas para controle e ordem de falas. É um espaço aberto a manifestações orais e escritas, conforme a dinâmica do evento. Para fins de planejamento do espaço ou envio prévio de manifestações, dúvidas e documentos, os interessados podem ainda entrar em contato por meio do correio eletrônico: nupema.regiao3@mppe.mp.br. É a primeira audiência pública sobre o tema do Núcleo de Proteção Especializada do Meio Ambiente (Nupema) do MPPE e tem como escopo principal avaliar os desafios inerentes para tornar compatíveis a atração de investimentos em tecnologia e a segurança hídrica, proteção das comunidades locais e adoção de salvaguardas socioambientais rigorosas, em consonância com o recente alerta emitido pelo Conselho Nacional do Meio Ambiente (Moção CONAMA nº 147/2026). O MPPE destaca que a participação popular e o controle social são fundamentais para garantir a proteção do meio ambiente ecologicamente equilibrado e o desenvolvimento sustentável em nosso Estado. O Nupema instaurou, em julho deste ano, procedimento para acompanhar a eventual implantação de data centers no Estado e avaliar seus impactos ambientais, econômicos e sociais, com atenção especial ao uso dos recursos hídricos. A iniciativa busca assegurar que o desenvolvimento tecnológico ocorra de forma compatível com a proteção ambiental e a segurança hídrica da população pernambucana, além de estimular a participação da sociedade no acompanhamento de projetos dessa natureza. O edital da audiência foi publicado no Diário do MPPE de 06 de novembro de 2026. artigo.texto: India's dependence on China for machinery and technology used in upstream solar manufacturing — from ingots and wafers to cells — and battery-cell production is emerging as a major vulnerability for its clean energy manufacturing ambitions. With access to Chinese supplies becoming increasingly uncertain amid frequent export curbs, Indian manufacturers are exploring equipment and technology partnerships with suppliers in other countries to diversify their sourcing, Moneycontrol has learnt. Industry representatives said Indian solar manufacturers had faced intermittent restrictions this year on access to Chinese manufacturing technology, equipment and technical support, affecting plans to set up upstream manufacturing facilities for wafers, ingots and polysilicon. More recently, on October 16, China introduced an interim pre-export registration requirement for specified solar technology transfers while proposing to prohibit or restrict exports of 12 photovoltaic manufacturing technologies. The proposed controls, covering selected polysilicon, wafer and cell manufacturing technologies and associated equipment, are expected to be taken up for a decision by the Chinese government after November 15. India has already built substantial solar module manufacturing capacity, with supply in this segment outpacing domestic demand. Cell manufacturing capacity is also expanding rapidly, with Union Minister for New and Renewable Energy Pralhad Joshi saying it is expected to reach 70 GW by December 2026 and cross 100 GW by May-June 2027. But, the next focus for the industry is deeper integration of the supply chain through domestic manufacturing of polysilicon, ingots and wafers — the key inputs used to produce solar cells. This is where India's manufacturing capabilities remain particularly limited, leaving expansion plans vulnerable to restrictions on access to Chinese technology and equipment. Industry scouts for alternatives to Chinese machinery To mitigate the risk of supply disruptions, the industry is scouting for technology and equipment partnerships beyond China. Subrahmanyam Pulipaka, Chief Executive Officer of the National Solar Energy Federation of India (NSEFI), told Moneycontrol that manufacturers were exploring tie-ups with suppliers in Germany, South Korea, Japan, Italy and Australia. However, the alternatives remain limited, as some manufacturers in these countries also outsource production to China, he said. Amit Manohar, Secretary General of the Indian Solar Manufacturers Association (ISMA), said Indian manufacturers were working to build resilience through diversified technology sourcing, global partnerships and stronger in-house engineering capabilities. “Companies are increasingly exploring equipment and technology partnerships across Europe, Japan, Taiwan and other markets, reducing concentration risks. This diversified approach ensures greater supply chain flexibility, technological adaptability and long-term manufacturing competitiveness,” Manohar told Moneycontrol. Building domestic machinery-making capabilities, however, will take time. “It will take at least three years in the best-case scenario and up to five years realistically,” Pulipaka said. China’s pricing power adds to the challenge The dependence also leaves Indian manufacturers exposed to pricing pressure across the solar value chain. Pulipaka said China had raised cell prices while lowering module prices when Indian manufacturers expanded module production, squeezing their margins. “Now, as India catches up in cell manufacturing, China has adopted a similar approach by raising wafer prices while lowering cell prices. This makes it costlier for Indian manufacturers to produce cells while allowing cheaper Chinese cells to compete with domestic products, putting local manufacturers at a disadvantage," he said, while adding that the strategy was aimed at choking India's domestic solar manufacturing industry. Machinery dependence runs deep across solar and batteries A NITI Aayog report prepared with Crisil Intelligence found that capital goods used in polysilicon, wafer and cell manufacturing are concentrated largely in China. Separately, a January report by The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI) found that more than 90% of high-end solar manufacturing equipment, including furnaces, PECVD/ALD tools and diamond-wire saws, is imported. The exposure extends to batteries as well. India imported $1.5 billion worth of battery-cell manufacturing machinery from China in 2022, according to an analysis by the International Institute for Sustainable Development (IISD). China was the leading supplier across several equipment categories, including calendaring, slitting, electrolyte-filling and cell-formation machinery.

artigo.texto: SoftBank tem prejuízo com perdas em investimentos e mudanças em data centers nos EUA O SoftBank Group registrou prejuízo no trimestre mais recente por causa de perdas com investimentos e baixas relacionadas a mudanças nos planos de aquisição de equipamentos de geração de energia para projetos de data centers nos Estados Unidos. A holding japonesa de investimentos em tecnologia teve um prejuízo líquido de 1,11 trilhão de ienes (US$ 7,06 bilhões) no trimestre encerrado em setembro. O resultado frustrou a estimativa de lucro líquido de 53,5 bilhões de ienes apontada em pesquisa com analistas da provedora de dados Visible Alpha. No mesmo período do ano anterior, a empresa havia registrado lucro líquido de 2,5 trilhões de ienes, impulsionado por ganhos bilionários com seu investimento na OpenAI. O grupo contabilizou uma perda de 597,2 bilhões de ienes decorrente de alterações no plano de compras de equipamentos ligados à geração de energia para projetos de data centers de inteligência artificial nos EUA. Segundo a companhia, sua unidade revisou a estratégia de aquisição diante da evolução dos requisitos dos projetos existentes e planejados. Os números decepcionantes somam-se a uma série de reveses enfrentados pela empresa nos últimos meses. Recentemente, a China bloqueou a aquisição de US$ 5,4 bilhões da divisão de robótica da gigante industrial suíça ABB, negócio anunciado em outubro de 2025 com o objetivo de combinar o potencial da IA com robôs. O SoftBank contava com a compra da unidade da ABB, fabricante de braços robóticos e outros dispositivos usados na manufatura e na logística, para liderar uma ofensiva mais ampla em aplicações físicas de inteligência artificial. Nos Estados Unidos, a empresa de data centers SB Energy, apoiada pelo SoftBank, adiou a data de sua oferta pública inicial de ações após enfrentar resistência em relação ao seu potencial valor. Enquanto isso, a Anthropic, rival da OpenAI, planeja avançar com seu IPO ainda neste mês, apesar da recente volatilidade do mercado ligada a investimentos em IA, informou o jornal The Wall Street Journal na segunda-feira. A própria OpenAI captou menos da metade do valor inicialmente almejado em sua última rodada de financiamento, a um valuation de US$ 1,25 trilhão, abaixo da meta original. Nos últimos anos, o SoftBank concentrou suas apostas na inteligência artificial, deixando para trás a estratégia anterior de investir em um portfólio diversificado de startups. Em outubro, a companhia informou ter injetado US$ 10 bilhões adicionais na OpenAI como parte de seu plano de investimentos previamente anunciado, elevando o total investido na criadora do ChatGPT para US$ 64,6 bilhões e sua participação acionária para cerca de 13%. Na semana passada, a unidade britânica de design de chips Arm divulgou resultados acima do esperado no segundo trimestre, impulsionada pela demanda por IA.

artigo.texto: Hitachi e BCR-i Brasil assinam contrato para resiliência energética de data centers O acordo se dá num momento em que o país tem despertado a atenção de investidores para o setor A Hitachi Energy e a subsidiária brasileira do BCR-i, grupo internacional focado na gestão de infraestrutura, serviços técnicos e soluções de eficiência operacional, assinaram contrato para aprimorar a disponibilidade, a confiabilidade e a resiliência da infraestrutura energética que atende segmento de data centers no Brasil. O acordo, chamado de "HMAX Energy", acontece no momento em que o país tem despertado a atenção de investidores para o setor de data center. “[Esse contrato] Nos permite combinar nossa expertise no fornecimento de energia limpa com soluções avançadas de manutenção preditiva”, disse, em nota, Raphael Campos, a frente do segmento de operação e manutenção da BCR-i Brasil. O contrato prevê conjunto de soluções de serviços da Hitachi, baseadas em inteligência artificial, e deve permitir que o BCR-i Brasil se antecipe a eventuais gargalos e problemas que possam atingir uma subestação de 560 megavolt-amperes operada pelo grupo, que atende um data center no Estado de São Paulo. “Os data centers estão no centro da era da inteligência artificial e operam com a expectativa de 100% de disponibilidade. Isso exige uma transformação na forma como a infraestrutura energética é gerenciada”, disse, também na nota, Fernanda Alves, gerente do hub de serviços da Hitachi para a América Latina.

artigo.texto: Oposição a data centers de IA celebra Midterms, mas diz que luta continua Pesquisa da CNN mostrou que cerca de um quarto dos eleitores americanos considerou a IA e os centros de dados cruciais para seu voto A moradora do Texas Maggie Elizabeth Hill ficou acordada até tarde na noite da eleição para acompanhar a divulgação dos resultados das eleições de meio de mandato dos Estados Unidos. Mas acordou cedo novamente na manhã seguinte, já pensando em como poderia trabalhar com os novos líderes democratas eleitos no estado para desacelerar o desenvolvimento de data centers de inteligência artificial. "Fiquei muito animada com os resultados", disse Hill, que formou no início deste ano o grupo de fiscalização de data centers Don't Drain Texas para ajudar comunidades rurais a resistir a projetos do setor. "Comecei a pensar: o que o vice-governador pode fazer? Quais são os nossos caminhos para o sucesso?" A rápida expansão dos data centers de IA se tornou uma questão central nos meses que antecederam as eleições de meio de mandato. Campanhas populares surgiram em comunidades de todo o país, levantando preocupações sobre os impactos locais de grandes projetos de novos data centers de IA. Grande parte da resistência também serviu como uma manifestação da desconfiança geral em relação à inteligência artificial e da frustração com o poder e a riqueza de bilionários do setor de tecnologia. Assim como Hill, opositores dos data centers em todo o país veem os resultados da eleição da semana passada — em que uma expressiva onda de candidatos democratas populistas venceu até mesmo em áreas tradicionalmente consideradas redutos republicanos — como um referendo sobre o tema e uma vitória significativa para o movimento. Eles afirmam que as preocupações com o aumento dos custos de eletricidade, os danos ao meio ambiente e o impacto dos data centers de IA sobre a qualidade de vida das comunidades próximas levaram moradores às urnas. Em todo o país, cerca de um quarto dos eleitores americanos afirmou que a IA e os data centers foram "cruciais" para seu voto nas eleições de meio de mandato, segundo pesquisa eleitoral da CNN. Quando questionados sobre a construção de data centers em suas comunidades, os eleitores se mostraram contrários por uma margem de aproximadamente três a um. Mas os opositores dos data centers afirmam que a luta não acabou. Agora, eles pretendem cobrar dos políticos recém-eleitos o cumprimento das promessas de conter ou estabelecer novas regras para a construção de data centers — ou pressioná-los a adotar medidas ainda mais rígidas. Muitos defendem uma moratória sobre a construção desses empreendimentos, enquanto outros buscam apenas mais transparência e maiores benefícios para os moradores das áreas próximas durante o processo de desenvolvimento. "Sou independente e certamente votei tendo os data centers no topo da minha lista. E conheço muitas pessoas de comunidades rurais que tradicionalmente votam nos republicanos e disseram que essa questão as fez mudar de posição", afirmou Hill à CNN. Uma questão central nas eleições Vários candidatos venceram disputas difíceis depois de colocar os data centers no centro de suas campanhas, incluindo os senadores democratas eleitos Sherrod Brown, de Ohio, e Annie Andrews, da Carolina do Sul. Os democratas também conseguiram uma grande vitória no Texas, estado de Hill, ao vencer a disputada corrida para o Senado e derrotar republicanos que ocupavam os cargos de governador e vice-governador. "Quando os políticos deixam de falar pelas pessoas ou de responder a elas, você vê uma recalibração, e acredito que foi isso que certamente aconteceu" nas eleições de meio de mandato, disse Nick Owens, advogado e fundador do Conserve Ohio, grupo que se opõe à construção de grandes data centers. Owens, republicano durante toda a vida e delegado do presidente Donald Trump na Convenção Nacional Republicana de 2024, acrescentou que os democratas fizeram um trabalho "mil vezes melhor" ao falar com os eleitores sobre os data centers antes da eleição. Enquanto isso, os candidatos republicanos tiveram de lidar com uma associação com Trump, que classificou as preocupações sobre os data centers como uma "farsa" e afirmou que as comunidades que se opõem a eles devem querer continuar "atrasadas e pobres". Em Ohio, a governadora democrata eleita Amy Acton fez campanha defendendo uma "moratória condicional" para o desenvolvimento de data centers. A proposta exigiria, entre outras condições, que os desenvolvedores arcassem com os custos de geração de energia e se comprometessem com medidas de transparência para que seus projetos fossem aprovados. Mas Owens afirmou que seu grupo vai pressioná-la a ir além, usando como modelo a moratória de um ano adotada pela governadora de Nova York, Kathy Hochul, sobre a construção de novos data centers de IA no estado. Ele também espera que Brown possa contribuir para avanços na legislação federal sobre o setor, considerando sua experiência anterior no Senado. "Nossa luta não muda" Em todo o país, muitos ativistas se opõem aos data centers porque querem preservar as terras e os recursos naturais de suas comunidades. É o que motiva Nancy Thellman, cuja fazenda familiar, localizada em uma área agrícola do Condado de Douglas, no Kansas, fica a cerca de 15 minutos de carro de um projeto proposto de data center de grande escala. "Temos pessoas que estão se esforçando muito para manter suas fazendas, preservar suas habilidades e manter a próxima geração no campo, para que os alimentos possam continuar sendo produzidos", disse Thellman. Ela está preocupada com a possibilidade de "data centers chegarem e retirarem vastas áreas de terras agrícolas de alta qualidade da produção para uma finalidade que não é totalmente compreendida ou conhecida para o futuro". Thellman e seu grupo popular, o Douglas County Data Center Watchdogs, estão otimistas de que os resultados eleitorais no Kansas lhes darão uma chance maior de pressionar os legisladores estaduais a revi

artigo.texto: Astella, do Grupo ABL, inaugura data center em Curitiba com investimento R$ 60 milhões Entre 2027 e 2028, grupo brasileiro de tecnologia prevê investir mais R$ 300 milhões em centros de dados com recursos próprios e expandindo a operação a outros estados A empresa Astella, do Grupo ABL, estreia no mercado de centros de dados para serviços de nuvem e inteligência artificial com a inauguração de um data center em Curitiba (PR). O grupo investiu R$ 60 milhões na operação entre 2025 e 2026, em energia, refrigeração e cibersegurança do data center. Até 2028, a meta é injetar mais R$ 300 milhões no negócio, com recursos próprios, expandindo a operação para outros estados. O data center inicia um projeto de rede nacional e descentralizada de computação em nuvem, inteligência artificial e soberania de dados, diz o presidente do Grupo ABL, Agnaldo Lopes, ao Valor. “Em 2025, decidimos retomar a operação de data center na esteira desse movimento do mercado para atender à demanda da IA. Vimos uma oportunidade de retomada”, afirma. O centro de dados com capacidade inicial de 3,5 megawatts e está instalado em um edifício de 16 andares e 8.800 metros quadrados de área útil, no centro de Curitiba. O prédio foi vendido pela Vivo, do Grupo Telefônica, ao grupo ABL em 2018. O imóvel era o principal data center da Vivo no Paraná desde a aquisição da GVT pela operadora. O primeiro projeto da Astella prevê uma rede em forma de estrela que leve o tráfego de dados do data center de Curitiba a outros pontos de conexão de rede (nós) localizados em regiões que não possuem grande concentração de centros de dados. A ideia também é conectar essa rede aos pontos estratégicos de troca de dados como São Paulo e alguns estados da região Nordeste até o final de 2028, acrescenta o executivo. O Paraná possui cinco data centers em operação, enquanto São Paulo reúne 133, segundo os dados atualizados no fim de agosto pelo Mapa de Datacenters do Brasil, criado pelo centro de inovação do Rio de Janeiro em parceria com o site Startups. Fundado em 2000, o grupo ABL atuou no setor de data center no passado. "Em 2015, nós inauguramos um dos primeiros data centers de nuvem privada no Paraná", recorda Lopes, sócio fundador e majoritário da companhia. A empresa também foi provedora de acesso à internet em banda larga, entre 2014 e 2021. A operação foi adquirida pela Copel, que criou o provedor Ligga Telecom, vendido em fevereiro à Brasil Tecpar. A soberania dos dados é um dos pilares da atuação da Astella. "Quando olhamos para o mercado vimos que 80% das estruturas atuais pertencem a grandes empresas internacionais", afirma Lopes. "Entendemos que precisamos criar um modelo que atenda estrategicamente também a soberania nacional", ele acrescenta. As operações de data centers são financiadas com capital próprio, informa Lopes. O executivo controla o Grupo ABL, com 90% do capital, e detém 100% da Astella. O grupo de capital fechado projeta fechar o ano de 2026 com um faturamento de R$ 100 milhões, o que pode representar um crescimento de 28,2% ante o resultado de R$ 78 milhões em 2025. A margem de lucro antes de juros, impostos, depreciação e amortização (Ebitda na sigla em inglês) estimada para 2026 é de 58%, ante margem, Ebitda de 57% no ano passado. A companhia não informou o valor do lucro líquido.
