artigo.texto: A Amazon Web Services (AWS), divisão de computação em nuvem da Amazon, anunciou na última quarta-feira, 11, um polo de data centers no Chile. A iniciativa, na prática, cria a chamada Região AWS América do Sul (Chile), a partir de um investimento de mais de US$ 4 bilhões no país. Segundo a empresa, a infraestrutura poderá ser usada por desenvolvedores, startups, empresas de diversos portes, agências públicas, instituições educacionais e organizações sem fins lucrativos. A lista de clientes inclui BancoEstado, BTG Pactual, Cencosud, Consorcio, Itaú e Ripley. A expectativa é de que, nas próximas semanas, a região esteja disponível para clientes de todo o mundo. Na fase inicial, a nova infraestrutura suporta serviços essenciais de computação, armazenamento, redes e bancos de dados. Ainda serão adicionados serviços de Inteligência Artificial (IA). A região possui três zonas de disponibilidade – grupos de infraestrutura independentes localizados na região metropolitana, cada um com sua própria energia, resfriamento e segurança física –, o que deve contribuir para o armazenamento e a execução de aplicações no território chileno. A AWS estima que a operação vai contribuir com mais de US$ 7,5 bilhões para a economia do Chile e sustentar uma média de 4,1 mil empregos diretos e indiretos em tempo integral por ano, levando em conta a construção, a manutenção, a engenharia, os serviços de telecomunicações e a operação dos data centers. "Cada Região AWS é construída com os mesmos padrões de segurança e resiliência usados pelas organizações mais exigentes do mundo, e, a partir de hoje, essa infraestrutura está aqui no Chile, e do Chile para a América Latina e o mundo", destacou Paula Bellizia, vice-presidente da AWS para a América Latina. Na América Latina, além do polo no Chile, a AWS também tem regiões em São Paulo, em operação desde 2011, e no México, ativada em 2025. No geral, a rede global contempla 124 zonas de disponibilidade e 39 regiões de infraestrutura, mais de 1,8 mil pontos de presença e quase 20 milhões de quilômetros de fibra óptica.

artigo.texto: Naver and NHN also remain at just the 100MW scale, leaving a gap with overseas mammoth operators South Korean companies have unveiled plans to build gigawatt (GW)-scale data centers to meet growing artificial intelligence (AI) demand, but their current capacities remain at just tens to hundreds of megawatts (MW). Meanwhile, overseas operators have already surpassed 1GW, raising concerns that Korean companies could face a vicious cycle of losing ground in customer acquisition and delaying expansion schedules. According to earnings announcements and quarterly reports released by the companies as of Nov. 13, KT and SK Telecom currently operate data centers with capacities of 152MW and 137MW, respectively. These figures represent just 13% to 15% of their stated 1GW targets. During its third-quarter earnings conference call, KT said it plans to secure more than 1GW of additional data center operating capacity by 2031. Of its 911MW pipeline of new projects, investment decisions have been finalized for 200MW. SK Telecom faces a similar situation. Through SK Horizon, the company plans to expand its capacity to 318MW, including existing facilities and data centers under construction in Ulsan and Guro. The figures raise questions about the feasibility of SK Group’s separately announced vision to build AI data centers with a combined capacity of up to 15GW. Naver operates GAK Chuncheon in Chuncheon, Gangwon Province, and GAK Sejong in Sejong. GAK Chuncheon has a power intake capacity of approximately 40MW, while GAK Sejong had a capacity of 47MW as of October 2025. Naver plans to expand the latter to more than 130MW by 2029. According to a report published by Samsung Securities on Nov. 10, the major data centers operated or secured by NHN Cloud have a combined power capacity of 38MW, including 12MW in Pangyo, 6MW at the National AI Data Center in Gwangju and 20MW at Factory X in Yangpyeong, Seoul. NHN Cloud plans to expand its AI data center operating capacity, including existing facilities, to 100MW by the end of 2027. Reaching the scale of a major 1GW data center operator would therefore require substantial capital investment and time for these South Korean companies. Overseas, massive data center operators with capacities exceeding 1GW have already emerged. According to third-quarter results released on Nov. 10 local time by U.S. AI cloud company CoreWeave, its active data center capacity reached 1.7GW. The company has also secured 4.6GW of contracted power capacity through agreements with data center operators. CoreWeave’s data center expansion is backed by actual demand. Third-quarter revenue surged 168% from a year earlier to 4.9 trillion won. Its revenue backlog based on customer contracts reached 177 trillion won. CoreWeave Chief Executive Officer Michael Intrator said during the earnings conference call that qualified customer demand under discussion through the end of 2027 was 10 times greater than the company’s available supply capacity. South Korean companies are also lagging in securing customers. During its third-quarter earnings conference call, Naver announced that it had signed a contract for 20MW of power capacity. That represents part of the 200MW it plans to supply by 2028 in partnership with Brookfield and others. The contracted 20MW accounts for just 10% of the planned capacity. According to a report released in July by global real estate services firm CBRE Korea, the pre-lease rate for data center capacity scheduled to come online in the Seoul metropolitan area in 2027 was just 16%. “If you listen closely to what companies say about their future plans, they talk about expanding data center capacity in stages as they confirm demand,” the head of a South Korean cloud company said. “They cannot immediately build gigawatt-scale data centers when demand remains uncertain.” The executive added, “Securing sufficient demand to recover the enormous investment required for expansion is critical, but competing with global operators that already control massive capacity will not be easy.”

artigo.texto: O mercado brasileiro de data centers ganhou um novo concorrente: a Astella, novo negócio do grupo ABL dedicado à infraestrutura digital, chega com a previsão de investir R$ 1 bilhão no setor em dez anos. A empresa estreou na quarta-feira, 11, ao anunciar um complexo em Curitiba com capacidade inicial de aproximadamente 3,5 megawatts (MW), podendo alcançar 5 MW em uma futura expansão. A unidade, levando em conta infraestrutura de energia e computacional, é orçada em cerca de R$ 50 milhões. Na prática, a empresa está aproveitando uma infraestrutura anteriormente utilizada por operadoras de telecomunicações e investindo na modernização do ambiente. A instalação é um edifício de 8,8 mil m² e 16 pavimentos. Segundo a Astella, Curitiba foi escolhida por dispor de infraestrutura para operações críticas, conectividade e localização estratégica para atender a região Sul. A operação foi projetada para suportar demandas de processamento de Inteligência Artificial (IA) – o data center conta com sistema de refrigeração líquida e racks de alta densidade. Expansão nacional O data center paranaense é só o começo. A estratégia da Astella prevê a construção de uma rede nacional de centros de dados, infraestruturas de borda e pontos de processamento. A curto prazo, o planejamento prevê investimentos adicionais de R$ 300 milhões até 2028, em seis novas localidades. A ideia da empresa é aproximar processamento e armazenamento dos locais onde os dados são gerados e consumidos. Por isso, aposta em um modelo de unidades regionais interligadas por conectividade de alta capacidade e baixa latência. "Estamos transformando quase três décadas de experiência em tecnologia, conectividade e infraestrutura crítica em uma plataforma preparada para uma nova demanda do mercado. A inteligência artificial está mudando a escala e a localização da capacidade computacional, e nossa estratégia é construir uma infraestrutura nacional capaz de acompanhar essa transformação com segurança, conectividade e eficiência", afirma Agnaldo Lopes, presidente do grupo ABL. Por trás da Astella, o grupo ABL está no mercado há 26 anos, com atuação em tecnologia, telecomunicações, nuvem, infraestrutura crítica e energia.

artigo.texto: CATL Builds an Ecosystem Around the Battery: Transit Deals, European Storage and an Aviation Niche Published on 11/11/2026 at 01:31 | Editorial boerse-global.de CATL is pushing past the simple sale of battery cells. In a burst of announcements spanning public transport, home energy storage and electric aviation, the Chinese battery giant has sketched out a strategy in which the battery becomes the starting point for a wider set of services — swapping, servicing, recycling and grid interaction — rather than the end product itself. The most concrete piece of that puzzle arrived in the form of strategic cooperation agreements with four Chinese transit operators: Benxi Passenger Transport Group, Changzhou Transit Group, Guiyang Public Transport Group and Lanzhou Public Transport Group. According to media reports, the arrangements cover battery supply and exchange, customer service, citywide battery-swap networks, recycling, and vehicle-to-grid interaction. The breadth is the point. Rather than a one-off delivery notice, the deals tie a battery's deployment to its upkeep and its eventual disposal — a linked chain that only pays off if CATL can actually coordinate the various tasks in day-to-day operations. From the vehicle to the grid The larger idea running through the transit pacts is the coupling of mobility with energy supply. A swap network touches fleet operations; vehicle-to-grid interaction pulls the power system into the frame. That logic gains weight if the operators adopt these building blocks together and extract practical value from them. For investors, the question shifts accordingly: how much value can CATL create around a battery once it has been delivered? The answer hinges on the role the company genuinely takes on in swapping, servicing and recycling. The tighter those tasks can be woven together, the more convincing the strategic case for the package. The citywide approach matters in particular because it places the individual battery in a broader operational context. The test, ultimately, is execution at each transit operator. A related thread runs through CATL's home-storage ambitions. On 4 November, CATL, Ampace and Octopus Energy signed a memorandum of understanding to explore smart storage solutions for Europe, with the UK, France and Spain as the initial focus. Octopus Energy describes the plan as linking its software platform and electricity tariffs with the battery technology and hardware from CATL and Ampace. Here too the approach reaches beyond a single technical product: the collaboration would carry strategic weight for CATL if hardware, controls and household tariff design mesh sensibly. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying CATL? Storage at scale and a foothold in aviation The same theme recurs at utility scale. On 29 October, CATL gave the TENER+ energy storage system its global debut at All Energy Australia, signing memoranda with Hitachi Energy, EPEC Group and UNSW Sydney to implement large battery storage projects and their grid connections. Grid integration is thus a recurring concern across very different applications — a sign of a coherent strategic direction, provided CATL can successfully interlock its battery technology with its partners' contributions. Aviation is the newest frontier. On 3 November, CATL agreed to work with Blue Vector Intelligent Technology on a custom-built aviation battery for the latter's SKYLA V30 electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft. Blue Vector selected CATL as the exclusive battery partner for the model, so the arrangement covers both development of the specially adapted battery and CATL's sole-supplier role for that aircraft's battery needs. Buyback progress Alongside the deal flow, CATL disclosed the state of its share repurchase programme on 3 November. As of 31 October, the company had bought back a total of 19.6 million A-shares at a cost of RMB 5.36 billion, according to its own figures. CATL at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now. What unites the transit agreements, the European storage memorandum and the Australian grid projects is the embedding of the battery in its surroundings — software and tariffs in the home, swapping, service and grid links in transport. That points to a plausible direction for CATL, so long as partners combine their respective contributions into offerings that work in practice. The yardstick for the stock is delivery on those connections: supply, operation and recycling coming together, and the agreed cooperation holding up in the everyday business of each partner. artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no SoftBank registra prejuízo de US$ 7 bilhões após perdas com data centers nos EUA e queda das ações da Intel Publicado 10/11/2026 • 11:24 | Atualizado há 20 horas Nos bastidores da Nvidia: o primeiro dia de Jensen Huang de volta ao escritório após a revelação do caso extraconjugal Senador acusa Trump de defender o CEO da Nvidia, Jensen Huang, em detrimento da segurança nacional Caso envolvendo Jensen Huang amplia pressão sobre negócios da Nvidia na China Nvidia contrata escritório de advocacia Wachtell Lipton para liderar a investigação do caso Jensen Huang Laços da Nvidia com Trump entram na mira após relatos de que Jensen Huang foi alvo da inteligência chinesa KEY POINTS Foto: Divulgação O SoftBank registrou prejuízo líquido de 1,12 trilhão de ienes (US$ 7 bilhões) no segundo trimestre do ano fiscal, divulgado nesta terça-feira (10). O resultado foi pressionado por perdas relacionadas à aquisição de equipamentos para data centers de inteligência artificial (IA) nos Estados Unidos e pela desvalorização das ações da Intel. O conglomerado japonês também registrou uma perda de 597,2 bilhões de ienes (US$ 3,7 bilhões) nos seis meses encerrados em 30 de setembro, devido a mudanças nos planos de aquisição de equipamentos de geração de energia para projetos de data centers de IA nos EUA. O SoftBank afirmou que realizou investimentos antecipados para garantir o fornecimento de equipamentos de geração de energia para seus projetos de data centers de IA nos Estados Unidos, diante de preocupações com possíveis escassez e longos prazos de aquisição. Leia também: Por que a China barrou o negócio de US$ 5,4 bilhões do SoftBank? A disponibilidade de energia está se tornando uma das principais limitações para a expansão dos data centers de IA, à medida que as redes elétricas ficam sobrecarregadas com pedidos de grandes consumidores de energia, como essas instalações. Os pagamentos acumulados por equipamentos de geração de energia destinados aos projetos de data centers de IA nos EUA, incluindo o PORTS-Pike Technology Campus, no condado de Pike, em Ohio, totalizavam US$ 9,48 bilhões no fim de setembro. “Fizemos investimentos-ponte antecipadamente para garantir equipamentos de geração de energia, diante da expectativa de escassez”, afirmou um executivo do SoftBank durante a teleconferência de resultados da companhia. Veja o desempenho do SoftBank no segundo trimestre do ano fiscal: A receita avançou 13,3% no semestre encerrado em 30 de setembro, impulsionada pelo crescimento dos negócios de telecomunicações e computação em inteligência artificial. A empresa informou que o segmento SoftBank registrou aumento nas vendas em todas as suas operações, enquanto a receita da divisão de computação em IA também cresceu. O segmento Vision Fund passou a registrar prejuízo de 81,58 bilhões de ienes no segundo trimestre do ano fiscal, ante lucro de 2,38 trilhões de ienes no mesmo período do ano anterior. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC O Vision Fund 1 registrou perda de US$ 20 milhões em investimentos no trimestre, apesar de um ganho de US$ 1,3 bilhão com a ByteDance. O resultado foi influenciado pela queda das ações de empresas de capital aberto que integram seu portfólio, incluindo Coupang e Grab. Os fundos Vision Funds registraram ganhos de investimento de 85,45 bilhões de ienes, uma queda acentuada em relação aos 2,81 trilhões de ienes do mesmo período do ano anterior. O Vision Fund 2 apresentou ganhos de investimento de 89,26 bilhões de ienes, enquanto o Vision Fund 1 registrou perdas de 3,86 bilhões de ienes em seus investimentos. Até o fim de setembro, o investimento acumulado do SoftBank na OpenAI somava US$ 54,6 bilhões. O valor justo da participação era de US$ 99,6 bilhões, com ganho acumulado de US$ 45 bilhões, segundo a companhia. O SoftBank afirmou que uma possível elevação da avaliação da OpenAI após uma nova rodada de financiamento ainda não havia sido incorporada aos resultados, pois dependia de um anúncio oficial. A nova avaliação poderá ser refletida no terceiro trimestre do ano fiscal, com potencial para elevar o valor líquido dos ativos da companhia e melhorar sua relação entre dívida e valor dos ativos (loan-to-value, ou LTV). “ O ChatGPT tem sido continuamente uma arma da OpenAI, especialmente para os consumidores”, afirmou o executivo do SoftBank durante a teleconferência de resultados, ao destacar o crescimento da base de usuários do chatbot. Leia também: SoftBank registra lucro acima do esperado após ganho de US$ 8,2 bilhões com Intel As ações do conglomerado japonês fecharam em alta de 13,9% nesta terça-feira. O avanço ocorreu em meio à valorização de empresas asiáticas de tecnologia, incluindo Samsung Electronics e SK Hynix, após uma recuperação das ações do setor em Wall Street na noite anterior. Em relação aos investimentos em infraestrutura de IA, o SoftBank destacou um contrato de arrendamento de 20 anos com a OpenAI para oito gigawatts de capacidade de tecnologia da informação (TI) em um projeto de data center em Ohio. Sobre as preocupações com o consumo de água no data center planejado no Texas, o SoftBank afirmou que está adotando medidas para reduzir o uso do recurso por meio de um sistema de circuito fechado com resfriamento a ar. A companhia também mencionou planos de contratar trabalhadores e adquirir insumos localmente. Antes da divulgação dos resultados, o SoftBank Group anunciou, na segunda-feira (9), planos com a Grab e a empresa malaia PETROS para investir, em conjunto, US$ 1,85 bilhão em capital inicial no desenvolvimento de infraestrutura de inteligência artificial na Malásia. artigo.texto: Data center é o espaço físico que armazena toda a estrutura de computação necessária para o processamento, armazenamento e transmissão segura de dados digitais. Eles são importantes para a manutenção de serviços de internet e de ferramentas como a inteligência artificial, o que explica o rápido crescimento no número de data centers em todo o mundo. Dentro de um data center, é possível encontrar racks com elementos como switches, firewalls e servidores, bem como bancos de baterias, painéis elétricos e sistemas de refrigeração. Atualmente mais de 180 data centers estão em atividade no Brasil. Devido ao crescente uso da inteligência artificial, o país busca dar continuidade ao seu processo de desenvolvimento tecnológico por meio da atração de novos data centers. Para isso, criou uma medida conhecida como Redata, que foca na oferta de incentivos fiscais com contrapartidas. Contudo, há muitas críticas com relação a essa política por conta dos impactos ambientais dos data centers. Leia também: Por que tem se falado em uma bolha econômica em torno da IA? Tópicos deste artigo Resumo sobre datas centers - Data center é o espaço físico onde ficam as máquinas e equipamentos de computação que realizam o armazenamento, o processamento e a transmissão segura de dados digitais. - São importantes porque mantêm o funcionamento dos serviços de internet e as ferramentas de inteligência artificial, cuja demanda cresceu de forma acelerada nos últimos anos. - A capacidade instalada de data centers cresceu cinco vezes entre 2005 e 2025. O atual número de data centers no mundo passa de 13 mil, maioria dos quais está nos EUA. - Dentro de um data center tem, entre outros: - racks, onde ficam itens como painéis de conexão, servidores, firewalls e switches; - banco de baterias e painéis de energia elétrica; - sistemas de ventilação e de refrigeração; Anuncie aqui - equipamentos para o controle de umidade. - Três dos principais tipos de data centers são: - data centers corporativos, que ficam no interior das próprias empresas; - data centers de colocação, que são espaços compartilhados por várias companhias; - data centers hiperescala, que são espaços de grande dimensão construídos exclusivamente para as operações de uma única empresa. - A rápida difusão dos data centers tem gerado debates e críticas sobre sustentabilidade desse modelo de estabelecimento por conta do elevado consumo de energia e de água. - Os data centers também geram poluição sonora e produzem ilhas de calor por conta da elevação da temperatura média do ar, causando alterações no microclima. - O Brasil tem mais de 180 data centers, mas aprovou uma medida que promete isenções fiscais para a instalação de novas unidades no território nacional. Anuncie aqui O que é um data center? Data center é um espaço físico onde ficam instaladas todas as máquinas e os equipamentos de computação responsáveis pelo armazenamento, processamento e transmissão segura de dados digitais de serviços em nuvem e de ferramentas como a inteligência artificial (IA). Em função da rápida modernização dos sistemas de propagação de informações e de comunicação que aconteceu nas últimas décadas, cresceu, na mesma proporção, a demanda por softwares e serviços de armazenamento em nuvem. Não obstante essas sejam redes que existem e se multiplicam no ciberespaço, elas demandam um outro tipo de rede, dessa vez, física, para se manter. Essa rede física é mantida em data centers. Por que data centers são importantes? Os data centers são importantes porque eles mantêm o funcionamento dos serviços de internet que nós utilizamos todos os dias. Uma boa parte do nosso sistema moderno de comunicação depende diretamente de aplicações que são mantidas e aperfeiçoadas por meio desse tipo de infraestrutura. Segundo informações da Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA, em inglês) trazidas pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE)|1|, o número de usuários da internet aumentou em 78% somente entre 2015 e 2022, quando o tráfego global se expandiu aproximadamente seis vezes. Dentro do atual período técnico em que estamos inseridos, empresas, sistemas financeiros e mesmo governos desenvolveram uma alta dependência de ferramentas de TI para a sua gestão. Então, além de serem parte indissociável desse ecossistema de gerenciamento, os data centers são fundamentais para a garantia da eficácia e, sobretudo, da segurança no processamento e armazenamento de informações que, na maioria das vezes, são sensíveis e/ou confidenciais. Esses espaços físicos também são necessários para o funcionamento da inteligência artificial. As ferramentas de IA, entretanto, são bastante complexas e resultam em um trabalho mais intenso do que aquele desempenhado pelas máquinas que compõem os data centers convencionais. Dada a difusão acelerada das ferramentas de IA, que tem sido empregada tanto para atividades corriqueiras quanto para o gerenciamento de empresas e em setores estratégicos, como o energético, os data centers têm se multiplicado em um ritmo semelhante. Para evidenciar a importância dos data centers dentro do presente contexto tecnológico e informacional, basta analisarmos os dados que mostram a evolução da capacidade energética instalada nos data centers. No ano de 2005, essa capacidade ficava em torno de 20 GW, enquanto 20 anos mais tarde, em 2025, ela cresceu para 114,3 GW, segundo dados da IEA|2|. Essa capacidade corresponde a cerca de 13 mil data centers, a maioria dos quais fica nos Estados Unidos (5 mil), na Índia (348) e no Canadá (299)|3|. O que tem dentro de um data center? As seguintes estruturas e equipamentos são encontrados dentro de um data center: - Racks, que é onde ficam todos os equipamentos utilizados para o processamento e armazenamento de dados, como patch panels (painel de conexões), switches, acesso remoto, firewalls, servidores, roteadores, fonte de alimentação de energia (UPS ou nobreak), unidades de distribuição de energia e sistemas de ventilação e refrigeração. artigo.texto: Data Center São Carlos pode receber R$ 2,2 bi São Carlos pode receber um investimento de R$ 2,2 bilhões para a instalação de um Data Center, conforme declaração do secretário João Muller nesta terça-feira, com exclusividade ao SÃO CARLOS AGORA. O anúncio aponta a existência de um grupo empresarial interessado em aportar os recursos no município. A informação foi divulgada em primeira mão e sinaliza um potencial avanço na infraestrutura digital da região. O que é um Data Center O Data Center é o “cérebro” físico da internet e da computação em nuvem, indispensável para operar redes sociais, bancos, serviços públicos digitais e ferramentas de inteligência artificial. Trata-se de uma instalação que concentra servidores e equipamentos de rede para processar e armazenar grandes volumes de dados. Sem essas estruturas, a oferta de serviços online e a transformação digital de empresas e governos seriam inviáveis. A chegada de um empreendimento desse porte coloca São Carlos em posição estratégica no setor de tecnologia. Investimento bilionário em negociação O secretário João Muller afirmou nesta terça-feira, com exclusividade ao SÃO CARLOS AGORA, que existe um grupo empresarial disposto a investir R$ 2,2 bilhões para instalar um Data Center em São Carlos. O valor representa um aporte significativo para a economia local, com potencial de gerar empregos diretos e indiretos durante a construção e a operação. A fonte não detalhou o nome do grupo nem o cronograma previsto para a concretização do projeto. A expectativa é que novas informações sejam divulgadas conforme as negociações avancem. Impactos na arrecadação municipal A implantação de um Data Center pode elevar a receita municipal por meio do ISS (Imposto Sobre Serviços), relacionado à construção e à operação, além de impulsionar o IPTU e, em alguns casos, a participação no ICMS, fortalecendo o orçamento público local. Esses tributos incidem sobre diferentes etapas do empreendimento, desde a obra civil até a prestação de serviços de hospedagem de dados. Para os cofres públicos, o incremento pode representar mais recursos para investimentos em áreas como saúde, educação e infraestrutura urbana. A administração municipal ainda não divulgou estimativas oficiais de arrecadação. Modernização da infraestrutura tecnológica A chegada de grandes operadoras exige melhorias nas redes de fibra óptica e nas subestações de energia elétrica, modernizando a infraestrutura tecnológica da região. Essas adequações beneficiam não apenas o Data Center, mas também empresas e moradores que dependem de conexão estável e energia de qualidade. O investimento em infraestrutura pode atrair outras empresas de tecnologia e serviços digitais, criando um ciclo virtuoso de desenvolvimento. A fonte não detalhou quais operadoras estariam envolvidas no processo. Desafios de energia e água Por outro lado, há um consumo intensivo de energia e água. Essas estruturas demandam grandes volumes de eletricidade para os servidores e de água para os sistemas de refrigeração, o que pode pressionar a rede local se não houver planejamento. Especialistas alertam para a necessidade de avaliar a capacidade das concessionárias e dos recursos hídricos antes da instalação. O poder público e o grupo investidor precisarão apresentar soluções sustentáveis para mitigar esses impactos. A fonte não detalhou medidas de eficiência energética ou hídrica previstas para o projeto. Perspectivas para o setor empresarial Para empresários e comerciantes da região noroeste paulista, o anúncio sinaliza oportunidades indiretas em serviços de apoio, como fornecimento de materiais, logística e manutenção especializada. A instalação de um Data Center pode aquecer a demanda por mão de obra qualificada e serviços técnicos, beneficiando pequenas e médias empresas locais. Entidades como ACSP, CDL e Sebrae poderão acompanhar o desdobramento do projeto e orientar seus associados sobre possíveis nichos de atuação. A concretização do investimento ainda depende de etapas formais e da confirmação do grupo empresarial. Perguntas Frequentes Qual é o valor do investimento previsto para o Data Center em São Carlos? O investimento previsto é de R$ 2,2 bilhões, conforme anunciado pelo secretário João Muller. Quais benefícios fiscais um Data Center pode trazer para São Carlos? A implantação pode elevar a receita municipal por meio do ISS, impulsionar o IPTU e, em alguns casos, aumentar a participação no ICMS. Quais são os possíveis impactos negativos da instalação de um Data Center em São Carlos? Há consumo intensivo de energia elétrica e água, o que pode pressionar a rede local se não houver planejamento adequado.

artigo.texto: 19,6% ao ano. Essa é a taxa de crescimento anual composta projetada pela Frost & Sullivan para o mercado de data centers de colocation na América Latina entre 2024 e 2029, período em que as receitas do segmento devem avançar de US$ 1,47 bilhão para US$ 3,59 bilhões. Mais do que sinalizar a expansão da infraestrutura digital, essa projeção evidencia a pressão por arquiteturas capazes de acompanhar a evolução das cargas de trabalho, especialmente aquelas impulsionadas pela inteligência artificial. Nesse cenário, ampliar a capacidade computacional sem repensar a arquitetura de rede pode limitar o desempenho, a escalabilidade e a eficiência dos investimentos. A conectividade deixa de ser apenas uma camada de suporte e passa a ocupar uma posição estratégica no desenho dos data centers da próxima geração. A inteligência artificial é um dos principais fatores por trás dessa mudança. Os ambientes desenvolvidos para treinamento e inferência de modelos demandam padrões de comunicação distintos dos observados em aplicações corporativas tradicionais, com intenso tráfego entre servidores, baixa latência e alta previsibilidade de desempenho. Para as redes, o desafio vai além de aumentar a velocidade da conexão. É preciso garantir que os servidores troquem informações com rapidez e eficiência, evitar sobrecargas e manter a operação estável mesmo diante de picos de demanda. Isso exige uma arquitetura preparada tanto para o intenso fluxo de dados entre os próprios servidores quanto para a comunicação com sistemas externos. O desenho da rede deve, portanto, acompanhar as necessidades de cada data center, considerando o tipo de aplicação, o volume de processamento e a possibilidade de expansão futura. Essa transformação exige também uma mudança na maneira de operar a infraestrutura. À medida que os ambientes se tornam mais distribuídos, virtualizados e dinâmicos, a observabilidade de rede passa a ter papel estratégico: monitorar apenas a disponibilidade dos equipamentos ou a utilização média dos links já não é suficiente. É necessário correlacionar telemetria, latência, perda de pacotes, filas, padrões de tráfego e desempenho das aplicações para identificar gargalos antes que eles comprometam os serviços. Combinada à automação e à inteligência artificial, essa visibilidade abre caminho para redes autônomas, capazes de detectar anomalias, recomendar ajustes e, dentro de políticas previamente estabelecidas, executar ações corretivas. Em infraestruturas críticas, a autonomia precisa ser construída com critérios claros de segurança, rastreabilidade e reversibilidade das mudanças. Na América Latina, essa discussão ganha relevância diante da expansão dos mercados de colocation e hyperscale, especialmente no Brasil, no México, no Chile e na Colômbia. No Brasil, o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), instituído pela Lei nº 15.504/2026, acrescenta um vetor potencial de crescimento. Ao prever incentivos tributários para equipamentos destinados a essas instalações, sob determinadas condições, o regime pode favorecer investimentos em infraestrutura digital, computação em nuvem e inteligência artificial. As contrapartidas previstas de pelo menos 10% da capacidade efetiva de processamento, armazenamento e tratamento de dados instalada ao mercado interno deverá gerar mais investimentos em infraestrutura e sustentabilidade nos próximos anos. Do ponto de vista de alguém que acompanha esse setor desde seus inícios e testemunhou de perto a transformação do mercado, vejo como fundamental que as redes sejam pensadas como parte central do projeto do data center, desde as decisões iniciais de arquitetura até a operação cotidiana. Isso exige soluções que combinem desempenho, disponibilidade, segurança e flexibilidade para acompanhar o crescimento da demanda, sem gerar complexidade operacional ou custos desnecessários. Aqui, o papel dos fornecedores de tecnologia é apoiar as empresas na escolha e na implementação de arquiteturas alinhadas às necessidades de cada ambiente, com capacidade de expansão e recursos de automação e observabilidade que simplifiquem a gestão da infraestrutura. Mais do que entregar conectividade, o desafio é oferecer uma base tecnológica preparada para sustentar novas cargas de trabalho, proteger a continuidade dos serviços e garantir que os investimentos em data centers se traduzam em eficiência operacional e valor para os negócios. * Sobre o autor – Roberto Murakami é VP de Redes e Telecom da NEC na América Latina. As opiniões expressas neste artigo não refletem necessariamente a visão de TELETIME.

artigo.texto: With artificial intelligence use increasing, Cal Poly’s second Real Estate Day focused on how data centers could affect communities across the Central Coast . Hosted by Cal Poly’s Real Estate Initiative, the event featured panel discussions with business professionals, Cal Poly faculty and local government officials, who shared their perspectives and expertise on data center development and answered questions from attendees. Data centers are large buildings that house computer systems that store information, run internet programs and train AI models. These facilities have the potential to generate local tax revenue, create construction jobs and attract private investments to surrounding areas. Data centers also have environmental impacts, requiring substantial amounts of land, water for cooling and fossil fuels for producing energy, according to Lincoln Institute of Land Policy. READ MORE: The environmental cost of the Cal State’s new AI initiative Hamed Ghoddusi, director of Cal Poly’s Real Estate Initiative, said the event aimed to bring the community together to discuss important issues and learn from one another. “We don’t have many events where people get together to have informed discussions like this,” Ghoddusi said. “I think we really need more of this.” Ghoddusi estimated that more than 200 people were in attendance at one point during the event. Thomas Fowler, an architecture professor who spoke on one of the panels, said his students are designing data center concepts for a class project. “I think it’s important for students to get information outside of the classroom in addition to being inside of the classroom,” Fowler said. “It’s rare that they would be working on a project that there would be a half-day seminar about the topic.” Matthew Hanley, a business administration senior concentrating in real estate finance, said he attended the event to learn more about developments in commercial finance. “They’re going to be built and what matters is that people know what’s going on,” Hanley said. The panels also explored the potential economic benefits of data center development. Stockton Mayor Christina Fugazi, who participated in one of the panels, discussed data center development revenue’s potential to help fund local infrastructure improvements, including road repairs. Business administration sophomore Andrew Silvas said the panels acknowledged the duality of data centers. He also expressed concern that cheaper technology could lead to increased usage and demand for more data centers, potentially creating what he described as a “scary world.” Henry Knudson, a computer science senior and member of Cal Poly’s AI Ethics Lab, said he attended the event to hear perspectives beyond the concerns and skepticism about AI he often encounters in the lab. “Being able to hear industry professionals talking about why we might need the speed that we do and what the benefits for communities might be was pretty interesting,” Knudson said. Knudson said the AI Ethics Lab is also working on a project involving data centers, which motivated him to learn more about their potential impacts. “I think this is comparable to the industrial revolution of the past,” Knudson said. “It’s really important that you get involved so that you don’t just experience the effects of it later if we don’t do it right.”

artigo.texto: Arctic data centers: Buy, Sell or Hold? Is the Arctic’s data center boom a smart investment for local communities, or will the costs outweigh the returns? At an Arctic Today-moderated panel during the recent Arctic AI Summit in Kirkenes, Norway, three experts delivered three very different verdicts: Buy, Sell and Hold. Justine Vanhalst, co-founder of Icelandic start-up Hringvarmi, which aims to turn data center waste heat into locally grown food, voted Buy, meaning Arctic people should welcome the centers. However, her vote came with conditions. Professor Lars Ailo Bongo of UiT, The Arctic University of Norway, and co-founder of the Sámi AI Lab at the Sámi University of Applied Science, delivered a resounding Sell, advising people to say no to building the centers in their backyards. Meanwhile, Mads Qvist Frederiksen, executive director of the Arctic Economic Council, opted for a Hold. These contrasting opinions show the underlying tension between the economic promise of major investment and the potential environmental and social costs for the Arctic communities involved. Why the Arctic and why now? AI is driving unprecedented global demand for computing infrastructure and Arctic countries offer an attractive value proposition for data center developers: naturally cold conditions for cooling, an abundance of open space for construction, and access to low-carbon electricity. Developers also choose the northern countries for their safety, political stability and reliable connectivity. However, negative environmental impacts are already being seen across the region. In Finland in September, Google plans to invest €13 billion in data center expansion, which according to their Finnish country manager would be the largest single investment in Finland’s history. By October, the project had hit a speed bump after more than 500 hectares of forest (about 740 football fields) were cleared without the correct environmental impact studies and approvals. In response, the Finnish police have now launched a criminal probe into the suspected breach. Hold: Not So Fast This kind of risk reward dilemma is familiar to Qvist Frederiksen, who was able to list myriad economic benefits for countries like Finland, not least that Google’s investment came with a forecasted €3.6 billion in annual GDP contributions for the construction phase. He also pointed to Greenland, where the government is actively seeking data center investment and exploring expanded hydropower capacity to attract developers. “For years, we’ve been screaming for investment,” he told the audience. “Now someone is coming in trying to invest. Do we want to say no?” Maybe not no, but not so fast. His instinct is to welcome direct investment while his HOLD verdict suggests a need for caution. Some investments bring substantial economic benefits, while others leave communities with higher energy costs and very few new jobs. Qvist Frederiksen referred to Bell Canada’s planned US$50 billion data center investment in Saskatchewan as a success case where investors are sourcing their own energy rather than drawing on existing community supplies and creating 4,500 high-quality jobs. (Although, as Bongo points out, in emissions terms, this is still a huge new CO2 source.) In contrast to Bell, Qvist Frederiksen cited the cryptocurrency mining facility in Norway that brought no meaningful benefits to the local community, while generating heavy noise pollution and higher electricity prices. BUY, but with conditions For Vanhalst, the opportunity lies in turning a costly byproduct of data centers into a valuable local resource. Or as she puts it, “turning data into dinner.” Her Icelandic startup, Hringvarmi, is developing modular farms that use excess heat from the centers to grow fresh produce, reducing food imports while creating jobs and new business opportunities. “We’re connecting all these sectors together,” Vanhalst told the audience. “We need the data centers, the municipalities and the local people who want fresh food. By using existing resources, we can create the right environment for local food production.” She pointed to a separate initiative in Akureyri, northern Iceland, where a data center is in discussions with the municipality about using waste heat to warm a swimming pool or keep a natural grass football playable through winter. However, her BUY verdict comes with conditions. “It’s more like BUY/HOLD,” she said. “It’s too simple to just say we have the Arctic, we have the energy, so let’s do it. We need to consider where the energy comes from, the land, the environment and whether the community supports the project.” For Vanhalst, realizing these benefits will depend on effective regulations, responsible energy use, and building local partnerships rather than simply hosting the infrastructure. Sell: Who really benefits? For Bongo, the central question is whether the Arctic risks becoming a supplier of energy and land for someone else’s digital economy. “Who stands to benefit from the Arctic’s land and energy resources?” he asked. “The wind farm might be owned by a German company, the data center by the British, and the main customer might be one of the big American tech companies. Then what does the local community get in return?” Bongo, co-founder of the Sámi AI Lab, pointed out that his AI lab’s electricity needs are equivalent to those of just one or two freezers, a stark contrast to the energy demands of large commercial data centers. He warned that expanding renewable energy production to power such facilities could place further pressure on Sámi lands, where development has already led to conflicts over Indigenous rights. He pointed to Norway’s Fosen wind farm controversy and the Norwegian Supreme Court ruling that wind energy development in this project violated Sámi reindeer herders’ fundamental human rights. “We cannot simply say that AI is so important, and that we need so much green energy that we can ignore human rights,” he said.

artigo.texto: Tudo que você precisa saber sobre os mercados regulado e voluntário, como eles funcionam e se conectam. O carbono entrou na conta Durante décadas, o carbono foi um custo invisível pago pelo clima e pela sociedade. Hoje ele tem preço, valor de mercado e impacto direto no balanço das empresas. Com o mercado regulado brasileiro (SBCE) saindo do papel, o Artigo 6 do Acordo de Paris em operação e créditos voluntários podendo entrar no sistema regulado, as fronteiras entre esses mercados estão cada vez mais porosas. E a discussão saiu da agenda ambiental para entrar nas decisões de investimento, financiamento e gestão de risco. O Guia Reset de Mercados de Carbono explica como cada mercado funciona, como os preços se formam e onde estão os riscos e as oportunidades. artigo.texto: asharkyu/Shutterstock Save for later Print Download Share LinkedIn Twitter The energy storage market is expanding at a speed that would have seemed impossible just a few years ago. Yet, government targets have not kept pace with the market's growth. Storage is no longer a peripheral technology whose deployment can be left until renewable generation is built. It is becoming a central part of how electricity systems will operate, how much value they can extract from renewable power and how reliably they can meet growing demand. With COP31 focused on accelerating electrification, the gap between storage deployment and government ambition raises questions about whether power systems can deliver on those commitments. Ember’s analysis of national 2030 storage targets shows how far countries have come and how far they still have to go. The combined ambition of countries and the EU has reached 822 gigawatts, nearly three times the 284 GW assessed when governments agreed the Global Energy Storage and Grids Pledge at COP29 in 2024. But that total remains 45% below the pledge’s 1,500 GW goal. More revealing still is where the increase has come from. China and the EU account for most of the increase in national storage targets worldwide. The global headline suggests a broad shift in ambition. The underlying picture is much more concentrated. Global Storage Ambition Rests on 2 Markets China has raised its 2030 storage ambition from 130 GW to 460 GW under its 15th Five-Year Plan. The target combines 300 GW of new-type energy storage, mostly lithium-ion batteries, with 160 GW of pumped hydro. The EU, meanwhile, established its first bloc-wide storage target at 200 GW in June 2026. These decisions are significant. China’s target reflects the need to integrate its rapidly expanding renewable capacity, while the EU’s agreement explicitly links storage to reducing gas demand and making better use of renewable electricity. But the concentration of ambition matters. Since COP29, only eight countries and the EU have increased or introduced 2030 storage targets. Many other major markets have made little change to their plans. The result is a global total that looks much stronger than the underlying policy shift. Two major economies have moved decisively, while much of the rest of the world has yet to follow. That matters because the energy transition is not being built in two markets alone. Countries are pursuing different combinations of solar, wind, electrification and grid investment. They will not all need identical storage technologies or deployment pathways. But they do need to understand what their own power systems require and plan accordingly. A global pledge is only as strong as the national plans on how to deliver it. The Market Is Already Moving Faster Than the Plans Annual storage additions reached a record 118 GW in 2025, 108 GW of them batteries, and installed capacity reached 430 GW by the end of the year. The pace of change is remarkable. It took four years for annual battery additions to rise from around 10 GW to 100 GW. Solar took nine years to cross the same threshold, while wind took 15 years. Falling costs have helped drive this expansion. Battery storage costs have declined by roughly 20% per year on average over the past decade, improving the economics of projects and opening up new opportunities for power systems. Current deployment also puts the shortfall in national targets into perspective. If annual additions remained at the 2025 level through to 2030, global installed storage capacity would reach around 1,020 GW. That would exceed the combined national targets by almost one-quarter. Reaching the 1,500 GW global pledge will require further growth. But our analysis suggests that the necessary acceleration is well within reach of recent market performance. Battery additions have grown at almost 80% a year since 2020. To reach the 1,200 GW of battery storage envisaged in the International Energy Agency’s net-zero scenario update, annual additions would need to grow at only about one-fifth of that rate. The market has already demonstrated that it can grow at extraordinary speed. The question is whether governments are planning for the power systems that this growth makes possible. Solar Policy Without Storage Planning Is Incomplete The consequences and benefits are clearest in solar markets. Solar power is generated mostly during the day, but electricity demand continues into the evening and overnight. Batteries can shift some of that daytime generation to periods when it is needed, reducing curtailment, easing pressure on grids and allowing existing renewable capacity to deliver more useful electricity. Storage and solar are therefore not separate policy choices. They are complementary parts of a power system. Building more solar without planning for flexibility risks leaving some of its potential untapped. Of the 20 largest solar markets by capacity in 2025, 12 have a 2030 storage target and eight do not. Some of these markets are already deploying storage at scale. The US has installed roughly 52 GW of utility-scale battery power capacity, while Germany has around 30 GWh of battery storage. Market signals can drive projects where the economics are attractive. But they do not necessarily ensure that the right amount and type of storage will be built in the right locations and on the right timelines. Nor do they guarantee that storage deployment will be coordinated with new generation, transmission infrastructure and changing patterns of demand. Credible targets can provide a direction around which these decisions are made. Storage Belongs at the Center of Energy Planning The stakes will grow as electricity takes on a larger role across transport, buildings and industry. The Global Electrification Pledge proposed by the COP31 presidency aims to raise electricity’s share of final energy demand from around 20% to 35% by 2035. artigo.texto: Battery storage opens evening electricity markets to solar: Ember November 11, 2026 | Electrification, News Battery storage is pushing solar power beyond daylight hours and into electricity markets long dominated by fossil fuels, according to a report from energy think tank Ember. The analysis, published August 12, finds solar and batteries already supplied roughly a quarter of evening electricity demand in California and Bulgaria during the first half of 2026. Globally, batteries expected to be installed this year could shift 34 per cent of new daily solar generation into evening hours, based on solar growth during the first six months. That compares with 18 per cent in 2025 and just 4 per cent in 2021. Ember cautions that the estimate is a theoretical ceiling. It assumes all the new batteries are used to shift solar electricity. Actual performance depends on how storage is operated and whether electricity market rules allow batteries to earn revenue from multiple services. The findings point to a new phase of solar expansion. Solar supplied just over 10 per cent of global electricity in the first half of 2026, nearly double its 5.6 per cent share three years earlier. On an average day, it met more than a quarter of demand between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m., before falling to almost nothing overnight. That concentration creates problems in markets already producing abundant midday solar electricity. Wholesale prices can turn negative, generators may be forced to curtail output, and returns on additional solar projects weaken. Batteries can store that electricity for later use, reducing waste and allowing solar to compete during evening demand peaks. In California, solar and batteries met more than a quarter of demand between 7 p.m. and 9 p.m. in the first half of 2026, up from 6.8 per cent in the same period of 2023. Bulgaria reached 24 per cent during those evening hours. In Chile, batteries helped solar meet more than 10 per cent of electricity demand through the evening and into midnight. “Solar’s role in global power systems can be far bigger than previously thought possible,” Ember analyst Kostantsa Rangelova said in the report. Deployment is accelerating. Ember cites projected global battery additions of 459 gigawatt-hours in 2026, a 50 per cent increase from 307 gigawatt-hours last year. But installing equipment is only part of the challenge. Batteries can earn money by shifting electricity between low-price and high-price hours, supporting grid stability and providing capacity when needed. Rules that let operators combine those revenue streams can improve utilisation. China illustrates the gap. Standalone batteries averaged 299 charge-discharge cycles in 2025, while batteries installed alongside generation averaged just 199. Ember compares that with international best practice of about 350 cycles annually. Storage also has limits. Today’s batteries primarily address daily fluctuations, leaving prolonged cloudy weather and seasonal shortages as continuing challenges. Ember says electricity systems will still need a complementary mix of wind, hydro, nuclear and longer-duration storage. The next stage of solar growth will depend increasingly on deploying batteries and integrating them into electricity markets, the report concludes. That makes market reform central to further expansion.

artigo.texto: Missoula County accepts report in pursuit of data center regulations Martin Kidston (Missoula Current) Members of the public praised Missoula County for its temporary ban on data centers and urged it to extend its moratorium until new zoning is adopted to temper the industry's environmental and social impacts. Commissioners on Thursday moved toward that action by accepting the findings of a report, which in summary found that data centers “have very real impacts” on health, safety and the environment. Accepting the report positions the county for its next step, which may include another year-long moratorium while it crafts new zoning to lasso the industry and its impacts. “There will be no gap,” said Commissioner Dave Strohmaier. “Either we have permanent zoning in place by the end of this moratorium period, or, in the more likely case and in a separate action from today, we'll extend the moratorium.” The study conducted by Missoula County found that data centers can have a significant impact on health, safety and the environment, and the interim ban adopted by the county earlier this year was appropriate. County officials released the study last month, roughly four months after adopting its initial moratorium. What happens next hasn't been determined, though Thursday's acceptance of the study sets the stage for another ban and potential zoning. Become a Missoula Current Sustaining Contributor “We know we're not immune and insulated from what happens at the state level,” said Abby Huseth with Climate Smart Missoula. “Overall, we really support the report because it offers the most durable pathway to getting regulations on the books, which can protect our community for the long term.” While the county is looking to take action, its choices may be partially limited by state law. The report cites a number of state policies, which enshrine a county's right to adopt zoning regulations to protect public health and safety. But in 2025, the Legislature also adopted the Right To Compute Act, limiting what measures a local government can take to restrict data centers. Under that scenario, a permanent ban on data centers won't be likely. “We've been advised by the county's legal council that the act likely makes an outright local ban untenable,” said Svein Newman, the county's climate action program manager. “The county itself cannot address all the identified impacts. The state likely has purview over air quality and water quality. They largely regulate discharge permits and limit the county's authority there.” But the county may have room to adopt zoning to address other concerns like noise, backup power, water use and a data center's location. It may also set renewable energy standards, which it did two years ago by requiring data centers and cryptocurrency operations to offset their power with 100% newly created clean electricity. The Legislature convenes in two months and the county, along with advocates of stricter regulations on data centers, will be watching to see what laws may or may not emerge. “We already know there will be a lot of bills about data centers, from water impacts to local control and more,” said Newman. “The last I looked there were already 50 filed bill-draft requests related to data centers and that number seems to be growing rapidly.” The study identified three types of data centers from large to small. It also identified 13 potential impacts including climate change, water quality and quantity, noise, thermal effects, land use, electronic waste, wildlife and light pollution, among others. Some on Thursday questioned the will of state-level leadership to address such impacts. Others spoke over concerns around “military industrialism,” “computational centers for digital neural networks” and a “high-tech surveillance police state.” Ben Catton of the Montana Environmental Information Center noted the Montana Public Service Commission's approval of the $15 billion merger between Northwestern Energy and Black Hills Corp. With that merger now set, he encouraged the county to follow the report's recommendations, which include engaging with both the PSC and the Legislature. “We'd like to continue to engage in the development of regulations and we strongly support the extension of this moratorium,” said Catton. “We'd love to continue to see engagement at the PSC now that the merger has been approved. We know that's largely to attract data-center development. We might be more of a target than we already are.” The county report recommends that it remain engaged with the PSC – an all Republican body whose interests were questioned on Thursday. “The county should continue its involvement (with the PSC) to help require data centers in Montana to pay their own way, essentially to ensure electrical costs associated with data-center power and transmission are contained to those customers and not shifted onto other customers like residential ratepayers,” Newman said.

artigo.texto: Proposed 'data center' project could come to Greenville County A proposal is making its way through the Greenville County application process that looks to develop a building into a project resembling a data center The proposal The application, which was in front of the Greenville County Planning Commission in October, lists Steven Pearce of McGuireWoods Consulting for Robert Moser of Prime Storage as the applicant, and according to the application, developers have a portfolio of taking existing storage assets to develop a proposed "Inference Point." The proposed location is a Prime Storage location along Wade Hampton Boulevard next to a Texas Roadhouse and backing up to a residential street. The application goes on to say developers plan to take existing storage assets to develop that inference point, which is a low-latency use to assist with medical procedures. It claims a $100 million development would use 5 megawatts of power Developers claim this can all happen inside of the building without knocking it down. What is an 'Inference Point'? We researched Inference Point and found it was a trademarked project by Edge Inference, LLC, based in Saratoga Springs, New York. According to the website, the company has had several similar projects across the country. Their website says an inference point is a "Small piece of local infrastructure, inside a building that already stands, that works out AI answers for the people, hospitals, schools, and businesses around it. In an instant, because it is close" The website also says it serves a local community that is close to the physical location of the center, and answers are given instantly because, "they never leave town." The Inference Point website also claims the machines are quiet and use no city water. How much power does it use? Where they differ, according to the site, is that an Inference Point is a 'tenant in an existing building' and focuses on answering questions for nearby people instantly, not housing and storing data for worldwide customers. We also wanted to know how that power usage compares to similar proposals in the Upstate. Here is research from WYFF4 Reporter Alex Land. In Spartanburg, a data center along Tyger River Industrial Drive would use up to 65 megawatts. Another project at the former R.R. Donnelly Industrial property would also use around 65 megawatts. The project has passed through the Greenville Planning Commission with approval in October but still needs a final thumbs-up from the Greenville County Council. Councilmembers say the project is facing second reading on Nov. 17.

artigo.texto: In delivering the Benchmark Lifetime Achievement Award 2026 to CATL (HKG:3750) Chairman Robin Zeng, former recipient and long-time colleague Bob Galyen says Zeng has helped transform batteries from a niche technology into a global industry. Gaylen, CATL’s former CTO, credits him with bringing electrification to scale and positioning batteries at the heart of the modern economy. The award was delivered at Benchmark Week 2026 in Shanghai, held on 10–11 November at the Pudong Shangri-La. Zeng founded CATL in 2011, recognising that batteries would become an essential part of the global economy. Over the last 15 years, he has grown the company around that vision. Zeng was also named to the TIME100 Climate 2025 list for his leadership in business climate action. In 2023, he received a Nobel Sustainability Trust award recognising his contributions to transportation electrification and the energy transition. Galyen notes that Zeng recognised early on the need to electrify at scale and has since focused on making battery technology reliable, affordable, and available across income levels. Zeng points to five factors that matter for EVs: safety, performance, lifespan, cost, and environmental impact. That last factor extends to the company’s own operations, not just the impact of EV adoption. CATL says it achieved carbon neutrality across its core manufacturing operations in 2025 and aims to reach full value-chain carbon neutrality by 2035. A rising tide for the battery ecosystem In line with the event’s theme of collaboration across the battery value chain, Zeng says the industry can only achieve long-term success if it grows together. Rather than concentrating profits in one part of the supply chain, he believes value should be shared so that participants can continue investing, innovating, and scaling. Zeng likens the approach to ensuring everyone has enough oxygen to survive. A healthy industry, he says, relies on miners, processors, manufacturers, automakers, and technology providers all benefiting from growth. That philosophy extends beyond CATL. While acknowledging the geopolitical pressures affecting the industry and growing competition for control of battery supply chains, Zeng says no single country or business can dominate the energy transition alone. Achieving carbon neutrality requires nations and industries to work together, share expertise, and share the value created. Galyen agrees, noting the opportunities for communities and economies. He says global expertise is needed and that the West has much to learn from China in this area. CATL has put those principles into practice through partnerships around the world that allow participants to learn from each other. Innovation drives the next chapter For Zeng, the next phase of the battery industry will be driven by innovation. Since the early 2000s, falling prices and more efficient manufacturing have helped bring batteries and EVs into the mainstream. Zeng notes that long-term growth still depends on the industry’s ability to innovate, develop new technologies, and improve upon existing ones. He describes the battery sector as a “teenager”, with much more room to grow. As demand for electrification continues to rise, innovation across the supply chain remains a key challenge for industry leaders. AI can be a major enabler, Zeng notes, helping researchers identify new materials, accelerate laboratory work, and uncover opportunities for new battery technologies. Zeng believes that lithium-ion batteries will continue to play a dominant role, but sees growing opportunities for alternative chemistries such as sodium-ion, particularly in energy storage and urban transport. The end use will ultimately determine the most suitable chemistry, with producers matching batteries to each application and customer. Battery swapping is another innovation Zeng highlights, allowing users to access different batteries depending on their needs. Looking ahead, both Zeng and Galyen see opportunities in new materials, improved surface chemistry, and innovations such as low-cost graphene. As electrification expands, they expect the industry’s next breakthroughs to emerge through materials research and development, AI, and collaboration across industries and borders. Write to Amy Rotman at Mining.com.au Main image: Mining.com.au

artigo.texto: QuantumScape Unveils Osprey Solid-State Battery Platform, Shares Rebound From 52-Week Low QuantumScape Corp (QS) introduced a new all-solid-state battery platform called Osprey on Nov. 11, saying early testing showed its cells held roughly 80% of their original capacity after 1,000 full charge cycles at just one atmosphere of pressure. The stock rose on the announcement, recovering from a 52-week low. The San Jose, California-based company said the results are the first publicly disclosed data showing a cell with a sulfide-based cathode cycling 1,000 times at that pressure. It published the findings and test conditions in a white paper released alongside the announcement. Osprey builds on QuantumScape's existing QSE architecture, keeping the ceramic separator and anode-free lithium-metal design while adding a solid cathode. The platform is engineered to accommodate a range of cathode chemistries, and the company has tested it with cathodes developed both internally and by its automotive customers. The pressure requirement has been a central obstacle to commercializing sulfide-based solid-state cells. Sulfides can react with lithium metal, which shortens cell life, and cells using them typically must be held under high pressure to operate, a condition that is impractical inside a vehicle. "The industry has invested heavily in sulfide-based batteries but keeps hitting the same fundamental limits. As the data shows, Osprey can address these limitations," said Siva Sivaram, QuantumScape's president and CEO. In early testing, Osprey cells charged from 10% to 80% in five minutes, according to the company, and operated at temperatures below minus 4 degrees Fahrenheit. QuantumScape projects the design could reach a volumetric energy density of about 1,100 watt-hours per liter. The company credits the combination of its ceramic separator and the solid cathode for the faster charging and wider operating temperature range. Note: Figures as reported by QuantumScape from early testing and company projections. The commercial structure may carry the most weight for investors. Osprey is positioned as an open platform that creates licensing and joint development opportunities for existing customers and extends QuantumScape's offering to developers working on sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries. The ability to test customer-supplied cathodes gives partners a way to evaluate their own materials inside QuantumScape's cell design. Cells based on the QSE platform are already shipping to customers. QuantumScape describes Osprey as its longer-term platform for all-solid-state battery development, giving it a starting point for pursuing multiple cell designs as partner work proceeds. "We believe Osprey can unlock the full potential of all-solid-state batteries, and our goal is to make it the leading platform for solid-state battery development," Sivaram said. The announcement lands in a solid-state battery race where automakers and cell makers have poured capital into sulfide electrolytes without yet delivering a commercially viable product. A design that cycles under low pressure, charges quickly and tolerates cold would address several of the barriers that have kept solid-state cells out of mass-market vehicles. For QuantumScape, the open-platform model could broaden its revenue base beyond its own cell manufacturing through licensing and co-development fees, though the disclosed results come from early testing rather than production-ready cells.

artigo.texto: South Korea's Samsung, Hyundai Motor Join Forces on Solid-State Battery Mass-Production Processes, Filing 9 Joint Patents Battery cooperation between Samsung and Hyundai Motor Group is moving beyond supply contracts into joint design and next-generation technology development. After jointly filing patents that simultaneously raise the safety and energy density of electric-vehicle battery packs, the two sides have entered a phase in which they are jointly securing not just materials research but mass-production process technology for next-generation solid-state batteries. According to the Korea Intellectual Property Rights Information Service (KIPRIS), a patent titled "Battery Pack and Vehicle Including the Same," jointly filed by Hyundai Motor, Kia and Samsung SDI, was published on the 22nd of last month. Its core is a gas vent at the bottom of the battery cells and a separate channel at the lower part of the battery pack. The structure vents high-temperature gas generated in a thermal-runaway situation to the outside while merging the previously separate gas-venting space and impact-protection space into one to raise energy density. The patent was designed around Samsung SDI's flagship prismatic battery. Five Hyundai Motor and Kia researchers and two Samsung SDI researchers are named as inventors. The key point is that the two companies' cooperation has expanded beyond simple cell supply to joint design of battery packs tailored to vehicles. Samsung SDI signed its first EV battery supply contract with Hyundai Motor in 2023. Under the terms, Samsung SDI will supply prismatic batteries made at its Hungarian plant for Hyundai Motor and Kia's Europe-bound EVs for seven years from this year through 2032. The number of models actually using them is also growing. Starting with Kia's EV2, the number of vehicles using Samsung SDI batteries has expanded to three models, including Hyundai's Ioniq 3 and Genesis's top-tier electric SUV, the GV90. The move is seen as a result of Hyundai Motor and Kia — which have mainly used pouch-type cells — rating the prismatic battery's energy density and safety highly. Cooperation is also taking concrete shape in next-generation solid-state batteries. Hyundai Motor, Kia and Samsung SDI jointly filed a total of nine solid-state-related patents, including divisional applications, from 2022 through last year, two of which were registered last year. Initially the focus was on coating technology to protect sulfide-based solid electrolytes that are vulnerable to moisture, but from 2023 the research scope widened to battery life improvement and mass-production processes. A representative example is the joint filing of temperature-measurement technology for the high-temperature warm isostatic pressing (WIP) process needed to manufacture solid-state batteries, along with battery-cell preheating and transfer devices. Solid-state batteries replace liquid electrolytes with solid ones to improve safety and energy density, and their applications could expand beyond EVs to humanoid robots and other uses. Euisun Chung, chairman of Hyundai Motor Group, said in August regarding the group's electrification strategy: "EVs will go their own way as EVs, but we are also researching solid-state batteries, so that part has to come out before we can move to a more efficient direction." Note: Publication and registration dates and contract terms are based on the Korea Intellectual Property Rights Information Service and industry confirmation. Executive-level exchanges underpin the broadening of the two groups' cooperation. On the 9th, Samsung Electronics hosted "HMG Appreciation Day" at its Seocheon Training Center in Yongin, Gyeonggi Province, inviting key Hyundai Motor Group executives. Samsung Electronics Vice Chairman Jeon Young-hyun and Hyundai Motor Group Vice Chairman Jang Jae-hoon presided over the event, which was attended by 177 people, including executives, senior managers and spouses from both groups. It was the first time Samsung has held a large-scale invitation event for a specific South Korean group. At the event, Vice Chairman Jang said, "Samsung and Hyundai Motor Group are expanding the possibilities for cooperation beyond vehicle components such as automotive electronics, audio and batteries to future industries such as robots and energy," adding, "I hope we will respect each other's strengths, pool our efforts and take on future challenges together." Vice Chairman Jeon responded, "I hope Samsung's technology, spanning components to finished products, will come together to open up new value and infinite possibilities." The two companies' ties date back to 2020. In May 2020, when Chairman Chung was senior vice chairman, he visited Samsung SDI's Cheonan plant and discussed next-generation EV batteries with Samsung Electronics Chairman Lee Jae-yong, and two months later Lee paid a return visit to Hyundai Motor and Kia's Namyang Research Institute. This exchange is seen as having paved the way for the 2023 supply contract. A relationship that had been kept at arm's length — partly because of Samsung's foray into the auto business in the 1990s — has turned into a cooperative framework under third-generation management. Robots are cited as the next point of contact for cooperation. In February last year, Hyundai Motor, Kia and Samsung SDI signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to jointly develop high-performance batteries dedicated to robots. Under the structure, Samsung SDI handles materials and cell design, while Hyundai Motor and Kia's Robotics Lab applies them to actual robots and verifies performance. Humanoids must deliver large bursts of power while fitting batteries into a narrow body, and because they move in the same spaces as people, safety against impacts and repeated joint movement is also required. The challenge is to simultaneously secure energy density, output, weight, safety and charging speed. Hyundai Motor Group plans to deploy Boston Dynamics' humanoid

artigo.texto: Japan's Elecom Launches Mobile Battery with Gel-Electrolyte Semi-Solid-State Battery, Quadrupling Cycle Life Elecom will release the DE-C102 series of 10,000mAh mobile batteries in mid-November 2026, featuring a "semi-solid-state lithium-ion battery" made with a gelled electrolyte. The units have an integrated cable, are open-priced, and are scheduled to sell for ¥7,480 (approximately $47), tax included, on the company's direct-sale website. Unlike the liquid electrolytes widely used in conventional mobile batteries, the semi-solid-state battery sharply reduces the amount of flammable organic electrolyte used. Even in the event of a short circuit, the design is said to suppress the generation and external release of flammable gases. Improved chemical stability has also extended cycle life fourfold, from about 500 cycles in conventional products to roughly 2,000 cycles in testing. The body features a "Health Monitor" whose LED changes color according to the number of charge and discharge cycles, letting users check battery health and gauge when to replace the unit. It also includes "Thermal Protection," which monitors and controls temperature in real time while powered, and a multi-layer protection circuit that automatically shuts down when an abnormality is detected. Note: Output and operating temperature range are based on the company's published figures. In addition to an integrated cable about 0.1m long, the body has a USB Type-C port and a USB-A port. It supports a pass-through function that prioritizes charging the connected device without routing through the battery, as well as a low-current mode for low-power devices such as wireless earbuds. On the environmental front, the body uses recycled plastic, and the packaging uses paper materials with no plastic. The product is also covered by the collection program of JBRC, a general incorporated association, and can be dropped off at participating collection stores. In the mobile battery market, concern about safety issues such as ignition and swelling is growing. Semi-solid-state batteries are a technology that companies are considering adopting because they can reduce the risk of electrolyte leakage. Elecom is emphasizing long life and safety, positioning the product as one suited to longer replacement cycles. The price is ¥7,480 (approximately $47), tax included, equivalent to about $48 (roughly ¥7,700) for overseas markets. Whether Elecom can capture consumers who prioritize safety and durability will be the focus of future sales.
