artigo.texto: Supported by SpaceX Plans $74 Billion Investment to Build Data Centers in Texas and Arizona Elon Musk’s rocket and artificial intelligence company has spent billions to develop the giant warehouses full of computer servers that power the technology. SpaceX said on Thursday that it planned to invest $74 billion to build new data center campuses in Arizona and Texas as the company continued to pour money into the global artificial intelligence race. The projects, proposed by Elon Musk’s rocket and A.I. company, would be among some of the largest data center projects in the United States. In Texas, SpaceX plans to invest $24 billion in a data center campus on 444 acres of company-owned land near the Starbase rocket site in the Rio Grande Valley. The data center in Texas will generate its own power rather than rely on the public grid, the company said in its announcement. It is not immediately clear whether the project needs any further regulatory approvals. In Arizona, SpaceX plans to build a $50 billion campus in Cochise County, which will create 5,500 construction jobs and 1,000 permanent jobs, the company said. The Arizona project still requires approval from the county. SpaceX, which went public this year in the biggest initial public offering in history, has quickly grown its business leasing out computing power to other A.I. companies like Anthropic and Google. In October, SpaceX reported that its A.I. business accounted for more than half its revenue. Anthropic has committed to paying up to $120.5 billion through 2029. Google is also paying SpaceX $920 million per month for computing power. SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment. SpaceX’s A.I. unit — xAI — has been at the forefront of the data center build out and operates four data centers near Memphis, Tenn., and Southhaven, Miss. Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and other tech giants have spent tens of billions of dollars on their own data center campuses. The build outs have proved costly. SpaceX said in October that capital expenditures had risen to $19.6 billion during the third quarter, nearly three times its spending from the previous year. Mr. Musk said in October that the company had also closed $40 billion in debt financing to help fund the chips needed for its data centers. SpaceX’s chief financial officer, Bret Johnsen, has said the company will continue to spend heavily on its data center build out. In October, he said the company was likely to spend $35 billion to $40 billion in the three months ending in December. I'm a New York Times reporter, covering Elon Musk's companies with a focus on AI and emerging technology from New York. Related Content Advertisement

artigo.texto: Japan's AIST and Partners Develop Robotic System That Automates Synthesis of All-Solid-State Battery Materials, Processing 10 Samples in a Row The research group of Senior Researcher Yuki Yamaguchi at Japan's National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology (AIST), together with Denso Wave (Agui, Aichi Prefecture), Aichi Institute of Technology and the Aichi Center for Industry and Science Technology, has developed a "human-collaborative automated experiment system" that performs mechanochemical synthesis of all-solid-state battery materials as a seamless automated process. The partners announced the system in November 2026. It handles powders sensitive to moisture and oxygen inside a glove box under an inert gas atmosphere and can process up to 10 samples consecutively on a single command. The aim is to reduce reliance on manual work by researchers and boost the efficiency of materials exploration. Mechanochemical reactions are a technique that harnesses the mechanical energy generated when powder is crushed in a ball mill to drive chemical reactions. The series of tasks — weighing raw material powders and grinding beads, packing them into a container and running them through a planetary ball mill — has been replaced by robots. Because the solid electrolytes and electrode materials used in all-solid-state batteries react easily with moisture and oxygen in the air, the entire apparatus is housed in a glove box filled with inert gas. The hard part of automation was handling the powder. Delicate motions such as scooping powder with a spatula are difficult for robots to reproduce. Denso Wave developed an end tool dedicated to powder handling, while Aichi Institute of Technology designed automation modules to handle peripheral tasks such as opening and closing the ball mill containers. The joint research framework combined AIST's expertise in ceramics and battery materials with the Aichi Center for Industry and Science Technology's materials evaluation platform to integrate the component technologies. The system's throughput is 10 samples per command. The planetary ball mill handles two samples per run, and the design executes this five times in succession. From transporting reagent storage containers and ball mill containers to the grinding process and subsequent sample storage, the system performs the work automatically without interruption. Conditions such as reagent quantities, bead type and amount, mill rotation speed and processing time can be changed for each sample, allowing systematic investigation of diverse combinations. Reproducibility of experimental know-how is another feature. The system can automatically reproduce tacit knowledge such as how to select reagents and beads, weighing procedures and the order of operations, while also managing experiment parameters centrally as digital data. Such data can be used as explanatory variables for materials informatics (MI) and process informatics (PI), paving the way for AI-driven condition optimization. Note: Compiled based on the announcement. All-solid-state batteries are next-generation storage batteries expected to offer high safety and energy density, but developing the solid electrolytes and electrode materials that determine performance requires comprehensively investigating a wide range of compositions and processing conditions. Conventionally, researchers have repeated experiments by hand, which has been one factor holding down development efficiency. In 2023, AIST also used an automated powder-weighing device and a collaborative robot to speed up the search for conditions in a chemical sintering process that proceeds at 100°C or below; the latest work extends that technology to mechanochemical synthesis and all-solid-state battery materials. The research group plans to broaden the target materials and experimental processes and to refine the system so it can be applied to ceramics materials development in general. From fiscal 2029 onward, the partners are considering installing it as an experimental facility available for shared use, as part of a materials evaluation and development platform that regional companies can access. All-solid-state batteries are a field where major automakers and battery manufacturers in Japan and abroad are competing to achieve mass production, and the speed of materials development affects competitiveness. This initiative, combining experiment automation with data accumulation, offers materials exploration sites — where it is hard to rack up trial runs — the option of continuous, hands-free experimentation. Bridging to mass-production processes is essential for practical application, and attention will focus on whether making the equipment more versatile and opening it to regional companies can raise the level of Japan-originated materials development infrastructure.

artigo.texto: The data center industry is awaiting the commercialization of solid-state transformer technology, which skips power conversion steps and limits energy loss. The tech is already in use in electric vehicle charging and is about a year away from commercialization for data centers, where the voltages in question are much higher and the demand variances are swingier. According to Jeffries, the U.S. market for solid-state transformers will be about $4.3 billion per year by 2030 and would eliminate $1.39 million in costs per megawatt for data centers, which adds up for data centers that may be over 1,000 megawatts. Though many existing data centers are under construction already without the tech, the companies working on solid-state transformers believe that given that savings — and the chance to free up space for more processing — they’ll be able to plug in nicely into existing builds.

artigo.texto: Mark Trahant Substack Congress may soon make it harder for communities to have that better conversation about data centers, or for that matter, energy projects. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will probably make it to the floor for a vote next week after getting enough votes to get past any filibuster. The basic idea of the legislation is that it takes too long and their are too many rules to get projects constructed. One of the champions of the legislation is the Bipartisan Policy Center: “For decades, reform has been on the agenda, and there is widespread recognition that a permitting system created to protect the environment against industrial pollution more than 50 years ago has morphed into a system that is bad for both the economy and the environment. Reviews that once were completed in weeks or months now take years or decades. And delays on heavily polluting projects now also hold up and block clean energy technologies and conservation projects. But even with this new understanding, reforms have proven controversial and a bipartisan deal has been elusive.” This legislation is supposed to be that compromise. But the cost to the environment, to tribal sovereignty, and to community engagement is high. Earth Justice makes the case that Congress should start over after the new year. “The Trump administration’s playbook is to move fast and break things. This version of BAAJA would still turbocharge that playbook. It would enable presidents to rush through deeply harmful projects, and it would constrain future presidents from repairing the damage. It also fails to provide fixes that fully honor Tribal sovereignty and restore basic protections for water, wetlands, and species. “The Senate is expected to vote on BAAJA very soon. Earthjustice is urging senators to shelve this version, then come back in the new year and give these reforms the full attention they require.” The legislation is being rushed — not unlike the pace of construction of data centers. Instead of a new law that makes it easier and quicker to build data centers, we need a collective moment to pause and think. (Indeed in a weird twist, this legislation may lead more communities to turn down projects because the standardized template won’t work on a local level.) It’s the perfect metaphor. Rush a bill for an industry in a rush. Read the room The law firm Foley & Lardner outlined a few of the challenges in a memo: “One of the clearest signals from the election results is that data centers have become a political issue, including in markets that have historically welcomed large-scale infrastructure investment. “That shift could translate into greater scrutiny of proposed projects and, in some markets, slower development. “Developers should increasingly expect communities and regulators to look closely at how a project will affect local resources and residents. Concerns surrounding electricity costs, access to power, water consumption, and broader community impacts are likely to remain important considerations as projects move through the development and permitting process. “Against that backdrop, projects that enter the process with strong community support, secured power, and demonstrable economic benefits will be better positioned to advance. “The result may not be an end to development, but a higher bar for getting projects approved and built.” These are the very challenges that are opposite world from The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. A reader of this newsletter pointed out in comments that tribes and communities can respond by enacting ordinance before the new permitting law goes into force. Marc from The Steward’s Walk: “The bill’s trade of full cost for less local control swaps a veto for a payment. A county that loses the power to stop a project keeps only what its own code already prices. Should tribal nations write data center ordinances before the bill reaches the House?” “Great points. I think the earlier the better for code ordinances. Tribes are still hoping to kill the permitting bill. (Run out the clock strategy)” Marc from The Steward’s Walk: “An ordinance written now holds whether the clock runs out on the bill or not, so the code work is the one step that pays under both outcomes. Thank you for the answer.” This is an important point. What gives the industry so much leeway is that tribes, states and local jurisdictions are using zoning rules that work better for an industry of the past. (Another advantage tribes have no matter what happens with the legislation is that most land deals would be a long term leases rather than private property, so specific “asks” that would not be allowed under the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would be requirements in the lease not regulation.) Data centers need to have different rules and taxing structures designed for this era. What about corruption? One way the the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act fails to read the results from the last election is a rush to develop without new safeguards to prevent public corruption. Earth Justice lists a “fatal flaw” in the legislation this way: “Section 1401 of the bill would still give the Trump administration very broad authority to fast-track projects of all kinds (not just clean energy projects). And, it would still constrain future administrations from reconsidering them — even if they were granted illegally.” So a public official, from the president on down the line, can invest in a specific industry or company and yet have the broad power to approve a deal without any recourse later. Makes no sense. And it’s not theoretical. “Officials across the Trump administration also stand to profit from the White House’s support for AI and data centers. For example, 380 of President Donald Trump’s political appointees or their spouses hold stocks or have other financial connections to Nvidia, which has become the world’s most valuable company thanks to the data center boom

artigo.texto: Mini data centers – O Governo Federal vai investir R$ 46,3 milhões no desenvolvimento de uma tecnologia nacional para tornar data centers mais eficientes, seguros e sustentáveis. Aprovado pelo Conselho Gestor do Fundo para o Desenvolvimento Tecnológico das Telecomunicações (Funttel), o projeto prevê uma plataforma inteligente para gerenciar e distribuir dados entre diferentes estruturas, incluindo mini data centers em várias regiões do país. Batizada de Prisma, a iniciativa utilizará inteligência artificial (IA) para definir onde as informações devem ser processadas e distribuir os recursos computacionais conforme a demanda. A tecnologia busca reduzir gastos com energia, custos operacionais e tempo de resposta dos sistemas, além de reforçar a proteção de dados estratégicos. LEIA: Inteligência artificial facilita invasões e aumenta alcance de hackers “Investir em tecnologia nacional é garantir que o Brasil tenha mais autonomia para proteger suas informações e desenvolver soluções para os desafios do futuro. Com o apoio do Funttel, estamos fortalecendo a inovação brasileira e criando condições para uma infraestrutura digital mais moderna, segura e sustentável, reduzindo nossa dependência de tecnologias desenvolvidas no exterior”, afirma o ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho. Os recursos serão administrados pela Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (Finep), enquanto o desenvolvimento ficará sob responsabilidade do Centro Brasileiro de Inovação em Tecnologias da Informação e da Comunicação (CPQD), em Campinas (SP). A expansão dos mini data centers permitirá processar informações mais perto de onde são geradas e utilizadas, beneficiando setores como saúde, defesa, segurança pública, educação e telecomunicações. Eficiência energética e autonomia tecnológica O projeto também pretende diminuir o impacto ambiental dos data centers, que demandam grandes quantidades de energia para processamento e refrigeração. Entre os resultados esperados estão a redução das emissões de carbono, maior resistência a falhas no fornecimento elétrico e proteção contra ataques cibernéticos. A plataforma deverá incluir sistemas de armazenamento de energia e mecanismos de governança de informações críticas, seguindo padrões internacionais de segurança e as diretrizes da Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD). artigo.texto: Swiss battery developer Unbound Potential has begun installing its first external pilot system at Gesundheitspark Thalwil, near Zürich. The stationary battery uses the company’s membrane-free redox flow technology and will store surplus electricity generated by the health and sports centre’s photovoltaic installation. Stored energy will be released when required. The installation follows almost four years of research and development and represents the technology’s first deployment outside Unbound Potential’s own test environment. The company said operating the system under real-world conditions would provide data on its performance and reliability as it works towards commercialisation. Unbound Potential: a simpler cell design by eliminating the membrane The company claims that eliminating the membrane used in conventional redox flow batteries enables a simpler cell design, with the potential to reduce manufacturing costs and resource consumption. The company is targeting stationary, long-duration applications, including renewable-energy integration and grid support. The pilot is being supported by the Municipality of Thalwil through its Climate Funding Programme. Gesundheitspark Thalwil, which operates what Unbound Potential described as the municipality’s largest photovoltaic system, is providing the host site. Dr David Taylor, CEO and co-founder of Unbound Potential, said: “Having our first pilot battery go into operation here in Thalwil, where everything started, means a great deal to us. “After almost four years of development, our technology is being deployed for the first time at an external partner. It is a big moment for our entire team.” The system had arrived at the site and was being installed and prepared for commissioning when the announcement was made. The company did not disclose its rated power, energy capacity, intended storage duration or commissioning date. Unbound Potential was founded in January 2023 and employs 28 people. It said it had raised more than CHF14 million ($17.5 million) in investment and grant funding from backers including the Migros Pioneer Fund, Germany’s Federal Agency for Disruptive Innovation, SPRIND, and the Swiss Innovation Agency, Innosuisse. Photo: Unbound Potential’s first membrane-free redox flow battery pilot is being installed at Gesundheitspark Thalwil in Switzerland, where it will store surplus electricity from the site’s solar array. Credit: Unbound Potential

artigo.texto: Microsoft data center in Washington state brings "a kind of boom" despite growing AI pushback Opposition to data centers helped propel Democratic candidates who pledged to stall new construction to victory in last week's midterm elections. More than half of voters said artificial intelligence and data centers were a significant factor in their votes, according to a CBS News exit poll. But one town says it has benefited from data centers, despite the pushback growing across the nation. For 20 years, Microsoft has operated its Columbia Data Center in Quincy, Washington, where Mayor Paul Worley told CBS News its presence has created "a kind of boom" for the area. Additional tax revenue from the project has funded a new high school and hospital, and helped improve other critical services, he said. Microsoft president Brad Smith told CBS News about the pledge it makes to the communities where it builds and operates data centers. "Basically, we will put the community first," he said. "We will not do anything that will increase the electricity rates of our neighbors. We'll ensure that we replenish more water, we put more water back into the community than we use." He also highlighted the role data centers play in powering every action we take on our phones and other connected devices. "Every time we tap on our phone, it's connecting through an app, it's pulling data from something like this," he said. The industry, he said, needs to better inform opponents of data centers about the essential services the facilities enable. "They're part of daily life, just like electricity is," Smith said. Why Quincy? The nearby Columbia River provides hydropower that has led seven additional companies to choose Quincy for their data centers. It hasn't been entirely smooth. To accommodate the roughly two dozen data centers that have entered the area over the past two decades, some residents have been asked to vacate their homes. Electricity rates per kilowatt-hour have risen by roughly 55% over the past 20 years, according to the Grant County public utility. While that marks a steep increase, it's still lower than the average increases in national and state electricity rates over the same period. In Washington, electricity rates rose 107% over the same time period. Nationwide, they rose 66%. Smith said he believes it is the company's "fundamental responsibility" to manage the industry's growth and the impact on residents' rising utility costs. "You can't make the challenges go away, but you can be broad-minded, you can [be] committed, and you can take steps to manage growth well," he said. For example, Microsoft pledges to replenish or give communities back more water than it uses. It also commits to paying for its own electricity and ensuring that its usage doesn't increase neighbors' utility rates, Smith said. He added that the facilities create local jobs, too, though many are temporary construction positions. According to Microsoft, the company employs roughly 700 people, or almost 9% of Quincy's roughly 8,000 residents. Questions to ask Yale professor of environmental and energy economics Kenneth Gillingham outlined the questions communities should ask data center developers before they come to town. They include: - What type of technology is it using for cooling? - How large will it be? - How is it going to generate its electricity? Meanwhile, Microsoft's Smith has a clear message for Americans who say they don't want data centers in their backyards. "Give us a chance to talk through what we want to do, and give us a chance to prove that we can do this in a way that will put the community first," he said. "We have to persuade you. But the people that you've elected, they're the ones who are gonna make a decision, not us."

artigo.texto: A German university has introduced a solar carport equipped with 237 kilowatts-peak (kWp) of photovoltaic capacity and a 200-kilowatt-hour (kWh) sodium-ion battery for excess energy storage. Located at the Diepholz campus of the Private University of Applied Sciences for Business and Technology (PHWT), the new installation was officially inaugurated on November 9. It has a total of 90 covered spaces and a battery system that uses sodium instead of lithium. The structure is home to the first sodium-ion battery storage system in the state of Lower Saxony, and the third in the country. It will reportedly allow the campus to store electricity for later use, especially during periods of high demand. PHWT representatives highlighted the facility’s most striking feature. “The existing parking lot is arranged in a semicircle with two rows of parking spaces,” they said. “The aim was to incorporate this unusual geometry into the roof design.” A massive solar twist To bring the unusual design to life, solar energy company PfefferKnecht came up with a custom metal structure that follows the parking area’s curved layout. Local engineering firm and longstanding university partner, Böckmann Maschinenbau, then erected the structure. According to PHWT, the carport’s roof covers roughly 12,378 square feet (1,150 square meters) and incorporates glass-glass photovoltaic modules. These panels provide around 230 kWp of installed solar capacity. More from Energy See All An additional bicycle shelter contributes another 7.3 kWp. The bicycle facility can accommodate 20 bikes. “A patented feature of the structure is that the individual photovoltaic modules also serve as a seamless, waterproof roof covering,” PHWT said. “This eliminates the need for an additional roofing membrane underneath.” The construction is also complemented by integrated LED lighting for the parking spaces. Moreover, the energy storage system consists of two sodium-ion battery cabinets supplied by Swiss green energy company Phenogy. Together, they offer 200 kWh of storage capacity and a charging and discharging power of 100 kW. The sodium-ion technology relies on widely available sodium-based materials and does not require lithium, graphite or cobalt. This makes the batteries less flammable and resistant to high and low temperatures. Completed in record time The system is expected to help the university become more energy independent and rely less on grid electricity. According to PHWT, stored electricity can cover peak demand periods, and potentially reduce energy costs. While the project’s development took nearly 18 months, the actual construction was completed within a 10-week window during the semester break. The effort was initiated by Dennis De, PhD, PHWT President Professor, and Andreas Knecht, PfefferKnecht’s Managing Director. PfefferKnecht planned and implemented the solar structures under its Lichtkraft brand. The entire construction process involved laying the foundations, erecting the steel frame, installing solar panels, and setting up the electrical systems. The new solar carport site complements an existing sustainable energy concept at the Diepholz campus,” PHWT officials said in a press statement. “The campus already uses an ice-based thermal energy storage system for heating and cooling.” PHWT hopes to become a leader in sustainable energy solutions beyond Lower Saxony. “The facility also highlights how innovation, sustainability, and industry collaboration can work together,” PHWT concluded.

artigo.texto: Riverside Council Enshrines Temporary Data Center Ban Language While City Researches AI The Riverside City Council Tuesday voted 5-2 to adopt a resolution barring the city from accepting data center proposals, since the land use is not currently included in city code. Riverside has joined a number of other cities in the county in temporarily banning data centers, though the council took a much different approach than its neighbors. The Riverside City Council Tuesday voted 5-2 to adopt a resolution barring the city from accepting data center proposals, since the land use is not currently included in city code, while a council-led committee researches artificial intelligence (AI) policies, foregoing a second option to impose a 45-day temporary moratorium. “We need to pause the moving forward of development so [we] can figure out, and do that deep dive, and do that research, and set those regulations, and set those parameters,” Councilmember Philip Falcone said at the November 10 council meeting. “To not do them in tandem is disjoint and, I think, not strategic.” Councilmembers Chuck Conder and Sean Mill voted against the resolution — although Mill, in a phone call with The Riverside Record, said he chose to vote against the resolution because he preferred establishing a temporary ban like other cities across the county have done. The council’s decision to move forward with the resolution followed a now-updated agreement between the city of Riverside and a nonprofit organization that previously mentioned a possible data center as part of its proposal. The agreement originally said the nonprofit, and its for-profit counterpart, would “contemplate” the development of a data center after establishing an office in the city. The CEO for both organizations previously told the city’s Economic Development Committee the idea was to create a data center meant for community use — which would have been contained within a typical office server room — to help with training residents on emerging technologies. Falcone, who championed efforts to restrict data centers within city limits, said at the September 14 Land Use Committee meeting that the agreement pushed him to request that staff bring forward a temporary data center ban to the council for discussion. He said he felt a ban would preserve commercial land for sectors he believed would bring more jobs, prevent an electrical grid overload and protect the city’s water supply. The following day, the council voted to create a 13-month AI working group tasked with developing a “forward-looking” strategy to address AI’s rapid growth and outline how the city should utilize the technology in the future. Councilmember Steven Robillard, who is leading the working group, said the group plans to tackle data center policies in the coming months. That decision led city staff to return to the Land Use Committee in October to ask for clarification on how to proceed with the dueling requests. After a discussion, the committee directed staff to bring forward two options: establish an urgency ordinance to impose a temporary 45-day moratorium on the approval of any data center developments that could be extended for up to two years total or adopt language that highlights the city is technically prohibited from accepting data center proposals at this time due to current city code. “There [are] no proposals on the table right now,” Robillard said at the November 10 meeting. “I think the resolution sends the proper message that we currently don’t have a zoning that allows for data centers, we need to discuss the entire conversation in-and-around AI, and its related uses including data centers, and, until we do that, approving the data center doesn’t make any sense.” During public comment, residents and environmental advocates said they supported placing restrictions on data center development due to their concerns with potential long-term negative impacts on the community. However, several union representatives said they were opposed to a ban, citing recently signed California laws placing restrictions on the facilities and concerns that any prohibitions would eliminate job opportunities for union members. “If we utilize the latest technologies like closed loop systems for cooling and a clean energy infrastructure, they could be successful,” Anthony Zambrano, an International Union of Operating Engineers Local 12 representative, said. “In my opinion, no one builds these systems better than union labor.” Conder, throughout his reelection campaign, said he was a proponent of data centers. At a community forum held last month, Conder said he believed the technology has been rapidly improving and could be built to minimize harm to both communities and the environment. “Not all data centers are a million square feet,” Conder said at the November 10 meeting. “They can be as small as a medium-sized box truck that delivers in town here.” He also said, both at the November 10 council meeting and in statements throughout his campaign, that he believed much of the opposition to data centers was funded by foreign governments that prefer to have the facilities built in their countries. An investigation into the claim by NPR found little evidence of a coordinated Chinese campaign to stop data centers in the U.S. The next AI ad hoc committee meeting is scheduled for December 3. The group will continue to meet over the next year to discuss AI-related topics, including data centers, and is set to present a list of policy recommendations for the full council to review later next year. artigo.texto: Indonesia and Norway have entered into a Mitigation Outcome Purchase Agreement (MOPA) at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye. The agreement, facilitated by the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI), marks Indonesia’s first MOPA designed to operationalise Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement. It is backed by the Norwegian Article 6 Climate Action (NACA) Fund under GGGI’s Carbon Transaction Facility. Discover B2B Marketing That Performs Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms. According to the parties involved, the deal is expected to count among the largest carbon market transactions yet conducted under the Paris Agreement’s cooperative framework. The signing ceremony took place at the Indonesia Pavilion during COP31. It was witnessed by Indonesia’s Minister of Environment and Head of the Environmental Protection Agency Moh Jumhur Hidayat, and Norway’s Climate and Environment Minister Sigrun Aasland. Following this agreement, GGGI is set to collaborate with the Indonesian government, the state electricity company PT PLN (Persero), and the Norwegian Ministry of Climate and Environment to establish the arrangements necessary to implement the deal. Hidayat said: “Through this cooperation, we seek to mobilise carbon finance to support Indonesia’s energy transition and contribute to the achievement of our national climate targets. “This cooperation will also support efforts to strengthen Indonesia’s SRUK (Carbon Unit Registry System) and ensure transparent recording and tracking of international transfers. “Our priority is to ensure that this cooperation delivers credible mitigation outcomes, upholds environmental integrity, and is implemented in line with Indonesia’s national climate commitments.” The MOPA will support the Generation-Based Incentive (GBI) Program in Indonesia, a results-based crediting mechanism built to encourage investment in additional clean, grid-connected electricity. The GBI Program is applicable to a range of renewable energy technologies, with an initial emphasis on floating solar photovoltaic projects, reflecting Indonesia’s current priorities. The mechanism is designed to offer additional incentives to power producers when existing pricing does not cover the costs for eligible projects. It also focuses on encouraging projects paired with battery energy storage systems to deliver renewable electricity during periods of high emissions. Participation in the GBI Program is voluntary, with eligible Independent Power Producers able to apply if they fulfil specific financial, technical, and regional criteria. All projects must also demonstrate additionality, measurable emission reductions, and sustainable development impacts. A digital monitoring, reporting, and verification system underpins the programme, providing data that is subject to independent audit before carbon payments are issued based on performance. Emissions reductions achieved through the programme are aggregated and authorised to be traded as Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes. This is done in cooperation with the Norwegian Ministry of Environment, within the framework of the Norwegian Global Emissions Reduction initiative. The agreement aims to address financial, regulatory, and grid-related challenges that have hindered Indonesia’s renewable energy uptake and highlights a strategy to enhance grid stability and accelerate a shift towards a low-carbon power sector.

artigo.texto: Expansão em Belo Jardim elevará a capacidade de fornecimento de sistemas de armazenamento de energia para mais de 8 GWh por ano. Empresa atua em parceria com a chinesa CATL e mira o primeiro leilão nacional de baterias. A expansão do mercado de armazenamento de energia no Brasil abriu uma nova oportunidade para a indústria nordestina. O Grupo Moura anunciou um investimento estimado em R$ 200 milhões para ampliar sua estrutura de fabricação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, conhecidos como BESS, em Belo Jardim, no Agreste de Pernambuco. Com a ampliação, a companhia pretende alcançar uma capacidade de fornecimento superior a 8 GWh por ano. O projeto combina tecnologia da chinesa CATL com montagem, integração e atividades industriais realizadas no Brasil. A princípio, a iniciativa ocorre às vésperas dos primeiros leilões brasileiros destinados à contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias, previstos para os dias 2 e 4 de dezembro de 2026. Belo Jardim entra na disputa por um novo mercado de energia O investimento amplia a atuação de uma empresa que já possui uma trajetória de quase sete décadas na fabricação de baterias. Fundada em 1957, em Belo Jardim, a Moura construiu no município um complexo industrial que atende diferentes segmentos, incluindo os mercados automotivo, industrial e de armazenamento de energia. Segundo informações da companhia, a expansão de aproximadamente R$ 200 milhões reúne investimentos recentes e um novo ciclo de modernização da estrutura produtiva. Além disso, a empresa já possui experiência em mais de 40 projetos de armazenamento instalados no Brasil, com aplicações em setores como indústria, agronegócio, saúde, saneamento e entretenimento. Parceria com empresa chinesa combina tecnologia e produção local A Moura atua ao lado da CATL, fabricante chinesa de baterias e sistemas de armazenamento de energia. A parceria entre as empresas começou em 2020, inicialmente com serviços de assistência técnica, manutenção e pós-venda de baterias de lítio. Agora, a cooperação também envolve o fornecimento de sistemas para os projetos que disputarão o leilão brasileiro. Nesse modelo, a CATL participa com sua tecnologia e experiência internacional, enquanto a Moura assume a industrialização e a integração dos equipamentos em Pernambuco. A estratégia busca atender às exigências de conteúdo nacional previstas para uma das modalidades do certame. Conteúdo nacional pode chegar a 60% Um dos diferenciais do projeto é a tentativa de ampliar a participação da indústria brasileira na cadeia de armazenamento de energia. De acordo com o diretor de operações de lítio do Grupo Moura, Spartacus Pedrosa, a empresa trabalha com uma rota de montagem e integração que pode atingir entre 50% e 60% de conteúdo local, conforme os critérios de nacionalização. Entretanto, a estratégia também pode facilitar o acesso dos equipamentos às linhas de financiamento do BNDES, desde que cumpram os requisitos de credenciamento. Primeiro leilão brasileiro de baterias acontece em dezembro A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica aprovou os editais dos dois primeiros leilões de reserva de capacidade voltados a sistemas de armazenamento em baterias. O primeiro certame, em 2 de dezembro, será destinado a projetos que atendam às exigências de conteúdo nacional. Já o segundo, previsto para 4 de dezembro, terá regras diferentes de nacionalização. Os contratos terão duração de 15 anos, com início do fornecimento previsto para agosto de 2028. Os sistemas deverão disponibilizar potência por até quatro horas em cada ciclo, podendo ser acionados até duas vezes por dia. Dessa forma, as baterias poderão armazenar energia e devolvê-la ao sistema elétrico nos momentos de maior necessidade. Mercado desperta interesse de empresas A dimensão da oportunidade aparece no cadastramento realizado pela Empresa de Pesquisa Energética. Em agosto de 2026, a instituição informou que recebeu 6.091 projetos para os leilões, somando 296.807 MW de potência. Além disso, o volume demonstra o interesse do mercado por soluções de armazenamento, embora nem todos os projetos inscritos necessariamente participem ou vençam os certames. LEIA TAMBÉM: - Frutas, mel e celulose do Nordeste ganham o mercado da Europa - Estudo revela a situação das rodovias no Nordeste; veja como está por estado - Starbucks anuncia três lojas em Fortaleza e volta expansão no Nordeste - Nordeste ganha loja de gigante com 4 mil lojas pelo mundo; confira onde Investimento amplia importância industrial de Pernambuco Portanto, a ampliação da fábrica reforça a presença de Pernambuco em uma cadeia produtiva relacionada à transição energética. Além da produção de baterias, Belo Jardim concentra atividades de montagem, tecnologia e reciclagem. Em 2025, o Governo de Pernambuco informou que o Grupo Moura contava com 4.114 colaboradores no estado. Afinal, o novo investimento pode ampliar a demanda por profissionais especializados, fornecedores industriais e serviços técnicos. Entretanto, a empresa ainda não divulgou o número de empregos adicionais que pretende gerar com a expansão. Com a entrada em um mercado de maior escala, Belo Jardim passa a disputar espaço em uma atividade estratégica para a modernização do setor elétrico brasileiro. O desafio agora será transformar a capacidade industrial anunciada em contratos efetivos, produção local e novas oportunidades econômicas para o Agreste pernambucano.

artigo.texto: Irondale considers new regulations for data centers Irondale city officials are preparing to discuss proposed regulations for data centers during a public hearing at Irondale City Hall on Tuesday, Nov. 17, at 6 p.m. Mayor James D. Stewart Jr. said the regulations aim to address common concerns raised by the community. "Our regulations, I would say, address the main things that people want to discuss all the time," Stewart said. The proposed ordinance includes measures to limit water usage, require companies to provide their own power and restrict noise pollution. Generators would only be allowed to operate between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., with noise levels capped at 50 decibels during the day and 45 decibels at night—even during emergencies. "If you need an example, that's you and I having a conversation. That's how loud that is," Stewart said. Additionally, companies would be required to enter into a community benefit agreement, outlining how their operations would positively impact Irondale. "That spells out how those data centers would benefit the city of Irondale, and what some of the things are that they are required to be able to do to make sure that the community receives goodwill and that they are good corporate citizens during that time," Stewart said. Stewart noted that no companies have approached Irondale about building a data center, but emphasized the importance of having regulations in place beforehand. "We feel that it is the proactive measure to be able to do this. Also, our community is more protected when we have something in place than when we don't," he said. The Jefferson County Mayor's Association is also working on similar legislation to create uniform rules across all 36 municipalities in the region, Stewart said. "When people look to come to our region, they will see that we're unified. We have one agreement and hopefully the strengths in numbers will help to determine if they really want to be in the Dale or in Center Point or Birmingham and we're not competing against each other," Stewart said. Transparency has been a concern for several data center projects in the area, and the ordinance addresses this by classifying data centers as conditional use developments. This means any potential project would require city council approval and a public hearing before moving forward. The Irondale City Council will vote on the ordinance following Tuesday's public hearing.

artigo.texto: A homeowner in the United Kingdom considering spending an extra £2,000 ($2,670) on home battery storage received an unexpected recommendation from their solar installer: buy less capacity. In the installer's view, another battery module would probably cost more than the homeowner would save by avoiding occasional peak-rate electricity purchases. Here's what to know On Reddit, they wrote that they had been considering 15 kWh or 20 kWh as backup capacity given their daily winter consumption of about 14 kWh. However, their solar installer recommended only going with a 10 kWh capacity. "His advice is the cost to buy that little bit extra from grid is probably cheaper than adding another battery," the original poster wrote. "The extra cost might not make sense for ROI/savings." In addition to asking whether Redditors agreed with the solar installer's advice, the OP also wondered how easy it would be to add extra battery capacity down the line. For homeowners considering making the move to battery backup, EnergySage makes it easy to explore battery products and compare competitive installation estimates. EnergySage has partnered with electrification company Qmerit to help homeowners secure the best available battery-storage pricing. What commenters said When it came to the question of capacity, opinions were divided, though some acknowledged that it ultimately came down to what the OP's goals were. For one commenter, 10 kWh was too little capacity for their own goal of powering the entire house during an outage. While a suitably configured battery can keep household essentials running during outages, when paired with solar panels, it can also offer even greater energy independence, including off-grid use with certain systems. For the original poster, however, the priority was not whole-home backup but saving money on their electricity bill. By charging their home battery when rates were cheapest and using that electricity to power their home when rates were high, the OP hoped to limit the impact of soaring energy prices. Not all household electricity use has to be supplied by storage, another commenter explained. Solar generation consumed immediately and grid electricity used during cheap-rate periods both reduce the amount of energy that needs to pass through the battery. For households seeking a smaller backup option, Pila offers a plug-and-play alternative at a substantially lower price point than whole-home backup systems. Other considerations A 10 kWh starting point seemed more reasonable to the homeowner after a commenter raised the panels' potential contribution. Confirming that solar was part of the installation, the OP noted that even 1 to 2 kWh of winter generation could help offset consumption on heavier-use days. For charging and discharging power, commenters advised checking the battery stack's own specifications rather than relying on the inverter's rating. That distinction is particularly important when running several appliances. In one commenter's hypothetical example, an 8 kW inverter would still have only 5 kW available from a pair of battery modules delivering 2.5 kW each. As for the OP's question regarding battery expansion at a later date, one commenter noted that, for their setup, space for new modules had been an issue. Ultimately, that commenter had to have an inverter moved because it blocked the battery additions. The upgrade also required firmware updates, and the commenter recommended checking the manufacturer's commissioning and warranty requirements. Where can I learn more? Other U.K. homeowners have also been comparing the cost of battery storage with the savings it could deliver. • A U.K. homeowner sought retrofit battery storage after an installer said batteries weren't worthwhile. • A U.K. homeowner exploring battery-only storage to avoid peak electricity rates received a G98/G99 warning. • After solar was ruled out, a U.K. homeowner considered battery-only storage for savings. • A U.K. homeowner's 10-kWh battery payback estimate stretched from three years to five. • A U.K. homeowner's £6,999 battery quote drew scrutiny over £3,000 in installation costs. artigo.texto: Em 9 de novembro de 2026, sete dos nove prédios do campus norte do complexo da AWS perto de New Carlisle, em Indiana, estavam concluídos e operacionais. As obras continuavam em outras partes do projeto. Segundo a reportagem do South Bend Tribune, os prédios em operação já desenvolviam, treinavam e executavam modelos de IA para a Anthropic, parceira da AWS. O que operava e o que ainda estava previsto Naquele período, a AWS previa colocar os outros dois prédios do campus norte em operação no primeiro semestre de 2027. No campus sul, a previsão era que oito dos nove prédios entrassem em operação nas semanas seguintes à reportagem; o último tinha como meta o início de 2027. O terceiro local, chamado SBN 210, ainda não havia entrado em obras. Bill Schalliol, diretor de desenvolvimento econômico do condado de St. Joseph, disse que o clima de inverno poderia adiar trabalhos substanciais até a primavera. Para acompanhar o avanço do complexo, vale separar as fases: operação no campus norte, metas de entrada em operação no sul e SBN 210 ainda sem obras naquele momento. O plano do terreno ainda podia mudar O projeto previa 32 prédios distribuídos por três locais, mas o número final ainda estava em planejamento. Schalliol disse que mudanças no desenho poderiam resultar em prédios maiores e em uma quantidade menor deles. A AWS planejava retirar 4,82 acres de áreas úmidas existentes, cerca de 1,95 hectare, e criar 10,2 acres, aproximadamente 4,13 hectares, para compensar a intervenção. Bijay Niraula, representante da AWS, apresentou o plano a um conselho de recursos hídricos do condado em 22 de outubro de 2026. Empregos e expectativa para as obras A reportagem atribuiu a Andre Woodson, gerente de políticas e relações externas da Amazon, a informação de que a AWS havia contratado mais de mil funcionários permanentes. Separadamente, Bill Schalliol havia informado que, em maio, o total passava de 900 e que 80% eram moradores de Indiana. Na cobertura de novembro de 2026, autoridades do condado estimavam que a construção ainda levaria de dois a três anos.

artigo.texto: Mark Trahant Substack There’s a story about Napoleon Bonaparte I have always liked. Something along the lines of “I know he’s a good general, but is he lucky.” Lucky. So often in my career I have been in the exact right place at the right time, being at places where I didn’t plan. Lucky. Last week I was honored with a Rural Power award by Groundswell and its Rural Renaissance Roadshow. Kenrick J. Escalanti, Quechan, nominated me for this honor to “recognize individuals whose leadership, ideas, storytelling, and service are helping shape a stronger and more equitable future for rural communities.” Instead of a mail-order plaque, the group gifted me a unique embroidered jean jacket to wear proclaiming “Rural Power.” Way cool. Here’s the lucky part. I have been thinking a lot about the debate going on in tribal and rural communities about data centers. It’s absolutely fine for tribes to pause or just say no. But could there also be a deeper conversation, what do we need when it comes to data storage, AI, and a digital future? Where is the richer conversation? Turns out that was the theme of the conference: “At the Data Center Crossroads.” The awards’ panel was first evening of the conference; a start of the conversation. And one of the first questions from the audience asked where I stood on data centers. I jumped right into the deep end. Two things. First, we need a better conversation about data centers and where they should be located. And, second, no elected official should ever sign a Non Disclosure Agreement. I think that runs counter to the public good. Transparency is an important value and the lack of it is exactly why we are having a terrible conversation about what’s needed and why. Data Centers at scale “What is a data center and what do people know?” asks Sherry Stout, program manager for the National Laboratory of the Rockies. She works with state and tribal governments. “So first and foremost, 38% of people statistically in this room, you live within five miles of a data center and you just might not know it,” she says. “If you ask what national polls say 35% of people would say that they have heard —quote — a lot about data centers in this past year. And why is that? … there’s 632 local governments have taken up the issue of data centers this year alone. It’s these very conversations that are so twisted. Data centers are pitched as inevitable on private and public land and many of the people involved won’t answer questions because they’ve signed those NDAs. Sherry Stout: “People are encountering news stories. They’re encountering political processes. They’re encountering social media that’s all about data centers. We’re seeing states that have paused large scale data centers and we’re seeing moratorium that are placed to say we need to pause and figure out what are these things? How are they affecting us and how do we need to go forward? There’s also, let’s just talk about the reality. There are a few very visible, very poorly done examples of data centers and those are going to drive conversations like it or not. NDAs are becoming a greater and greater issue. I spent a lot of last week with some of the hyperscalers talking about the issue of NDAs and it used to be in business that NDAs would actually speed things along because you would have some of that non-compete. But now the second a community finds out that their council has an NDA with a hyperscaler, that has changed the conversation and transparency is really changing. How we think about data transparency and what’s going on is really changing. Then there’s also just some of the reality of there’s a huge worldwide debate right now on the future of artificial intelligence or super intelligence if you work in the federal world. Data centers often can be the face, the physical manifestation of that conversation.” Billions, not millions Pearl Eva Walker is a member of the Memphis City Council where a huge generative A-I data center, Colossus, was built by Space X — Elon Musk —for Grok and is now leases computer capacity to Anthropic. Walker said the bill for that lease is $1.5 billion per month. (Soon to be Colossus 2 and Colossus 3.) More than 7,500 construction workers are building the facilities. That number of workers has caused significant impact to the communities in Memphis, including those across the line in Mississippi that don’t get the same benefits. “… God didn’t create data centers and they are not all good,” Walker said. “How do they become better? Hopefully all good. That’s up to us.” When all this started there were not many community rules in place. So the community had to develop legislation as the data centers were under construction while learning about the impacts as (or after) they happened. That leaves few paths forward for to protect the public. “What do municipalities need to know? If you’re thinking that a data center could come to your city or town, you need to check on the legislation that you have first concerning data centers,” she said. That means a comprehensive legislative plan that outlines what companies have to do and how to hold them accountable. Council Member Walker: “We’ve been accused of signing NDAs. I have not signed an NDA. I have not been asked to sign an NDA. Why? Because they didn’t need us for anything. Why not? Because we didn’t have any guardrails and moratoriums or anything that kept them from coming in. And then on the other side, there were entities such as the chamber that helped them come into the city and maneuver certain spaces and circumstances. But you want to start with the zoning because they can’t do anything without a parcel. So keep that in mind. The Paul Laurie location, it’s been zoned for commercial industrial since the 1950s. And we are in the process of doing some rezoning for the entire city already. And it will include zoning specific to data centers. That is very important because that’s going to guide your municipality, your leadership, the business

artigo.texto: Officials discuss data centers in the Tri-State Former Evansville mayor and two state lawmakers talk jobs, electricity costs, nondisclosure agreements and community input EVANSVILLE, Ind. (WFIE) - A former Evansville mayor and two state lawmakers joined a conversation about data centers. Watch us when we are live, right here ⬇️ Lloyd Winnecke, former Evansville mayor and CEO of the Evansville Regional Economic Partnership, took part. So did Indiana State Rep. Alex Burton and Kentucky State Sen. Robby Mills. The discussion covers jobs and pay, data center interest in the Tri-State, electricity costs for homeowners, nondisclosure agreements, possible health impacts and what residents want in their communities. Winnecke was asked about construction and permanent jobs, the types of jobs and what they pay. He also was asked about nondisclosure agreements and public access to information on companies officials are talking with. Burton was asked about data center interest in the Tri-State and whether local officials should consider a moratorium until more is known about potential health impacts. Mills was asked who guarantees homeowners will not pay for data center electricity use. He also was asked what constituents want when it comes to a data center in their community. artigo.texto: The Western Australian Government has awarded $15 million through the Investment Attraction Fund (IAF) New Energies Industries Round 2 to Australian Vanadium Limited (AVL) to establish a high-capacity, relocatable vanadium electrolyte manufacturing facility in the state. The project will expand AVL’s capacity to produce vanadium electrolyte to support large-scale battery installations as well as increasing local content in the vanadium flow battery supply chain. Related article: AVESS wins grant to explore vanadium flow battery manufacturing in Indo-Pacific Vanadium flow batteries use liquid vanadium electrolyte solutions in separate tanks to both store and release electricity. Skilled employment and training opportunities in advanced manufacturing, chemical processing, engineering, construction, commissioning, and plant operations will be created, while its modular and relocatable design enables deployment across regional and industrial centres throughout WA. The IAF funding will also support the development of grid-scale vanadium flow batteries and long-duration energy storage infrastructure in the state. WA State Development and Economic Diversification Minister David Michael said, “The Investment Attraction Fund continues to play a critical role in attracting projects that strengthen Western Australia’s industrial capabilities and support our energy transition. “By supporting AVL’s electrolyte manufacturing capability, we’re creating new opportunities in advanced manufacturing while helping position WA at the forefront of long-duration energy storage technologies. Related article: Western Australia doubles renewable energy target to 75% “The development of a high-capacity vanadium electrolyte facility will support local jobs, strengthen our manufacturing capability, and provide the foundations for future grid-scale battery projects across the state.”

artigo.texto: Governo apresenta na COP 31 resultados da implementação do mercado de carbono Secretaria Extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono apresenta, na Turquia, resultados da implementação do mercado no país e lidera diálogos globais na presidência da Coalizão Aberta para Mercados Regulados de Carbono O Governo Federal, por meio da Secretaria Extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono (SEMC) do Ministério da Fazenda, apresenta os resultados da primeira fase de implementação do Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE), que será concluída nos próximos meses. A apresentação ocorre durante a 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudança do Clima (COP 31), realizada em Antália, na Turquia, até 20 de novembro. Na agenda internacional, a delegação técnica divulga os avanços da Coalizão Aberta para Mercados Regulados de Carbono (OCCCM), proposta pelo Brasil em Belém (PA), durante a COP 30. A iniciativa já reúne países que representam quase metade do PIB mundial e visa garantir a interoperabilidade entre os mercados nacionais de carbono e construir uma precificação mundial do carbono. Mercado regulado O modelo de mercado regulado adotado pelo país de teto e comércio (cap-and-trade, em inglês) traz cotas de emissão de carbono para grandes empresas que vão sendo reduzidas ao longo dos anos e oferecem possibilidade de comercializá-las. O Mercado Regulado brasileiro constitui um dos instrumentos do Plano de Transformação Ecológica (PTE). Estimativas do Banco Mundial indicam que o mercado regulado de carbono no Brasil pode gerar expansão cumulativa de 5,8% no Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) até 2040 e de 8,5% até 2050, além de proporcionar uma redução de 27% nas emissões dos setores regulados até meados do século. Instituído pela Lei nº 15.042/2024, o SBCE prevê a adesão gradual do setor produtivo. Em outubro, o Ministério da Fazenda divulgou o cronograma para os setores industriais iniciarem o monitoramento de emissões e adotarem as exigências de Mensuração, Relato e Verificação (MRV). As regras alcançam operadores com emissões a partir de 10 mil tCO2e ao ano, atingindo menos de 1% das empresas brasileiras. “O SBCE oferece previsibilidade regulatória para a atração de investimentos sustentáveis. Ao reduzir sua poluição e estruturar um mercado regulado com padrões técnicos consistentes, o país transforma compromissos climáticos em modernização industrial e avanço para uma economia de baixo carbono”, afirma a secretária extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono, Cristina Reis. Retração nas emissões — A participação brasileira na conferência ocorre em um cenário de retração nas emissões brutas de gases de efeito estufa (GEE). Dados do Programa de Monitoramento dos Biomas Brasileiros (BiomasBR), do Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais (Inpe), apontam que a taxa de desmatamento na Amazônia recuou 41,8% no período 2025/2026, somando 3.335 quilômetros quadrados, o menor índice da série histórica iniciada em 1988. No Cerrado, a redução foi de 23,8%, atingindo 5.516,69 quilômetros quadrados, a menor taxa desde 2001. Segundo o Sistema de Estimativas de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (SEEG), iniciativa do Observatório do Clima, a contenção da perda vegetal respondeu pela queda de 6% nas emissões brutas do país em 2025. Cooperação internacional No cenário multilateral, a Coalizão Aberta para Mercados Regulados de Carbono completa o primeiro ano de atividades. Criada na COP30, em Belém (PA), a coalizão é presidida pelo Brasil e copresidida por China e União Europeia. O grupo reúne jurisdições responsáveis por 42,2% das emissões mundiais de GEE e 49 trilhões de dólares do PIB global. Em Antália, a delegação brasileira lidera reunião de alto nível da OCCCM com novas adesões de países-membros previstas. O Plano de Trabalho 2026-2027 da coalizão foi aprovado em setembro, em Wuhan, na China. A agenda oficial prevê ainda a assinatura de Memorando de Entendimento (MoU) para a adesão do Banco Asiático de Investimento em Infraestrutura (AIIB) à OCCCM, em sessão no Pavilhão dos Bancos Multilaterais de Desenvolvimento. O AIIB passa a ser o primeiro banco multilateral de desenvolvimento sediado na Ásia a integrar formalmente a governança da coalizão. Newsletter — A secretaria disponibilizou na primeira semana da COP31 a nova edição da newsletter MercadoDeCarbono.GOV, boletim que compila as entregas da primeira fase de implantação do SBCE e pode ser acessado no portal do Ministério da Fazenda. artigo.texto: ANACONDA - Anaconda’s chief executive wants to squash any rumors that a data center is coming to the Smelter City. He even went as far as proposing a one-year moratorium on any data centers coming here until it can be further examined. Watch full story here: “Data centers are not popular. There’s a lot of questions about data centers, a lot of questions that I personally don’t have answers for right now,” Anaconda Chief Executive Bill Everett said. To help him get more answers, Everett proposed adopting a 12-month ban on data centers locating in Anaconda-Deer Lodge County. This would give county officials time to examine potential impacts of facilities like this have on the community. According to the proposed resolution presented at the Nov. 10th Commissioners meeting, “data centers may create public nuisance, public health, and/or environmental impacts that the county has an obligation to prevent.” “It’s a good idea to do it, give ourselves a little breathing room before we get into a difficult situation, litigation or something,” Commissioner Ed Beaudette said. Everett added that rumors about the county considering proposals for a new data center are false. “The rumor’s actually grown that now there’s a data center going to be built east of town and west of town, which, obviously, is not true either,” Everett said. Some residents at the meeting told MTN News they are relieved the county is considering taking the time to learn more about data centers before making a permanent decision. The commission noted it may be about three weeks for a public hearing to be held on the proposed resolution.

artigo.texto: US elections show strong resistance to AI data centers By LIA ZHU in San Francisco | China Daily | Updated: 2026-11-12 09:17 Ambitions to expand AI infrastructure in the United States face a growing local challenge after voters backed restrictions on data centers in the midterm elections, reinforcing what experts describe as an emerging constraint on development. On Nov 3, voters favored limiting data center development in 40 of 41 local ballot measures, according to Ballotpedia. The measures included outright bans, temporary moratoriums and voter approval requirements. The results reflect growing public concerns over the noise, land use and environmental impact of large data centers, as well as their impact on electricity and water bills. They also contrast with the federal policy push. In July last year, US President Donald Trump signed an executive order prioritizing the rapid construction of AI data centers and supporting energy infrastructure through streamlined federal permitting and access to federal land. However, public opposition has grown rapidly. "I've never seen an issue where the public sentiment has moved as quickly as it has as opposition to data centers in the past year," said David Sandalow, inaugural fellow at Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy, at an energy conference before the midterms. Sandalow cited a December study he coauthored examining state legislation on data centers. It found that incentives to attract the facilities dominated the laws enacted. Last year, more state legislatures were trying to attract data centers than pursuing any other policy related to the facilities, he said. The political landscape has since shifted. With Democrats wresting control of both chambers of Congress from Republicans in a "blue wave", experts said the election results could give incoming officials greater political support to tighten development rules. Democrats have pledged to clamp down on the massive, energy-hungry facilities. The potential policy changes could extend across national, state and local levels, according to a Brookings Institution analysis of the election's implications. It identified possible measures, including extended moratoriums, mandatory protections against higher electricity costs, a reconsideration of tax exemptions, and greater scrutiny of projects previously eligible for automatic approval. Texas offers an example of how opposition to data centers is reshaping political debate. Republican Governor Greg Abbott announced a moratorium on data center construction this year before losing his reelection bid to Democrat Gina Hinojosa. Hinojosa, who made data centers a key part of her campaign, has outlined several planned restrictions on the facilities, including voiding contracts that affect water supplies and requiring data centers to pay taxes on electricity. "It's a very dramatic change," Sandalow said of the opposition to the facilities at the recent US-China Green Energy Summit at Stanford University. "This is going to be the constraint going forward. And part of this is driven by data centers moving into these suburban areas." The issue has also emerged as an early test for Congress. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is designed to speed up permitting reviews while requiring large data centers to pay for the energy they use. The Senate held a procedural vote on Monday to gauge support for advancing the legislation. However, the bill faces a more difficult path following the midterms. Investment firm TD Cowen has lowered its estimate of the likelihood of its passage from 40 percent before the elections to 25 percent. Investment hurdles The election results could also create additional challenges for AI infrastructure investment, particularly as newly elected state officials consider restrictions on data center development, according to a post-election analysis by Morgan Stanley. Decisions governing US data center projects rest largely with state utility commissions, legislatures and county boards. Additional state regulations could create a more fragmented environment, the analysis said. Sandalow said the changing nature of AI computing could further intensify local opposition. In the next five years or so, a greater share of computing is expected to be devoted to inference — when trained models can make predictions or decisions on new, previously unseen data — rather than large-scale model training, he said. Applications such as autonomous vehicles require relatively low latency, meaning data centers need to be located closer to where their computing capacity is used. "To the extent that we're locating data centers in suburban areas, that's going to cause a lot of opposition," he said.

artigo.texto: Lawmakers in New Jersey will consider a ban on data center non-disclosure agreements after the state Senate passed an identical bill in October. The ban aims to encourage greater transparency around data center developments in New Jersey. At the end of October, the New Jersey Senate passed Bill 4304. The bill stipulates that data center applicants and their agents shall not enter into any agreement, including non-disclosure agreements, with approving authorities, municipal agencies, or property sellers that has the purpose of concealing the details of data center developments. “Transparency is crucial during the data center development process, especially since these projects can have a major impact on our communities,” said Senator Linda Greenstein (D-Mercer/Middlesex) in a press statement in October. “This legislation establishes clear consequences for applicants who attempt to conceal data center development plans and makes clear that these agreements have no place in the approval process.” The bill further states that data center developers applying for approval will have to attest that no party to the property transaction has entered into an agreement with the seller that obfuscates the details of the project or prevents public review of the development plans for the property. “As data center development continues to expand across New Jersey, communities deserve a voice in how these projects affect their neighborhoods,” said Senator Brian Stack (D-Hudson). “This legislation will help ensure residents and local officials have the opportunity to review proposed developments and understand their potential impacts before projects move forward.” Following the passing of Bill 4304 in the Senate, it has now been referred to the Assembly Science, Innovation and Technology Committee, which meets on Monday November 16, 2026. The Assembly has its own version of this bill, Bill 2774, which was introduced on January 13, 2026 as a carry-over from December 2025. Once the Senate’s bill was referred to the committee, the two were classified as the same or similar. Save for the sponsors of the bill, the Senate’s version and the Assembly’s version are identical. New Jersey lawmakers join a growing number of states pushing back against data center developments. In August, w.media reported that Pennsylvania governor Josh Shapiro had signed what he called the strictest guardrails for AI data center developments in the US. The guardrails require developers to pay the full cost of new electricity generation, transmission, distribution, and other infrastructure, and to commit to open, transparent engagement with local residents and leaders. Earlier this year Texas governor Greg Abbott directed the Public Utility Commission of Texas (PUCT) and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) to conduct a verification audit of all data center projects moving through ERCOT’s interconnection process. The governor also ordered the two bodies to assess the extent to which data centers are paying their own way or depending on state financial incentives. The history of pushback also appears to have elevated fears that incoming Democratic governors and senators, elected during the midterm elections last week, will stall or stop data center developments. These fears reached a breaking point last week when US$ 2.5 trillion in market value evaporated.

artigo.texto: Juntamente com outras certificações obtidas de acordo com as normas UL, IEC e NFPA, a VinEnergo reafirma sua posição como marca líder em segurança e qualidade no campo de baterias para armazenamento de energia em particular e em soluções de energia verde em geral. O sistema BESS desenvolvido pela VinEnergo é fabricado na fábrica de armazenamento de baterias VinES em Ha Tinh , equipado com tecnologia de resfriamento líquido ativo para controlar com precisão a temperatura das células da bateria, reduzir as diferenças de temperatura entre as células e prolongar a vida útil do sistema. Além disso, o sistema incorpora uma solução proativa de prevenção e combate a incêndios, capaz de detecção precoce, alerta, isolamento de incidentes e ativação automática do mecanismo de supressão de incêndio desde o estágio inicial, garantindo a máxima segurança do sistema. Para obter a certificação de segurança UL 9540, o sistema BESS da VinEnergo passou pelo rigoroso teste UL 9540A, que avalia o potencial de fuga térmica, incêndio e liberação de gases dentro do sistema de armazenamento de energia. Os resultados do teste fornecem uma base técnica crucial para avaliar os níveis de segurança e apoiar o processo de certificação UL 9540. Além da certificação UL 9540, o Sistema de Armazenamento de Energia em Baterias (BESS) da VinEnergo obteve outras certificações internacionais de prestígio, como UL 1973, IEC 62619, IEC 63056, e relatórios de testes como IEC 62933-5-2, NFPA 68 e NFPA 69. Em particular, a avaliação e a certificação são realizadas pela UL Solutions (Underwriters Laboratories) - uma organização líder mundial em ciência da segurança de produtos, testes, inspeção e certificação, com mais de 130 anos de experiência global. A certificação UL 9540 é um passo significativo na estratégia da VinEnergo para levar seus produtos BESS aos mercados internacionais, especialmente aqueles com altas exigências de segurança, qualidade e padrões técnicos, como América do Norte, Europa e Ásia. A Sra. Nguyen Huong Giang, Diretora-Geral Adjunta Permanente da VinEnergo, afirmou: “Identificamos as soluções de armazenamento de energia como uma área tecnológica fundamental, que contribui para a modernização da rede elétrica e promove a transição para fontes de energia limpa no Vietnã.” A VinEnergo está a desenvolver as suas capacidades em todo o processo, desde a investigação e desenvolvimento e produção até à integração de sistemas BESS em aplicações e operações práticas, reforçando assim a posição das empresas vietnamitas no mercado internacional de energia.” Atualmente, a VinEnergo fornece e instala mais de 1,6 GWh de baterias de armazenamento de energia para diversos grandes projetos de empresas de energia do Grupo de Eletricidade do Vietnã, bem como para empresas nacionais e internacionais, como Marubeni, MM Mega Market, Usina Termoelétrica Nghi Son 2, etc. Recentemente, a VinEnergo também colocou em operação um sistema de armazenamento de baterias de 45 MWh combinado com energia solar para seu complexo fabril no Parque Industrial de Vung Ang (Ha Tinh).
