artigo.texto: The Oakland City Council on Tuesday extended a pause on data centers for almost another year, giving city officials more time to study the impacts of computing facilities and develop rules governing where and how they can operate. The council voted unanimously to extend the existing temporary moratorium for an additional 10 months and 15 days, effective until Oct. 5, 2027. The moratorium is not a permanent ban on data centers; rather, it temporarily suspends new approvals for such facilities. Separately, council members also declared an emergency ordinance prohibiting the city from approving permits, zoning changes, and other land-use agreements for the construction of data centers. “We’re seeing an uprising across the country when it comes to how data centers are operating,” District 3 Councilmember Carroll Fife said during the council meeting. “It was imperative that I take immediate action to protect Oakland residents from what we’ve seen in other parts of the country.” The council’s vote comes a little more than a month after it unanimously approved an initial 45-day moratorium on Oct. 6, following hours of public comment from residents concerned about electricity and water consumption, increased air and noise pollution, and other potential impacts of data centers. That moratorium was set to expire on Nov. 20. The extension, introduced by Fife, buys time for the city to research the impacts of data centers on the local energy grid, water supply, air quality, and compliance with local and state laws. It also gives the city a chance to determine whether it should update Oakland’s current zoning and land use regulations to accommodate the facilities. Dozens of community members spoke in support of the moratorium extension and against AI data center development in Oakland. Many residents, including Jamal Khan, a member of the Alliance of Californians for Community Empowerment, said Oakland is an easy target for billionaires and developers who prioritize profit over the well-being of vulnerable people. “We’re not talking about proposing a data center over there in Marin County on Skywalker Ranch,” Khan said. “This is part of a design to disenfranchise us again.” Cathy Leonard, a District 1 resident, warned that West Oakland seniors and children, who experience higher rates of asthma and cancer than those in other neighborhoods, would experience more noise and air pollution if data centers come to Oakland. “Let’s bring some productive businesses to Oakland that actually help us, not kill us. These centers are killers,” she said. Not everyone supported the moratorium. Mindy Pechenuk, a District 4 resident who ran unsuccessfully for mayor, argued data centers could create more jobs for young people and boost the local economy. She said developers could build a facility at the former Oakland Army Base. In an agenda report released ahead of Tuesday’s council meeting, Fife argued that the city’s existing infrastructure was not designed to accommodate the “extraordinary” demands of large-scale data centers. The city has yet to determine whether its power grid, water supply, and emergency response systems could support data centers without affecting services for residents, businesses, schools, and hospitals. The city’s planning code also does not specifically define data centers or outline rules about their operations, including requirements for water efficiency, energy use, noise reduction, backup generators, and environmental protections, according to the report. The extension, Fife wrote, is necessary because “data centers have the potential to impose significant negative impacts on local water and electrical resources, air quality, and community livability.” City officials have already received inquiries about establishing data centers in new and existing buildings, according to Fife’s report. Though the document does not provide any names of individuals or companies, one developer, Behring Companies, made headlines in August when it proposed siting a data center inside a downtown Oakland building. Activist group says West Oakland survey shows broad opposition to data centers An hour before the council meeting, Care 4 Community Action, an Oakland-based civic engagement group that grew out of Carroll Fife’s 2020 City Council campaign, held a press conference outside City Hall to go over the findings of a survey they conducted with West Oakland residents about data centers. The group says it knocked on more than 2,400 doors across West Oakland last month. Of the 424 people who spoke with organizers, 73% said they supported a full ban on new artificial intelligence data centers in the city. Other findings from their survey include: - 46% worried about rising electricity and utility bills - 47% were concerned about jobs being replaced by AI - 51% expressed concern about rents going up and residents being displaced because of data center development - 73% wanted the city to establish water and energy use standards before the moratorium expires Forty-five percent of residents who spoke with canvassers said they have lived in West Oakland for at least a decade, according to a news release from Care 4 Community Action. At the press conference, organizers said they supported the moratorium extension because they believe the city needs more time to assess the long-term impacts of data centers. “Forty-five days is not enough to make decisions that can impact West Oakland for generations,” said Bradley Gentry, a Care 4 Community Action organizer who spoke with over 50 residents as part of the effort. Stacy Hogg-Stewart, a District 3 resident whose family has lived in West Oakland for 80 years, said community members deserve transparency when it comes to new development in their neighborhoods. “We’re not against new development, but we deserve to know what the costs of having a data center in West Oakland are,” Hogg-Stewart told The Oaklandside. artigo.texto: Supported by The Latest Ploy: Bringing Data Centers to Your Actual Backyard An energy company believes they can tap into homeowners to deliver compute without the acrimony. With communities across the country mounting opposition to data centers, technology firms are desperate to find places where they can stash their servers without facing a public outcry. One company has a bold proposal: How about your backyard? That’s the premise behind a micro-data center developed by Span, a San Francisco energy company. Called XFRA, the unit is about the size of an HVAC system and looks like one, too: a gray metal casing, with a condenser fan behind a grille. Inside are 16 processors made by Nvidia, the same kind that fill an ordinary data center. It doesn’t require a constant input of water and is about as loud as a dishwasher. According to the company, it would take about 8,000 of these home units to match the power requirements of a large data center — only without, Span hopes, attracting intense acrimony. The company’s backers hope to mitigate opposition by paying host homeowners’ electrical and internet bills, and by installing one of its proprietary “smart” electrical panels, which direct current more efficiently. Some experts doubt that XFRA will work as smoothly as promised, or that it can entice enough customers to make a dent in the nation’s soaring need for processing power, known in Silicon Valley shorthand as “compute.” Span executives say they aren’t fazed, and about 100 units are now being tested, ahead of a market rollout sometime next year. “The idea that people are fundamentally against A.I., I don’t think is actually well supported by the research,” said Ryan Harris, Span’s chief revenue officer. “I think that they’re against the idea that the infrastructure necessary to power this technology is being forced on them.” Related Content Advertisement

artigo.texto: Resumo - Itaú BBA vê WEG (WEGE3) favorecida pela expansão de data centers no Brasil - Banco mantém recomendação outperform e preço-alvo de R$ 56 para a ação - Projeto Scala AI City, perto de Porto Alegre, já tem aval da ANEEL para 5 GW - Em certos equipamentos elétricos, o tempo de entrega pode chegar a três anos - Servidores de data center sofrem carga tributária de cerca de 70% no país - Programa Redata poderia reduzir essa carga para perto de 20%, estima o BBA A WEG (WEGE3) pode se beneficiar do avanço da inteligência artificial (IA) e da expansão dos data centers pelo mundo. Essa é a avaliação do Itaú BBA, que colocou a companhia entre suas principais apostas nos setores de transportes e bens de capital. O banco reiterou recomendação outperform, equivalente a desempenho acima da média do mercado, e estabeleceu preço-alvo de R$ 56 para a ação. A análise foi divulgada após uma reunião do banco com a Scala, uma das principais desenvolvedoras de data centers de grande porte da América Latina. Segundo o BBA, a procura crescente por equipamentos e a oferta limitada de fornecedores nacionais favorecem a fabricante brasileira. Além disso, os longos prazos de entrega de componentes elétricos ampliam a vantagem competitiva da WEG. Como a companhia já possui estrutura de produção no Brasil, ela está bem posicionada para atender à demanda gerada pelo novo ciclo de investimentos em infraestrutura digital. A Scala também destaca a disponibilidade de energia elétrica no Brasil como um diferencial competitivo. O cenário contrasta com o dos Estados Unidos, onde as restrições de oferta de energia são mais severas. Na cadeia de fornecimento elétrico dos data centers, a WEG já responde por uma parcela expressiva dos equipamentos, posição que poucas empresas nacionais conseguem alcançar. Capacidade de energia favorece expansão dos data centers A administração da Scala informou que o Scala AI City, projeto que pretende construir próximo a Porto Alegre, já recebeu autorização da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (ANEEL) para contar com 5 gigawatts (GW) de energia. Essa capacidade deve permitir a expansão gradual do empreendimento nos próximos anos. Entretanto, a disponibilidade de equipamentos ainda representa um desafio para o setor. Segundo estimativas da Scala, um empreendimento de 1 GW pode esperar cerca de oito meses pela entrega de transformadores. Em contrapartida, o prazo para determinados equipamentos elétricos pode chegar a três anos. Diante desse cenário, a desenvolvedora avalia que fabricantes com operações instaladas no Brasil, como a WEG, levam vantagem sobre concorrentes que ainda precisam estruturar sua produção no país. Os analistas do Itaú BBA também chamam atenção para a valorização das empresas fornecedoras de equipamentos. Fabricantes como a Vertiv, por exemplo, negociam a múltiplos superiores aos das operadoras de data centers. Para o banco, essa diferença indica que o mercado pode atribuir maior valor às companhias responsáveis pelo fornecimento da infraestrutura necessária aos centros de dados do que às próprias operadoras. Redata pode reduzir custos para data centers no Brasil A tributação dos equipamentos também aparece como um fator importante para a expansão do setor no país. Segundo os dados apresentados pela Scala, os servidores de data centers enfrentam atualmente uma carga tributária efetiva próxima de 70%. O impacto é relevante porque esses equipamentos representam cerca de 80% dos investimentos em bens de capital de um centro de dados. Na avaliação da administração da Scala, a carga tributária ajuda a explicar por que aproximadamente 40% das cargas de trabalho brasileiras ainda operam no exterior. Nesse contexto, o Itaú BBA avalia que o Redata, programa voltado ao estímulo de investimentos em data centers no Brasil, pode reduzir a tributação dos servidores para cerca de 20%. Com uma carga menor, os custos de implantação dos centros de dados também diminuiriam. Consequentemente, empresas que hoje mantêm parte de sua infraestrutura fora do país poderiam considerar o mercado brasileiro uma alternativa mais competitiva. Para o BBA, esse movimento pode ampliar os investimentos em infraestrutura digital no Brasil e, assim, criar oportunidades para fornecedores nacionais de equipamentos, como a WEG.

artigo.texto: Severn residents express concerns over proposed data center expansion Residents in Anne Arundel County are voicing concerns about a proposed expansion to an existing data center, fearing its impact on Severn and their utility costs. Miguel Ruiz, who has lived in Severn for seven years, said he has seen the area evolve significantly during his time there. "There is definitely a lot of change," Ruiz told WBAL-TV 11 News. Ruiz shared his frustration about the addition of the data center, which he passes by daily. "This is a beautiful place, and if they're going to keep on putting that stuff, those monsters here, it's going to destroy the beauty of the place," Ruiz told WBAL-TV 11 News. Ruiz also noted changes in his utility costs. "My energy bills have gone up sky-high. (My) water bill, (it's) unbelievable. It's like the service is the same, but the prices are still going up," Ruiz told WBAL-TV 11 News. "I don't agree to it. I hope it doesn't happen and we'll do whatever we can for it not to be accomplished." The data center's developer is exploring plans for the expansion. A county representative confirmed the proposal in a statement sent to WBAL-TV 11 News on Tuesday. Shanice Corlette, who lives in an apartment complex next to the site, expressed her concerns about the proposal. "It's not good for the area," Corlette said. Corlette plans to move out of the neighborhood next summer and hopes her next home will not be near a data center. "I'll be out of here by next summer, so hopefully, where I move next, I won't have to deal with that," Corlette told WBAL-TV 11 News. Corlette added that she believes the expansion plans will draw more attention from residents. "I definitely think a lot more will be concerned. It's definitely going to be raising eyebrows," Corlette told WBAL-TV 11 News. The proposal comes after the Anne Arundel County Council approved an extension of its data center moratorium, which prevents new data center developments through January 2028. However, the moratorium does not apply to expansions of existing facilities. A county representative told WBAL-TV 11 News that the proposed expansion will go through the standard review, comment and approval process. Ruiz said he expects the project to face resistance from residents. "We just need more information to make people more aware so we can do something about it." "I think that most of these people would be willing to fight it because the bills are getting too extraordinary," Ruiz told WBAL-TV 11 News. Corlette emphasized the need for more information about the project. "We just need more information to make people more aware so we can do something about it," Corlette told WBAL-TV 11 News. The project engineer declined to comment on the expansion plans when reached by email.

artigo.texto: Sacramento residents push back against data center growth as SMUD considers new protections Sacramento residents voiced concerns about electricity costs and environmental impacts Wednesday as the Sacramento Municipal Utility District (SMUD) discussed proposed protections for customers amid growing demand from data centers. Protesters gathered outside SMUD headquarters, while residents questioned utility officials during a board committee meeting. "I'm retired. I'm on a fixed income. I don't know how much more I can pay for," resident Catherine Keeney said. According to SMUD, approximately 16 data centers currently operate within its service area. Two additional proposed data centers, each requiring more than 50 megawatts of power, are in the early feasibility stages. SMUD is considering principles that would require large energy users to cover costs associated with connecting to the electric grid, rather than passing those expenses to existing customers. "We want to make sure that we remain committed to our longstanding policy that the costs for these larger projects are not passed on to existing customers," SMUD spokesperson Gamaliel Ortiz said. Ortiz emphasized that SMUD does not decide whether data center projects are approved. Those land-use decisions fall to local jurisdictions, while SMUD is responsible for providing electricity to approved projects. Residents also raised concerns about water consumption, pollution and whether increasing electricity demand could jeopardize SMUD's goal of achieving zero-carbon electricity by 2030. Some protesters called for a moratorium on new artificial intelligence data centers. Ortiz emphasized that Wednesday's meeting was informational and no decision was made. The SMUD board is expected to vote next week on whether to adopt the proposed principles, not on approval of individual data center projects. artigo.texto: Subscribe to The Y’all — a weekly dispatch about the people, places and policies defining Texas, produced by Texas Tribune journalists living in communities across the state. McALLEN — SpaceX is planning to build a $24 billion data center and power plant just outside of Brownsville on property that the city had just de-annexed earlier this year at the company’s request, circumventing Brownsville’s data center moratorium that went into effect last week. On Monday, the city of Starbase, which later annexed land where the project will be built into their city limits, notified the public that SpaceX is building a $24 billion “gas-fired power plant and super-compute facility.” The $24 billion investment is expected to cover the initial phases of the project which could include future expansions, according to the Monday notice which stated that the Starbase city commissioners are scheduled to hold a public hearing in December in which they will consider tax breaks for the project. The 444.45 acres of land where the project will be located was the subject of local scrutiny over the summer, when SpaceX asked the city of Brownsville to de-annex that land. In exchange, the company offered to fund $220 million for city water and wastewater projects. A SpaceX representative didn’t provide details as to why the company wanted the land, located near the Port of Brownsville out of Brownsville’s city limits, but the company pressured the city to approve the de-annexation quickly or else the $220 million would be off the table. The city agreed, but the move drew widespread condemnation from residents and environmental activists who believed the city was allowing SpaceX to further take over land in the area. Soon after the city approved the deal, speculation circulated online that SpaceX planned to build a data center on the property and wished to circumvent a data center moratorium that was advancing within Brownsville. That speculation appears to have been correct all along. In response to the news, the South Texas Environmental Justice Network, announced a protest against the project, arguing that the new facilities would pollute the air, use up water and increase energy bills for residents. Other residents responded positively, seeing the project as a source for more jobs. “There’s a lot of people that need jobs in our community and SpaceX has contributed to those jobs,” said Janie Melendez, a Brownsville resident and school teacher. She previously served on the Texas Republican Party’s executive committee but said her politics don’t influence her view on data centers and SpaceX. “Since SpaceX moved in, my home has tripled in value,” she said. “But I’m one of those [people] that tries to find a balance in everything.” SpaceX did not respond to questions regarding the project. What the future holds for data centers in Texas However, a majority of Texans oppose data center construction, which has received a wave of pushback across the state due to concerns over how much power and water they require to operate at a time when utility bills remain high and water scarcity fears mount. In response to public backlash, several communities have issued temporary moratoriums on data centers. As criticisms of these facilities grew, Gov. Greg Abbott directed operators of the electric grid in August to pause requests for data center connections to the grid until the data centers could be audited. However, not all data centers rely on the state’s power grid and therefore could still move forward by supplying their own electricity. The gas-fired power plant that SpaceX plans to build could provide power to its data center to avoid connecting to the state’s power grid. Abbott also ordered the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to stop issuing permits for data centers, though critics say that some permits have continued to advance through the permitting process. Data center developers could face stronger headwinds under Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who said she would issue a ban on all data center approvals until state legislators can pass laws “to protect Texans,” she said in a video posted on X. Brownsville approved its own 90-day moratorium which went into effect last week, temporarily hitting pause on data center applications within the city and its extraterritorial jurisdiction. Had the 444.45-acre tract of land remained within Brownsville’s city limits, the SpaceX project likely would have had to find a different location. The city of Brownsville said it stood by its decision to de-annex the property, which was based on “information and circumstances presented at the time,” the city said in a statement. That included the property’s location, municipal service considerations and potential long-term benefits to Brownsville. The city further noted that the land was privately owned and its sale to SpaceX was a transaction between private parties. The $220 million that the city received for the de-annexation will fund critical water infrastructure which the city said would help ensure their water supply keeps up with their future growth. “The City recognizes the concerns raised about data center development and takes those concerns seriously,” the city said. “It remains committed to evaluating those concerns and protecting water resources, evaluating infrastructure impacts and ensuring responsible growth that serves Brownsville’s long-term interests.” Further, the city assured that any future de-annexation requests will be evaluated independently under state law and the city commission will take the circumstances and legal requirements into consideration before taking action. “Residents should have confidence that their concerns about data center development, water resources, energy consumption and responsible growth are being taken seriously,” the city said. “Our responsibility is to ensure that Brownsville’s growth is intentional, that residents’ interests remain a priority, and that decisions involving our c

artigo.texto: Astella planeja R$ 1 bi em data centers em 10 anos Rede começa por Curitiba, terá novos nós no Amapá e Mato Grosso e já conta com cliente-âncora voltado a treinamento de IA. A Astella, empresa do Grupo ABL voltada a data centers e infraestrutura digital, projeta investir cerca de R$ 1 bilhão ao longo da próxima década na expansão de sua rede nacional. O primeiro nó começa a operar em Curitiba, com capacidade inicial de aproximadamente 3,5 MW e possibilidade de chegar a 5 MW, enquanto Amapá e Mato Grosso estão entre os próximos destinos previstos para 2027. O plano de longo prazo foi detalhado por Agnaldo Lopes, presidente do Grupo ABL. Segundo ele, o valor de R$ 1 bilhão considera o conjunto de todas as unidades que a empresa pretende implantar. Para o horizonte mais próximo, a previsão é de R$ 300 milhões adicionais até 2028 em seis novas localidades. A operação do Paraná recebeu cerca de R$ 50 milhões, considerando Curitiba e Maringá. O investimento foi menor do que seria necessário em uma instalação construída integralmente do zero pois boa parte da infraestrutura já existia e foi modernizada. Cliente-âncora será de IA A Astella já possui um cliente-âncora para a unidade de Curitiba, embora a empresa ainda não revele o nome. “Será para processamento de inteligência artificial”, afirmou Lopes. Em seguida, esclareceu que a carga será destinada a treinamento de IA e operará em modelo de colocation. A empresa acredita que os projetos já em negociação possam ocupar toda capacidade disponível em aproximadamente oito meses. “Os projetos já estão na mesa, e eu acredito que em oito meses nós estamos com a nossa capacidade já tomada”, disse Lopes. A unidade está instalada em um edifício de 8,8 mil m² e 16 pavimentos e foi preparada para crescer de forma modular conforme a contratação de clientes e de energia. Amapá e Mato Grosso entram em 2027 “A próxima unidade será no Amapá, e depois nós desceremos para o Mato Grosso. Essas próximas duas estrelas estão previstas para 2027”, afirmou Lopes. Diferentemente de Curitiba, onde o data center está separado da unidade de geração, os novos projetos deverão adotar modelo off-grid, com a infraestrutura computacional instalada junto à geração de energia. “Nos outros projetos, nós vamos fazer off grid. Nós vamos criar o data center junto com a unidade geradora de energia”, disse o executivo, confirmando que Macapá deverá seguir esse modelo. A estratégia energética do grupo inclui geração própria renovável. Uma usina solar de aproximadamente 2,7 MWp já está conectada à rede e integra o modelo de fornecimento da operação. Receita pode crescer até 40% em 2027 Lopes estima que a expansão dos data centers possa elevar o faturamento do grupo entre 38% e 40% em 2027, caso os contratos atualmente previstos se concretizem. “A nossa expectativa, já dentro do que a gente tem hoje, é que o grupo vai ter um aumento de faturamento, já em 2027, em torno de 38%, 40%”, afirmou. A rede terá foco nacional e prevê unidades distribuídas e interligadas para armazenamento, processamento, replicação de dados e continuidade operacional. A unidade de Curitiba também será conectada à infraestrutura da Megaport. Segundo Lopes, a rede da empresa alcança mais de 1,2 mil data centers no mundo, ampliando as opções de interconexão da Astella com ambientes internacionais. Redata fica para etapa de GPUs próprias A Astella ainda não utiliza os incentivos do Redata, mas pretende recorrer ao programa em uma etapa posterior. “Ainda não, mas certamente nós vamos tentar utilizar”, respondeu Lopes ao ser questionado sobre a utilização do regime. Segundo ele, a intenção é recorrer ao programa quando a empresa avançar para operação de nuvem própria e infraestrutura com GPUs próprias. Na unidade atual, os equipamentos de processamento ficarão sob responsabilidade do próprio cliente, enquanto a Astella fornece a infraestrutura física, energia, conectividade e refrigeração. Lopes destacou que a compra direta de servidores e GPUs exigiria um volume de investimento significativamente maior. Refrigeração será híbrida O data center de Curitiba foi preparado para suportar cargas de maior densidade associadas à IA. Segundo Lopes, a refrigeração será híbrida, combinando air cooling e liquid cooling. A instalação possui três reservatórios que somam 80 mil litros de água, usados em circuito fechado para retirada de calor. O executivo afirmou que a água permanece circulando no sistema e que a necessidade de reposição ocorre principalmente por evaporação. Em plena carga, a estimativa citada por ele é de perdas entre 8% e 10%. Soberania dos dados A Astella também pretende posicionar a rede como infraestrutura para armazenamento e processamento de dados no Brasil. “Um dos nossos objetivos é exatamente esse, criar um modelo de negócios em que os nossos dados, sejam os dados das empresas, sejam os dados do governo, fiquem realmente no Brasil. Trafeguem dentro do Brasil”, afirmou Lopes. O grupo informou que mantém pedido junto ao Ministério da Defesa para obter enquadramento relacionado a atividades estratégicas de segurança. Segundo a empresa, a iniciativa integra a intenção de atender clientes privados e públicos com requisitos de soberania, segurança e continuidade operacional.

artigo.texto: O mercado regulado de carbono brasileiro pode acrescentar 5,8% ao Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) até 2040 e 8,5% até 2050, além de reduzir em 27% as emissões dos setores submetidos ao sistema até meados do século, segundo estimativas do Banco Mundial divulgadas pelo Ministério da Fazenda. Os números foram reportados pelo Monitor do Mercado e apresentados pela Secretaria Extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono (SEMC), vinculada à pasta, durante a COP31, em Antália, na Turquia. A conferência ocorre até 20 de novembro e marca a apresentação dos resultados da primeira etapa de implementação do Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE). O desenho do mercado combina limite de emissões, cotas negociáveis e regras de monitoramento, com o objetivo declarado de criar incentivo econômico para a redução de poluentes e dar previsibilidade a investimentos de baixo carbono. O que o SBCE muda para as empresas Criado pela Lei nº 15.042/2024, o SBCE estabelece um teto para as emissões de gases de efeito estufa de empresas de setores regulados. As companhias recebem cotas de emissão, que diminuem gradualmente ao longo dos anos e podem ser comercializadas entre os participantes do mercado. Quem emitir abaixo do limite pode vender o excedente; quem precisar de mais cotas pode comprá-las. Em outubro, o Ministério da Fazenda divulgou o cronograma para que os setores industriais iniciem o monitoramento das emissões e cumpram as exigências de Mensuração, Relato e Verificação (MRV). O conjunto de procedimentos define como as empresas devem medir, registrar e comprovar a quantidade de gases de efeito estufa lançada na atmosfera. As regras alcançam operadores com emissões a partir de 10 mil toneladas de CO₂ equivalente por ano. Segundo o governo, esse grupo representa menos de 1% das empresas brasileiras. A secretária extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono, Cristina Reis, afirmou que o sistema oferece previsibilidade regulatória para atrair investimentos sustentáveis. A expectativa do governo é que a implementação contribua para a modernização industrial e para a transição a uma economia de baixo carbono. Projeção de PIB e agenda global As projeções do Banco Mundial foram divulgadas pelo Ministério da Fazenda em um momento de implementação gradual do sistema. O ganho estimado de 5,8% do PIB em 2040 e de 8,5% em 2050 é acompanhado pela expectativa de redução de 27% nas emissões dos setores regulados até meados do século. A participação brasileira na COP31 também marca o primeiro ano da Coalizão Aberta para Mercados Regulados de Carbono (OCCCM), iniciativa apresentada pelo país durante a COP30, em Belém (PA). Presidido pelo Brasil e copresidido pela China e pela União Europeia, o grupo reúne jurisdições responsáveis por 42,2% das emissões globais de gases de efeito estufa e por US$ 49 trilhões do Produto Interno Bruto mundial. O Plano de Trabalho 2026-2027 da coalizão foi aprovado em setembro, em Wuhan, na China. Durante a COP31, a delegação brasileira conduz uma reunião de alto nível e prevê a entrada de novos participantes. Também está prevista a assinatura de um Memorando de Entendimento para a adesão do Banco Asiático de Investimento em Infraestrutura (AIIB). Segundo o Ministério da Fazenda, a instituição será o primeiro banco multilateral de desenvolvimento sediado na Ásia a integrar formalmente a governança da coalizão. Desmatamento recua e ajuda o balanço de emissões Além do mercado de carbono, o Brasil apresentou na conferência dados recentes sobre a redução do desmatamento. Segundo o Programa de Monitoramento dos Biomas Brasileiros (BiomasBR), do Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais (Inpe), a taxa de desmatamento na Amazônia caiu 41,8% no período 2025/2026, para 3.335 quilômetros quadrados. O resultado é o menor da série histórica, iniciada em 1988. No Cerrado, a redução foi de 23,8%, com área desmatada de 5.516,69 quilômetros quadrados. De acordo com os dados apresentados pelo governo, esse é o menor índice desde 2001. O Sistema de Estimativas de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (SEEG), iniciativa do Observatório do Clima, atribui à contenção da perda de vegetação uma contribuição para a queda de 6% nas emissões brutas do Brasil em 2025. O conjunto de números apresentado na COP31 reúne a projeção de impacto macroeconômico, o cronograma de adaptação das empresas e os dados de desmatamento. O mercado regulado tem implementação gradual, enquanto a coalizão internacional busca ampliar a coordenação entre jurisdições que respondem por parcela relevante das emissões e do PIB global.

artigo.texto: The rumors aren't true, Anaconda Chief Executive Bill Everett assured the public Tuesday night: No data centers are coming to town. Nevertheless, Everett said at the city commission meeting that he plans to seek a 12-month moratorium on data centers coming to Anaconda to ensure further examination of the issue. The commission plan to hold a hearing on the proposed moratorium in about three weeks. Data centers have emerged as a flashpoint in communities across Montana. In Butte, a proposal by Sabey Data Center fell apart in April after neighbor REC Silicon exercised a right-of-refusal to buy the 620-acre site where the project was planned. A citizens group had launched a petition requiring public approval of data centers in response to the plan. Last month, the Missoula City Council approved a moratorium on data centers, and a local AI is suing to overturn the measure. In Broadview, developer Quantica broke ground in October on a massive data center on 5,000 acres south of town. The project has been met with protests and angry public comment at Yellowstone County commissioners' meetings.

artigo.texto: New Dem regulators plan to take on Georgia Power’s data center gas boom Georgia residents are angry at the state’s unchecked data center boom and rising electric bills — and they voted accordingly in last week’s election. Democrats won every statewide race in Georgia, including two seats on the Public Service Commission. Republicans had held a majority at the powerful utility regulator for 30 years. The winning candidates, Commissioner-elect Shelia Edwards and reelected Commissioner Peter Hubbard, have made clear that their top priority is to rein in rising electricity bills from Georgia Power, the state’s biggest utility. That likely means the new Democratic majority will challenge Georgia Power’s plans to enact one of the largest fossil-fuel expansions in the nation. In December 2025, the Republican-led PSC approved Georgia Power’s plan to build nearly 10 gigawatts of new gas-fired power plants and batteries to serve proposed data centers. It did so despite recommendations from commission staff to approve only about one-third of that capacity right away, given the speculative nature of the data center growth projections that the utility used to justify its buildout. All three Democrats on the five-member commission have signaled opposition to those plans. The two Democrats already on the commission, Hubbard and Alicia Johnson, tried earlier this year to get the PSC to reconsider the planned gas buildout but were thwarted by the GOP majority. The five new gas-burning plants planned as part of that buildout could cost customers an estimated $50 billion to $60 billion over their multi-decade lifespan and lock in significant amounts of new greenhouse gas emissions, according to estimates from the Southern Environmental Law Center. Hubbard, who worked for 16 years in utility planning and renewable energy project development, has conducted his own analysis that found a “cost-optimized portfolio” prioritizing solar, batteries, and energy efficiency could meet expected demand and save billions of dollars compared to the utility’s gas-heavy approach. Georgia Power’s expensive gas buildout would exacerbate the affordability challenges its customers already face. The PSC has approved six rate hikes from Georgia Power in the past few years, increasing typical residential utility bills by 33%, or more than $500 a year on average. The utility, which earns a set rate of return on what regulators allow it to spend on power plants, has seen profits swell over that same time. “Georgia Power is making billions while Georgia families are struggling,” Edwards, who owns a communications consulting firm, said during an Oct. 28 press event hosted by the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, a nonprofit advocacy group. “Something is fundamentally wrong with that picture.” Controlling data center costs — and making them pay their own way In February, the PSC voted 3–2 against a motion brought by environmental advocates to reconsider the 10-GW gas buildout, with Hubbard and Johnson voting to block the expansion. The Democratic commissioners argued that the utility had failed to prove that data center growth justified the cost. Nor was their opposition enough to discourage Georgia Power. Just months later, in April, the utility submitted a new request to the PSC seeking permission to add somewhere between 2 GW and 6 GW of additional “dispatchable capacity resources.” Utility critics fear this new round will also tilt toward a preponderance of gas power plants instead of solar, batteries, or other cleaner options. Georgia Power says that its broader customer base will be insulated from cost increases related to its gas buildout, and that growing electricity sales will put “downward pressure” on customer rates. Last year, the all-Republican commission approved a rule that would allow Georgia Power to force data centers and other large customers to cover the costs of the new power plants and grid infrastructure built to serve them. Other utilities and state regulators have made similar pledges via “large load tariffs” meant to force data center developers to commit to paying a significant portion of their costs if they don’t get built or shut down early. “We know our customers depend on us to keep energy reliable and affordable for their homes and businesses,” Rick Anderson, the utility’s senior vice president and senior production officer, said in an April announcement. “As we continue to invest in diverse, flexible generation resources, we also continue to work with new large-load customers who are driving much of this growth on appropriate contracts that are designed to cover the cost to serve them.” But the utility’s critics say it has failed to prove that its contracts with data centers really do protect customers. They also contend that the Republican majority on the commission has rebuffed repeated demands for more transparency into how the requirements might be enforced. Those concerns were heightened earlier this year when OpenAI revealed its plans for a 3.2-GW data center in southeast Georgia. The PSC’s three Republican commissioners outvoted Hubbard and Johnson to approve that contract in August, despite concerns that Georgia Power had failed to publicly reveal the terms under which OpenAI would be held responsible for paying the cost of the utility’s investment in grid and power plant infrastructure to serve it. The few details that Georgia Power has since disclosed haven’t allayed those concerns, said Maggie Shober, research director at the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy. “They have a statement saying, ‘The customer pays its full cost over the life of the contract,’ but no information on minimum bills, termination service, exit fees. It’s just, ‘Trust us, guys,’” she said. But trust is hard to come by these days. Last week’s election made clear just how large a swath of the public has turned against data centers. artigo.texto: On 3 November 2026, voters in ten U.S. states decided more than 40 local ballot questions on data centers, and opponents prevailed in nearly all of them on preliminary results. The one locality reported as an exception was Harwood, North Dakota. For universities, national laboratories and research offices that plan AI and high-performance computing capacity, the vote is a signal about local permitting risk, though it does not change any research funding rule. What happened According to Route Fifty’s report of 4 November 2026, more than 40 local votes on data centers took place the previous night, and opponents were successful in “virtually all 40 ballot measures across 10 states” on preliminary results. Route Fifty attributes the 40-plus figure and the ten-state total to the preliminary results compiled by the Data Centers on the Ballot tracker, run by Redbud Consulting, which notes that it can trail county election offices. Route Fifty reports that Ohio had the most votes, with almost 20 towns, cities and counties voting, and that in every Ohio race data center opponents appeared to have been victorious. It also names Emporia, Kansas, where a prohibition passed with just over 60 percent, and Alhambra, California, which was on track to ban data centers with many votes still uncounted. Illinois, Maine and New Jersey are also named among the states. The exception and the counting caveat In Harwood, North Dakota, about 75 percent of 430 voters, per the North Dakota secretary of state’s office as cited by Route Fifty, rejected a charter amendment that would have required independent review and a public hearing before large industrial projects, including data centers, were adopted. It would have applied only to future projects, not to the campus already approved there. Route Fifty also notes that some of the votes were advisory and not binding on local officials. Totals differ between outlets and will move as counts finish, so treat any single ratio as provisional. The figures above are the ones Route Fifty reported; the tracker, not a news summary, is the place to check final results. Background: how many measures were expected Before the election, Ballotpedia’s News (21 September 2026) counted 38 local data center measures across 35 jurisdictions in 30 counties in eight states, 34 of them scheduled for the 3 November general election. Ohio led with 20 measures across 17 jurisdictions. Ballotpedia reported that 31 of the 38 qualified through citizen petitions and seven were referred by local governing bodies, and that nine were advisory questions. The post-election counts reported afterwards are larger than that pre-election figure, and this page does not attempt to reconcile the two. What it means for researchers, universities and research offices The sources above report local ballot outcomes only. They do not mention universities, national laboratories or research computing. The following points are editorial interpretation, not findings of those sources. - Siting risk is local and political. Facilities that need rezoning, charter changes or development agreements can be stopped by a local vote. Institutions planning new on-campus or adjacent compute halls should check whether their jurisdiction can put such questions to voters and how its zoning process works. - Commercial capacity may be harder to add near you. Researchers who rely on cloud or colocated AI capacity depend on where providers can build. Research offices negotiating long-term compute commitments may want contract terms that account for delayed or relocated capacity. - Community engagement becomes part of the plan. Research infrastructure proposals that involve substantial power or water demand may benefit from early public consultation. Route Fifty’s coverage of the exit polling notes that NBC polling found 56 percent of voters called AI and data centers a crucial or major factor. - Nothing here changes grant rules. This is a local land-use story. Funder policies on computing costs and infrastructure are unaffected by it. For related background, see the CASRAI pages on data management plans and research data management. Sources - Route Fifty, “Voters reject data centers in local ballot initiatives”, 4 November 2026 (read 12 November 2026) - Data Centers on the Ballot, tracker by Redbud Consulting (read 12 November 2026) - Ballotpedia News, “Ohio leads states in number of local ballot measures on data centers for 2026”, 21 September 2026 (read 12 November 2026)

artigo.texto: Partnership will bring advanced BESS solutions to Indian customers and lay the groundwork for local manufacturing SHENZHEN, China and Â PANAJI, India, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Pai Kane Energy (PKE), the clean energy business of India's Pai Kane Group, and Shenzhen Gooree Energy Storage Technology Co., Ltd. (Gooree), part of BTR New Material Group, today signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) for strategic cooperation covering 5 GWh of battery energy storage systems (BESS) for the Indian market by 2030. The MOU was signed jointly at Gooree's offices in Shenzhen. Under the MOU, the two companies will work together to develop India's energy storage market. They will jointly develop BESS products designed for Indian conditions, including the climate, grid requirements and the needs of commercial, industrial and utility customers. PKE will lead product development, sales, project delivery and after-sales service in India, working with its network of EPC and channel partners. Gooree will contribute its product technology, engineering and system integration expertise. The partnership is designed to grow in phases. As deployments scale, the companies plan to move to assembly in India and then explore joint investment in a local manufacturing facility, in support of the Government of India's Make in India and energy storage goals. India has committed to 500 GW of non-fossil power capacity by 2030, and non-fossil sources already account for more than half of the country's installed capacity. As this share grows, energy storage is becoming essential to integrate renewable power, manage peak demand and keep supply reliable for businesses and utilities. Kapil Kane, Co-Founder & CEO, Pai Kane Energy, said:Â "This is a long-term partnership built on trust, transparency and a shared commitment to India. By combining Gooree's technology with Pai Kane's market presence and partner network, we can give Indian customers storage solutions that are safe, reliable and built for local conditions, and over time, made in India." Kevin Zhuo, CEO, Gooree, said:Â "India is one of the most important energy storage markets in the world. In Pai Kane Energy we have found a partner that understands the market deeply and shares our long-term vision. Together we will bring world-class BESS products to Indian customers and build a strong local foundation." About Pai Kane Energy Pai Kane Energy is the energy storage and clean energy business of the Pai Kane Group. It delivers battery energy storage solutions to commercial, industrial and utility customers across India through a network of EPC and channel partners. PKE began operations in 2026 and is based in India, the UAE and China. With design centers and labs in China and an extensive network across the region's battery supply chain, it builds innovative, grid-native products for India and the rest of the world. The Pai Kane Group was founded in 1989 by Atul Pai Kane with the establishment of its flagship company, Power Engineering (India) Pvt. Ltd. The Group manufactures capital goods for the power and infrastructure sector at five plants in India and one in the United Kingdom, with capacity to manufacture 10,000 generator sets every year. It has deployed more than 1 GW of power equipment in 86 countries. A long-established name in India's generator manufacturing industry, the Group acquired British manufacturer Wardpower in March 2018. About Gooree Shenzhen Gooree Energy Storage Technology Co., Ltd. is a green energy technology company specialising in energy storage system solutions, and a joint venture subsidiary of BTR New Material Group Co., Ltd. Gooree's offering combines hardware and software in integrated energy storage systems, together with smart energy operation and full lifecycle service management. Its portfolio covers commercial, industrial and utility-scale systems, and includes BESS built on semi-solid battery technology. BTR New Material Group was founded in August 2000 and is headquartered in Shenzhen. It supplies anode materials, cathode materials and advanced new materials used in batteries for electric vehicles, consumer electronics and energy storage, and has been the world's largest anode material supplier every year since 2010. In 2025, BTR reported revenue of about CNY 17 billion and anode material sales of around 600,000 tonnes. It has production facilities in Indonesia and Morocco. Media contact Dhanusha Prabhu - [email protected]

artigo.texto: Yokohama-based EGI Battery KK launches its Japan Technical Center to strengthen R&D, materials science, and supply-chain capabilities to support advanced lithium-ion battery development, manufacturing, supplier partnerships and customer relationships across Asia Pacific. ANN ARBOR, Mich., Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- EGI Battery, a U.S.-owned lithium-ion battery cell company, today announces the establishment of EGI Battery KK, its Japanese subsidiary, and the official opening of its Japan Technical Center in Yokohama. Japan's history of battery innovation, advanced manufacturing know-how and experienced talent make it a strategic location to bolster EGI's technical operations. EGI Battery KK's Technical Center will initially focus on conducting research & development, evaluating advanced battery materials, and strengthening supplier relationships and technology partnerships to support EGI's advanced battery cell development and commercialization efforts. "Building better batteries takes more than a breakthrough in the lab. It takes capabilities to connect materials, engineering and manufacturing to produce batteries which enable our customers' technology," said Tom McGuckin, CEO of EGI Battery. "Establishing EGI Battery KK is a strategic investment in those capabilities. By connecting Japan's deep battery expertise with the manufacturing operations we are building in Michigan, we aim to bring the next generation of advanced lithium-ion batteries into production and expand what our customers can achieve." EGI Battery KK also establishes a local base for working directly with customers and partners across Asia Pacific. The team will help connect regional market needs with EGI's cell development and commercialization efforts. McGuckin added, "This regional presence deepens collaboration between our technical development activities and our customers' applications." Junji Tabuchi, President of EGI Battery KK, will lead the Yokohama operation, including its technical partnerships and regional business development activities. Tabuchi brings more than 35 years of lithium-ion battery experience across UBE Corporation, NEC TOKIN and E-One Moli Energy, including leadership of battery materials R&D at UBE. "The opportunity is not only to develop better battery materials, but to turn those advances into cells that can be manufactured reliably and meet demanding customer requirements," said Tabuchi. "Our initial focus is on materials, R&D and our supplier partnerships. We are intentionally building a strong technical foundation in Japan so we can move promising research and engineering into commercial production." As the Japan operations develop, EGI Battery KK plans to expand into cell design, with a focus on electrodes, and then battery manufacturing capabilities. These future capabilities will leverage the center's initial materials, supply-chain and R&D activities, strengthening EGI's ability to develop and validate new battery technologies. The Japan Technical Center complements EGI's manufacturing expansion in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Through a phased approach, EGI is building the production capabilities and technical expertise needed to manufacture advanced lithium-ion pouch cells at scale. The Japan operation's initial materials evaluation, R&D and supplier collaboration will support that work, strengthening the connection between battery innovation and U.S. production. About EGI Battery EGI Battery is a lithium-ion battery company delivering the power that makes the next generation of drones, robots, aircraft and vehicles possible. Its team brings decades of combined lithium-ion experience, from materials science and cell design to high-volume manufacturing, giving EGI the know-how to develop innovative cell technology and produce it at scale. To meet growing demand and build a more resilient battery supply, EGI is scaling manufacturing at its Zeeb Manufacturing Center in Ann Arbor, Michigan, where fill and formation is already running and full cell production begins in 2027, providing customers with a direct path to NDAA-compliant cells. The company also operates a technical center in Yokohama, Japan, dedicated to battery materials research and development. The Yokohama team evaluates advanced materials, builds partnerships with suppliers and technology companies, and serves as a local base for customers across Asia. Learn more at egibattery.com. SOURCE EGI Battery Inc.

artigo.texto: A Baterias Moura se aliou à chinesa CATL para produzir sistemas de armazenamento de energia em sua planta industrial em Belo Jardim (PE). Na unidade a empresa já fabrica baterias para veículos. A companhia brasileira é a maior fabricante de baterias do País. A CATL também é fabricante de baterias para veículos automotores, mas detém avançada tecnologia do chamado BESS (battery energy storage systems; sistema de amazenamento de energia em baterias) – a empresa é líder global de sistemas desse tipo. O objetivo da parceria é atender a demanda que será proporcionada com o inédito Leilão de Reserva de Capacidade (LRCAP) por meio de novos sistemas de armazenamento de energia (SAEs), realizado pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) e voltado ao Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), a rede de produção, transmissão e distribuição de energia elétrica do país. O certame será realizado nos dias 2 de dezembro – atendendo critérios de conteúdo local – e 4 de dezembro – para fornecedores internacionais. Há um número recorde de cadastrados para participar do certame: mais de 6 mil projetos, totalizando 296 GW em capacidade. A contratação do governo no leilão pode chegar a 4 GW, segundo fontes do mercado. A previsão de investimento da Baterias Moura para o projeto em Belo jardim é de R$ 200 milhões e prevê a ampliação da planta. Spartacus Pedrosa, diretor de operações de lítio do grupo, a estimativa é de que em meados do ano que vem a fábrica já possa fornecer sistemas para participantes do leilão baseados em armazenamento de energia. O executivo ressaltou ainda que a parceria prevê atingir as exigências de conteúdo local dos sistemas para atender o leilão. A Moura anunciou atender em 8 GWh às empresas participantes do leilão. A empresa brasileira já possui linhas de baterias baseadas em sistemas de armazenamento, mas são voltadas para clientes industriais, comerciais e condomínios. Agora, amplia a atuação com atendimento ao Sistema Interligado Nacional. Ressalta-se que com a chinesa CATL a Baterias Moura já desenvolvia projeto de eletrificação de veículos.

artigo.texto: STOCKTON — The San Joaquin County Board of Supervisors could extend its moratorium on data centers for another 10 months when it reconvenes next week. The board was scheduled to vote on the extension Tuesday, but at least four supervisors were needed to approve the measure. With only three supervisors present, the board continued the discussion to Nov. 17. Although supervisors could not approve the extension, they voted 3-0 to accept a 10-day report prepared by Community Development Department staff outlining steps taken to address the conditions that led to the moratorium. Those steps include a preliminary review of data center development characteristics, such as facility size, electrical demand, water use, cooling systems, backup power generation, battery storage and noise. Staff also reviewed how other jurisdictions regulate data center development to identify potential tools and standards that could apply to the county. Other work includes identifying possible zoning requirements, conditional use permits, noise standards, water and energy considerations, and backup power requirements. The department also plans to finalize an outreach strategy, including public meetings, to gather input from residents and business owners. Data centers are specialized, secure facilities that house computer systems, servers and data storage used for cloud computing, artificial intelligence and business applications. They support a wide range of online services, from streaming to financial transactions. One concern surrounding the facilities is their water consumption, particularly the amount needed to cool servers and prevent overheating. According to the Environmental and Energy Study Institute, large hyperscale data centers can use as much as 5 million gallons of water daily — comparable to the water use of a city with 10,000 to 50,000 residents. The county’s Community Development Code currently has no definition of a data center. Staff previously said it would need at least six months to research the facilities and develop potential regulations. The board approved a 45-day moratorium on Oct. 6. The proposed 10-month extension would continue to exclude ordinary server rooms that are accessory to another permitted business, telecommunications facilities, government emergency communications facilities, hospitals, schools and facilities owned or operated by public utilities. Manteca resident Aaron Meridian urged supervisors to approve the extension when they reconvene, citing the county’s importance as an agricultural resource and its reliance on water. He noted that the Eastern San Joaquin Groundwater Basin has been classified as critically overdrafted. “We cannot spend water we do not have on server buildings,” he said. “Sure, people will tell you the county needs data centers to keep up. Keep up with who? We are not behind, we are already ahead. We do not need to rip out our orchards or pave over our farm land like other counties are doing.” Supervisor Mario Gardea said the moratorium would give staff time to research data centers and provide supervisors with the information needed to make an informed decision. “It’s a very hot topic out there, but before we’re put into a position to make a decision, we’ve got to make sure we’re educated,” he said. “I don’t think any of us up here truly know what is considered a large data center.” Supervisor Robert Rickman said the community deserves answers about how the facilities could affect water supplies, agriculture, public infrastructure and public safety. He also noted that staff reported at least 40 community members had expressed interest in participating in public outreach forums about data centers. “At the end of the day we need to hear from the public, and it’s nice to see that we do have a lot of interest, it appears,” he said. “People do want to be included. We need to understand these reports before deciding whether, or under what circumstances, these facilities should be allowed in San Joaquin County.” Staff expects to present a report on data centers to the board by June. Supervisors Paul Canepa and Steve Ding were absent from Tuesday’s meeting.

artigo.texto: China is taking steps to expand its role in global carbon markets through two new developments announced at COP31 in Türkiye. The country has joined Türkiye and Ethiopia in launching an initiative to strengthen international cooperation on high-quality carbon credits. It has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the International Emissions Trading Association (IETA), which aims to boost the growth and global reach of its domestic voluntary carbon market (VCM). Both announcements were made on November 11, 2026, in Antalya. Together, they signal China’s growing interest in international carbon market cooperation and the rules under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. The new initiative aims to improve cooperation between countries and promote high-quality carbon credit markets. The IETA agreement will boost dialogue, technical cooperation, and knowledge sharing. This will connect China’s market operators with international participants. The developments come as China works to strengthen its domestic carbon market and build closer links with global trading systems. China, Türkiye, and Ethiopia Launch Global Carbon Market Initiative China, Türkiye, and Ethiopia jointly launched the Initiative for Enhancing International Cooperation on High-Quality Carbon Crediting Markets at the COP31 China Pavilion. The initiative aims to encourage cooperation on developing and using high-quality carbon credits. It also provides a platform for countries to exchange knowledge and experience as they expand their carbon market systems. China’s Vice Minister of Ecology and Environment, Li Gao, highlighted the country’s support for multilateral cooperation during the launch. He also described carbon credits as a global public good, saying: “We welcome governments, international organizations and relevant institutions to join us in delivering a new global public good for climate action.” The partnership brings together China, the host of COP31, and Ethiopia, which is set to host COP32 in 2027. Türkiye’s participation also connects the initiative with the current climate conference presidency. The three countries are seeking to promote greater cooperation in carbon credit development and market practices. This includes improving the quality of credits and encouraging wider participation in international carbon markets. However, the initiative should not be confused with a new international carbon trading agreement. Its launch doesn’t automatically allow cross-border credit transfers. It also doesn’t create a system that connects the carbon markets of the participating countries. Instead, it creates a basis for further cooperation and dialogue. IETA and Beijing Green Exchange Target Greater CCER Cooperation On the same day, IETA and the China Beijing Green Exchange (CBGEX) signed a MoU. This agreement will help develop and internationalize China’s Certified Emission Reduction (CCER) scheme. Under the agreement, the two organizations will promote dialogue among policymakers, regulators, and domestic and international market participants. They will also work together on technical cooperation, knowledge sharing, and high-integrity carbon market practices. The partnership could help international market participants better understand China’s domestic crediting system and its rules. It may also support greater cooperation between Chinese institutions and global carbon market organizations. CBGEX plays a central role in this effort. China’s Ministry of Ecology and Environment (MEE) allows it to run the national voluntary greenhouse gas emission reduction trading system. The exchange manages the trading platform for CCERs, which are credits generated by approved domestic emissions reduction projects. These credits can boost income for projects that follow China’s rules on measurement, verification, and registration. The MoU is a strategic cooperation agreement. It does not automatically make CCERs eligible for international trading or use under Article 6. Any cross-border transfer would still need to meet the relevant national and international rules. China’s Domestic Carbon Markets Gain Trading Activity The two COP31 announcements build on China’s efforts to strengthen its domestic carbon market. China operates two main systems. Its national emissions trading system (ETS) covers major industrial emitters and requires them to manage their emissions allowances. The separate national voluntary carbon market allows eligible projects to generate CCERs from verified emissions reductions or removals. China restarted its national voluntary crediting market in January 2024. It had paused new project registrations in 2017 to review its rules and methods. The first batch of new CCERs was registered in March 2025. According to the MEE, these credits came from nine offshore wind and solar thermal projects. They totalled 9.48 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e). - Trading has since increased. In 2025, the voluntary market had 8.84 million tonnes of CCER transactions. This totaled 626 million yuan, roughly $89 million. The average transaction price was 70.76 yuan per tonne. China’s compliance market has also grown. In 2025, its national ETS covered 3,378 key emitters across the power, steel, cement, and aluminum sectors. Trading volume reached 235 million tonnes of emissions allowances, worth 14.63 billion yuan. These figures show the scale of China’s domestic carbon market. They also provide a foundation for its efforts to increase international cooperation. Article 6 Could Create New Opportunities for China China’s growing international engagement comes as countries work to implement Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. Article 6 allows countries to cooperate in meeting their climate targets. Under Article 6.2, countries can transfer internationally transferred mitigation outcomes (ITMOs) through bilateral or other cooperative arrangements. artigo.texto: Riot Platforms is likely to see significant upside from its new powered land lease, according to Jefferies. The investment firm upgraded the digital infrastructure stock to buy from hold. It also hiked its price target to $28 from $13, implying 59% upside from Monday's close. "We are upgrading RIOT to BUY on a Corsicana lease with highly favorable economics (avg. 33% yield)," analyst Jonathan Petersen said in a note to clients. "The powered land lease lets RIOT monetize the site with less execution and financing risk. It also cuts capex to $6M per IT [megawatts] versus $11-15M for a typical data center build." RIOT YTD mountain RIOT year to date The powered land lease will be valid for 15 years, beginning in September 2027. The agreement will earn 33% average yield per year at half the usual capital, he added. Riot can fund the project with project debt or by a tenant in exchange for a rent credit. "We see RIOT's Corsicana deal as a reset for the market," the analyst wrote. "Pairing ready power with the tenant's modular solution improves speed to market, while the powered-land structure reduces RIOT's capital needs and shifts meaningful execution risk to the tenant." Jefferies' call falls in line with consensus on Wall Street. All 23 analysts covering Riot have a buy or strong buy on the stock, LSEG data shows. Shares have jumped 39% year to date.

artigo.texto: Parcerias Smartbird garante capacidade em data center da Expedient para implantações de IA em 2027 Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google A Smartbird assinou um acordo plurianual de hospedagem de equipamentos em data center com a Expedient, garantindo mais de 3,7 megawatts de capacidade de TI em um data center nos Estados Unidos para implantações de infraestrutura dedicada de IA planejadas para o primeiro semestre de 2027. O acordo oferece à empresa uma base física para seu serviço de IA empresarial, na esteira de suas recentes parcerias tecnológicas com a Supermicro e a WEKA. Anunciado em 12 de novembro, o acordo trata de uma limitação prática na implantação de IA: comprar equipamentos de computação não garante um local capaz de fornecer energia, refrigeração e operação para eles. A Smartbird afirma que a instalação da Expedient pode acomodar sistemas de alta densidade, incluindo racks com refrigeração líquida. A capacidade deve atender às oportunidades no pipeline ativo de clientes da Smartbird. O anúncio não identifica a instalação, não divulga os termos financeiros do acordo nem especifica quais aceleradores serão instalados. Por que a capacidade de data center é importante para a IA A capacidade em megawatts indica a capacidade elétrica disponível para os equipamentos de TI. Ela não se traduz diretamente em uma quantidade de GPUs nem na capacidade de inferência de um modelo. Esses fatores dependem dos servidores escolhidos, dos equipamentos de armazenamento e rede que os acompanham e de como a carga de trabalho os utiliza. A refrigeração é igualmente decisiva. A concentração de aceleradores em espaços reduzidos gera muito calor em uma área pequena, o que torna a capacidade da instalação de dissipá-lo parte da arquitetura computacional. A refrigeração líquida transfere calor por meio de um circuito de fluido, em vez de depender exclusivamente do fluxo de ar pelos servidores. A capacidade de acomodar esses racks amplia a variedade de sistemas que uma instalação pode receber, embora o anúncio não esclareça qual será a configuração final da Smartbird. “O acesso à energia e à capacidade de data center preparada para IA é um dos requisitos mais importantes para fornecer infraestrutura em escala”, afirmou Nadia Carlsten, presidente e CEO da Smartbird. Para os clientes, a questão operacional é saber se a capacidade computacional, a energia, a refrigeração e os cronogramas de implantação estão alinhados. Garantir a capacidade da instalação elimina uma dependência desse processo; ainda assim, a instalação do hardware, a integração e o comissionamento determinam quando um cluster poderá começar a realizar trabalho útil. Como funciona o modelo de infraestrutura gerenciada da Smartbird Em seu site, a Smartbird descreve um serviço que abrange projeto de infraestrutura, aquisição, instalação, testes, operações e expansão. O processo começa com a carga de trabalho do cliente e coordena capacidade computacional, armazenamento, rede, energia e refrigeração para atender a esses requisitos. Após a implantação, o serviço inclui monitoramento, manutenção e otimização de desempenho, além de aumentos de capacidade e atualizações de hardware conforme a evolução das cargas de trabalho. A proposta comercial é oferecer às empresas uma infraestrutura dedicada sem exigir que montem e operem por conta própria todas as camadas. Isso é importante para a IA porque os gargalos mudam de uma camada para outra. Durante o treinamento, os aceleradores precisam de um fluxo constante de dados e de comunicação rápida entre os sistemas participantes. Durante a inferência, a capacidade de memória, a latência das respostas e o número de solicitações simultâneas afetam a eficiência com que o hardware atende aos usuários. O resultado útil de um cluster depende do funcionamento conjunto do sistema, não apenas das especificações dos aceleradores. A colaboração anteriormente anunciada da Smartbird com a Supermicro abrange plataformas computacionais e integração em escala de rack. A parceria com a WEKA acrescenta a infraestrutura de dados e memória NeuralMesh à oferta de clusters dedicados da empresa. O acordo com a Expedient abrange a camada de instalações que sustenta essa pilha tecnológica. O que a Expedient oferece à implantação A Expedient opera uma rede de data centers nos Estados Unidos e oferece serviços de nuvem, hospedagem de equipamentos em data centers e infraestrutura gerenciada. Seu serviço de hospedagem de equipamentos em data center permite que organizações instalem seus equipamentos em suas instalações e contem com energia, conectividade, segurança física e suporte operacional no local. A fornecedora informa que oferece redundância N+1 ou 2N para os componentes dos data centers. Essas abordagens disponibilizam capacidade de reserva ou sistemas duplicados para manter o serviço quando algum equipamento fica indisponível. A empresa também oferece conectividade privada entre suas instalações e equipe disponível 24 horas por dia, todos os dias. Esse portfólio mais amplo de serviços explica o papel da Expedient, mas o anúncio não especifica o projeto exato de redundância nem a configuração da rede para a instalação da Smartbird. O acordo tampouco estabelece que os produtos de software de IA oferecidos separadamente pela Expedient farão parte do serviço da Smartbird. Dos acordos com parceiros aos clusters em operação As implantações planejadas para o primeiro semestre de 2027 são o próximo marco. A capacidade de TI reservada define onde os futuros sistemas poderão operar; ela é diferente da capacidade computacional já comissionada e em operação para atender clientes. A abordagem da Smartbird reúne fornecedores especializados em diferentes componentes da infraestrutura: sistemas de computação, a camada de dados e, agora, as instalações físicas. artigo.texto: Ouça este conteúdo Em meio à expansão da inteligência artificial e à crescente demanda por infraestrutura de processamento de dados, o Grupo ABL, de Curitiba, está apostando em um novo negócio para disputar espaço no mercado brasileiro de data centers. A companhia lançou na quarta-feira (11) a Astella, plataforma de infraestrutura digital que integra serviços de armazenamento de dados, computação em nuvem, processamento de inteligência artificial, conectividade e geração de energia. O projeto já recebeu R$ 50 milhões em investimentos no Paraná, considerando a estrutura do data center, localizado no Centro de Curitiba, e uma usina de energia solar em Maringá, no Noroeste do estado. A inauguração marca o início de uma estratégia de expansão nacional, com previsão de outros R$ 300 milhões em aportes até 2028, destinados à implantação de operações em seis novas localidades brasileiras. Para os próximos dez anos, o Grupo ABL projeta um plano de investimentos de R$ 1 bilhão. A operação começa com capacidade energética de aproximadamente 3,5 megawatts (MW), podendo chegar a 5 MW conforme a ocupação e a ampliação da infraestrutura. O data center ocupa um edifício de 16 pavimentos e 8.800 metros quadrados, que já abrigou estruturas de grandes operadoras de telecomunicações e passa por um processo de modernização para atender às novas exigências do mercado digital. Durante o evento de lançamento, acompanhado pela Gazeta do Povo, Agnaldo Lopes, presidente do Grupo ABL, destacou que a iniciativa representa um novo capítulo na trajetória de uma empresa que nasceu em Curitiba há 26 anos e participou da expansão do mercado de telecomunicações no Paraná. "Estamos transformando quase três décadas de experiência em tecnologia, conectividade e infraestrutura crítica em uma plataforma preparada para uma nova demanda do mercado. A inteligência artificial está mudando a escala e a localização da capacidade computacional, e nossa estratégia é construir uma infraestrutura nacional capaz de acompanhar essa transformação com segurança, conectividade e eficiência", afirmou. Inteligência artificial muda as exigências dos data centers A popularização da inteligência artificial está transformando o mercado de data centers. Tradicionalmente utilizados para armazenar informações, hospedar sistemas e disponibilizar servidores para empresas, esses ambientes precisam agora atender também a aplicações que exigem maior capacidade de processamento, consumo energético elevado e sistemas mais eficientes de refrigeração. É nesse cenário que a Astella pretende se posicionar. A infraestrutura de Curitiba foi preparada para receber equipamentos de alta densidade, com soluções de refrigeração líquida, além de oferecer serviços de colocation, modalidade em que empresas instalam seus próprios servidores em ambientes especializados, e computação em nuvem. A proposta também contempla infraestrutura para processamento de inteligência artificial, aplicações com unidades de processamento gráfico (GPUs), recuperação de dados e continuidade operacional. Durante a apresentação, Agnaldo destacou que o objetivo não é atuar apenas como fornecedor de espaço físico e energia para servidores. "Nós não seremos um data center padrão onde se vende energia. Nós iremos vender inteligência", afirmou. Segundo o executivo, a operação foi dimensionada para comportar diferentes configurações de equipamentos e serviços. Em simulações apresentadas durante o lançamento, a estrutura poderia abrigar aproximadamente 4,3 mil servidores físicos ou suportar até 137 mil máquinas virtuais, caso sua capacidade fosse direcionada integralmente a essas modalidades. Os números representam cenários teóricos de utilização máxima, não a quantidade de equipamentos já instalada. A empresa pretende ampliar gradualmente sua capacidade, acompanhando a contratação de clientes e evitando antecipar investimentos elevados em infraestrutura sem demanda confirmada. Energia própria é aposta para reduzir custos e dar previsibilidade Um dos principais diferenciais apresentados pelo Grupo ABL está na integração entre infraestrutura digital e geração de energia. A operação inclui uma usina solar localizada em Maringá, instalada em uma área de aproximadamente 30 mil metros quadrados, com capacidade de geração de 2,7 megawatts-pico (MWp). A unidade já está conectada à rede elétrica e integra a estratégia de abastecimento do data center de Curitiba. Como a geração solar ocorre durante o dia e o processamento de dados exige fornecimento ininterrupto de energia, o modelo também contempla o uso da rede de distribuição e a contratação de energia no mercado livre. A estratégia busca reduzir a exposição às oscilações dos preços de energia, um dos principais componentes de custo desse tipo de operação. "Quem controla o ativo controla custo, quem controla custo controla previsibilidade", resumiu Agnaldo durante a apresentação. Na avaliação do empresário, essa condição poderá permitir contratos de longo prazo com maior estabilidade de custos para os clientes, fator considerado importante para empresas que dependem de infraestrutura tecnológica funcionando ininterruptamente. Agnaldo também ressaltou que a disponibilidade de energia se tornou um dos principais critérios para a localização de novos data centers no mundo, especialmente diante da expansão da inteligência artificial. Curitiba como alternativa à concentração em São Paulo A escolha de Curitiba para sediar a primeira operação da Astella está relacionada tanto à origem paranaense do Grupo ABL quanto à estratégia de descentralização da infraestrutura digital brasileira. Segundo os dados de mercado apresentados pela companhia, grande parte da capacidade nacional de data centers está concentrada em São Paulo e em outros estados do Sudeste. A empresa entende que essa distribuição abre espaço para instalações regionais capazes de atender empresas com menor distância entre os locais de processamento e de utilização dos dados.
