artigo.texto: Jackson County townships move to set data center rules JACKSON COUNTY, Mich. (News 10) - Townships in Jackson County are writing new data center rules before a developer proposes a project in their communities. Napoleon Township passed a 12-month moratorium on new data center projects this week. Summit Township, after its own six-month pause, approved new rules on noise, water use and setbacks. Why townships can’t simply say no Michigan’s Zoning Enabling Act says a zoning ordinance can’t have the effect of totally prohibiting a land use when there is a demonstrated need for it, with limited exceptions. In practice, townships generally can’t shut out data centers entirely, but they can write rules about where and how they’re built. Summit Township writes rules Summit Township Supervisor John Griffin said he wants his community to be prepared, as a nationwide data center boom brings new developments to Michigan. “We practically had nothing on the books. So, it’s like, well, let’s get ahead of this as opposed to just have something plunked down in front of us,” Griffin said. Before the change, Summit’s ordinance allowed data centers by right in all commercial districts. Griffin said the township went with a six-month moratorium, and the new rules took about seven to eight months to finish. “We just thought, let’s put some good guardrails in there,” Griffin said. The township board voted to update its zoning ordinance to make the requirements for developers clear. “It respects the property rights of property owners and developers, but it protects the township as far as health and safety” Griffin said. What the ordinance covers The ordinance targets three concerns: water, electricity and noise. Among its requirements: - Size tiers: Data centers are sorted into small, medium, large and hyperscale based on the size of their footprint, including outdoor power and cooling equipment. - Setbacks: Hyperscale centers, over 100,000 square feet, must sit 300 feet from residential districts and from homes in agricultural districts. Large centers, 50,000 to 100,000 square feet, must sit 100 feet from residential districts. Smaller centers follow existing setbacks. - Water: Data centers generally must use closed-loop cooling or municipal water. - Noise: Sound can’t average more than 55 decibels an hour at the nearest home, not counting backup generators during testing or outages. - Power: Developers must get assurances from their energy supplier that the project’s electric needs can be met. The township says it defers electricity pricing to the Michigan Public Service Commission. - Public input: Before the Planning Commission hearing, a developer must hold a public open house or meeting with at least 15 days’ notice. - Expert review: Every applicant must fund outside experts for the township’s review: the lesser of 0.1% of the project’s estimated cost or $15,000 for small and medium projects, or $75,000 for large and hyperscale projects. Griffin said the township expects to lose about $95,000 in state revenue sharing next year. He said data centers can bring financial benefits to townships, but the rules are meant to protect neighbors. Griffin said there are currently no data center proposals before the Summit Township board. Stream News 10 Lansing on your favorite devices! artigo.texto: India has received 22 bids for 10 GWh of advanced chemistry cell (ACC) manufacturing capacity dedicated to grid-scale stationary storage, in a government tender that strengthens the country’s effort to build domestic battery infrastructure for renewable energy. The Ministry of Heavy Industries said the bids came from companies including Reliance Industries, ACME Solar Holdings, Amara Raja Advanced Cell Technologies, Exide Energy Solutions, JSW Neo Energy and Vikram Solar. The 10 GWh capacity is part of the broader target to establish 50 GWh of ACC manufacturing capacity in India under the National Programme on Advanced Chemistry Cell Battery Storage. The Ministry said the grid-scale allocation is intended to meet the country’s growing energy-storage requirements as renewable-energy capacity expands. According to the Ministry, the additional storage capacity is expected to support energy security and deepen the domestic value chain for ACC technologies. Grid-scale storage can be used to hold electricity and make it available when generation and demand do not match, although the statement did not specify the technologies, project locations or commissioning schedules proposed by the bidders. The ACC battery-storage Production Linked Incentive scheme was approved by the Union Cabinet in May 2021 with a total budgetary outlay of ₹18,100 crore. The programme is intended to develop domestic manufacturing capabilities and attract large Indian and international companies to establish a globally competitive ACC manufacturing ecosystem. The request for proposal was floated on the Central Public Procurement portal on July 15, 2026. A pre-bid conference was held on July 29, and the deadline for submitting bids was November 10. The technical bids were opened on November 11 at the Ministry of Heavy Industries in the presence of bidders, the Ministry said. The bidding process is being conducted online through a two-stage Quality and Cost-Based Selection mechanism. This means the proposals will be assessed through both technical and financial considerations, although the Ministry’s statement did not disclose the evaluation timetable or the next steps for selecting companies. Other bidders named by the Ministry include Avaada Electro, Fujiyama Power Systems, Megha Engineering and Infrastructures, Waaree Energy Storage Solutions, Godawari New Energy, Renew Photovoltaics, Sun Drops Energia, GK Energy, JPM Energy Solutions, Lineage Power, Mahendra Sponge and Power, Nsure Reliable Power Solutions, Sai Bioenergy, Shirdi Sai Electricals, Utex New Energy and Zetsol Energy. The Ministry said the participation reflects industry interest in India’s ACC manufacturing potential and its objective of building a technologically self-reliant, globally competitive and sustainable battery ecosystem. The immediate milestone is the evaluation of the technical bids under the online tender process; the statement did not provide a date for final allocation of the 10 GWh capacity.

artigo.texto: Local opposition to data center construction in the United States has grown throughout 2026. According to Data Center Watch, at least 120 projects worth around $198 billion were blocked or delayed in the first half of the year. Meanwhile, the number of local opposition groups rose to 843 across 49 states. Data centers are the physical foundation on which AI is run, and as a result, the ability to build and operate this infrastructure has become an important global benchmark. The U.S. leads the global data center market with 5,044 facilities as of October 2026 (with the figure rising further in November). The United Kingdom and Germany followed with more than 550 data centers each, while China and France both had fewer than 450 facilities. The same hyperscale providers fueling AI revenue growth are building this capacity, expanding aggressively to secure compute advantages over competitors. However, this expansion is not without issues. In a March 2026 survey by Gallup, 71 percent of U.S. respondents opposed the construction of data centers in their local area. A further survey in April 2026 sought to understand people’s reasons for favoring or opposing the local construction of data centers. Concerns were primarily centered on resource use. Half of opponents cited the impact on energy and water consumption, while others pointed toward quality of life, costs and broader economic effects. Support, in turn, is largely driven by economic factors. Two thirds of those in favor cited reasons such as job creation, local investment and tax revenue, while a further 17 percent pointed to technology benefits. While data centers are critical to supporting AI and digital services, their physical footprint is increasingly visible. Economic gains are clear at a macro level, but local communities often experience the costs more directly. As a result, the next phase of AI growth depends less on whether companies want to build and more on whether energy supplies are sufficient and surrounding communities allow it. artigo.texto: This signal was most prominent in Texas, where Gina Hinojosa, a relatively unknown state legislator, campaigned heavily in opposition to these projects and toppled Greg Abbott, a three-term incumbent governor. Abbott had embraced the data-center boom and only called a pause in August amid alarming poll numbers. The problem is the U.S. needs to keep building data centers, which house thousands of computer servers, to process the clicks and taps that underpin modern life and to harness the productivity gains of an artificial intelligence revolution that is already taking hold in the economy. Productivity gains are what drive wage increases without spurring inflation and are the basis for the high U.S. living standards compared with the rest of the world. The consequence of the election should not be the demonization of data centers but the opportunity to build them with community concerns in mind. What shouldn’t be lost amid all the noise is that data-center construction is booming despite the mounting opposition that morphed into a bipartisan issue and left few politicians to defend these crucial projects — not even the governor of business-friendly Texas. Two suppliers closely tied to data centers, Vertiv Holdings Co. and Amphenol Corp., both reported that third-quarter orders doubled from a year ago, with no visible cracks in demand. The value of U.S. data-center construction jumped 90 percent in September from a year earlier, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. Data-center construction won’t stop, but the results of the midterm election give communities the upper hand in negotiating where and how they will be built, tempering the mad dash to put up these projects and halting some of the community-unfriendly solutions, such as deploying loud jet-aircraft engines as a quick way to generate off-grid electricity. The builders of data centers will be wise to heed the message that they must be more transparent on how these projects will use energy, consume water and create noise. More scrutiny of large projects is welcome to head off abuses that could take place if developers had free rein to build these facilities. Unfortunately, politicians latched on to the public’s concern and then amplified it into irrational fear that now has people discussing these projects as if they were nuclear waste dumps. The opposition has been fueled by the simplistic sound bites, and even disinformation, that flood the social media where many people obtain their news. The biggest obstacle for data centers is access to vast amounts of uninterrupted power supply, which has sparked fear that residential electricity bills will skyrocket. The answer is straightforward: Generate more electricity and shield households from cost increases. More than 200 companies, including the largest power producers and hyperscalers, signed a Ratepayer Protection Pledge at the White House in March, which, among other things, promised that data-center power needs wouldn’t push up residential rates. These promises aren’t mandatory, but the backlash should be fierce if they’re broken. Early signs are encouraging. In a deal to expand Google’s data-center campus in West Memphis, Arkansas, Entergy Corp. plans to add capacity to the grid that it says will result in $500 million of savings for customers beginning in 2028. In addition, Google pledged $25 million over five years for the local community, including workforce training. Similarly, Duke Energy Corp. last month reached a deal with several of the largest tech companies that will protect customers in North Carolina from some data-center costs, including infrastructure such as substations and transmission lines. Water use is often cited by opponents of data centers as a serious drawback, but this has been blown out of proportion. Data centers don’t use nearly as much water as traditional industries including agriculture, chemicals or food and beverages. Besides, recycling technology can reduce data-center water use to negligible amounts. This is where good governance can locate a project away from residential neighborhoods and insist on robust water recycling. Oracle Corp. is using closed-loop cooling technology that doesn’t require continuous water supply for data centers it’s building in Michigan, New Mexico, Texas and Wisconsin. Acoustic panels could help mitigate the low humming noise that opponents cite. The benefits of data centers have been lost in the overheated rhetoric of the midterms. These facilities generate local tax revenue and have a relatively light environmental footprint and social impact. They don’t pollute as much as traditional heavy industries, such as steel, glass or chemicals. They don’t generate heavy truck traffic like typical industrial plants and warehouses do. Most people and politicians support manufacturing more goods in the U.S. Those plants use electricity, consume water, make noise and create more traffic — all of which create local challenges that can be overcome. Should we just throw up our hands and quit making goods altogether? That would be irrational and unwise. The data-center boom will continue because AI has unleashed unprecedented demand that needs to be met. These facilities form the infrastructure backbone of our modern lives and, just as the water faucet and light switch are expected to work, it’s easy to take that for granted. Done right, these facilities will drive the digital revolution while most communities won’t even know they’re there, humming along 24/7 and processing every tap and click. ©2026 Bloomberg L.P. artigo.texto: Minneapolis City Council approves regulations for data centers, but fails to pass complete ban The Minneapolis City Council on Thursday narrowly approved new rules for data centers, but failed to pass an outright ban. In a 7-6 vote, the City Council passed a compromise policy that would create two downtown districts and give council members the opportunity to allow or deny development of specific data centers. The regulations say that the facilities cannot be bigger than 150,000 square feet if it uses renewable energy, or 50,000 square feet for non-renewable energy. The data center must also operate in an existing space, and it cannot be the primary use of a building. Council members Elliott Payne, Robin Wonsley, Soren Stevenson, Jason Chavez, Aisha Chughtai, Jamison Whiting and Aurin Chowdhury approved the regulations. "I think it gives us the conditions to ask a developer what are the things that they're going to put in place to ensure they're going to be a good neighbor?" Chowdhury said. The Council at first considered a full ban on data centers, but the measure failed to pass with six yes votes and seven no votes. Whiting voted against the ban but cast a vote in favor of the compromise policy. The city put a five-month moratorium on data center development back in June. That pause expires on Nov. 21. The measure will head to Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey's desk. Frey and other city staff have said data centers give the city a chance to use vacant buildings and help boost the tax base. The City Council said approximately 1,600 residents weighed in on data centers in comments. Earlier this week, a group rallied outside City Hall in opposition to centers. "They have not proven to be of benefit to the well-beings of regular residents," Wonsley said at the rally. "When we're talking about environmental impact, noise pollution, when we're talking about their consumption of energy that raises residents' utility bills, when we're talking about the contamination of their water sources."

artigo.texto: 16 state senators author sweeping legislation on data centers Senate Bill 338 would address water use, grid connections and tax incentives for large data centers AUSTIN, Texas (KLTV) — Texas senators have filed legislation that would place a range of restrictions on large data centers. Senate Bill 338 generally targets data-center sites with at least 100,000 square feet of facilities. It addresses cooling methods, water reporting, electric-grid connections, tax incentives and construction permits. The bill would require covered facilities to use approved cooling methods, including dry cooling, closed-cycle recirculating cooling and certain systems using desalinated or treated water. Operators would have to estimate their cooling-water needs and sources upfront and report actual use and sources annually. For covered large-load data centers connecting to the ERCOT transmission grid, utilities would have to disconnect a site that uses an unapproved cooling system or fails to submit required reports. The bill would also generally limit municipal property-tax abatements for data centers to no more than 50% of the otherwise eligible property value. Other conditions would apply to certain tax incentives and local grants or loans. State regulators could halt construction or deny or suspend certain stormwater-permit authorizations if a data center does not or will not comply with applicable utility rules. Fifteen Republicans and one Democrat have signed on as authors. Copyright 2026 KLTV. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Residents of Sutton expressed shock and outrage this week when they learned one of Robert Kraft’s companies had proposed building a massive data center complex in their small town 10 miles south of Worcester. But the idea was first discussed in public over a year ago when Sutton’s Select Board was encouraging a packaging company owned by the Kraft Group to develop a large parcel of land it owns on the north side of town, according to videos of public town Select Board meetings reviewed by the Globe. It’s not clear when the Krafts took up the idea, which was discussed Tuesday at a Select Board meeting. In December, a Kraft representative at a Select Board meeting said they had not formally presented any plan to Sutton officials. But there’s no doubt its $16 billion data center plan — potentially one of the largest in the country — has crashed headlong into the powerful political backlash nationwide against the energy-hungry facilities used to develop and run artificial intelligence systems. The Kraft Group did not respond Wednesday to requests for comment. The 383-acre parcel has been used for industrial purposes since the 1930s, according to town filings with the Worcester County Register of Deeds. Before the Krafts owned it, it housed a cement factory and a gravel pit. In 2022, Sutton had given the Kraft company, Unified Global Packaging Group, a tax incentive deal to build a huge warehouse on part of a 383-acre parcel it bought for $9.5 million in 2020. But by 2025, Unified told the town it couldn’t find a tenant for a warehouse and it would have to reboot its plans. At a meeting in March of last year, then-Select Board member Normand Champigny floated some advice on attracting a new major tenant — a data center. He had a modest-size one in mind, known as a co-location facility, or colo. In the meeting video, he said they’re not like the giants: “When I think of [a big tenant], I think of, for instance, a colo like Amazon Web Services.” Amazon’s cloud computing and AI unit lease data centers all over the world. Representatives of the Kraft Group and Unified present at the meeting did not react to the suggestion at the time, according to the video. Another 18 months later, however, they embraced the idea of installing not just a co-location data center, but a massive, AI-capable data campus that would rank as one of the largest in the entire country. Earlier in the meeting, Champigny also suggested the Kraft family should leverage its network of connections to find a tenant for the lot. “I know Jon Kraft is very engaged,” he said, referring to Robert Kraft’s son Jonathan Kraft, who is president of the Kraft Group. To that, the Kraft representative told town officials they were “leveraging those relationships all the time.” Champigny, who is no longer on the board, made his suggestion well before the major backlash against data centers erupted this year. But he foresaw at the time one concern residents might ultimately have: There would be a “a water constraint” because the centers require so much water for cooling. Still, he’d heard that using recycled water “could be the answer.” The current Kraft proposal includes the idea of using recycled water to avoid tapping town supplies. That didn’t mollify Sutton residents who appeared in droves at a Select Board meeting to oppose the new Kraft proposal on Tuesday night. “A facility of this scale would require vastly substantial quantities of water,” said Jessica Herbert, who grew up in Sutton and now resides in neighboring Millbury. Herbert said even if the water will be recycled from waste water, that raises questions over treatment and environmental harm. Reached on Wednesday, Champigny told the Globe he never imagined a data center of the size proposed by the Kraft Group. Co-location facilities are much smaller, he noted, than “the monstrosity” of an AI data center. His first preference for the property would be a sports complex, maybe with tennis courts, soccer fields, and restaurants, he said, modeled after Patriot Place in Foxborough. Ultimately, Sutton residents will get to weigh in, he said. “Town Meeting is their meeting,” he said. “That’s going to have the final say.” Regardless of Champigny’s intentions, whispers of a data center project loomed over the town and persisted throughout the months that followed. At a Select Board meeting on Dec. 9, 2025, members of the public expressed their disdain for a data center — although there was no official proposal on the table. At that meeting, Select Board member Jesse Limanek implied that some data center concept might be in the works but didn’t offer details. “As far as I know, the only ones who received that information were members of our board,” he said cryptically. “If that information somehow got out into the public and it’s incorrect, unfortunately that meant, you know, one of your elected officials shared information that they received in confidence,” he told attendees, according to video of the meeting. At that same meeting, Matthew Piekarski, the Kraft Group representative, said of the rumors: “We have not formally presented anything to the town. We haven’t talked to the town with regards to any specific opportunities within Lot 1 itself.” Limanek has not responded to requests for comment from the Globe. Representatives from Unified were present at that meeting as well. Len McAleer, Unified’s chief operating officer, reiterated at the December meeting that any project built on the empty lot would have to be in “the best interest of the town.” “Data center, no data center, whatever it happens to be, we’re going to put in that area what is in the best interest of the town and us,” McAleer said at the meeting. This week, Town Manager Austin J. Cyganiewicz told the Globe that he first officially heard of the mega-data-center proposal in late October. artigo.texto: AMD pronta para expansão de data centers na América Latina Região representa menos de 2% do mercado mundial de servidores, mas quase 8% dos gastos com nuvem, segundo executivo da fabricante. A AMD prevê uma expansão dos investimentos em data centers na América Latina, impulsionada pela demanda por IA e pela necessidade de manter determinadas cargas de trabalho em infraestrutura local. Segundo Nicolás Cánovas, líder da fabricante para a região, a América Latina representa menos de 2% do mercado mundial de servidores, mas responde por quase 8% dos gastos globais com serviços de nuvem. Os indicadores foram apresentados durante o AMD Partner Summit 2026, realizado entre 9 e 11 de novembro, na região de São Paulo. O encontro reúne representantes de cerca de 70 empresas parceiras e marca os 30 anos de atuação da companhia no Brasil. Para Cánovas, a diferença entre os dois indicadores mostra que a região expandiu sua capacidade computacional principalmente pela contratação de serviços de nuvem, sem desenvolver infraestrutura local na mesma proporção. “A América Latina, além de continuar crescendo como uma região focada em nuvem, terá que desenvolver seus próprios data centers para hospedar as cargas de trabalho e as informações sensíveis”, afirmou. Segundo o executivo, a tendência é de maior utilização de arquiteturas híbridas, que combinam serviços de nuvem e servidores próprios conforme os requisitos de cada aplicação. Os percentuais apresentados por Cánovas não vieram acompanhados do detalhamento das bases estatísticas utilizadas. Atualmente, a AMD registra crescimento das vendas para infraestrutura de processamento. No terceiro trimestre de 2026, a receita global da fabricante alcançou US$ 13,4 bilhões, alta anual de 45%. O segmento de data centers respondeu por US$ 8,5 bilhões, crescimento de 97% em relação ao mesmo período de 2025, impulsionado pelas vendas de processadores EPYC e aceleradores Instinct. Energia e Redata entram na avaliação dos investimentos A disponibilidade de energia, os custos operacionais e as condições regulatórias estão entre os fatores apontados pela AMD para a expansão da infraestrutura computacional na América Latina. Cánovas afirmou que as restrições de espaço físico e de acesso à energia em mercados como Estados Unidos e Europa contribuem para ampliar o interesse pela região. O executivo destacou a importância de políticas públicas, marcos regulatórios e oferta de energia limpa para viabilizar novos projetos. Questionado sobre o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Data Center (Redata), Sergio Santos, diretor-geral da AMD Brasil, manifestou apoio a iniciativas de incentivo à produção local e à atração de tecnologia. “Qualquer programa do governo que incentive a produção local e traga mais tecnologia para o país é sempre bem-vindo”, declarou. Santos também apontou a composição da matriz energética brasileira como um fator considerado nas decisões de investimento e afirmou esperar que projetos em discussão comecem a se materializar em 2027. AMD quadruplica eficiência energética em IA A necessidade de ampliar o processamento sem aumentar proporcionalmente o consumo de eletricidade também orienta o desenvolvimento de produtos da AMD. Em comunicado divulgado em agosto, a fabricante informou ter alcançado, até meados de 2026, uma melhora estimada de quatro vezes na eficiência energética de seus sistemas de IA em relação a 2024. O resultado superou a meta intermediária de três vezes estabelecida para o período. A companhia trabalha com o objetivo de ampliar em 20 vezes a eficiência energética de sistemas de IA em nível de rack até 2030, considerando cargas de treinamento e inferência e utilizando 2024 como referência. Nas projeções apresentadas pela AMD, dois racks de sua futura arquitetura poderão oferecer capacidade computacional equivalente à de 570 racks de referência de 2024. Para a carga de treinamento utilizada no estudo, a fabricante estima uma redução de 20 vezes no consumo elétrico durante o uso e de até 28 vezes na intensidade de carbono. A estratégia envolve mudanças nos processadores, nas memórias, nas interconexões, no software e na arquitetura dos sistemas. Durante o Partner Summit, Santos relacionou a evolução dos processadores à possibilidade de modernizar instalações existentes e liberar capacidade elétrica para novas aplicações de IA. Segundo o executivo, dependendo da carga de trabalho, as soluções da AMD permitem consolidar até 11 servidores antigos em um único equipamento. No ano anterior, a relação apresentada pela fabricante era de sete para um. “Dependendo da carga de trabalho utilizada por uma empresa ou por um hyperescaler, podemos fazer uma consolidação de até 11 para um”, afirmou. Santos explicou que o aumento da densidade de processamento pode reduzir a quantidade de equipamentos necessários, a ocupação física e os custos de refrigeração. A companhia também considera métricas como desempenho por watt, desempenho por dólar e custos de licenciamento nas avaliações de infraestrutura. AMD amplia participação e rede de canais no Brasil Além dos investimentos em infraestrutura, a AMD está expandindo sua atuação no mercado corporativo brasileiro, especialmente entre pequenas e médias empresas. Segundo Santos, a companhia contratou mais de 12 profissionais para reforçar sua equipe de canais e ampliou seu programa de parceiros comerciais, buscando maior integração com as redes de distribuição de fabricantes como HP, Dell e Lenovo. A estratégia está associada à adoção de IA pelas empresas, incluindo aplicações executadas em servidores e computadores com processamento local. “A IA vai muito além do nosso chip. Ela faz parte do ecossistema”, afirmou Santos. O executivo destacou que a comercialização dessas soluções exige que revendedores e integradores ofereçam serviços de implementação, segurança e suporte técnico, além do fornecimento de equipamentos. “Se você vende apenas a caixa, qualquer cliente pode procurar na internet e comprar mais

artigo.texto: BYD’s new EV may be about the size of a Toyota Camry, but it’s playing in a whole different league when it comes to technology. BYD debuts new Cloud Carriage body control system BYD launched the second-generation Seal 07 last week, calling it “the new choice for a class-leading luxury experience.” It’s available in battery electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains, with prices starting at 139,900 yuan (about $21,000) for the plug-in hybrid and 149,900 yuan (around $22,500) for the fully electric version. Both versions measure 5,080 mm long, 1,960 mm wide, and 1,495 mm high, with a 2,960 mm wheelbase, which is slightly longer than the Toyota Camry. Don’t let the price fool you, however, the vehicle is packed with BYD’s latest breakthrough technology. The new Seal 07 EV uses a 76.7 kWh second-generation BYD Blade LFP battery that provides a CLTC range of up to 481 miles (775 km). Thanks to the second-gen Blade Batteries and BYD’s Flash Charging technology, the vehicle’s battery can charge from 10% to 70% in just five minutes. A full recharge, or going from 10% to 97%, takes just nine minutes. The Seal 07 is also BYD’s first vehicle to debut with its new Disus-M Intelligent Magnetorheological Body Control System. The setup features a front double-wishbone suspension and an enhanced rear five-link suspension. It works alongside BYD’s road-surface sensors that use LiDAR, plus its iTAC 2.0 Intelligent Torque Adaptation System. Zhang Zhuo, the general manager of BYD’s Ocean sales division, offered a better look at how the system works in real life in the video shown above. BYD said the system provides ultra-fast response times down to the millisecond. The advanced suspension system adjusts damping force across a wide range of 100 to 10,000 Nm. It’s equipped on the all-electric Flagship Seal 07 variant, while lower-priced versions have the Disus-C intelligent body control system. The top-spec EV model with the Disus-M setup starts at 172,900 yuan ($26,000). Still, not too bad for what you get. Inside, the new Seal 07 adopts BYD’s new interior design, including a 15.6″ floating center infotainment screen, a 10.25″ instrument cluster, and two rear passenger entertainment screens. BYD added a few premium extras, including a built-in 6.8L smart refrigerator, zero gravity seats, and driver headrest audio. Top comment by Dan B Quite impressive for sure. What's more impressive is that GM/Cadillac first offered magnetic ride control back in 2002 (a full 24 years ago!!). It may not have been quite as advanced as this system in 2026, but still one of the most advanced suspension systems offered to date for a line of vehicles. I really want this car!! I truly hope BYD will be able to sell this in the USA soon. The Seal 07 also debuts BYD’s Smart Ecosystem 2.0, including “Diva,” a smartwatch that lets drivers interact with the vehicle and manage functions remotely. Higher-priced versions are available with BYD’s God’s Eye B intelligent driving system, which includes a roof-mounted LiDAR. The setup provides safety and convenience features like Navigation on Autopilot in the city and on highways, plus full-scenario intelligent parking. For a limited time, BYD is offering a “Super trade-in price” special, starting at 145,900 yuan ($22,000) for the new Seal 07 EV and 135,900 yuan ($20,500) for the PHEV version.

artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA Exowatt redesenha seu sistema solar térmico P3 para data centers de IA Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google A Exowatt anunciou o P3 Gen 2 em 12 de novembro de 2026, com o redesenho de seu sistema solar térmico modular para projetos de concessionárias de energia e grandes consumidores, incluindo data centers de IA. A empresa também apresentou o Exobloc, um bloco padronizado de validação de 1 MW, e detalhou os planos para Athena, um empreendimento de data center de 2,4 GW no oeste do Texas. Segundo a Exowatt, o P3 Gen 2 incorpora aprendizados obtidos com a implantação do P3 Gen 1 e mais de 7.000 horas de testes. A arquitetura revisada tem como objetivo melhorar o desempenho, simplificar a instalação e a manutenção e facilitar a fabricação. Seu fator de capacidade mais alto aumenta a quantidade de energia firme que o sistema pode fornecer. O P3 capta a luz solar na forma de calor, armazena esse calor por longos períodos e o converte em eletricidade quando necessário. A captação solar, o armazenamento e a geração são integrados a uma arquitetura padronizada, que pode ser fabricada em escala e montada em sistemas maiores para atender à demanda dos clientes. A Exowatt chama esse método de neotérmico, diferenciando a captação de calor solar e o despacho baseado em armazenamento da geração térmica convencional. O CEO e cofundador Hannan Happi afirmou: “A IA está criando uma demanda por energia mais rapidamente do que a rede consegue ser construída. Acreditamos que a resposta é transformar a infraestrutura energética em produtos: torná-la padronizada, replicável e menos cara à medida que a escala aumenta.” Isso posiciona o Gen 2 como parte de uma estratégia mais ampla de fabricação e implantação de infraestrutura energética para IA. Exobloc e software de gestão de energia O bloco Exobloc foi projetado para que os clientes testem o desempenho do P3 e seu funcionamento em conjunto com outros recursos energéticos em condições reais, antes de avançar para instalações maiores. O objetivo declarado pela Exowatt é reduzir os riscos da implantação e acelerar a expansão por meio desse processo de validação. A Exowatt também está desenvolvendo um sistema de gestão de energia com IA para coordenar o P3 e outros recursos de geração e armazenamento como uma única usina despachável. O projeto combina monitoramento e controle em tempo real, previsão e despacho automatizado, permitindo que o software ajuste a geração, o armazenamento e o fornecimento de energia à medida que as condições mudam. Os controles críticos funcionariam no local, em uma arquitetura que prioriza a computação de borda e opera independentemente da conectividade com a nuvem, enquanto protocolos padrão do setor permitiriam a integração com a infraestrutura energética existente. Assim, o projeto combina a continuidade local dos controles essenciais com a coordenação de uma composição variável de recursos energéticos. O plano de Athena para o oeste do Texas Segundo a Exowatt, Athena é o primeiro local do ExoRise, seu braço de desenvolvimento de data centers, lançado em janeiro de 2026. O projeto no oeste do Texas faz parte da estratégia Frontier Land da empresa, que tem como alvo o desenvolvimento de infraestrutura de IA em regiões com abundância de terras e recursos renováveis e potencial para construir capacidade energética em escala. Segundo a Exowatt, o local foi projetado para funcionar com 80% de energia renovável. A combinação de recursos proposta reúne mais de 800 MW de energia solar no local e em áreas adjacentes, geração eólica com alto fator de capacidade e geração do P3, além de 2,4 GWh de armazenamento. Está prevista uma conexão separada à rede da ERCOT como parte do Batch Zero, com 1.200 MW distribuídos em duas fases. Os três anúncios apresentam uma estratégia integrada: redesenhar o hardware, validá-lo em blocos padronizados e coordená-lo com outros recursos por meio de software. Athena oferece um projeto específico para essa abordagem, embora sua combinação de recursos energéticos e conexão à rede ainda sejam planos. Para concretizar as ambições de expansão da Exowatt, o Exobloc é a etapa prática de validação: implantações maiores de energia para IA exigem evidências de que o P3 funciona e se integra conforme previsto em condições reais.

artigo.texto: Captona, a North American energy transition investment firm, has partnered with Sunrun to finance 9,400 residential solar and storage projects across more than 20 US states. The preferred equity investment covers 74 MW of solar generation and 110 MWh of battery storage. Sunrun said the project-level financing structure is designed to facilitate tax credit monetization and senior debt placements. Earlier this month, Sunrun expanded its distributed power plant in Puerto Rico to more than 60,000 customers. It now represents nearly 70,000 home batteries capable of delivering 45 MW of dispatchable power for up to four hours to support grid stability. Philippines-based renewable energy developer RASLAG Liwayway has secured a Certificate of Authority (COA) from the Department of Energy (DOE) for its proposed 98.24 MW AC/132.034 MW DC solar power project integrated with 25 MW/120.38 MWh of BESS. The project is located in Nueva Ecija, Philippines. It will be developed in two phases, each combining approximately 67.09 MW DC/49.92 MW AC of solar capacity with a 12.5 MW/60.19 MWh BESS. The COA follows an assessment of the project's technical and financial feasibility and marks a step toward implementation, RASLAG said. Denmark’s European Energy has agreed to sell a 50% stake in its 323 MW solar portfolio in the country to pension investment companies administered by Danish pension provider Sampension. The portfolio comprises the operational 148 MW Glejbjerg and 175 MW Holsted solar parks in Vejen, along with a planned 87 MW/351 MWh BESS. The transaction will strengthen the existing partnership between the companies, says European Energy, which also includes joint investments in Latvia and Greece. The deal is expected to close in December 2026. UK-based independent power producer (IPP) Elgin has acquired its sixth project in Italy, a planned 72 MW facility in Belvedere di Aquileia, Udine, in the Friuli Venezia Giulia region. The project will combine a 57 MW agrivoltaic plant with a 15 MW BESS, with an estimated construction cost of €46 million. The facility will use elevated solar modules and monitoring technologies to enable electricity generation alongside continued agricultural activities. Elgin said the acquisition supports its goal of developing more than 3 GW of renewable energy projects in Italy by 2030. UK-based project developer Ampeak Energy has completed the delivery of all batteries and key components for its 240 MWh Afon Wysg 1 (AW1) BESS project in Wales. Located at Uskmouth Sustainable Energy Park, the project includes 55 battery units supplied by e-STORAGE, a subsidiary of Canadian Solar, along with 36 inverters and associated grid infrastructure. It is expected to be energized in November 2026 and enter commercial operation in Q1 2027. Ampeak also plans to expand the project to 480 MWh. Jinko ESS, the energy storage arm of Chinese solar manufacturer JinkoSolar, has delivered BESS with a combined capacity of approximately 65 MW/260 MWh across Australia. These projects are located in Victoria, New South Wales, and South Australia. The projects include standalone battery systems and solar-plus-storage installations. Jinko ESS has supplied its flagship SunTera G2 liquid-cooled battery systems and served as the BESS integrator, while Spain-based Ingeteam provided the power conversion systems. Jinko ESS said it has delivered more than 600 MWh of storage capacity in Australia. Revolta AG, a German technology startup developing battery systems and power electronics, has installed and commissioned its first 10 kWh sodium-ion home battery storage system at a customer site in Germany. The system, near Aschaffenburg, comprises five battery modules. It is installed at a property that already houses around 20 kW solar PV system and a small hydroelectric power plant. Revolta says the installation marks the commercial launch of its residential sodium-ion storage solution. It plans to commission additional systems at selected customer sites across Germany in the coming weeks. Revolta is the recipient of funding from the State of Hesse under the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) to develop sodium-ion AC battery for households, even those without rooftop solar. This includes rental apartments. Spanish renewable energy company Umbrella Global Energy has expanded its contract with ceramics manufacturer Pamesa Grupo Empresarial by €11.6 million to extend the Pamesa Net Zero project in Spain. The expansion will add 6.71 MW of solar PV capacity and 51 MWh of BESS across Pamesa’s additional industrial sites and existing facilities. The project integrates solar generation, battery storage and intelligent energy management technology supplied through Umbrella subsidiaries IM2 Energía Solar and Turbo Energy. The expansion builds on an initial €73.6 million contract signed in 2025, covering 80.56 MW of solar generation and 366.84 MWh of storage. Alinta Energy, an Australian energy retailer and power generator, has commissioned its 100 MW/200 MWh Wagerup BESS project in Western Australia. The facility has been operating commercially since September 2026. Alinta said the project faced challenging site conditions that required design changes, including raising the battery platform and constructing retaining infrastructure. It adds storage capacity to Alinta Energy's generation portfolio.

artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA Modine inicia a produção de chillers no Texas para data centers de IA Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google A Modine anunciou o início da produção comercial em 11 de novembro de 2026, em uma nova fábrica de chillers da Airedale, com 682.000 pés quadrados, em Grand Prairie, Texas, ampliando a capacidade de fabricação nos Estados Unidos de equipamentos para refrigeração de data centers. A unidade, construída especificamente para esse fim, é dedicada à fabricação de chillers de 2 MW e 3 MW com resfriamento livre. A capacidade adicional é voltada a provedores de nuvem em hiperescala, operadores de colocation e ambientes de computação de IA de alta densidade. O presidente e CEO Neil D. Brinker descreveu o lançamento como um marco no plano de expansão da capacidade da Modine nos Estados Unidos e afirmou que instalar capacidade perto dos clientes tem o objetivo de apoiar a entrega de sistemas de refrigeração projetados sob medida. Ampliação gradual da produção em Grand Prairie A linha de produção inicial está em operação. A Modine tem como meta colocar quatro linhas em operação até o fim do atual ano fiscal, condicionada ao comissionamento dos equipamentos, à preparação da força de trabalho e a outras considerações operacionais. Atualmente, a unidade opera em um turno, com planos de ampliar sistematicamente a operação para três turnos. A Modine espera que Grand Prairie se torne a maior unidade de fabricação de chillers da Airedale em sua rede global. Os chillers fazem parte de um portfólio mais amplo da Airedale, que inclui resfriadores secos, unidades de distribuição de líquido refrigerante e controles inteligentes. Segundo a Modine, os sistemas são projetados para atender a demandas térmicas complexas e de alta densidade, maximizando a eficiência energética e hídrica. Investimento na capacidade dos Estados Unidos por trás da unidade A Modine anunciou o investimento de US$ 100 milhões em 29 de julho de 2025, prevendo então que os recursos seriam aplicados nos 12 a 18 meses seguintes para ampliar a capacidade de fabricação de produtos de refrigeração de data centers na América do Norte. O plano abrangia uma nova unidade na região de Dallas, a expansão da fábrica em Grenada, Mississippi, e a possível reutilização de unidades existentes da Performance Technologies em Franklin, Wisconsin, e Jefferson City, Missouri. O plano também incluía melhorias nas capacidades de engenharia, desenvolvimento de produtos e testes, além da criação de novos empregos e do apoio à realocação e à requalificação de funcionários existentes. Eric McGinnis, então presidente do segmento Climate Solutions da Modine, descreveu a expansão como uma estratégia de produção local para atendimento local, concentrada nas regiões onde a Modine observava a maior demanda. Planos para a unidade de Grand Prairie e para o emprego A cidade de Grand Prairie anunciou a escolha do local pela Modine em 14 de outubro de 2025, identificando o endereço 2100 Refuge Way como a localização e projetando a criação de mais de 1.000 novos empregos, com remuneração anual média de US$ 66.760. A Modine mencionou a localização na região de Dallas–Fort Worth, a infraestrutura de transporte, a proximidade do Aeroporto Internacional de DFW, o acesso a uma força de trabalho qualificada, apoiado por programas regionais de treinamento, e a colaboração com funcionários da prefeitura. O cronograma original da cidade previa o início das obras no quarto trimestre de 2025 e o começo das operações no primeiro trimestre de 2026. O início da produção anunciado ocorreu depois dessa previsão operacional inicial. No mesmo anúncio de investimento, Brinker definiu como meta da administração que a receita total de data centers se aproximasse de US$ 2 bilhões no ano fiscal de 2028. Grand Prairie transforma parte desse programa em capacidade operacional; a dimensão de sua contribuição no curto prazo para essa meta depende agora da conclusão de uma ampliação condicionada ao comissionamento dos equipamentos e à preparação da força de trabalho.

artigo.texto: Ars Technica will host a live discussion on drone attacks on data centers on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, at 1:00 p.m. Eastern Time. The session carries the title “Drone attacks and data centers: New Risks for Big Tech.” According to the announcement, drone and missile strikes have damaged data centers in Eastern Europe and the Middle East this year. The same announcement says those strikes disrupted cloud services for millions of people. It also says some Amazon Web Services customer data was permanently deleted. That last detail matters most. An outage is a bad afternoon, while deleted data is a business problem that never fully heals. We cover this story four days before the stream, so many questions remain open. Our earlier report on Sberbank’s AI plans after an Oct. 14 drone hit showed how fast the topic moved from theory to boardroom planning. This analysis lays out what the announcement confirms, what it leaves blank, and what cloud buyers should do while the facts firm up. Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. What Ars Technica Is Hosting on November 17 This Ars Live session tackles a risk that cloud customers rarely put in a spreadsheet. The event will stream on YouTube and will take audience questions. Ars Technica reporter Jeremy Hsu joins the discussion, and Joseph Jarnecki, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), appears as the outside voice. The table below collects every event detail we can confirm. Anything missing from it, such as a run time or a full guest list beyond the two names, stays unconfirmed. Readers who want to ask a question should plan to submit it live. The announcement does not describe a pre-submission form, so we will not claim one exists. What the Announcement Says About Drone Attacks on Data Centers Strip the announcement to its factual core and four claims remain. Drone and missile strikes damaged data centers this year. The damage happened in Eastern Europe and the Middle East. Cloud services went dark for millions of people. Some AWS customer data was permanently deleted. The announcement also names the incident groups on the agenda. Those include Amazon facilities in the Middle East, plus Russian and Ukrainian data-center attacks. That framing tells us the discussion covers more than one conflict zone and more than one operator type. It spans a hyperscale cloud provider on one side and national infrastructure in an active war on the other. The announcement gives no confirmed count of damaged sites. It offers no tally of affected customers, no outage totals, and no figure for how much data disappeared. We treat any precise total circulating on social media as unconfirmed until Ars Technica or the operators publish one. Drone warfare has already reshaped adjacent infrastructure questions. Our look at Ukraine’s fiber-optic drones and the pressure on fiber supply shows how battlefield technology can collide with the physical backbone of digital services. Data centers sit on that same backbone, which makes them a natural point of overlap. The AWS Data Deletion Detail Changes the Conversation Cloud sales pitches lean on durability. Customers hear that data gets copied across machines and buildings so a single failure never costs them anything. The announcement’s line about permanently deleted AWS customer data cuts against that story, at least for the customers who were affected. We do not know which customers lost data, how much they lost, or why their copies failed to survive. We also do not know whether those customers had configured cross-region copies. That last point decides how the story reads. If the lost data lived in a single location by choice, the event shows a customer configuration gap. If it lived in a protected setup and still vanished, it shows a provider design gap. Either answer carries a lesson. Under the shared-responsibility model that major clouds describe, the provider secures the facility while the customer decides how many copies of their data exist and where. A strike on a building forces both halves of that arrangement into the open. Recovery planning gets less attention than it deserves, and the cost of ignoring it shows up in client behavior. Our piece on how ransomware recovery shapes client trust at managed service providers makes the point that customers judge a vendor by how it handles the bad day. A physical attack is a different threat from ransomware, but the trust math works the same way. What Is Confirmed and What Is Not Breaking stories attract numbers that nobody can source. The table below separates what the announcement supports from what it does not, so readers can weigh claims they see elsewhere. A fair reader should notice the pattern. Every confirmed item is qualitative, and every missing item is a number. That gap is normal this close to an event, yet it limits how far any analysis can go. We build our reasoning on the structure of the problem instead of on invented totals. Who Is Speaking: Jeremy Hsu and Joseph Jarnecki Jeremy Hsu is the Ars Technica reporter attached to the discussion. Joseph Jarnecki holds a senior research fellow post at RUSI, a British defense and security think tank. The pairing makes sense. One voice brings technology reporting, and the other brings a security-policy lens. We found no on-record quotation from either person in the available material, so this article attributes no statements to them. Expect the live stream to supply their actual views. Readers should treat any paraphrase of their positions published before November 17 as speculation. Their presence does signal how the topic is now framed. A defense research institution joining a tech-news event suggests the discussion treats data centers as strategic infrastructure, not just as commercial real estate. That shift in vocabulary is itself news for the cloud industry. Why Physical Attacks Break the Cloud’s

artigo.texto: Global Carbon Council (GCC) joins as a founding member of the UNCTAD-convened network, alongside leading financial institutions, exchanges and carbon market organizations, to strengthen market integrity, advance international cooperation and mobilize climate investment for developing economies. Antalya, Türkiye – The Global Carbon Council (GCC), the first independent carbon crediting standard established in the Global South, headquartered in Qatar and internationally recognized under UN ICAO's CORSIA scheme and ICVCM, has joined a global coalition of leading financial institutions, exchanges and carbon market organizations as a founding member of the Global Carbon Market Network, officially launched at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye. The launch ceremony was held at the Arab Climate Pavilion, jointly hosted by GCC and the League of Arab States in the COP31 Blue Zone, bringing together hundreds of participants in person and virtually, including climate experts, government representatives, financial institutions, carbon market organizations, standard-setting bodies and other stakeholders. The launch featured keynote addresses by Mr. Pedro Manuel Moreno, Acting Secretary-General of UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD); Ms. Nan Li Collins, Chair of the UN Sustainable Stock Exchanges Initiative and Lead of the World Investment Forum; H.E. Eng. Salim bin Nasser Al Aufi, Minister of Energy and Minerals of the Sultanate of Oman; Mr. Sammy Sau Kuen Yeung, Commissioner for Climate Change of Hong Kong SAR (China); and Dr. Yousef Alhorr, Founding Chairman of the Global Carbon Council (GCC). Their participation highlighted the importance of international cooperation in strengthening carbon markets and advancing climate finance. Convened by UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD), the network aims to strengthen connections between carbon markets, improve transparency and investor confidence, and facilitate climate finance for mitigation projects, particularly in developing countries. The Global Carbon Market Network addresses persistent market fragmentation caused by differing regulatory frameworks, standards, registries and trading systems. Rather than establishing another carbon market or competing standard, it seeks to connect existing voluntary and compliance markets, improve interoperability and promote consistent market practices. Its launch comes as emissions trading systems and carbon taxes cover nearly 30% of global greenhouse gas emissions and generated more than USD 107 billion in public revenue in 2025. Yet stronger market connections are needed to translate carbon pricing into greater investment in measurable emissions reductions and sustainable development. Speaking at the launch, Dr. Yousef Alhorr, Founding Chairman of the Global Carbon Council (GCC), emphasized the importance of cooperation, market integrity and equitable access to climate finance. “The future of carbon markets will not be determined by how many markets we create, but by how effectively we connect them, build trust and translate carbon transactions into measurable climate impact. The Global Carbon Market Network represents an important step towards overcoming fragmentation, strengthening international cooperation and unlocking climate finance, particularly for developing countries. “At GCC, we believe market integrity, transparent infrastructure and institutional readiness must advance together. Through our expertise in Article 6 readiness, capacity building and digital MRV, we aim to support more inclusive and credible carbon markets. Ultimately, success must be measured not simply by the volume of carbon traded, but by genuine emissions reductions, tangible benefits to local communities and progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals.” From Market Fragmentation to International Cooperation The network will promote cooperation among carbon market institutions, exchanges and financial stakeholders, focusing on market integrity, emissions measurement and verification, digital technologies and interoperability. Stronger connections between registries, trading platforms and financial institutions could reduce transaction costs and improve market access for project developers. The initiative also recognizes the role of non-state actors, including private sector institutions and financial intermediaries, in mobilizing climate finance beyond traditional public funding. Ahead of the launch, UNCTAD Acting Secretary-General Pedro Manuel Moreno expressed hope that the network would make carbon pricing a more effective instrument for reducing emissions and mobilizing climate finance for developing countries. "Carbon markets can play a role in putting a price on emissions and mobilizing finance for climate action, but their effectiveness depends on trust, integrity and functioning market infrastructure," said Nan Li Collins, UNCTAD's Director of Investment and Enterprise and Chair of the UN Sustainable Stock Exchanges Initiative. A Global Coalition of Founding Members The Global Carbon Market Network brings together institutions from Africa, Asia, the Middle East, Europe and Latin America, representing a diverse range of carbon market and financial stakeholders. Alongside the Global Carbon Council (Qatar), founding members include: Astana International Financial Centre Authority, Capacity Building Alliance for Sustainable Investment (China), Casablanca Finance City (Morocco), Climate Impact X (Singapore), Colombian Association of Carbon Market Actors (ASOCARBONO), Financial Services Development Council (Hong Kong, China), Indonesia Stock Exchange, Johannesburg Stock Exchange, Macao International Carbon Emission Exchange, Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority, UK Carbon Market Forum, Verra, and Voluntary Carbon Market Company (Saudi Arabia). artigo.texto: BMW Group has contracted Samsung SDI in Europe and LG Energy Solution (LGES) in the US as additional cell suppliers for its Gen6 high-voltage batteries. Following the nominations, the car maker will receive European-produced cells from CATL, EVE Energy, and Samsung SDI, whilst LGES will deliver cells within the US. The appointments follow the company's "local for local" principle, whereby components are acquired close to vehicle assembly locations wherever possible. Both manufacturers will supply BMW Group from their established regional plants beginning in the late 2020s. BMW stated that targeted localisation across Europe, Asia, and North America reduces transit distances and bolsters supply security, while a globally diversified network supports flexibility and resilience. Assembly of the Gen6 high-voltage batteries will take place at five newly constructed facilities adjacent to vehicle plants in Debrecen, Hungary; Shenyang, China; Woodruff, US; San Luis Potosí, Mexico; and Irlbach-Straßkirchen in Lower Bavaria, Germany. Series production of the batteries commenced in Shenyang last month. Following Debrecen and Irlbach-Straßkirchen, Shenyang is the third location in the new global production network for Gen6 battery technology. BMW added that localising industrial value creation remains highly complex, particularly for cell production, requiring heavy investment and supply arrangements with global technology leaders willing to set up operations locally. It added that fostering regional battery ecosystems over the long term depends on feasible political regulations and attractive local conditions for the necessary industrialisation periods. The group also retains internal development, production, and recycling capabilities at three Bavarian competence centres. The Battery Cell Competence Centre in Munich investigates new cell technologies, whereas the Cell Manufacturing Competence Centre in Parsdorf tests near-series cells and evaluates high-quality, resource-efficient production. In Salching, German circular economy service provider Encory will construct and operate the Cell Recycling Competence Centre, recovering raw materials using BMW's direct recycling method to reintegrate into production. BMW purchasing and supplier network management board member Nicolai Martin said: "We aim to ensure our products' global competitiveness and to be successful in different markets. To achieve this, we operate as locally as possible in our value chains, leveraging the potential of our global procurement markets. Through our battery cell partnerships, we are actively strengthening value creation in Europe and the US." artigo.texto: SAN JOSE, Calif., Nov. 11, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- QuantumScape Corporation (NASDAQ: QS), a global leader in solid-state lithium-metal battery technology, today announced Osprey: its next-generation open platform for all-solid-state batteries. Osprey cells have delivered the world’s first public data demonstrating a sulfide-based cathode cycling 1,000 times under just one atmosphere of pressure - an unmatched capability that is necessary for automotive solid-state batteries. Osprey pairs the QS proprietary ceramic separator and anode-free lithium-metal design with a solid cathode, creating an all-solid-state cell. Osprey builds on the company’s QSE platform, and opens new licensing and co-development options for current QS customers and expanding its offering to developers of sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries. QS technology has demonstrated an enhanced safety profile compared to conventional lithium-ion cells, along with low operating pressure and excellent energy retention. Osprey’s all-solid cathode, paired with the proprietary QS ceramic separator, enables additional performance benefits, including faster charging, operation across a wider range of temperatures, and projected energy densities up to ~1,100 Wh/L. In early testing, Osprey cells have demonstrated: - Cycle life: 1,000 full charge cycles with ~80% capacity retention under gold-standard testing conditions - Fast charging: 10% to 80% in five-minutes - Low pressure: Requires only one atmosphere of pressure - Cold-weather performance: Operational to less than -20 °C (-4 °F) More information, including test results and conditions, can be found in a new white paper. The battery industry has long pursued all-solid-state batteries using sulfide-based electrolytes, but this has yet to result in a commercially viable technology. Sulfides can react with lithium metal, which shortens battery life, and they typically need to be held under high pressure to operate, which is impractical for vehicles and many other applications. Osprey is conceived as an open platform capable of working with a range of cathode chemistries. QS has tested Osprey with all-solid cathodes developed both in-house and by its automotive customers, laying the groundwork for multiple technology pathways for solid-state battery development. "Osprey is the result of years of frontier R&D efforts, and we’re excited to share it publicly for the first time,” said Dr. Siva Sivaram, president and CEO of QS. "The industry has invested heavily in sulfide-based batteries but keeps hitting the same fundamental limits. As the data shows, Osprey can address these limitations. We believe Osprey can unlock the full potential of all-solid-state batteries, and our goal is to make it the leading platform for solid-state battery development.” QS is already working with partners across the automotive industry on development using the Osprey platform. Cells based on the company’s QSE platform are shipping to customers today, and Osprey represents its long-term technology solution for all-solid-state battery development. About QuantumScape Corporation QuantumScape is on a mission to revolutionize energy storage to enable a sustainable future. The company’s next-generation solid-state lithium-metal battery technology is designed to enable greater energy density, faster charging and enhanced safety to support the transition away from legacy energy sources toward a lower carbon future. artigo.texto: Reno pauses new data center approvals as officials weigh water, power rules RENO, Nev. — Reno’s decision to pause new data center approvals has intensified questions about how much water and power the facilities could require — and which agencies actually have the authority to decide whether more can be built. RELATED: No new data centers in Reno: Council adopts temporary moratorium, starts drafting rules Data centers are large facilities that house computer servers and related equipment that support internet services, cloud computing and artificial intelligence. Centra, the company building a data center off Keystone Avenue, describes its facilities as “engineered from day one to support modern digital services and AI workloads.” As the region weighs what rules should apply to future projects, the Truckee Meadows Regional Planning Agency is studying how data centers could affect Northern Nevada. Jeremey Smith, the agency’s director of regional planning, said the agency’s role is not to approve or deny projects, but to provide research and recommendations. “In the data center conversation specifically, our role is to research, provide factual information about data centers and growth in the region of data centers,” Smith said. “And we were asked to come up with recommendations and best practices.” Smith said data centers are tied to growing technology use. “We’re working as a society and we’re using our phones, we’re use more computers,” he said. “It’s underpinning the digital economy, if you will.” One concern highlighted in the research is electricity demand. “The power demand is unprecedented for data centers. I mean, it’s huge,” Smith said. RELATED: NV Energy’s new long-term plan highlights massive power demand tied to data centers NV Energy said the potential demand tied to data center proposals in Nevada totals 22,000 megawatts — roughly enough to power 20 million average U.S. homes at once. Jeff Brigger, NV Energy’s vice president of business development, said the utility is required to serve customers. He also said data center developers would be responsible for major upfront costs tied to the infrastructure needed to supply them. “They also would pay upfront costs for the transmission infrastructure that we need to build to serve them essentially, growth pays for growth,” Brigger said. Water is another major issue. The Truckee Meadows Water Authority plans for the region’s water needs, and about 80% to 85% of the water it provides comes from the Truckee River — a key reason residents have been asking how much water additional data centers could use. Danny Rotter of TMWA said the data centers currently in progress account for a relatively small amount of water use. “The six data centers that we have underway right now use only about 22 acre-feet, or about 50 to 60 homes’ worth of water,” Rotter said. While public utilities provide information and plan for the resources a data center would need, local leaders use those plans when making final decisions about whether projects can move forward. Newly elected Mayor Kate Marshall said she opposes placing data centers in Reno neighborhoods, including the Keystone Avenue area. “Data centers don’t belong in our town. They don’t belonging in your neighborhood. They don’t belong near your child’s school or next to your grocery store. And they certainly didn’t belong on Keystone Avenue,” Marshall said. Reno’s moratorium on new data centers runs through Aug. 31, 2027 — or until the city adopts regulations and rules for approving new data centers

artigo.texto: Critical minerals price swings stall energy storage projects Fri, 13th Nov 2026 (Today) DLA Piper has published research showing that 23% of energy storage participants have seen viable projects deferred or cancelled because of volatile critical minerals prices. The survey identifies price instability as a significant barrier to investment across the sector. Based on responses from 550 participants across the energy storage supply chain, the research found that 52% view critical minerals price volatility as a major constraint or a dealbreaker for investment. Of that group, 12% said it was the primary constraint or an outright dealbreaker. The effect appears to extend beyond early investment decisions. The survey found that 28% of respondents reported delays to project delivery, while the same proportion said they were struggling to secure bankable long-term offtake agreements. Another 27% said investment decisions had been pushed back, and 26% reported a higher cost of capital. The data comes as scrutiny of critical minerals supply chains intensifies, with market participants weighing exposure to raw material price swings alongside regulatory and financing risks. Respondents identified the difficulty of committing capital in the face of uncertain future commodity prices as the biggest obstacle to investment. Regional divide The survey found marked differences between markets. In the UK, 56% of respondents said volatility was a major constraint and 16% described it as a dealbreaker. In the US, 46% called it a major constraint and 18% a dealbreaker. Germany stood apart from the other markets surveyed. Just 8% of German respondents described volatility as a major issue, and it was the only market in which no respondent called it a dealbreaker. Italy was also more likely to treat volatility as a minor factor, while in Australia more than half of respondents said it was one of several material considerations rather than the defining risk. The research also identified China as more likely to classify volatility as a minor concern, reflecting its position in the global supply chain and its influence over benchmark indices. Alex Jones, Energy and Natural Resources partner at DLA Piper, said: "While financing difficulties and regulatory delays remain key challenges, our research suggests that price volatility is now one of the most significant factors holding back investment in energy storage. "Unpredictable pricing pressures are creating a domino effect across the sector, reducing investor confidence, constraining financing and structuring, and ultimately contributing to project delays, repricing and, in some cases, abandoned projects." Supply response Participants also reported strategic changes as companies try to reduce exposure to swings in minerals markets. The survey found that 37% of developers, including hyperscalers, OEMs, utilities and independent power producers, are pursuing vertical integration to gain greater control over supply. Among mining and raw materials producers, 32% said they were taking the same approach. The report cited POSCO Holdings in South Korea as an example of this model, with operations spanning upstream resources, refining and recycling. The findings also showed that miners were the group most likely to respond to price spikes by applying more conservative valuations, at 34%. Another area of change is pricing structures. Respondents said many companies are reassessing contracts that rely on benchmarks shaped largely by the Chinese market and are exploring alternative reference points. Component-linked pricing, in which contracts refer to battery or cell indices rather than the spot price of the raw mineral, was the most widely supported alternative. It was backed by 37% of respondents overall and 46% of battery and technology manufacturers. Lenders were most likely to favour contractually guaranteed price floors, at 43%, while developers preferred hybrid structures combining different approaches, at 46%. Mining and raw materials producers leaned towards long-term fixed pricing with periodic resets, at 48%. Oliver Wright, Energy and Natural Resources partner at DLA Piper, said: "For years, companies have had to depend on supply chains they do not control, and recent volatility has shown how quickly pricing and supply terms can shift. "As a result, developers and miners are now actively working to secure the stretch of the chain they depend on most, from the mine through the refinery to the recycling plant, so that a squeeze upstream no longer disrupts their operations. But control over supply risks only solving part of the problem. For many niche critical minerals, there isn't an index, so you can't rely on index-based pricing. And where indices do exist, they are often influenced by China. That's why, based on our research, we expect the industry to shift what contracts are priced against, whether that is component-linked pricing, price floors or hybrid structures."

artigo.texto: The dust from last week's rout of AI-related stocks is settling. But the damage is done. Confidence in these companies' foreseeable futures is weakened. Even names outside the heart of artificial intelligence mania have been upended. Take GE Vernova (NYSE: GEV), for instance, which simply makes power-generating equipment used by some AI data center owners. Shares of this industrial outfit are down 25% since their early October high, with much of this setback materializing just this month following concerning quarterly reports from Alphabet and Nvidia. There may be some degree of misunderstanding regarding GE Vernova's business, however, that needs to be clarified. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » An important detail You may be aware that GE Vernova manufactures a number of power-related solutions, ranging from transformers to wind turbines to hydropower equipment. But its leading product line right now is natural gas turbines, accounting for most of last quarter's $6.1 billion in revenue from its power division, which was nearly half of its total top line of $12.6 billion. Sales of this arm's wares improved 25% year over year, while orders for future deliveries of power equipment -- still mostly natural gas turbines -- jumped 178% to $21.8 billion. Yes, artificial intelligence data centers are now using gas turbines as secondary or even primary power sources, and yes, some data center owners and operators are purchasing this equipment from GE Vernova. That's why its stock's been so vulnerable to worries of a sudden slowdown in AI's anticipated growth. Just don't lose perspective on the matter. As CEO Scott Strazik said of Vernova's power division in last month's third-quarter conference call, "Demand also remains diverse, with approximately 100 customers in 25 different countries, of which approximately 80% are traditional customers and 20% are for data centers." In other words, GE Vernova isn't nearly as vulnerable to a contraction in artificial intelligence capital spending as the stock's recent sell-off suggests. Tailwind outside of AI There's some nuance to consider. While most of GE Vernova's gas turbine buyers are more traditional institutions like utility companies, many of these buyers are still purchasing this equipment to provide electricity to data centers. As Goldman Sachs notes, data center demand for power alone is set to more than double between last year and the end of 2027.

artigo.texto: O Acre deu um importante passo em direção à certificação internacional de seus créditos de carbono. Na terça-feira, 10, em Antalya, na Turquia, a governadora Mailza Assis participou de uma reunião com a ART Trees, entidade responsável pela validação de projetos de carbono, para discutir o progresso da auditoria necessária ao reconhecimento dos créditos jurisdicionais do estado. A reunião ocorreu durante a 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas (COP31). O encontro é um desdobramento das articulações realizadas em junho, durante a Semana de Ação Climática em Londres, onde Mailza se encontrou com Mary Grady, presidente da ART Trees. Também participaram da reunião Neide de Lima, presidente do Instituto de Mudanças Climáticas e Regulação de Serviços Ambientais (IMC), Victor Hugo Rondon, consultor internacional de mercados de carbono, Madson Cameli, chefe de gabinete, e Lúcia Madrid, diretora associada da ART. O principal objetivo da reunião foi atualizar o status da auditoria e alinhar procedimentos para avançar na certificação. O reconhecimento internacional permitirá ao Acre registrar créditos de carbono jurisdicionais, facilitando futuras negociações no mercado internacional. Mailza expressou sua gratidão pela disponibilidade da ART e reiterou o compromisso do governo em concluir o processo, afirmando que “estamos colocando um grande esforço, por meio do IMC, para concluir esse processo, que será muito importante para o desenvolvimento do Acre.” A auditoria está sendo conduzida por uma empresa independente que segue os critérios do padrão internacional ART Trees, que estabelece normas para a contabilização e verificação de reduções de emissões decorrentes do desmatamento e degradação florestal. Neide Lima destacou a importância de cumprir todos os requisitos previstos para a conclusão satisfatória da etapa, com o Acre atualmente na oitava de 11 etapas do processo de certificação. Entre os próximos passos, estão a finalização das verificações técnicas e a submissão dos resultados ao conselho deliberativo da ART. Uma nova fase da auditoria está prevista para o primeiro trimestre de 2027, quando auditores visitarão comunidades no Acre para realizar verificações. Neide também ressaltou a dimensão social do processo, enfatizando que os recursos obtidos com a comercialização dos créditos devem contribuir para o desenvolvimento das comunidades locais. Victor Hugo Rondon sublinhou a necessidade de assegurar que todas as exigências internacionais sejam cumpridas, levando em conta as prioridades sociais e ambientais do governo acreano. A Companhia de Desenvolvimento de Serviços Ambientais (CDSA) também será envolvida nas próximas etapas, especialmente nas estratégias relacionadas às negociações dos créditos certificados. O governo do Acre espera que a certificação abra oportunidades para atrair investimentos em agricultura familiar, extrativismo sustentável e iniciativas de preservação ambiental. A certificação envolve uma avaliação independente para assegurar que os resultados ambientais atendam aos requisitos estabelecidos, com cada crédito de carbono representando uma tonelada de dióxido de carbono equivalente (CO₂e) cuja emissão foi reduzida ou removida. O IMC continua promovendo agendas estratégicas durante a COP31, defendendo a valorização das comunidades e apresentando projetos de desenvolvimento sustentável para ampliar o diálogo com governos, investidores e instituições internacionais.
