artigo.texto: 10/11/2026 As negociações dentro do governo em torno do Redata (Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter) avançaram, segundo relataram interlocutores à Agência iNFRA. No entanto, há alguns aspectos relacionados ao setor elétrico que ainda precisam ser pacificados, dentre eles, a possível exigência de aquisição de energia nova para abastecimento dos data centers. A expectativa é que o decreto seja publicado ainda em novembro, após a participação do presidente Lula na COP31, na Turquia. O setor aguarda o governo definir se será necessário que os empreendimentos comprem energia de usinas novas, construídas para o seu abastecimento, ou recém-construídas, conforme o conceito de “adicionalidade energética”. O tema divide agentes no setor. Outra negociação ainda na mesa é quanto à cobrança de encargos dos data centers. Segundo interlocutores, os investidores querem ser isentos do pagamento da CDE (Conta de Desenvolvimento Energético) por meio da celebração de contratos de autoprodução por equiparação. Também é esperada a lista de fontes de geração que serão aceitas, com expectativas do segmento de gás natural para que a molécula seja incluída. Adicionalidade A exigência de novas usinas para atender os data centers não é um consenso. De um lado, há empresas que veem na adicionalidade uma possibilidade de expansão dos negócios. Do outro, há geradores com usinas que ficarão descontratadas que miram esse mercado e avaliam que erguer novas plantas de geração tiraria a competitividade dos projetos e acarretaria custos para o sistema elétrico. Na última sexta-feira (6), o presidente Lula falou sobre o tema e defendeu que os empreendimentos de data centers construam suas usinas. O presidente disse que os centros consomem muita energia e que “quem vier investir [que] construa a sua própria energia”. Ele continuou: “Não vai ser a energia do povo que vai ser usada para data center”. A preocupação está em linha com o que se observa em países onde o desenvolvimento de data centers já está mais avançado, como os Estados Unidos. Lá, a população viu a conta de energia aumentar em algumas regiões. Autoprodução Também circula nos bastidores que o Ministério da Fazenda levou à mesa de discussão uma proposta para que os empreendimentos sejam enquadrados como autoprodutores de energia. Dessa forma, os data centers ficariam isentos do pagamento da CDE – a conta que reúne os custos dos subsídios do setor elétrico. Com a possibilidade aventada, os técnicos do MME (Ministério de Minas e Energia) fazem agora o cálculo dos impactos dessa renúncia. Eles analisam se é possível “reduzir os danos”, disseram fontes. Na autoprodução por equiparação, o consumidor da energia se torna acionista da SPE (Sociedade de Propósito Específico) da usina. Dessa forma, é equiparado ao autoprodutor “clássico” – que investiu em geração própria para atender ao empreendimento consumidor. Gás natural Quanto às fontes de suprimento, a resistência de parte do governo federal à inclusão do gás natural está menor, segundo pessoas a par das tratativas. Agora, a tendência é que o decreto contemple o insumo, ainda que com condicionantes, como compensação pelas emissões de carbono. Os secretários-executivos dos ministérios de Minas e Energia, da Fazenda, da Indústria e Comércio e da Casa Civil reuniram-se na última semana, ocasião em que o MME defendeu o gás natural. Interlocutores afirmam que a Fazenda – que vinha travando a entrada do gás – passou a admitir a possibilidade de incluir a fonte. Falta, agora, fechar o modelo das condicionantes. No MME, a intenção é que as compensações de carbono mantenham os projetos de gás viáveis. No setor, no entanto, os agentes estão preocupados com os termos, que podem onerar os investimentos e acabar restringindo, na prática, a implementação de térmicas a gás para abastecer os data centers. Algumas possíveis formas de compensação aventadas nos bastidores são o uso de tecnologia de CCUS (Captura, Utilização e Armazenamento de Carbono, na sigla em inglês) ou a aquisição de créditos de carbono. Riscos Agentes ligados ao segmento de gás natural vinham demonstrando temor com a possibilidade de o gás ficar totalmente fora da regulamentação do Redata. Agora, admitem que esse risco é menor, mas ainda agem com cautela e dizem que será preciso ver os termos impostos pelo governo nas condicionantes. Uma regulamentação restritiva por causa das condicionantes, segundo um executivo, pode afastar investimentos em térmicas colocalizadas com data centers e pressionar as tarifas de energia. Isso porque os centros de dados poderiam ter de usar energia da rede nos horários com escassez de energia renovável, aumentando a demanda por potência. Caso o decreto vete ou restrinja o gás, o setor cogita buscar alterar os termos da regulamentação via Congresso. Isso poderia ser feito por meio de um PDL (Projeto de Decreto Legislativo). “Ficou claro que o Legislativo, ao aprovar o Redata, não quis restringir nenhum combustível de baixa emissão, como o gás natural”, comentou um agente termelétrico. Por outro lado, os geradores renováveis apontam que as termelétricas a gás natural emitem mais carbono do que os limites estabelecidos internacionalmente, de aproximadamente 0,10 tonelada de gás carbônico por MWh (megawatt-hora). Dessa forma, essas usinas não se enquadrariam na exigência da lei. Atraso O diretor de Relações Institucionais e Governamentais da Brasscom (Associação das Empresas de Tecnologia da Informação e Comunicação e de Tecnologias Digitais do Brasil), Sergio Sgobbi, diz que a demora na regulamentação tem afastado os investidores, que estão buscando outras alternativas. Ele aponta que é essencial a publicação das regras de habilitação e coabilitação dos empreendimentos, e a lista de equipamentos que terão os tributos federais desonerados para aquisição. “Enquanto a regulamentação não vier a público, tudo é incerto e, diante da incerteza, o investimento não vem. artigo.texto: Could tech giants eye Florida for data centers after midterms? AUBURNDALE, Fla. - A fierce political and environmental clash is brewing in Auburndale, where more than 1,000 residents mobilized against a proposed hyperscale data center amid fears that nationwide tech restrictions will drive massive industrial projects to Florida. Auburndale data center pushback What we know: More than 1,000 residents packed a public workshop Tuesday night to fight a proposed data center. Community members sounded alarms over persistent noise, environmental pollution, and declining property values. Midterm elections and data centers The backstory: Tech companies face tightening rules across the country following the recent midterm elections. Democratic governors in Texas, Georgia, and New Mexico plan to impose strict moratoriums and regulations on the sector. Florida emerged as an outlier after Republican Rep. Byron Donalds narrowly defeated Democrat David Jolly in the gubernatorial race with millions in tech industry backing. Donalds shifted his tone during the campaign from fully pro-business to remaining open to development while adopting caveats and restrictions. Florida remains highly attractive to developers because tech firms already operate across the state, alongside an existing multinational talent pool. The state also possesses robust power grids and extensive fiber-optic infrastructure that help hyperscale facilities manage extreme cooling demands. Shifting tech industry landscape What we don't know: Officials have not yet confirmed whether municipal leaders will approve or block the facility's construction permits. State authorities have not detailed how proposed statewide caveats will interact with local zoning ordinances. Balancing economy and community What they're saying: AI strategist Dr. Jill Schiefelbein emphasized that data center expansion transcends partisan labels. "When it comes to data centers, I don’t think this is a red state versus blue state issue at all," Schiefelbein said. "I think there are much more nuanced perspectives that go into it. Will companies be looking at Florida? Yes, 100 percent they will be. But will it become the next hotbed for data centers? Only time will tell." Schiefelbein added that state officials face a precarious balancing act between regional investment and neighborhood preservation. "I think there will be a fine line the government will have to walk between being pro-business—because there are some massive economic gains that can be realized by the state when you have tech and data centers move in—versus what the short, medium, and long-term consequences are for the everyday resident," Schiefelbein said. The Source: The information in this story was gathered from FOX 13 reporter Carla Bayron, who attended the public workshop and interviewed AI strategist Dr. Jill Schiefelbein, as well as public election statements from gubernatorial candidates.

artigo.texto: While many Americans resist, China embraces AI data center boom Ulanqab, China — Off a major highway on the outskirts of Ulanqab, in the Chinese province of Inner Mongolia, Hereford cows roam through corn fields scouring the ground for any dried up remains of the recent harvest. Hovering over the landscape are shiny new transmission towers linked by power cables that stretch along the plateau for as far as the eye can see. On the ridgeline, covered in snow, wind turbines spin, taking full advantage of the ever-blowing wind. The energy pulsing from the remote Chinese region — a combination of renewables and fossil fuels — will soon power multi-story data centers being constructed on farmland as part of a sprawling AI data center construction boom. The construction site is the size of a small American city. It is the biggest, and fastest growing infrastructure project anywhere in China right now. This corner of Inner Mongolia was famous for generations for growing potatoes. Now, it's fast becoming an AI hub, and Chinese officials hope the expansive, rugged landscape will help power the country's ambition to surpass the U.S. as the global leader in artificial intelligence. Baletu, a 72-year-old farmer, who has lived here for more than 40 years growing potatoes and corn, said the changes across his local landscape are positive. "It doesn't affect my farmland, not at all," he told CBS News. "It's good for the area." A short drive away, CBS News was able to see what all that wind power will soon be feeding. Trucks, cranes and thousands of workers are taking part in the construction project to create one of the biggest data centers anywhere in the world. We drove miles down new roads with multistory data centers going up on either side. Even from the road it was easy to spot the countless racks that will hold servers, semi-conductor chips and cooling and exhaust fans. There are dozens of data centers being built in Inner Mongolia, more than any other part of the vast nation. The reason they have chosen Ulanqab is because it offers cheap, abundant energy. Fossil fuels are still the main source of power here, but they also use renewables, including wind and solar. Ulanqab is one of the most consistently windy locations in the province. The climate is also cold all year, which helps keep cooling costs down, and land and labor are more affordable in the remote region. Experts cited by the Financial Times say data centers in China are built at about one-fifth of the costs incurred in the U.S., not least due to the much higher land and labor costs. As many as 30,000 workers have been brought in from across China to help build the AI hub, and in a country experiencing an economic downturn and high youth unemployment, these mass infrastructure projects are very much welcome. "Development is the best thing, especially when it provides job opportunities for many young people," a local businesswoman who sets up a lunchtime food stall outside the construction site told CBS News. While data centers in the U.S. face major community opposition, which could be emboldened by the "blue wave" of the Democrats' stunning midterm election performance, there are few hurdles for Chinese developers. While China's government doesn't generally tolerate protests of any kind, and it tightly controls messaging across all media, a United Nations survey last year found that as many as 80% of people in the country support data center construction. At least two-thirds of Chinese people use AI in their day-to-day life, as many embrace the technology and the infrastructure behind it. Under President Xi Jinping, AI development has become a national strategic priority for China. "There is no opposition to data centers in China. It's never heard of, whereas in the U.S., it has become a huge movement against data center building in neighborhoods," Henry Wang, founder and president of the Center For China and Globalization, told CBS News. Huawei, Alibaba, Byte Dance, Deepseek, Baidu, Z.ai, ZData and VNET — China's biggest AI companies — are all active in Inner Mongolia. In areas where construction has finished, fences are up and grounds are landscaped, and avenues through the humming data centers have been named after the AI tech giants. While Chinese firms' AI models are believed to be about six months behind their U.S. competitors, due largely to restrictions on the sale of high-end microchips, the gap is narrowing. China has more than double the power generation capacity of the U.S., and some experts believe access to power, not chips, will ultimately be the deciding factor in the global race for AI dominance. "Chips may not become the latest diving criteria," said Wang. "It may be that power is the bottleneck, and whoever goes through that first gets the advantage. And right now. China has the edge."

artigo.texto: Storey County weighs data center growth as jobs and tax revenue rise Concerns are growing in Storey County as more data centers move into the area, but local officials and industry advocates say the facilities are bringing major construction work and tax revenue to the rural county. RELATED: Reno pauses new data center approvals as officials weigh water, power rules Storey County Commissioner Clay Mitchell said there are fewer than 10 data centers operating in the complex. He said each project can support hundreds of construction jobs, even if the permanent workforce is much smaller. “The same data center that may employ 20 to 50 people when its running may take 500 to 800 to build,” Mitchell said. Mitchell also said some of the jobs tied to data centers do not require higher education. “So with a high school diploma, maybe a couple of technical certificates. We're finding starting wages in the $65,000- $75,000 a year range, average is six figures,” he said. WATCH: Mitchell said jobs are not the only draw for Storey County. “Even after the abatements that the state gives out, we have pretty significant tax revenue that comes through,” he said. Draft revenue numbers show Switch, described as one of the largest operators, paid more than $9 million in taxes during the 2025–26 tax year. Nearly $5 million went to Storey County. About $12 million in taxes were abated, meaning Switch received that amount in tax breaks. Mitchell said the abatements reduce certain taxes but do not eliminate all of them. “They pay the full freight on property taxes for the building and the land. What they pay in taxes on the equipment that goes in and on the building gets reduced significantly,” Mitchell said. Tray Abney, who leads the Nevada Data Center Alliance, said the tax revenue and jobs make data centers worth the tradeoffs, as long as they are built in appropriate locations. “As long as, again, you put these things in the right places,” Abney said. “You hear a lot of people say, I don't wanna live next to a data center. That makes sense. I don't wanna live to a gigafactory or any large industrial buildings, right? I will tell you that most local governments, if they have industrial zoning, 99% of their problem is taken care of.” Abney says the alliance works to educate public officials and be vocal about what the industry does and jobs they provide. He is working to bring the topic of data centers up at the next legislative session.

artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA PSI detalha a receita de seus data centers por trás de suas ambições de pesquisa em IA Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google A TechCrunch informou em 10 de novembro de 2026 que a Physical Superintelligence obtém sua receita atual usando suas ferramentas para otimizar data centers, enquanto busca construir, no longo prazo, um negócio baseado na descoberta de fenômenos físicos com auxílio de IA. O CEO Matt Pines descreveu o objetivo como transformar avanços da física teórica em tecnologias concretas. Os data centers são o primeiro campo de provas dessa abordagem, onde os sistemas de pesquisa em IA da PSI, que ela chama de físicos virtuais, podem atuar em sistemas físicos reais sujeitos a restrições operacionais mensuráveis. A PSI é uma empresa de benefício público, com segurança, verificação, desenvolvimento responsável e amplo benefício público estabelecidos em seu estatuto. Em sua página da empresa, informa ter mais de 25 pesquisadores e engenheiros e ter captado mais de US$ 58 milhões, em uma rodada liderada pela Breakthrough Energy Ventures. Data centers como campo de provas comercial O trabalho atual de otimização simula calor, energia, água e som, relacionando o desempenho das instalações e seu impacto nas comunidades à física de cada local. Em sua página sobre sua visão, a PSI afirma que constrói modelos de alta fidelidade de instalações em operação para que os físicos virtuais possam examinar o sistema por completo, identificar restrições ocultas e testar intervenções. Os resultados pretendidos incluem maior densidade computacional, uso mais eficiente da energia, melhor gestão térmica e maior eficiência de capital. As campanhas comerciais também fornecem subsídios para a pesquisa. Segundo a PSI, instalações em operação impõem restrições que não seriam propostas em simulações, e cada campanha treina os físicos virtuais usados nas campanhas seguintes. Assim, o negócio de data centers cumpre duas funções: gerar receita no presente e fornecer restrições práticas que ajudam a aprimorar o sistema de pesquisa. Um sistema de pesquisa baseado em verificação Pines descreveu um sistema de pesquisa eficaz como uma combinação de estruturas de software em torno de modelos, ferramentas, sistemas de memória e infraestrutura de simulação, que permite explorar um problema em amplitude e profundidade, considerando uma ampla variedade de alternativas. A PSI formaliza esse processo como uma Campanha Autônoma, um esforço contínuo que vai da definição do problema à formulação de hipóteses, verificação, experimentação, engenharia e implantação. Cada campanha tem marcos mensuráveis, etapas rigorosas de verificação e um caminho para a aplicação, enquanto os pesquisadores humanos escolhem as missões e os critérios de sucesso. A arquitetura separa a geração de candidatos da verificação. Entre as verificações estão as leis de conservação, a simetria, a consistência dimensional, a demonstração formal, a simulação, os gêmeos digitais — contrapartes virtuais de sistemas físicos — e as medições físicas. A PSI afirma que os verificadores que certificam um resultado também podem se tornar funções de recompensa, ou sinais de treinamento, para os físicos virtuais usados posteriormente, vinculando diretamente a avaliação ao aprimoramento do sistema. O anúncio de pesquisa de 6 de novembro de 2026 da PSI fornece um exemplo. A empresa afirmou que seu sistema desenvolvido internamente, executando um modelo da Anthropic que ainda não era público na época, produziu uma demonstração completa da conjectura de Aaronson–Ambainis no terceiro dia de uma execução; o Lean, um assistente de demonstração que verifica cada etapa, aceitou o resultado e, posteriormente, aceitou uma versão final após duas melhorias. Em aberto desde 2008, a conjectura trata das situações em que computadores quânticos podem ser exponencialmente mais rápidos do que computadores convencionais ao processar entradas aleatórias. David Turturean liderou o trabalho com acesso antecipado ao Claude Fable 5.2, que a Anthropic apresentou publicamente em 9 de novembro de 2026. A validação física continua sendo o teste comercial A demonstração também ilustra um limite à comercialização. A matemática e a ciência da computação podem expressar resultados em código validado, mas a física e as ciências da vida ainda exigem contato experimental com a natureza. Pines disse que a PSI está trabalhando em formas eficientes de validar resultados computacionais por meio de experimentos, resumindo a diferença com a observação de que “a natureza também tem voz nos seus modelos da realidade”. Pines também disse que a física teórica ainda não é, em sua maior parte, domínio das máquinas, apesar de ter apresentado aos investidores, de seis a nove meses antes, uma tese mais contundente, embora condicional. Essa ressalva é importante para os negócios da PSI: sua receita atual depende da otimização de instalações, enquanto sua ambição mais ampla exige descobertas validadas que possam se tornar dispositivos ou outras tecnologias. Pines relacionou um fato da natureza validado à possibilidade de construir um dispositivo com capacidades antes indisponíveis. Para a PSI, portanto, a questão comercial é saber se seu processo de geração e verificação pode produzir repetidamente resultados confirmados por experimentos, permitindo que o mesmo sistema de pesquisa passe da otimização da infraestrutura de IA à criação de tecnologias baseadas em nova física.

artigo.texto: A new global network will launch at the UN climate summit COP31 on 12 November in Antalya, Türkiye, aiming to tackle fragmentation in carbon markets and help channel more investment into climate projects, particularly in developing countries. Convened by UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD), the Global Carbon Market Network will seek to strengthen links between carbon and capital markets, improve transparency and credibility, and facilitate cross-border transactions. Carbon markets remain fragmented across different standards, registries and trading systems. Concerns over credit quality, transparency and double counting have weakened confidence and constrained market development, particularly in developing economies. Ahead of the official launch, UNCTAD Acting Secretary-General Pedro Manuel Moreno expressed hope that the Network would help make carbon pricing a more effective tool for reducing emissions and mobilizing climate finance for developing countries. Connecting fragmented carbon markets “Carbon markets can play a role in putting a price on emissions and mobilizing finance for climate action, but their effectiveness depends on trust, integrity and functioning market infrastructure,” said Nan Li Collins, UNCTAD’s Director of Investment and Enterprise and Chair of the UN Sustainable Stock Exchanges Initiative. The Network will promote cooperation among exchanges and market institutions, including technical work on market integrity, measuring and verifying emissions reductions, and digital technologies to improve transparency and reduce transaction costs. Why it matters now Carbon pricing is expanding. Emissions trading systems and carbon taxes now cover nearly 30% of global greenhouse gas emissions and generated more than $107 billion in public revenue in 2025. The UNCTAD-convened Network will not create a new carbon market or standard. Instead, it aims to connect existing markets and initiatives, including voluntary and compliance markets. Voluntary carbon markets have particular potential to channel private investment across borders. UNCTAD research shows that most voluntary carbon credits are generated by projects in developing countries and sold to buyers in developed countries. Stronger links between markets could help build confidence in these transactions and expand financing for projects that reduce or remove emissions in developing countries. Who is participating and what’s next? The Network’s initial activities include capacity-building programmes, market-practice benchmarking, a global synthesis report on the state of carbon markets, and engagement with emissions trading system regulators on technical and interoperability issues. Founding members span Africa, Asia, the Middle East, Europe and Latin America.

artigo.texto: West Sedgwick County group raises concerns about data center size, location Planning committee to discuss data centers in Wichita Thursday WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH) - The group ‘Renwick Area Against Data Centers in West Sedgwick County’ says its name is not the full story. “We are not anti-technology,” said Kaitlyn Gruenbacher, a member of the group. “We are not anti-data center. However, we do have some issues with these hyper-scale sites that they think are appropriate to put anywhere in the county.” Gruenbacher says they just want the data centers to be right for Sedgwick County. “This is laying the groundwork for how we’re going to see data centers in our community, if we want to see data centers in our community,” Gruenbacher said. The two main issues the group has are location and size. Right now, data centers can be placed anywhere, and there are no limits on their sizes. “Neighbors talk to neighbors, and we honestly were just trying to understand what was happening,” Gruenbacher said. Currently, a moratorium against data centers is in place in Sedgwick County. However, that does not bring comfort to Gruenbacher. “The moratorium right now only goes through December,” Gruenbacher said, “The moratorium also can be extended or it can be removed at any time, so it could end as soon as the commissioners feel that they have enough information.” On Thursday, the Advanced Plans Committee, a subcommittee of the Wichita-Sedgwick County Metropolitan Area Planning Commission, is meeting to discuss data centers. Gruenbacher is hoping the committee listens to the people. “I think best case scenario for the meeting tomorrow is that advanced plans chooses to listen to the public, and really take that feedback and show that they can take that guidence,” Gruenbacher said. The Advanced Plans Committee meeting will take place at 10 a.m. on Thursday in the Ronald Reagan Building, 271 W. 3rd Street, in downtown Wichita. Copyright 2026 KWCH. All rights reserved. artigo.texto: Trending A proposed natural-gas fired, electrical generating station in Oliver County would offer numerous economic benefits in the region, according to a project spokesperson who presented at the Minot Area Chamber EDC's Energy Committee meeting in Minot Monday, Nov. 9. Base Electron's proposed Missouri Bend Energy Center will be a 1,200-megawatt, natural gas-driven facility designed to support the electrical needs of a nearby data center, said Tyler Hamman, the company's vice president of Community Engagement and External Affairs. The generation plant will be somewhat larger than the state's current largest generating facility, lignite-fueled Coal Creek Station near Underwood, which is just over 1,100 megawatts. Another natural gas facility, Basin Electric's approximately 1,490-megawatt Bison Generation Station, is under construction in Williams County. Base Electron is working on permitting through the county and will be filing for permits with the North Dakota Public Service Commission and North Dakota Department of Environmental Quality. The hope is to break ground next spring, Hamman said. Operational startup could happen in the second half of 2030. Base Electron, headquartered in Plano, Texas, is an independent power producer, incorporated in December 2025. The company formed specifically to provide power generation for large industrial loads, particularly data centers. "We have the same co-founders as Applied Digital, but we're organized as a separate company," Hamman said. Base Electron's first anchor project is the proposed Applied Digital data center in Oliver County. The company plans to build a $2.4 billion steam turbine electrical plant in association with a long-term power purchase agreement with Applied Digital. "Those dollars are going to recycle several times throughout the community by the time it's all said and done. So, pretty significant investment for the region, a lot of construction jobs," Hamman said. "We're guessing it's probably going to be about 300 (workers) on an average rolling basis throughout the construction period, but we hope to get about 1,000 on site for a short period of time in 2028. Sixty to 70 full-time jobs once we finish operations. So, those will be anything from technicians, maintenance, operators, welders, boiler workers, etc. "And then, of course, you're going to have seasonal and cyclical maintenance every few years," he added. "That will bring 100 to 200 workers at a time during those periods." In addition, the project will generate both property taxes and an electrical generation tax. The use of natural gas will help sustain that piece of the energy industry while generating additional taxes, Hamman said. Base Electron has a natural gas agreement with WBI Energy, which plans to construct the Bakken East Pipeline to run about 350 miles from near Watford City to near Fargo. Hamman noted North Dakota has a large gas production industry that creates opportunity for a low-cost and secure supply of fuel to feed power facilities. Use of that natural gas helps address reliability concerns within the transmission grid, he said. Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO), the region's transmission organization, predicts the need for 15-20 gigawatts of power by 2035, creating opportunity for new power generation, Hamman said. "We've set ourselves up to capitalize on the energy infrastructure and the investment environment in North Dakota to utilize produced gas and meet the need for reliability," he said of Basin Electron. Hamman said the company chose a location enabling it to access transmission infrastructure already in place. Missouri Bend Energy Center will connect into an existing 345 kV power line. Base Electron acquired 312 acres, much of it to be used during the construction period. The operational footprint will be 30-50 acres, Hamman said. Applied Digital's data center will be about a mile north and will be served by the local utility. "But we're basically providing that power as a capacity backstop to the grid," Hamman said. Base Electron estimates a need for about a million and a half gallons of water a day. The intent is to draw water from Nelson Lake, located about eight miles from the proposed plant and fed by the Missouri River. If that option is not available, the draw would come directly from the Missouri River, 16 miles away. The usage represents a fraction of a percent of Missouri River flows, Hamman said. "We're using air cool condensing, which significantly reduces your water demand," he said. "There'll be a lot of recycling of the water." The proposed construction would come at a time when other regional construction will be happening on the Applied Digital data center, the River Run Energy Center gas-powered plant and data center campus in Mercer County and the Garrison spillway. It could result in a demand for 10,000 construction workers in a confined region in a short period of time, but Hamman said trade unions are confident they can provide the workers.

artigo.texto: Cincinnati council hears study on how to regulate data centers CINCINNATI (WXIX) - The City of Cincinnati is considering how to regulate data centers. A presentation Tuesday in council gave an overview of how data centers could be installed in the city. The city ordered a study to help guide council as members consider how to handle data centers if more are brought into the city. What the study found The Department of City Planning and Engagement representatives acknowledged that data centers may be a piece of important infrastructure, but not everyone wants them around. “We all use the internet. We use social media, we do Google search ... All of that uses data from data centers, so if we want to do that, we need data centers,” Councilman Mark Jeffreys said. About 400 people provided the city with feedback on the issue. “The primary message that we received from community members was a strong desire to see the zoning code prohibit data centers as a land use,” said Sophia Ferries-Rowe with the Cincinnati Department of City Planning and Engagement. The department said 28 data centers currently operate within the Greater Cincinnati area, with nine directly in the city. If more arrive, residents are concerned about increased heat, noise, energy bills and water utility bills, the study found. The study also found that more data centers could create jobs and help support local infrastructure, but they may have negative environmental impacts on carbon emissions. RELATED | Data centers multiply across Ohio, raising questions about costs and benefits Water use and costs “Why should citizens and property owners pay higher water bills to protect a billion dollar company?” Stephan Pryor said. Representatives with the Metropolitan Sewer District and Greater Cincinnati Water Works suggested that existing regulations already control how companies use water. They said the city could implement a reuse system that would allow water that is not fully treated to be rerouted directly to data centers and other uses not related to drinking water. They told Councilman Evan Nolan that it would require new infrastructure. “That could be expensive,” Nolan said. “Could be, yes, but other places in the country have had private investment,” said Scott Bessler, with the Metropolitan Sewer District. PREVIOUSLY | Cincinnati considers temporary halt on new data centers Next steps As the study continues, local leaders still have questions about how much energy and water current data centers use before setting any guidelines. “We need to put a cost associated with those, and if another data center is proposed to be built, we need to know what that cost is so we can offset it. It shouldn’t be on ratepayers,” Jeffreys said. The next step is more research, and city departments will put forth recommendations for the zoning rules. Another public engagement session will follow, and the recommendations will be refined before going before council. See a spelling or grammatical error in our story? Please click here to report it. artigo.texto: Quanta Services is growing faster than expected, driven by demand for power infrastructure, data centers and renewable energy. CEO Duke Austin sees potential for growth in the 20% range next year, while leaving the company's longer-term targets unchanged. Data centers and related projects account for roughly 10% to 15% of the business, and Quanta's revenue per megawatt on data center work has increased to about $4 million to $6 million as customers award it more work at each site. Quanta is investing in equipment manufacturing and supply to ease project bottlenecks, but that spending could weigh on free cash flow over the next couple of years. The company is also pursuing generation projects, with some work expected to begin in 2027. Vertiv's UIG Deal Targets the Next Big Constraint in AI Data Centers Quanta Services (NYSE:PWR) is growing faster than management anticipated at its March analyst day, driven by demand for power infrastructure and technology-related construction, CEO Duke Austin said at the Baird 2026 Global Industrial Conference. Austin said the company was ahead of the five-year plan it outlined at the event, which included a target for 15% to 20% compound annual growth in adjusted earnings per share. He said demand for power and computing capacity had developed more quickly than expected, while renewable energy work had remained stronger than anticipated. Data Center Delays Create Opportunity in These 3 Stocks "It's broad-based growth, faster than we thought," Austin said, pointing in particular to expansion in mechanical, electrical and plumbing, or MEP, work. Austin said Quanta expects to grow next year and sees an opportunity for growth in the 20% range, with potential to grow faster. He did not revise the company's longer-term targets at the conference. 3 Stocks Cashing In on AI While Everyone Watches NVIDIA Quanta serves utilities and large power users, including technology customers. Austin said the company self-performs about 85% of its work, has 95,000 employees and generates $41 billion in revenue. He said data centers and related work, including chip and Tesla projects, represent roughly 10% to 15% of the business. Electricians can move among data centers, pharmaceutical facilities and other projects, giving Quanta flexibility if demand shifts, he said. Austin said Quanta's revenue capture on data center work had risen to approximately $4 million to $6 million per megawatt from $3 million to $5 million, as customers ask the company to take on more work at each site. He expects that share to continue expanding. On transmission projects, Austin said Quanta had not yet started field work on 765-kilovolt lines and probably would not begin until sometime next year. He said the company's existing business was growing without that contribution. Supply Chain and Generation Investments Quanta has expanded into manufacturing and supply of equipment to keep projects moving when materials are scarce, Austin said. Its investments include transformers, circuit breakers and poles. The company formed a breaker joint venture with Hyosung HICO and acquired a pole manufacturer during the quarter, he said. Austin also discussed Quanta's fossil-fuel generation business, including a combined-cycle power plant program with NiSource. He said Quanta structured the work to manage risk and target a margin profile consistent with the segment, which he described as approximately 10% to 12%. Some generation work will start in 2027, Austin said, adding that other customers have expressed interest. He expects the business to become a meaningful platform, though not Quanta's largest segment. Cash Flow and Capital Deployment CFO Jayshree Desai said growth in renewables, MEP and engineering, procurement and construction work can support a more favorable free-cash-flow profile because those activities generally have more favorable working-capital characteristics than Quanta's typical utility master service agreement work. Desai cautioned that spending to expand transformer, breaker and offsite manufacturing facilities could pressure free cash flow over the next couple of years. The mix and growth rate of the company's businesses will influence the outcome, she said. Austin said Quanta could deploy capital through acquisitions or by buying back stock if the share price becomes disconnected from the business. He also expressed confidence in demand beyond the near term, saying he felt good about the outlook through 2029. artigo.texto: COLUMBUS, Ohio — The push against data centers has been well-documented. One independent tracker counts nearly 150 data center moratoriums in place all across the state. Opponents are concerned about a wide variety of issues, including the impact the centers have on the environment and their utility bills. At the same time, supporters point to the fact that those data centers are bringing billions of dollars in investment and new opportunities for construction workers. As data centers continue to expand across Ohio, so does the demand for the workers needed to build them. “We’ve got in-house architecture and engineering, licensed and stamped in all 50 states,” said Will Goodin, vice president of project development for Terrapin Construction Group. Terrapin Construction Group designs data centers across the country with four separate projects currently in Ohio. “And that’s inclusive of mechanical, electrical, plumbing as well as engineering, civil, so site work and structural work as well,” Goodin said. He said the growing number of data center projects is creating more business for his company, making over $100 million from design, construction and procurement of HVAC equipment this year, and they’re on track to triple that next year. “We’ve seen a huge uptick in not only design but also a lot of pre-construction, a lot of construction specifically in the data center asset class,” Goodin said. And it’s not just the construction crews. Goodin said demand for the specialized equipment needed to build these facilities is also high, with some supplies taking months to arrive. “There’s huge lead times depending on the types of equipment that you’re looking to source for your project. Anywhere from 18- to 50-plus weeks for any number of transfer switches, switch gears, chillers, things of that nature,” Goodin said. That demand creates opportunities for a wide range of skilled trades, including electricians, mechanical contractors, framers and carpenters. Goodin said the steady pipeline of projects is providing job security for his company and the subcontractors it relies on. But he recognizes the industry is not without controversy. “Depending on who you ask, it’s kind of a loaded, complicated issue but we’re very excited to be a resource for folks who are looking to get into this business and are expanding their current operations,” Goodin said. Across Ohio, communities are pushing back against data center development. As more communities consider putting development on pause, the question becomes: How many jobs do these facilities actually create once construction is over? Case Western Reserve University Economics Professor Jonathan Ernest said the initial construction phase can provide a significant employment boost. But he said once it’s built, that changes. “There are fewer people onsite for the longterm with lots of jobs in an area. So we’re not likely to get entire cities that are built around the one plant that everyone works at we’re not likely to get that with data centers because they don’t need that many capacity of people on site for the long run,” said Ernest. So, while the construction boom is creating opportunities for Ohio’s skilled trades, Ernest said communities should take a closer look at what those projects will mean for the local workforce once the facilities are up and running. According to the U.S. Data Center Map, there are 26 data centers currently being constructed, with another 54 in the planning phase.

artigo.texto: Tenaska, an energy company, gave a presentation hosted by Care NET in the Holston Electric Co-Operative (HEC) Auditorium on Monday, Nov. 9. The subject of the meeting was a new facility Tenaska is building in the Phipps Bend Industrial Park. The Bobwhite facility will be a battery energy storage system, known as BESS. Located in the southern end of the industrial park, the new construction will occupy about four acres of a six-acre plot. There will be about 75 jobs created during the two-year construction period. Bobwhite has been in the planning stages for about three years, and will begin construction in early 2028. Plans call for completion by the third quarter of 2029, with an investment by Tenaska of about $300 million. BESS provides a way to store electricity during times of low demand and provide it to the grid within seconds of high demand. At Phipps Bend, the battery collection will store about 225 MW of electricity. This can provide energy to thousands of homes and businesses during periods of high energy demand when the grid would otherwise be overloaded or when there is a weather-related extreme event. The batteries, composed of lithium, iron and phosphate, are about the size of the computer towers of years past. They sit on individual shelves within steel cabinets and are wired together in series. When construction is completed, there will be about 200 of these cabinets on site. Storage batteries have a functional life of about 20-25 years. After 20 years, Tenaska expects to take BESS apart, recycle as much as possible, and recondition the site. The presentation included a discussion on safety issues and the built in protections that are part of the units. Tenaska has already devoted a day to training the Surgoinsville Volunteer Fire Department on how to conduct emergency measures in case of fire. Forbes Magazine called Tenaska ”the biggest company you never heard of.” Tenaska, whose national headquarters are in Omaha, Nebraska, is a privately held company which is developing energy production facilities throughout the United States. Bill Kornrich, a Care NET member, introduced the Tenaska group. The presentation at HEC was delivered by Tyler Clark, Chief Engineer on the project, and Jamie Wagner, Manager of Community Relations. Standing on either side of the stage, they alternated explaining the power point presentation. This was followed by a lively question and answer period in which Mike Bonaccia, Tenaska’s Assistant Project Developer, stepped in to answer some questions. The event was catered by Jo Anderson from Sweet Tooth and Hale Springs Inn. Cookies were provided by Care NET members. Care NET is a regional conservation committee of the Sierra Club with members in Grainger, Greene, Hancock, and Hawkins counties. Care NET’s focus is in promoting clean air, water and soil. Meetings are held on the fourth Thursday of every month at 6 p.m. at St. Henry’s Catholic Church. ~Joanne Irvin and Bill Kornrich of Care NET contributed to this report.

artigo.texto: Data centers may be willing to be double charged for grid infrastructure, so long as those costs are paired with policy that makes it easier to build in the U.S. Tucked inside the Senate’s bipartisan permitting reform bill are provisions that would upend decades of federal power rules by directing data centers and crypto miners to pay for both the new transmission lines needed to serve them, as well as the cost of using the existing grid. Historically, charging a customer twice for the same capacity was considered an illegal practice. But that could change, as data centers disproportionately drive up demand for electricity across the U.S. and hyperscalers promise not to saddle other customers with the bill. The shift reflects a fraught moment in the race to power artificial intelligence, especially heading into the midterm elections next week. Energy affordability is top of mind for many voters across the U.S., whose opinion of data centers has soured dramatically this year, according to the latest polling by POLITICO. Half of Americans now oppose data centers being built within three miles of their home, up from 28% in January. Their concerns are rooted in rising utility bills, water use, air pollution, and AI’s impact on jobs and the broader economy. Controversial projects are affecting local races, including in states like New Mexico, Utah, and Wisconsin. “I think the data center industry will take this deal because they’ve already acknowledged that they need to cover their costs,” Tyson Slocum, director of Public Citizen’s energy program, told Latitude Media. “And at the end of the day, the bill will make it a lot easier to build the gas and renewable infrastructure needed to serve data centers.” President Donald Trump, a vocal supporter of data centers that underpin the global AI race, who says the U.S. needs to win against China, launched a voluntary ratepayer protection pledge in March. Tech giants, AI labs, and major utilities signed it, with the tech companies promising to either build or buy generation to power new data centers and pay for any new grid infrastructure to serve them. Trading extra cash for speed The Senate permitting deal, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, aims to actually enforce that pledge. And so far, at least two industry groups that represent companies including Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft have endorsed the legislation: the Corporate Energy Buyers Association and the Electricity Customer Alliance. However, the Data Center Coalition has not endorsed the bill. The group told Latitude Media in a statement that it’s still reviewing the legislation with its members. Amazon, Google, and Meta didn’t respond to a request for comment. Microsoft declined to comment. CEBA in a statement described BAAJA as a “generational opportunity” to build out U.S. energy through faster infrastructure permitting and improved transmission planning. Jeff Dennis, executive director of ECA — which represents tech companies and residential and industrial customers — said BAAJA strikes a balance between encouraging the build out of larger transmission lines in a more financially disciplined way, while setting the stage for long-term affordability. He noted that data center developers have already said they expect to pay their own costs, and then some. “They are willing to pay more than their own costs to make sure other customers are treated fairly,” Dennis said. BAAJA would require the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to rewrite a 1994 policy that allowed electricity customers to pay either the “embedded” costs of the existing grid, or the “incremental” cost of its expansion — not both. Instead, computational loads larger than 20 megawatts would be forced to pay both. States could charge a “surplus” on top of that, in order to lower other customers’ utility bills, and discriminate against data centers by treating them as a “less favorable” customer class to other large industrial, manufacturing, or commercial loads. The bill also would mandate that utilities hold data centers liable for capital costs, even if they exit agreements early for any reason, to make sure ratepayers aren’t left on the hook. Dennis said a final bill must ensure that data centers aren’t forced to shoulder so much of the costs that they ultimately decide to build off-grid. Some projects are already going that route, including those backed by Microsoft and Amazon, mainly powered by gas turbines and engines and backup diesel generators. “That could pose negative impacts to customers and removes a lot of investment in the grid we all rely on,” he said. A Senate aide told Latitude Media that key negotiators are working on a managers’ amendment to BAAJA, although it’s unclear whether it would revise the ratepayer protection section of the bill. Nidhi Thakar, CEBA’s senior vice president for policy, said the group supports BAAJA in its current form, but acknowledged there is some concern among its data center members about how much they’ll be forced to pay. “A lot of this will have to get worked out in a FERC rulemaking,” Thakar said. “That is where the deep details on how to allocate costs for new transmission lines will occur. So that rulemaking will be very critical.” The Senate is set to vote on the permitting bill on Nov. 9, the week after the midterm elections.

artigo.texto: da Agência iNFRA A Hitachi Energy assinou contrato com a BCR-i Brasil para fornecer serviços de monitoramento e manutenção preditiva de uma subestação de 560 MVA (megavolt-amperes) que atende a um data center no estado de São Paulo. O acordo é o primeiro da Hitachi Energy no Brasil para a solução HMAX Energy, que utiliza inteligência artificial e análise de dados para acompanhar o funcionamento de equipamentos elétricos. Segundo as empresas, o serviço permitirá monitorar os ativos da subestação em tempo quase real e identificar possíveis falhas antes que afetem o fornecimento de energia ao empreendimento. A parceria é de longo prazo, mas as companhias não informaram o valor do contrato nem sua duração. O acordo ocorre em meio à expansão da demanda de energia elétrica dos data centers no Brasil. Segundo projeções da EPE (Empresa de Pesquisa Energética) citadas pela Hitachi Energy, o consumo de eletricidade no SIN (Sistema Interligado Nacional) deverá crescer 4% ao ano até 2030, com a carga elétrica total chegando a 98,8 GW no período.

artigo.texto: Lubbock residents urge council to pass data center moratorium City council hosts first public hearing over proposed 90-day moratorium LUBBOCK, Texas (KCBD) - Residents urged the Lubbock City Council to pass a 90-day data center moratorium during the first of two public hearings on the proposal. The proposed moratorium followed a successful citizen petition organized through SAVE Lubbock this past summer. Residents raise concerns Fabian Mata, a north Lubbock resident, told city council Tuesday afternoon he does not trust the city to enforce its ordinances. “We don’t trust you when you say you’re going to put 1,000, 2,000, 5,000 feet [setback] in the data centers in north Lubbock because you don’t enforce any of the ordinances,” Mata said. Natalie Miller of the North and East Lubbock Coalition said while the moratorium proposal isn’t exactly what citizens asked for, she hopes council respects their wishes. “Citizens of Lubbock asked for 18 months. There was a compromise for 90 days, and that’s what the law would allow for. And so, we accepted that answer, and now we’re just asking to simply honor that,” Miller said. Zoning recommendations At its meeting last week, the Planning and Zoning Commission unanimously recommended that Lubbock require specific zoning for AI factories. The proposed rules would address landscaping, setbacks, noise and pollution limits, and data center decommissioning. Stephen Sanders of SAVE Lubbock said residents should be heard. “We don’t want a data center in those communities at all. But if we have to have one, it needs to be 1,000 foot setback,” Sanders said. The commission’s recommendations for large-scale data centers are scheduled to come before the council Dec. 1. Some residents said a moratorium would come too late because the Lubbock Economic Development Alliance has already approved a new data center inside city limits. That facility is smaller than the large-scale data centers the city is considering regulating. “We had no opportunity to say no because LEDA and you all had already spoken about it,” Stephanie Smith said. The second public hearing on the moratorium is set for Dec. 10, when council will have its first opportunity to vote on it. “Usually it’s the industry comes in first and then we study. We’re just saying let’s study this first, right?” Miller said. Copyright 2026 KCBD. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: In the final days of Joe Biden’s administration, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) filed a lawsuit alleging PepsiCo violated the Robinson-Patman Act. This largely dormant New Deal-era antitrust law prohibits wholesalers from giving large retailers preferential prices disproportionate to sales volume. Donald Trump’s second administration dropped the case soon after taking office, but a watchdog group, the Institute for Local Self-Reliance, petitioned the Southern District of New York court to unseal the Biden-era complaint in late 2025, and the court did. The details that emerged were explosive. Drawing on a trove of internal PepsiCo emails and other documents, Biden’s FTC accused the company of forging a secret pact with Walmart to ensure the big-box giant had unbeatable retail prices on PepsiCo products. PepsiCo allegedly did this by monitoring retail prices for its products and raising wholesale prices on retailers whose PepsiCo prices were too close to Walmart’s. As the Monthly reported in January, the alleged conduct carried profound implications for food pricing and affordability. Conventional wisdom holds that Walmart’s low prices reflect volume discounts and economies of scale used by the Bentonville, Arkansas-based retailer—America’s largest employer and largest grocery retailer by sales. But the PepsiCo suit, brought by the FTC under its then-Chair Lina Khan, presented evidence of the opposite of efficiency: PepsiCo’s painstaking micromanagement of prices to protect its most powerful buyer. For consumers, this raises the possibility that Walmart’s market power does not, at least in this case, discipline prices downward, but inflates them across the market. (Since the Trump administration dropped the suit, PepsiCo did not get to make its case in court, although it said in a statement at the time that it “has always and will continue to provide all customers with fair, competitive, and non-discriminatory pricing, discounts and promotional value.”) But before the FTC suit regarding PepsiCo was filed in January 2025, private plaintiff antitrust suits against Walmart and battery maker Energizer had already been underway for two years. These cases, which have received scant media attention, provide another set of allegations that Walmart may be influencing its suppliers’ pricing decisions in ways that harm consumers. Reached for comment, Walmart and Energizer did not respond. The plaintiffs in these suits, which include both smaller retailers and consumers, allege that Walmart pressured Energizer to monitor sellers’ prices to ensure they didn’t underprice Walmart’s. If they did, Energizer would discipline the sellers by raising their wholesale prices or limiting access to products. The plaintiffs allege the scheme is evidenced by price increases between 2019 and 2023 that exceeded what a normally competitive market would see, as well as internal corporate correspondence and pricing records describing the pressure Energizer allegedly faced from Walmart to hike prices on smaller retailers. The internal records and correspondence described in the legal filings seem to show that as early as January 2018, Energizer had allegedly developed an internal team, Project Atlas, to police customers who sold batteries below Walmart’s rate. One of the plaintiffs, a discount battery reseller called Portable Power, employed pricing strategies that were considered “disruptive,” according to an Energizer manager. To “resolve” the issue in Walmart’s favor, Energizer raised wholesale prices for headlamps on Portable Power by 50 to 85 percent as early as November 2018, telling the California-based reseller the increase aligned with internal pricing policy. This was the first of many Energizer moves to discipline Portable Power’s pricing, according to the reseller’s amended complaint. In the second quarter of 2019, Energizer again raised the wholesale prices of certain products—Max Alkaline and Ultimate Lithium batteries—by 8 percent for all its non-Walmart customers. The plaintiffs say this allowed Walmart to raise retail prices for the same Energizer products by an even greater margin—nearly 40 percent by the first quarter of 2020—while still maintaining price leadership. In January 2021, an Energizer sales representative forwarded an email from the company’s Project Atlas team to Portable Power’s CEO, Richard Petretti, informing the battery reseller that it was “in violation” of Energizer’s “pricing policies.” Energizer then hiked the prices it charged Portable Power and, according to the amended complaint, “told Portable Power the minimum price it had to charge—Walmart’s price—to avoid being terminated as a distributor.” Portable Power refused, and on February 1st, the Energizer sales representative warned Portable Power that it could no longer distribute certain Energizer products. When Portable Power’s CEO discussed the decision with the representative later that day by phone, the complaint alleges, the representative told him that “this is 1000% about Walmart and wanting the best price.” Energizer has filed counterclaims in the same lawsuit against Portable Power, accusing the company of illegally obtaining “trade secrets” from Energizer employees to bring and support the litigation. The two cases, PepsiCo and Energizer, show that Walmart’s business is “based on exercising market power over suppliers,” says Ron Knox, a senior researcher and policy advocate at the Institute for Local Self-Reliance. Indeed, other signs have emerged. As far back as 2017, Walmart reportedly demanded that prices from large consumer-goods companies selling through the retailer be 15 percent lower than competitors’ prices 80 percent of the time. Whether Walmart illegally pushed suppliers to raise prices on its rivals has not been adjudicated. The PepsiCo case is dismissed. artigo.texto: OKLAHOMA CITY – The Oklahoma City Council voted unanimously Tuesday to extend its existing moratorium on approvals for new large-scale data center projects through December 2027, continuing a pause that’s been in effect since April of this year. The moratorium officially blocks planning, zoning, and expansion applications for any data center exceeding 75 megawatts of electrical load, effectively halting any new “hyperscale” data center projects while City officials continue examining questions of potential utility strain, environmental impact, and noise pollution. “City staff will be researching best practices and working with a consultant and community stakeholders to update the zoning code, including the creation of a specific use unit for data centers,” Planning Director Geoff Butler said in a press statement. “Extending the temporary moratorium will give City Council time to evaluate the full scope of the potential impacts and determine appropriate regulations.” Some exemptions, including newly approved hyperscale data center The new extension comes hot on the heels of last month’s City Council approval of the city’s first hyperscale data center development, a 500 megawatt, multi-site mega-project planned by Beltline Energy on the far westerns edges of OKC, at NW 23rd St. and Frisco Rd., overlapping with parts of Yukon. That project was specifically exempted from the moratorium, as it had already been approved by Planning Commission and had entered the development pipeline before April’s vote to pause further data center approvals. The Beltline development was joined by two other projects that were retroactively exempted from the moratorium – the Scale Datacenters facility on the Expand Energy (formerly Chesapeake) campus, serving Cerebras AI, and the 7725 Connect development on W. Reno, housing the Rack59 Data Center. Both of those data centers fall well below the 75 megawatt usage threshold for the moratorium, however, and with no official large-scale expansion plans outlined, it remains unclear as to why they were exempted by name. Moratorium could be lifted with new Zoning Code The moratorium could also be lifted before December 2027 if the City of OKC’s impending Zoning Code overhaul outlines firm new regulations for data center operations in the city limits. “If there is a situation where we have a revised ordinance ready to accept applications, the moratorium could end earlier than the end of 2027,” Mayor David Holt clarified in discussion with City Manager Craig Freeman from the dais at Tuesday’s meeting. “But that’s not guaranteed.” Holt explained that the moratorium could, in fact, continue even after the approval of a new Zoning Code, if the council and City consultants determine that more study is still needed. “If we decided, as a policy matter, that even with the adoption, we still wanted to maintain this expectation,” he said, “we certainly could, in the new ordinance, say ‘this moratorium still lasts through 2027.’” Brett Fieldcamp is the owner and Editor in Chief of Oklahoma City Free Press. He has been covering arts, entertainment, news, housing, and culture in Oklahoma for nearly two decades and served as Arts & Entertainment Editor before purchasing the company from founder Brett Dickerson in 2026. He is also a musician and songwriter and holds a certification as Specialist of Spirits from The Society of Wine Educators.

artigo.texto: A melhoria dos mecanismos de gestão de emissões abre caminho para um mercado de carbono. Alterar a Lei de Proteção Ambiental e aprimorar as regulamentações sobre emissões criará um arcabouço legal sincronizado e transparente, ajudando o mercado de carbono nacional a operar com mais eficácia. Aprimorar as instituições e padronizar a gestão de emissões. A transição verde impõe novas exigências à gestão estatal e às atividades produtivas e empresariais. À medida que as normas ambientais se tornam cada vez mais uma condição para o acesso ao mercado, a redução das emissões não é apenas uma responsabilidade a cumprir, mas também está diretamente ligada à competitividade das empresas. A Conclusão nº 75-KL/TW, de 28 de julho de 2026, do 14º Comitê Central do Partido Comunista do Vietnã, identifica a proteção ambiental, a adaptação às mudanças climáticas e a transição verde como a base e a força motriz para a inovação de modelos de desenvolvimento, a melhoria da qualidade do crescimento e o aumento da competitividade da economia . A conclusão estabelece uma meta para 2030: a economia verde representará 10% do PIB, a proporção de energia renovável no fornecimento total de energia primária atingirá pelo menos 26,1% e as emissões nacionais de gases de efeito estufa serão reduzidas em pelo menos 9% em comparação com o cenário sem intervenção. Para alcançar esses objetivos, é crucial aperfeiçoar a estrutura institucional e os instrumentos econômicos para a redução de emissões. Em consonância com essa direção, o Ministério da Agricultura e do Meio Ambiente está elaborando um projeto de lei revisado e emendado sobre a Proteção Ambiental para institucionalizar novas políticas, remover obstáculos à aplicação da lei , promover a descentralização e a delegação de poderes e reduzir os procedimentos administrativos. Notavelmente, o projeto adiciona regulamentações ao mercado interno de carbono de forma transparente e aberta, em consonância com as práticas internacionais. Paralelamente à alteração da Lei, o Ministério da Agricultura e do Meio Ambiente está elaborando um Decreto que detalha diversas disposições da Lei de Proteção Ambiental relativas à resposta às mudanças climáticas, esclarecendo especificamente as normas sobre gestão de emissões e funcionamento do mercado de carbono. O projeto concentra-se em quatro grupos principais de políticas: adaptação às mudanças climáticas, gestão de emissões de gases de efeito estufa, desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono e proteção da camada de ozônio. Especificamente, instalações com emissões superiores a 3.000 toneladas de CO2 equivalente por ano estão sujeitas a requisitos de inventário. Diversas instalações nos setores de energia, indústria, transporte, comércio e tratamento de resíduos também devem realizar inventários se atenderem aos critérios especificados. Na oficina de consulta sobre o projeto de Decreto, realizada em 10 de novembro, diversos ministérios, setores, associações e empresas contribuíram com opiniões para aprimorar a regulamentação, de modo a alinhá-la melhor às práticas de produção e negócios. Representantes do Ministério da Indústria e Comércio afirmaram que, por meio do programa piloto de alocação de cotas para usinas termelétricas, siderúrgicas e cimenteiras, é necessário um maior rigor na padronização dos dados de entrada, dos métodos de cálculo e dos procedimentos de avaliação. O Ministério recomendou uma avaliação completa dos resultados do piloto, o aprimoramento do banco de dados, a definição de prazos de implementação e o esclarecimento da autoridade e dos recursos necessários para a execução do projeto. Você também pode gostar Representantes do Grupo de Eletricidade do Vietnã ( EVN ) solicitaram esclarecimentos sobre os limites das fontes de emissão, o escopo das emissões diretas e indiretas, especialmente para usinas hidrelétricas e instalações de geração de energia em ilhas. A distinção entre instalações obrigadas a realizar inventários e aquelas com cotas alocadas também precisa ser claramente definida para evitar procedimentos desnecessários. Em relação ao método de alocação de cotas, um representante do Grupo Hoa Phat sugeriu que a indústria siderúrgica precisa diferenciar entre as tecnologias de alto-forno e forno elétrico. Para complexos integrados, o limite de emissão deve corresponder à produção de aço bruto, considerando também soluções para o aproveitamento do calor e dos gases residuais a fim de reduzir as emissões. Em relação ao setor elétrico, a EVN e representantes do Ministério da Indústria e Comércio propuseram a inclusão de uma disposição para o ajuste de cotas quando as usinas termelétricas precisarem aumentar a produção para atender às demandas de despacho e garantir a segurança energética nacional. Este é um fator que precisa ser considerado para assegurar que o mecanismo de gestão de emissões seja consistente com as necessidades operacionais do sistema elétrico e com a produção real. Os delegados também sugeriram a disponibilização pública das fontes de dados, coeficientes e métodos de alocação para que as empresas possam verificá-los e compará-los; e a inclusão de um mecanismo para feedback e resolução de reclamações quando surgirem discrepâncias. Em relação ao mercado de carbono, as principais áreas de preocupação incluem os padrões de crédito de carbono, os regulamentos de leilão, a compensação e a prevenção da dupla contagem para os mesmos resultados de redução de emissões. Representantes do setor florestal propuseram uma distinção clara entre emissão duplicada de créditos de carbono, uso duplicado e declarações duplicadas; e o estabelecimento de um mecanismo de contingência para o risco de reversão dos resultados de redução de emissões devido a incêndios florestais e desastres naturais. Facilitar transações e impulsionar os negócios. Juntamente com as melhorias institucionais, a infraestrutura para a negociação de carbono no mercado interno está sendo gradualmente formada. artigo.texto: Improving emission management mechanisms paves the way for a carbon market. Amending the Environmental Protection Law and improving regulations on emissions will create a synchronized and transparent legal framework, helping the domestic carbon market operate more effectively. Improving institutions and standardizing emission management. The green transition is placing new demands on state management and production and business activities. As environmental standards increasingly become a condition for market access, reducing emissions is not only a responsibility to comply with but is also directly linked to the competitiveness of businesses. Conclusion No. 75-KL/TW dated July 28, 2026, of the 14th Central Committee of the Communist Party of Vietnam identifies environmental protection, adaptation to climate change, and green transition as the foundation and driving force for innovating development models, improving the quality of growth, and enhancing the competitiveness of the economy . The conclusion sets a target for 2030: the green economy will account for 10% of GDP, the proportion of renewable energy in the total primary energy supply will reach at least 26.1%, and national greenhouse gas emissions will be reduced by at least 9% compared to the business-as-usual scenario. To realize these goals, perfecting the institutional framework and economic tools for emission reduction is crucial. In line with this direction, the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment is developing a draft revised and amended Law on Environmental Protection to institutionalize new policies, remove obstacles in law enforcement, promote decentralization and delegation of power, and reduce administrative procedures. Notably, the draft adds regulations on the domestic carbon market in a transparent and open manner, consistent with international practices. Alongside the amendment of the Law, the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment is drafting a Decree detailing several provisions of the Law on Environmental Protection regarding climate change response, specifically clarifying regulations on emission management and carbon market operation. The draft focuses on four main policy groups: adaptation to climate change, greenhouse gas emission management, carbon market development, and ozone layer protection. Specifically, facilities with emissions exceeding 3,000 tons of CO2 equivalent per year are subject to inventory requirements. Several facilities in the energy, industrial, transportation, trade, and waste treatment sectors must also conduct inventories if they meet the specified criteria. At the consultation workshop on the draft Decree on November 10th, many ministries, sectors, associations, and businesses contributed opinions to improve the regulations in a way that is more aligned with production and business practices. Representatives from the Ministry of Industry and Trade stated that, through the pilot program of allocating quotas to thermal power plants, steel and cement production facilities, further standardization of input data, calculation methods, and appraisal procedures is needed. The Ministry recommended a full evaluation of the pilot results, improvement of the database, consideration of implementation timelines, and clarification of the authority and resources for implementation. You may also like Representatives from the Vietnam Electricity Group ( EVN ) requested clarification on the boundaries of emission sources, the scope of direct and indirect emissions, especially for hydropower plants and power generation facilities on islands. The distinction between facilities obligated to conduct inventories and those allocated quotas also needs to be clearly defined to avoid unnecessary procedures. Regarding the quota allocation method, a representative from Hoa Phat Group suggested that the steel industry needs to differentiate between blast furnace and electric furnace technologies. For integrated complexes, the emission threshold should correspond to crude steel production, while also considering solutions for utilizing waste heat and gases to reduce emissions. Regarding the electricity sector, EVN and representatives from the Ministry of Industry and Trade proposed adding a provision for adjusting quotas when thermal power plants need to increase production to meet dispatching requirements and ensure national energy security. This is a factor that needs to be considered to ensure that the emission management mechanism is consistent with the operational requirements of the power system and actual production. The delegates also suggested making the data sources, coefficients, and allocation methods publicly available so that businesses can verify and compare them; and adding a mechanism for feedback and resolution of complaints when discrepancies arise. Regarding the carbon market, key areas of concern include carbon credit standards, auction regulations, offsetting, and prevention of double counting for the same emission reduction results. Representatives from the forestry sector proposed clearly distinguishing between duplicate carbon credit issuance, duplicate use, and duplicate declarations; and establishing a contingency mechanism for the risk of reversing emission reduction results due to forest fires and natural disasters. Facilitating transactions and creating momentum for businesses. Along with institutional improvements, the infrastructure for trading carbon in the domestic market is gradually being formed. artigo.texto: Aldo Soares Evangelista Em 15 de setembro de 2026 foi sancionada a Lei nº 15.504, o Redata, que suspende por cinco anos Imposto de Importação, PIS/Cofins e IPI sobre equipamentos de data centers, com renúncia estimada em R$ 5,2 bilhões em 2026. Em troca, a empresa deve operar com energia renovável ou “de baixa emissão”, gastar no máximo 0,05 litro de água de resfriamento por kWh, destinar 10% da capacidade ao mercado interno e aplicar em pesquisa no país 2% do valor comprado com o benefício.1 O problema está num parágrafo que passou sem debate: o § 7º do art. 11-B, inserido pelo Redata na Lei 11.196/2005, reduz em 20% essas duas contrapartidas para projetos no Norte, Nordeste e Centro-Oeste, que caem para 8% e 1,6%.2 Onde a floresta está, onde a água é o próprio território e onde o Estado mal chega, a lei exige menos retorno. O legislador chamou isso de incentivo regional. É o contrário. A Zona Franca de Manaus ensinou que isenção fiscal, mesmo com contrapartidas, produz uma ilha de produção cercada de carência quando nada a amarra ao território.3 O Redata repete a receita para a infraestrutura mais sedenta de energia e água deste século, e o faz quando o primeiro data center de inteligência artificial da Amazônia já está anunciado: Elea e Axia em Belém, 7,5 megawatts iniciais com expansão para 100, operação em 2027.4 O anúncio fala em cabos submarinos; não fala em água nem licenciamento. Os Estados Unidos mostram o fim dessa história. A isenção da Virgínia custou US$ 1,6 bilhão em 2025.5 A conta chegou: a Gallup mediu 71% de oposição a data centers de IA na própria comunidade,6 e Monterey Park baniu data centers com 88% dos votos.7 O país que inventou o modelo o está desmontando, enquanto o Brasil o importa com desconto para a Amazônia. O Direito Amazônico, campo que pensa a região a partir dela mesma, da realidade dos povos da floresta e dos rios, da sua história e biodiversidade, e não a partir de Brasília nem de uma visão eurocêntrica, tem uma objeção a fazer. O art. 170 da Constituição submete a ordem econômica à defesa do meio ambiente e à redução das desigualdades regionais; o art. 225 impõe ao poder público preservar os processos ecológicos essenciais. Uma lei que reduz a contrapartida justamente na região mais frágil inverte os dois comandos: trata a desigualdade como vantagem comparativa a ser vendida, não como déficit a corrigir. E ignora a física. A própria indústria admite que o resfriamento consome cerca de 40% da eletricidade de um data center e muita água, e recomenda instalá-los em regiões frias, onde o ar faz o trabalho do compressor.8 A Amazônia é o avesso disso: gastará mais água e energia por kWh do que qualquer outra região. E a energia “de baixa emissão” da lei pode ser gás. A saída não é proibir data centers na Amazônia, é inverter as contrapartidas: onde o impacto é maior, a exigência deve ser maior. Fundo local alimentado por percentual da receita, consulta às comunidades afetadas no licenciamento, publicação do consumo real de água e energia por bacia e circuito fechado de água com reúso, tecnologia que empresas brasileiras já usam, como condição do alvará, e data centers sustentável. Se nada mudar, a Amazônia vai repetir a Zona Franca em versão digital: uma ilha de servidores refrigerada com água de rio, cercada de gente sem água encanada e sem conexão com a internet de qualidade, treinando modelos que decidem a milhares de quilômetros. Desenvolvimento regional é quando a região fica com o desenvolvimento. Aqui, a Amazônia fica com a conta. Notas 1 BRASIL. Lei nº 15.504, de 15 de setembro de 2026. Institui o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata). Diário Oficial da União, Brasília, 15 set. 2026, ed. extra. A estimativa de renúncia (R$ 5,2 bilhões em 2026 e cerca de R$ 1 bilhão em cada um dos dois anos seguintes) consta do parecer da relatoria no Senado Federal, aprovado em 1º set. 2026. 2 Lei nº 11.196/2005, art. 11-B, § 7º, inserido pela Lei nº 15.504/2026: “Na hipótese de o estabelecimento da pessoa jurídica habilitada localizar-se nas Regiões Norte, Nordeste e Centro-Oeste, os compromissos de que tratam os incisos I e V do § 1º deste artigo serão reduzidos em 20% (vinte por cento)”. Os incisos I e V fixam, respectivamente, o mínimo de 10% do fornecimento efetivo de processamento ao mercado interno e o investimento no país de 2% do valor dos produtos adquiridos com o benefício; os 8% e 1,6% resultam da redução. O índice de eficiência hídrica (inciso IV) não é reduzido. 3 BRASIL. Tribunal de Contas da União. Acórdão 2.872/2021-Plenário (TC 042.406/2020-0), rel. Min.
