artigo.texto: Huawei Luterra S2 All-in-One Residential Energy Storage System Huawei has introduced the Luterra S2, a residential energy storage package that integrates a hybrid inverter, lithium iron phosphate batteries and AI-driven energy management into one system. Single-phase hybrid inverter options span 3 kW to 10 kW, while three-phase versions range from 5 kW to 20 kW. As many as three 20 kW inverters may be paralleled, yielding a combined maximum output of 60 kW. The LFP battery modules offer nominal capacities of 5.02 kWh and 7.03 kWh, corresponding to usable capacities of 4.9 kWh and 6.9 kWh. Rated charge and discharge power stands at 2.5 kW and 3 kW for the smaller module, versus 3.5 kW and 4 kW for the larger one. Ten-second peak discharge reaches 5 kW and 7 kW respectively. Dimensions are 590 mm x 255 mm x 290 mm for both modules, which weigh 46 kg and 57 kg. Across interconnected systems, the modular design accommodates as many as 48 battery packs, reaching a maximum nominal storage capacity of 336 kWh with the 7.03 kWh modules. Huawei stated that the batteries come with integrated energy optimizers and are engineered for more than 15 years of service. The company claims lifetime usable energy throughput of up to 5 MWh for every kWh of battery capacity. Inverter and Backup Specifications Silicon carbide power electronics and active neutral-point-clamped topology are used in the inverters. Per Huawei's preliminary specifications, single-phase models reach 98.6% maximum efficiency, while three-phase units reach 99%. Maximum PV input voltage is 600 V and 1,100 V respectively, with as many as three maximum power point trackers and up to 18 A of input current per tracker. Three-phase models accept up to 40 kWp of PV input power. In backup applications, switchover takes under 10 milliseconds, and continuous off-grid loads of up to 20 kW are supported. According to the preliminary specifications, the 20 kW three-phase inverter can supply peak backup output of up to 40 kW for 10 seconds. Cooling is passive, with no external fans, and claimed operating noise stays below 29 dB. The system runs at ambient temperatures between -25 C and 60 C and carries an IP66-rated enclosure with corrosion protection up to C5-M. Energy Management and Connectivity Huawei's AI Energy Management 2.0 platform draws on weather forecasts, electricity tariffs, household consumption data and battery status to optimize energy flows among PV installations, storage, electric vehicle chargers and heat pumps. Participation in virtual power plants is also supported. Connectivity options include EEBUS, SG Ready, OCPP and Modbus TCP. Additional software features include an AI-based assistant for homeowners, 3D modeling tools for installers and remote diagnostics. Cell-level thermal isolation, pressure relief and smoke evacuation channels are built into the battery system, together with continuous temperature monitoring of AC and DC terminals. Huawei said TUV Rheinland safety testing has been completed, covering thermal runaway, fire exposure and hydrogen explosion tests. The company also reported UL 9540A validation and compliance with IEC 63027 requirements for arc-fault protection. Pricing and market availability details have not been disclosed by Huawei. artigo.texto: One of the most resounding results of the midterm elections was that artificial intelligence (AI) is facing a big backlash from voters. Americans of both parties seem to agree on one big issue: They don't want AI data centers built in their backyards. According to data tracked by Ballotpedia, as of Nov. 4, voters decided on 47 local ballot initiatives to either support or limit the development of AI data centers. And 46 of 47 of these initiatives (98%) resulted in outcomes against the development of AI data centers. This is a big sign that the AI industry has a public relations problem. It's rare to get 98% of American voters to agree on anything, but in 98% of these local ballot measures, American voters expressed distrust of the AI build-out. A CNBC poll found that 56% of voters ranked data centers as a "crucial or major" factor in how they voted on Election Day. Many American voters are worried that AI data centers will raise utility costs. They don't want to offer up their local land and resources for data center construction without seeing economic benefits to their communities. And they support political candidates who are skeptical about AI data centers. In Ohio and Texas, newly elected Democratic governors have proposed moratoriums on new AI data center construction. Let's look at what the AI data center backlash means for investors -- and how you might want to position your portfolio as a result. A post-election sell-off in AI data center stocks The first few days after the Nov. 3 midterm election brought a big sell-off in AI-related stocks. The tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 dropped by 5.5% between Nov. 3 and Nov. 5, while the iShares Semiconductor ETF plummeted by about 15%. It's not just tech companies and chipmakers that are affected by the AI backlash. Construction manufacturer Caterpillar, a major pick-and-shovel AI stock that has benefited from the data center boom, lost about 11.3% during those two days after the election. Although all these names have recouped some of their post-election losses since Nov. 5, this is still a big sign that AI stocks are vulnerable to the will of the voters. If Americans are becoming hostile toward data centers, that could slow the AI boom -- and lead to downturns for other AI stocks. Warning signs of an AI data center slowdown Does the midterm election result mean that the AI boom is over? Not necessarily. But it could be heading for a slowdown. If states and local governments require more expensive regulations or slower approval processes for AI data centers, that could drive up costs and add delays for AI companies. If AI data centers are built more slowly and more expensively, there could be some new AI winners and losers in the short term. Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co., has been an enthusiastically bullish voice on the AI boom, which he calls the "AI Revolution." But on Nov. 4, as reported by CNBC, Ives wrote a research note that said: "For tech investors the big focus is will these mid-term elections slow the pace of the planned 800 to 1,000 datacenters across the US fueling the AI Revolution...the answer in our view is a clear YES." Ives also wrote that his firm now believes that "Big Tech capex growth rate now peaks in 2027 vs. our previous view that would not happen until 2028/2029." If the boom in AI capex ends in 2027, that could be bad news for semiconductor stocks and various pick-and-shovel stocks whose earnings have been boosted by hundreds of billions of dollars in corporate investment in data centers. CNBC also reported that Dominique Toublan, Barclays Investment Bank head of U.S. credit strategy, wrote in a note from Nov. 4 that "AI pushback is bipartisan but local, making the buildout pricier rather than stalling it," and that "scarce power favors the biggest balance sheets." How to invest in AI stocks after the midterms If you believe AI data centers are about to become more expensive to build and you agree with Toublan's view that companies with the "biggest balance sheets" are likely to benefit from this new dynamic, the best AI stocks to buy now might be the large-cap AI hyperscalers. If AI data centers become more expensive to build, the companies best equipped to build them are likely to be the well-established, cash-rich companies like Alphabet (GOOG +2.00%) (GOOGL +2.11%) rather than neoclouds like CoreWeave (CRWV +24.71%). CoreWeave has recently drawn investor concern about its high level of debt and rising interest expenses. A slowdown in the AI data center build-out could add to those pressures. The landscape of the AI trade just got more complicated with the midterm elections. If you still believe in tech stocks but don't want to invest too much in any one stock or sector, you could buy a tech ETF like the Invesco Nasdaq 100 ETF (QQQM +2.29%). This fund holds 103 stocks of the largest non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq. In the past five years, QQQM has delivered annualized returns of about 13.1%. QQQM Invesco NASDAQ 100 ETF NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/11/26 That 13.1% average annual return includes the bad bear market of 2022, when the Nasdaq-100 declined by about 33.1%. For long-term investors, QQQM is likely a good way to invest in the tech economy and perhaps own future big AI winners -- without concentrating too much on any one company or industry vertical. artigo.texto: AI data centers raise questions about water use, cooling Artificial intelligence can answer a question in seconds, but behind that speed is a physical network of computers, power lines and, in many cases, water. Data centers running AI generate enormous amounts of heat and keeping that equipment cool can place new demands on local water supplies, especially during hot weather or drought. Shirley Clarke, a Penn State Harrisburg professor, said cooling is a major issue. “The biggest part that people need to know about air and water is this issue around cooling the computer chips that we use, which take a tremendous amount of water depending on what cooling system we use,” Clarke said. How data centers stay cool When an AI program summarizes a document or answers a question, that work happens on computers housed in data centers. Those computers use electricity, and as they work, their chips give off heat. How that heat is removed can make a major difference in how much water a facility needs. One common method uses water that moves through tubes near the chips to carry heat away. In some systems, that water circulates in a closed loop. But the water can become too warm to reuse directly, so some facilities use cooling towers, where water is sent outside and allowed to evaporate. That breaks the closed loop and requires new water to be added. Another option uses fans to move air across equipment, which uses very little water but can require more electricity on very hot days. Experts say the amount of water used can vary widely depending on the model, the length of the response, the location, the weather, the cooling system and the electricity supply. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that all U.S. data centers — not just those running AI — directly consumed about 17 billion gallons of water in 2023. Questions for local communities For communities considering a data center, the biggest questions are where the facility would get its water, how much it would need on average and on the hottest days, and what happens when supplies are low. “You know, does it go to the residents to do what? Shower, to clean, to drink, to cook? Or does it go to the data center or is there a balance in there? And that's what many of the parties are going to have to be dealing with and the water systems are gonna have to deal with,” Clarke said. Location also matters. A facility drawing from a small stream or heavily used groundwater source may raise different concerns than one served by a larger supply. Groundwater can also replenish slowly, and even where water is available, a utility may need new pipes, pumps or treatment capacity. There is also debate about using treated wastewater for industrial cooling instead of drinking-water supplies. “The other problem we have with this really is we're just not equipped for it. Oftentimes the data centers are not built next to the treatment plants. So now we'd be looking at running another set of infrastructure to get the wastewater to that,” Clarke said. The question, experts say, is not whether every data center uses the same amount of water. They do not. The question for each community is how a proposed facility will be cooled, where its water and electricity will come from, and what protections will be in place when supplies are under stress.

artigo.texto: Mundo Indonésios protestam contra data centers por falta de água Enfrentando uma seca severa e escassez de água para necessidades básicas como cozinhar e tomar banho, os habitantes da ilha de Batam, na Indonésia, manifestam-se contra a rápida instalação de ‘data centers’ que impulsionam o avanço da inteligência artificial. A região vem sofrendo uma seca prolongada, intensificada pelo fenômeno climático El Niño, segundo o responsável pelo serviço local de abastecimento de água, em depoimento à AFP. Como em outras nações, a população atribui a culpa aos ‘data centers’, que são instalações que mantêm aplicativos e ferramentas de IA em funcionamento e utilizam água para resfriar seus equipamentos. Juniardi Adinda Sembiring Gurukinayan, comerciante local de 54 anos, relatou que inicialmente a chegada dessa indústria parecia positiva para Batam, mas com os cortes recentes no fornecimento de água, os moradores enfrentam dificuldades como ficar sem banho em algumas ocasiões. Ele destaca: “Não podemos preparar arroz sem água, nem cozinhar verduras”. Em um período crítico, dezenas de moradores realizaram protestos diante do Nongsa Digital Park, um complexo de ‘data centers’ e outras instalações que foi designado como zona econômica especial. Os residentes creem que a escassez hídrica está relacionada à construção dessas instalações, afirmou Juniardi. A seca causou uma queda acentuada no nível do reservatório próximo a Nongsa, enquanto uma pane elétrica agravou as interrupções no abastecimento, explicou Ginda Alamsyah, porta-voz da empresa operadora de água Air Batam Hilir. Esse parque tecnológico é abastecido por outro reservatório, o de Duriangkang, conforme fonte do setor industrial. Em setembro, as autoridades orientaram os empreendedores a instalarem sistemas para dessalinização da água do mar para uso na refrigeração, evitando assim a pressão sobre os recursos locais. Empresas como BW Digital, com sede em Singapura, DayOne e Princeton Digital Group operam ou planejam operar no Nongsa Digital Park. Gaw Capital Partners, com sede em Hong Kong, declarou estar ciente das preocupações dos moradores e que seus centros de dados adotam tecnologias eficientes e energias renováveis para minimizar impactos, incluindo sistemas de circuito fechado que reutilizam água. Na cidade costeira vizinha de Mata Ikan, moradores têm utilizado água do mar para higiene pessoal após evacuações, relata o manifestante Rahmat, de 52 anos. Sulastri, de 38 anos, conta que a crise hídrica, que já dura um ano e piorou nos últimos seis meses, faz com que precise usar água engarrafada para lavar utensílios domésticos. O governo disponibilizou água por meio de caminhões-pipa, porém a qualidade foi criticada por moradores, pois estava malcheirosa e com coloração amarelada. Autoridades locais não responderam aos questionamentos da AFP sobre a situação. O prefeito de Batam, Amsakar Achmad, afirmou que as interrupções no abastecimento não são consequência dos data centers, mas sim de fatores climáticos. A rápida expansão tecnológica e seus desafios Relatório da KPMG indica que a capacidade dos ‘data centers’ no sudeste asiático deve triplicar entre 2025 e 2030, o que poderá aumentar a pressão sobre recursos hídricos e energéticos, já fortemente dependentes de combustíveis fósseis. A Indonésia e a Malásia viram crescimento acelerado destes centros, especialmente após Singapura suspender novos projetos temporariamente. Ginda ressalta que a empresa de água apoia o desenvolvimento desde que haja gestão eficiente, incluindo melhorias nos reservatórios de Batam e técnicas como semeadura de nuvens para combater a seca. Impactos e mobilizações na Malásia Na região de Johor, considerada um grande polo emergente para infraestrutura de IA, a capacidade dos ‘data centers’ aumentou consideravelmente, causando preocupações ambientais. Projeções do governo indicam que até 2035 esses centros poderão consumir um terço da energia total da Malásia. Moradores protestam contra poluição por poeira e alagamentos provocados pela proximidade das instalações a áreas residenciais, enfatizando que a situação está em um momento crítico, segundo Mohd Fadhil Md Din, da Universidade Tecnológica da Malásia. Em Kota Damansara, um projeto de ‘data center’ foi suspenso após forte oposição da comunidade, com mais de 9.000 assinaturas em petição e pressões políticas. Jahaidi Harun, aposentado de 72 anos, destacou que além do barulho, o consumo elevado de água é sentido por todos quando não chove por um período prolongado.

artigo.texto: Production of Airedale® Chillers for Data Center Customers Begins at New Texas Facility RACINE, Wis. , Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Modine (NYSE: MOD), a diversified global leader in thermal management technology and solutions, today announced that it has commenced commercial production of Airedale® chillers at a new purpose-built advanced manufacturing facility in Grand Prairie, Texas. The 682,000-square-foot facility is dedicated to manufacturing state-of-the-art 2MW and 3MW chillers with free cooling for the data center market, directly supporting the rapidly expanding infrastructure needs of the world's leading hyperscale cloud providers, colocation operators, and high-density AI computing environments. "The launch of our Grand Prairie facility is an important milestone in the plan we announced last year to expand U.S. manufacturing capacity for Airedale cooling technologies," said Neil D. Brinker, President and CEO. "Scaling our capacity close to our customers enables us to partner with them to deliver the right highly engineered cooling solutions to help them advance their progress and achieve their performance objectives." The Grand Prairie site is expected to become the largest Airedale chiller manufacturing facility within the organization's global footprint. The first production line began operations this month, and the company is targeting four operational 2MW production lines by the end of the current fiscal year, subject to equipment commissioning, workforce readiness, and other operational considerations. The facility currently operates one shift, with plans to systematically scale to a fully operational, three-shift model. In addition to chillers, Airedale offers a comprehensive portfolio of mission-critical thermal management solutions, including dry coolers, coolant distribution units (CDUs), and intelligent controls, engineered to optimize efficiency across diverse data center thermal architectures. Airedale's purpose-built, premium systems address the most complex, high-density thermal demands of today's data center operators while maximizing energy and water efficiency. About Modine For more than 100 years, Modine has solved the toughest thermal management challenges for mission-critical applications. Our purpose of Engineering a Cleaner, Healthier World™ means we are always evolving our portfolio of technologies to provide the latest heating, cooling, and ventilation solutions. Through the hard work of more than 9,000 employees worldwide, our businesses advance our purpose with systems that improve air quality, reduce energy and water consumption, and use environmentally friendly refrigerants. Modine is a global company headquartered in Racine, Wisconsin (U.S.), with operations in North America, Europe, and Asia. For more information about Modine, visit www.modine.com. artigo.texto: VinFast's Unlimited-Mileage Battery Warranty Rewards the Freedom to Drive While most electric vehicle (EV) battery warranties come with strict mileage restrictions, VinFast is taking a distinctly different approach. Its 10-year, unlimited-mileage battery warranty offers American drivers one less thing to calculate as the odometer ticks upward. IRVINE, Calif. , Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Consider two drivers purchasing identical electric vehicles on the same day. One covers a modest 10,000 miles annually, while the other logs 25,000 miles between long commutes, family obligations, and weekend getaways. Four years in, both vehicles remain reliably on the road—yet only one driver still enjoys battery warranty coverage. Under a typical eight-year or 100,000-mile battery warranty, the high-mileage driver has already reached the coverage ceiling. Meanwhile, the lower-mileage driver retains protection for another four years before the time limit expires. It highlights a subtle paradox in vehicle ownership: the more heavily you rely on your EV, the sooner you risk losing coverage on its most critical component. Decoding the Fine Print America's reliance on driving is clear, though yearly mileage varies significantly. Federal Highway Administration data indicates that the average U.S. motor vehicle logged approximately 11,071 miles in 20241. However, lengthy commutes, frequent interstate travel, and active lifestyles push that figure much higher for millions of households. High mileage typically indicates a dependable vehicle doing its job, but standard warranty structures present a catch. Most automotive warranties operate on dual limits—years and mileage—expiring whichever threshold is crossed first. While an eight-year/100,000-mile policy sounds generous on paper, its real-world lifespan hinges entirely on driving habits: - 15,000 miles/year: Coverage expires in roughly 6 years and 8 months. - 20,000 miles/year: Coverage drops to 5 years. - 25,000 miles/year: Protection vanishes in just 4 years. The irony is clear: those who utilize their vehicles the most receive the shortest window of protection. Granted, an expired warranty does not mean a battery is nearing the end of its operational life. Industry research demonstrates that modern EV batteries are engineered to perform well past their warranty windows, often outlasting the vehicle itself. Nevertheless, physical durability and financial peace of mind are distinct. Even with high-end battery design, having a long-term safety net against unexpected issues provides vital reassurance. Removing the Mileage Ceiling VinFast offers an alternate path for American EV buyers. Available on its VF 8 and VF 9 electric SUVs, VinFast's 10-year battery warranty eliminates the mileage limit entirely under standard personal use. Complementing this is a new-vehicle limited warranty of up to 10 years or 125,000 miles (subject to standard terms and conditions). Under this model, logging 25,000 miles a year—accumulating 250,000 miles over a decade—will never prematurely void the battery warranty, simply because no ceiling exists. Long-distance commuters no longer need to track the odometer with concern, and frequent road-trippers can travel without worrying that extra miles are quietly eroding their coverage. Beyond the Battery This warranty framework forms part of a broader ownership package designed to streamline EV adoption. Alongside its comprehensive vehicle and battery protection, VinFast provides: - 24/7 Roadside Assistance for round-the-clock peace of mind. - Seamless Charging Access across a network of more than 250,000 public chargers throughout North America . By combining long-term financial protection with practical convenience, VinFast aligns its warranty coverage with the reality of how Americans actually drive: without limits. About VinFast VinFast (NASDAQ: VFS), a subsidiary of Vingroup JSC, one of Vietnam's largest conglomerates, is a pure-play electric vehicle ("EV") company with the mission of making EVs accessible to everyone. VinFast's product lineup today includes a wide range of electric cars, e-scooters, e-bikes and e-buses. VinFast is embarking on its next growth phase by rapidly scaling its distribution and franchised dealership network globally while expanding its global manufacturing footprint across North America, Europe, the Middle East, and Asia. artigo.texto: Battery storage is becoming an indispensable component of power grids and energy plants, but can it be scaled up quickly enough to meet the worldâs rapidly growing needs? As electrification of the global economy continues at pace, attention is increasingly focusing on battery energy storage systems (BESS) that ensure a consistent supply of energy. So even if renewable generation itself fluctuates, our businesses, factories, and homes have a reliable, and continuing, source of power. With energy demand rising across the world, battery storage is becoming the Net Zero transition’s next big challenge. How fast is the battery storage market growing? The global battery storage market is expanding rapidly â and it shows no sign of slowing down. According to the latest data from the International Energy Agency (IEA), battery storage is the âfastest growing power technology todayâ with 108 GW of new capacity deployed worldwide in 2025, a 40% increase on 2024 figures. This equates to an eleven-fold increase in the past five years[1]. The same trend is evident in figures from BloombergNEF[2], which notes that global deployment has set new records every year since 2014. According to the data, it took only four years for annual battery storage additions to increase from 10 GW to more than 100 â far quicker than the time it took solar and wind energy to achieve the same progress (eight and fifteen years respectively). The research also found that in 2025: - China continued to lead the global battery storage market, responsible for 54% of additions - The US was the next biggest player, accounting for 16% of new storage - Deployment in Australia increased by almost six times since 2024 - Saudia Arabia âleapfroggedâ some of its peers, working with Chinese suppliers Statistics such as the increase of more than three quarters (75.5%) in global shipments of battery energy storage systems (BESS)[3] provide further indications of the sectorâs current strong growth. And the trend is expected to continue over the next decade, with more than 300 GW of annual additions forecast for 2036[4]. Whatâs driving the growth of battery storage? The total amount of battery storage capacity around the world is increasing for a number of reasons: The rise of renewables: The integration of renewable energy into power systems is increasingly driving the growth of battery storage. The output of renewable sources such as solar and wind varies depending on the weather and time of day. Having the ability to store energy in batteries and then release it later allows suppliers to deliver power on demand and stick to generation schedules. Businesses can also reduce costs, and the load on their systems, by storing excess energy and releasing it during times of high demand. This âenergy shiftingâ has become the dominant application for battery projects, with its share of new projects increasing from around 40% in 2015 to more than 90% in 2025[5]. âAs deployment pivots towards energy shifting and renewables integration, the duration of utility-scale batteries is increasing, with a rising share of projects offering four hours of storage or more,â states the IEA[6]. Having the ability to store energy in batteries and then release it later allows suppliers to deliver power on demand and stick to generation schedules Artificial intelligence AI is another important factor in the growing need for new battery storage. As well as requiring large amounts of power, AI creates rapidly changing, unpredictable loads. Responding to these effectively requires energy storage, not merely as an emergency backup, but as an essential element of day-to-day operations. In a 2025 survey, almost half of industry respondents (49%) named âAI dynamic powerâ as a factor driving changes they were considering to their energy storage technology[7]. Grid complexity Booming sectors such as electric vehicles, AI and advanced manufacturing are creating a growing dependence on electric power globally. In turn, this is increasing the demands on, and complexity of, electrical grids. In many places, major improvement work is under way: in the European Union and the UK, for example, investment in grids is set to reach US$ 120 billion a year by 2030, according to McKinsey[8]. Alongside other technologies, battery storage can contribute to providing the flexibility needed to meet and manage energy demands efficiently. BESS also offers functions such as voltage and frequency regulation to help stabilize grids. Booming sectors such as electric vehicles, AI and advanced manufacturing are creating a growing dependence on electric power globally Falling costs The cost of battery storage projects is falling rapidly amid increasing manufacturer competition, improved designs and lower pack prices. According to Bloomberg NEF data, in 2025 the global benchmark cost of a four-hour battery project dropped by 27% year-on-year to a record low (US$ 78 per MWh). This follows a decade of substantially decreasing prices, with installed costs falling around 20% a year on average between 2004 and 2014[9]. Policy Government policies are a significant factor accelerating the growth of BESS, too. Net zero targets support widespread electrification, increasing demand on grids and driving the switch to renewables. Meanwhile, many governments have designed regulations or incentives specifically to support battery storage. In China, mandates to co-locate storage with renewable projects have underpinned much of the growth of BESS in recent years. These ended in 2025. In other countries (including Poland[10], Ireland[11] and Australia[12]) there are subsidies or effective requirements for battery storage. How are key countries around the world using battery storage? China is the world leader in battery storage, accounting for more than half of global BESS capacity by the end of 2025[13]. artigo.texto: Hyperscale Data Sells Remaining Bitcoin Reserves to Reduce Debt and Fund Michigan AI Data Center LAS VEGAS , Nov. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Hyperscale Data, Inc. (NYSE American: GPUS), an artificial intelligence ("AI") data center company ("Hyperscale Data" or the "Company"), today announced that as of November 8th, 2026, it had sold all of its remaining Bitcoin reserves at approximately $76,000 per Bitcoin. The Company sold approximately 211.56 Bitcoin and received gross proceeds of approximately $16.0 million. Since the Company initially sold a portion of its Bitcoin reserve in late July of 2026, the Company has sold approximately 1,113 Bitcoin for approximate proceeds of $74.4 million. Hyperscale Data is using the proceeds to pay down debt and fund the continued development of its Michigan AI data center. "Our highest priority is to energize the first 10 megawatts of critical IT capacity at our Michigan data center in December," said Will Horne, Chief Executive Officer of Hyperscale Data. "We believe bringing that capacity online is our quickest path to profitability. Selling our Bitcoin reserves reduces our exposure to Bitcoin price swings and gives us cash to pay down debt and fund the work in Michigan. We believe that's the best use of this capital for all our stockholders." Hyperscale Data continues to mine Bitcoin at its Montana mining site. Going forward, the Company expects any Bitcoin it holds on its balance sheet to come primarily from its own mining operations. The Company expects to file its Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, on or before Monday, November 23. In light of the recently announced proposed exchange offer for its Class A common stock (the "Exchange Offer"), the Company also expects to move its virtual Investor Day from November 12 to November 23. Management expects to update investors on debt reduction and progress toward the December energization target. When the Company commences the Exchange Offer, it will file the offer documents with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. Stockholders should read those documents when available. They will be accessible free of charge at www.sec.gov. For more information on Hyperscale Data and its subsidiaries, Hyperscale Data recommends that stockholders, investors and any other interested parties read Hyperscale Data's public filings and press releases available under the Investor Relations section at hyperscaledata.com or available at www.sec.gov. About Hyperscale Data, Inc. Through its wholly owned subsidiary Sentinum, Inc., Hyperscale Data owns and operates a data center at which it offers colocation and hosting services for the emerging AI ecosystems and other industries. Another of Hyperscale Data's wholly owned subsidiaries, Ault Capital Group, Inc. ("ACG"), is a hybrid private equity firm and operating company that acquires, finances, builds and actively manages businesses across financial services, digital assets, industrial services, hospitality, defense technologies and other sectors. Hyperscale Data currently expects the divestiture of ACG (the "Divestiture") to occur in 2027. Upon the occurrence of the Divestiture, the Company would be an owner and operator of data centers to support high-performance computing services, as well as a holder of the digital assets and the third wholly owned subsidiary of the Company, Omnipresent Robotics, LLC. Until the Divestiture occurs, the Company will continue to provide, through ACG and its wholly and majority-owned subsidiaries and strategic investments, mission-critical products that support a diverse range of industries, including an AI software platform, equipment rental services, defense/aerospace, industrial, automotive and hotel operations. In addition, ACG is actively engaged in private credit and structured finance through Ault Lending, LLC, a licensed lending subsidiary. Hyperscale Data's headquarters are located at 11411 Southern Highlands Parkway, Suite 190, Las Vegas, NV 89141. On December 23, 2024, the Company issued one million (1,000,000) shares of a newly designated Series F Exchangeable Preferred Stock (the "Series F Preferred Stock") to all common stockholders and holders of the Series C Preferred Stock on an as-converted basis. The Divestiture will occur through the voluntary exchange of the Series F Preferred Stock for shares of Class A Common Stock and Class B Common Stock of ACG (collectively, the "ACG Shares"). The Company reminds its stockholders that only those holders of the Series F Preferred Stock who agree to surrender such shares, and do not properly withdraw such surrender, in the exchange offer through which the Divestiture will occur, will be entitled to receive the ACG Shares and consequently be shareholders of ACG upon the occurrence of the Divestiture. artigo.texto: ATU-Ozark to provide âcritical’ training for data center jobs Arkansas Tech UniversityâOzark will provide âcritical facilities trainingâ through a partnership with El Segundo, Calif.-based Serverfarm, the company building a $6.6 billion data center in Clarksville, Ark. (Johnson County). The company says it will have more than 200 âpermanent, high-paying jobsâ at the facility when completed. According to an ATU-Ozark press release, the program will provide training for those seeking a career in data centers. The 180-hour training program is set to begin in January 2027, with Serverfarm helping to shape the curriculum âaround real-world job requirements.â The program combines 128 hours of lab and simulation training with 52 hours of classroom instruction in electrical power, cooling and refrigeration, backup systems, controls and maintenance. ATU-Ozark said the course is a first step toward a planned two-year associate decree program in critical facilities technology. âWhat makes this partnership especially exciting is our commitment to build upon this training to establish an associate degree pathway that will continue to meet the needs of students and strengthen our local workforce,â Dr. Sheila Jacobs, ATU-Ozark chancellor, said in a statement. âI am especially grateful to work with a team of people who are flexible and willing to do what it takes to meet industry needs and serve students.â According to ATU-Ozark, entry into the program requires no prior data center experience. The first class is expected to include 12 to 15 students, with eligible students able to receive Arkansas Workforce Challenge Scholarship funds to cover the cost of training. ATU Ozark staff will help with the scholarship application, the university noted. âEvery data center we operate depends on technicians who know how to keep power and cooling running around the clock,â Mike Whitman, vice president of operations, North America at Serverfarm, said in a statement. âWe worked side by side with ATU Ozark to translate what our facilities actually require into a curriculum, and to make sure students train on the same kinds of equipment they would find inside a working data center. We want our operations staff to come from the communities around us, and this program gives local residents a direct path into those careers.â Serverfarm CEO Avner Papouchado said the Clarksville facility will employ 2,000 people during construction, which is ongoing, and be home to 200 full-time jobs when operational. He also said the facility will have âapproximately 1,000 additional campus jobs.â Serverfarm says the 200 jobs will be based in Clarksville, and the 1,000 additional jobs will be created by vendors and will not be Serverfarm employees. Serverfarm said the first building will begin operations in the summer of 2027, with the entire facility operational by fall 2028. The large data center â about 1.2 million square feet on up to 463 acres when finished â has been a point of controversy in the city and county. Some residents were upset that city and county officials signed non-disclosure agreements with the company and the public was not aware of facility details until it was announced. An online petition was created at change.org to oppose the facility, with 1,030 verified signatures as of Nov. 12. Petition organizers said âlocals are being left in the darkâ about the potential negative impacts â water and sewer system demand, utility costs, noise â of the center. âThereâs been no public hearing on energy use, water needs, noise levels, or environmental impact,â petition organizers noted. âAnd the company still hasnât answered basic questions. â¦ This project could reshape Clarksville for decades, and residents deserve more than closed-door decisions and vague promises.â

artigo.texto: Munters announces investments to strengthen data center supply chain and capacity STOCKHOLM , Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Munters Group today announced it has entered into an agreement with Lordan, a producer of high-quality fin and tube heat exchangers, to establish a joint venture for coil manufacturing in the US. The company also said it plans to expand its facility for chiller production in Italy. US joint venture Munters will invest MUSD 9.5 (approximately MSEK 90) and hold 45% in the joint venture company, with Lordan holding the remaining 55%. The joint venture will now proceed to establish a facility for coil manufacturing near Munters Data Center Technologies' facility in Selma, Texas. Production is expected to begin in 12-18 months. "Coils are a critical component in many of our cooling products. Through this collaboration with a well-established expert in heat exchangers, we are ensuring a flexible supply of high-quality coils and related components for products such as CRAHs and fan walls," says Frank Pellegrino, President of Munters business area Data Center Technologies. "The proximity to our existing facility is an added benefit from an efficiency and environmental perspective, and we're excited about the potential for this joint venture to contribute to our in-house expertise around thermal management and heat exchange," adds Pellegrino. The agreement with Lordan is valid for seven years and includes commitments from the parties to produce and acquire a certain quantity of coils over that period, at preferred lead times and price levels. Lordan will be responsible for day-to-day operations at the facility while Munters will contribute with supply chain and staffing resources. Italy expansion Munters has also decided to expand its existing facility in northern Italy for manufacturing of chillers, to better meet growing demand in Europe for these products. The company is acquiring an adjoining site and will over the course of the coming year develop new production lines, R&D capabilities and testing facilities. The total investment is estimated at around MEUR 25. "This investment signifies our commitment to growing chiller capacity for Europe, as well as the importance of our Italian operations as a hub for expertise in this area," Pellegrino said. artigo.texto: LITEON Showcases High-Speed Optical Interconnect and Key Optoelectronic Technologies at electronica 2026, Advancing AI Data Center Infrastructure with Intelligent Photonics MUNICH , Nov. 11, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- LITEON Technology (2301) participates in electronica 2026, held in Munich, Germany, from November 10 to 13, showcasing its optoelectronic semiconductor technologies under the theme "Intelligent Photonics." The portfolio spans high-speed optical interconnects, high-efficiency isolation and power control, intelligent sensing, and AR optics, demonstrating LITEON's broad deployment of core optoelectronic technologies across AI data centers, high-efficiency energy management, and intelligent applications. "AI is accelerating the transformation of computing and energy infrastructure, while driving growing demand for high-speed, low-power, and highly reliable optical connectivity," said Sander Su, General Manager of LITEON's Optoelectronics Products Solutions. "With deep expertise in optical communications and optoelectronic semiconductors, LITEON is positioning ourselves as a Digital Photonics Integrator, continuously integrating technologies across key components, modules, and system-level applications to help customers address the growing demands for high-speed transmission, greater efficiency, and intelligent sensing in the AI era." As AI computing scales, data centers require higher bandwidth, lower latency, and greater energy efficiency. LITEON showcases its VHP External Laser Source (ELS) technology and ELSFP solutions supporting CPO and NPO switch architectures, providing high-performance, scalable optical connectivity for AI clusters and future data centers. Designed to accommodate different system configurations, liquid-cooling architectures, and integration requirements, the solutions help customers build more efficient AI networking infrastructure. LITEON also showcases isolation and power-control technologies for 800 VDC power systems and AI data center power architectures, extending its optoelectronic expertise from data transmission to power conversion and control. The portfolio includes Isolation Amplifiers, Gate Drivers, high-speed Photocouplers, Photo Relays, and reinforced isolation platforms, providing safe and reliable power conversion as well as precise signal sensing and control in high-voltage, high-power environments. These technologies also support solar inverters, battery management systems, EV charging, and industrial automation, enhancing safety, reliability, and energy efficiency across diverse applications. Beyond data centers, LITEON showcases Multi-Zone ToF, Direct ToF, Metalens Dot Projectors and SWIR sensing technologies for robotics, machine vision, industrial automation, autonomous navigation and AR/VR applications. The showcase also features next-generation AR optical technologies, including MicroLED display modules, full-color optical engines, waveguide integration and AR optical system design, demonstrating LITEON's ability to extend its optoelectronic semiconductor expertise from sensing components to optical modules and integrated systems, further expanding its presence in emerging applications such as smart wearables and immersive computing. artigo.texto: Gates Introduces Compact ThermalCool™ 2100SS Pump to Expand Data Center Portfolio 4U-Compatible Design Delivers High Performance for AI and High-Density Computing Applications DENVER , Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Gates Industrial Corporation Ltd. (NYSE: GTES), a global manufacturer of highly engineered power transmission and fluid power solutions, today introduced Gates ThermalCool™ 2100SS Pump, expanding the company's portfolio of liquid-cooling solutions for AI and high-density data center applications. The new stainless steel pump expands Gates participation across the data center cooling loop, adding a new, purpose-built active coolant circulation solution alongside its fluid conveyance and connection technologies. Higher rack densities are changing where data center cooling equipment is located and how much space it can occupy. Rack-mounted coolant distribution units (CDUs) integrate coolant circulation within the IT rack, which puts tight size and integration demands on every component. Gates developed the ThermalCool 2100SS Pump to meet those demands, combining substantial output with a 4U-compatible design while combining substantial coolant flow with integrated active cooling for the motor. Delivered in a platform configurable for different CDU architectures, these capabilities position Gates to serve a wider range of data center coolant circulation applications including those with high ambient temperature operating conditions. "As data centers pack more computing power into every rack, CDU manufacturers are facing infrastructure challenges that existing pumps weren't designed for," said Rebekah Headley, general manager of data centers at Gates. "We developed the ThermalCool 2100SS Pump in response to requirements from a leading CDU manufacturer, working as an engineering partner to address an emerging system need. That application-driven approach resulted in a configurable platform that takes the solution beyond the original application and into the broader data center cooling market." Key features of Gates ThermalCool 2100SS Pump: - High performance in a compact footprint: Up to 200 L/min flow at 3 bar in a 4U-compatible design. - Self-cooling architecture: Built for enclosed CDUs with limited airflow or high ambient temperatures, the motor is uniquely designed to be electrically dry and actively liquid-cooled by the coolant the pump already circulates, with no separate cooling circuit or fan required. - Engineered for data center reliability: Stainless steel construction, OCP-compliant wetted materials, IP55 protection and a rated 50,000-hour pump life support reliable, long-term operation. - Flexible, scalable integration: Configurable connections and mounting options fit different CDU layouts, while parallel operation and N+1 redundancy let customers scale capacity and help protect uptime. CANBUS and MODBUS communication support integration with CDU monitoring and control systems. The ThermalCool 2100SS Pump expands Gates' capabilities across the data center cooling loop, complementing its portfolio of hoses, UQDs, fittings and engineered assemblies. Together, these technologies strengthen Gates' ability to help customers engineer the fluid path from coolant circulation through rack-level connection and conveyance. The Gates ThermalCool 2100SS Pump is expected to be available globally in early 2027. For more information, to connect with a Gates engineer, or to request a sample, visit the Data Center Pumps Innovations page. About Gates Industrial Corporation Ltd. Gates is a global manufacturer of innovative, highly engineered power transmission and fluid power solutions. Gates offers a broad portfolio of products to diverse replacement channel customers, and to OEMs as specified components. Gates participates in many sectors of the industrial and consumer markets. Our products play essential roles in a diverse range of applications across a wide variety of end markets ranging from harsh and hazardous industries to everyday consumer applications, including virtually every form of transportation. Our products are sold in more than 130 countries across our three commercial regions: the Americas; Europe, Middle East & Africa; Asia-Pacific. For more information, visit gates.com. artigo.texto: Lawmakers eye data center moratorium as Virginia environmental coalition ramps up pressure ASHLAND, Va. (7News) — A coalition of more than a dozen environmental groups met in the parking lot of an animal shelter in Ashland, Virginia, Wednesday to call for a halt to any new data center construction within the commonwealth. Their backdrop: a data center approved in Hanover County with little-to-no public input. At a time when state lawmakers in Virginia are increasingly warming to the idea of pressing the pause button on Virginia's data-center build out, environmental groups are calling for a moratorium on new construction. ALSO READ | Virginia Democrats lay out 2027 agenda targeting affordability and data centers "We're here to say 'enough is enough. Our governor and our legislature need to pause data center construction to protect the Virginia we know and love," said Blair St. Ledger-Olson, Director of Advocacy and Campaigns for the Virginia League of Conservation Voters. More than one speaker Wednesday referenced shifting opinions within the Virginia General Assembly, as well as changing voter sentiment reflected in the midterm elections, a combination the coalition seeks to capitalize upon as Virginia lawmakers prepare to consider what one person Wednesday referred to as a "smorgasbord of legislative options." Senator Russet Perry, (D - Loudoun County) and Senator Glen Sturtevant, (R - Chesterfield), among others, are expected to back bills in the coming legislative session recommending a moratorium on data centers. With 685 data centers either built or in the planning stages, Virginia is far and away the data center capital of the world. Any new projects, the coalition insists, must protect the commonwealth's power, water and land. "We are paying more for power because of data centers, and the data centers are getting a sweet deal on the backs of Virginians," Nate Benforado, an attorney for the Southern Environmental Law Center said Wednesday. Jay Ford, a policy director with the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, cautioned that the 64,000 square mile Chesapeake Bay watershed sits at "ground zero." "Just this year, Virginia has faced historic strains on our water resources," Ford said. "We drink water from rivers and we drink it from ground water and both of those are under historic stress right now. " Julie Bolthouse, Director of Land Use for the Piedmont Environmental Council identified the commonwealth as "one of the fastest growing markets" in the nation's data center build out, "with about 280 million square feet of data centers space already approved locally." Bolthouse said that amount of land designated for data center development is "the equivalent of 1,500 Walmart supercenters or, if you're a football fan, 5,000 football fields." The question is whether the growing calls for a data center moratorium will sway the opinion of Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger, who has publicly supported greater restrictions on the industry through an executive order but not an outright pause on any new construction. Elena Schlossberg, who successfully battled a massive data center project in her home of Prince William County said Wednesday that Spanberger would do well to consider, what Schlossberg described as the shifting political winds. "If Governor Spanberger has higher aspirations, then I would recommend that she get on the right side of this issue," Schlossberg said.

artigo.texto: Minneapolis City Council to vote on data centers Thursday In less than 24 hours, the Minneapolis City Council will make a pivotal vote on whether to allow data centers in the city. The current proposal would require data centers to be in two downtown districts, be 150,000 square feet or smaller, only operate in existing office space, and not be the primary use of a building. In an update Wednesday, Council Member Jamal Osman pledged to work “to preserve the tighter size limit, the renewable-energy requirement, and public review in the final ordinance.” Others are still pushing for a total ban, which did not advance in Committee this week. On Wednesday, Council Member Soren Stevenson said, “If a full ban fails again tomorrow, we will bring back a proposal that includes overlay zoning again as well,” which he explained would allow City Council members and the Planning Commission to hold public hearings when evaluating a proposed data center development on a case-by-case basis. Stevenson said he and the others plan to bring forward more amendments to “do everything we can to protect Minneapolis from the interests of AI and Big Tech.” There is a moratorium in place, but that expires in about two weeks. The City Council implemented the pause to allow the city to create new data center standards. “Will small-scale data centers be a cure-all for revenue generation? I’ve already said no,” said Council Member Elizabeth Shaffer. “Is it a step in the right direction for some revenue generation and property tax relief? Yes.”

artigo.texto: Modelos e plataformas de IA Siemens eleva metas de crescimento com o avanço da IA industrial e a demanda por data centers Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Siemens elevou suas metas de crescimento de médio prazo em 12 de novembro de 2026, após os pedidos comparáveis aumentarem 25%, alcançando o recorde de €108,2 bilhões no exercício fiscal encerrado em 30 de setembro de 2026. A empresa associou as ambições mais elevadas à IA industrial, à digitalização, à eletrificação e à demanda por data centers. Para o grupo, excluindo a Siemens Healthineers, a meta de crescimento comparável da receita agora é de 7%–11%, ante 6%–9%, enquanto a ambição para o EPS pre PPA passou de crescimento de um dígito alto para crescimento de dois dígitos. EPS pre PPA corresponde ao lucro básico por ação antes da contabilização da alocação do preço de compra; o crescimento comparável exclui os efeitos da conversão cambial e das mudanças no portfólio. Data centers e software impulsionam a aposta em IA A Smart Infrastructure apresentou a evidência trimestral mais clara da demanda por data centers. Seus pedidos do quarto trimestre cresceram 39% em base comparável, chegando a €8,7 bilhões, com contratos maiores de eletrificação e produtos elétricos firmados com clientes de data centers, principalmente nos Estados Unidos e na Europa. A receita comparável aumentou 15%, para €7,2 bilhões, à medida que essas áreas executaram suas grandes carteiras de pedidos. A apresentação para investidores da Siemens informou um crescimento de três dígitos nos pedidos de data centers no exercício fiscal de 2026. Os data centers agora representam 20% da exposição da receita da Smart Infrastructure, tornando-se seu segundo maior segmento vertical, atrás dos clientes industriais. A empresa atribuiu o impulso sustentado à expansão da infraestrutura de IA. Grandes contratos ferroviários também contribuíram substancialmente para o recorde de pedidos do grupo. Os pedidos da Mobility aumentaram mais de 200%, chegando a €10,7 bilhões no quarto trimestre, incluindo um pedido alemão de €2,4 bilhões para trens de alta velocidade e serviços de manutenção. Além da eletrificação, a receita dos negócios digitais da Siemens, que abrangem software específico para cada segmento, IoT e serviços digitais, cresceu 16%, alcançando €10,9 bilhões. A Siemens também informou que seu Eigen Engineering Agent duplicou a velocidade dos trabalhos de engenharia na fabricante de máquinas ANDRITZ Metals, oferecendo um exemplo de cliente para sua estratégia de IA industrial. Lucro industrial recorde contrasta com queda no lucro líquido O lucro dos Negócios Industriais aumentou 13%, atingindo o recorde de €13,3 bilhões no exercício fiscal de 2026, mas o lucro líquido caiu para €9,5 bilhões, ante €10,4 bilhões. O valor do ano anterior incluía um ganho de €2,1 bilhões com a venda da Innomotics, o que ajuda a explicar por que o lucro industrial recorde não se traduziu em um aumento do resultado final. Perspectivas para o exercício fiscal de 2027 dependem dos investimentos em IA A Siemens inicia o exercício fiscal de 2027 com uma carteira recorde de pedidos de €143 bilhões. A empresa prevê crescimento comparável da receita de 9%–11% e EPS pre PPA de €10,20–€10,80, em comparação com a base comparável de €9,27 no exercício fiscal de 2026, excluindo a Siemens Healthineers. A previsão exclui a Healthineers porque a Siemens pretende desconsolidar o negócio por meio de uma cisão direta durante o exercício fiscal de 2027. Por isso, o valor de €9,27, e não o resultado divulgado pelo grupo, é a referência pertinente para comparar as perspectivas de lucro. A administração parte do pressuposto de que a expansão econômica global continuará, impulsionada principalmente por investimentos em IA e infraestrutura digital, programas de investimento público e uma retomada da atividade industrial. A Siemens também espera que a intensidade de capital seja substancialmente maior do que no exercício fiscal de 2026, medida pelos gastos de capital, incluindo arrendamentos operacionais, em relação à depreciação e à amortização, sobretudo devido à expansão da capacidade da Smart Infrastructure. As metas mais elevadas tornam a conversão da carteira de pedidos e a expansão da capacidade os principais desafios operacionais do exercício fiscal de 2027, enquanto a cisão planejada da Healthineers alteraria o perímetro de negócios usado para medir o crescimento e os lucros da Siemens.

artigo.texto: O governador de Mato Grosso, Otaviano Pivetta (Republicanos), divulgou nesta quarta-feira (11) imagens de sua presença na 31ª Conferência das Nações Unidas sobre Mudanças Climáticas (COP31), sediada em Antália, na Turquia. O deslocamento do chefe do Executivo estadual tem como finalidade central a captação de investidores estrangeiros e a obtenção de validação para créditos de carbono originados da diminuição do desmatamento em território mato-grossense. A projeção do governo aponta para a possibilidade de fechar negócios na ordem de R$ 4,1 bilhões. Em manifestação publicada nas redes sociais, Pivetta declarou: “Estamos na COP 31 com uma missão importante: apresentar o trabalho de Mato Grosso na redução do desmatamento e buscar reconhecimento internacional para nossos créditos de carbono. Também vamos conversar com investidores e mostrar que é possível unir conservação ambiental, desenvolvimento e novas oportunidades para o nosso Estado”. Nas imagens divulgadas, o governador surge ao lado de membros da comitiva do Estado, ressaltando a relevância do contato com representantes de outros países. A proposta governamental prevê a certificação de cerca de 50 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono que deixaram de ser lançadas na atmosfera em decorrência da queda do desmatamento. Conforme números apresentados pelo Estado, a supressão de vegetação na área mato-grossense da Amazônia registrou redução de 46,7% quando comparados os períodos de 2024/2025 e 2025/2026. A expectativa de arrecadar US$ 750 milhões, montante equivalente a aproximadamente R$ 4,1 bilhões, está condicionada à certificação dos créditos e à efetivação de acordos comerciais. Para dar suporte a essas tratativas, Pivetta enviou à Assembleia Legislativa o projeto de lei nº 1.156/2026, que propõe a instituição da Companhia Mato-grossense de Ativos Ambientais S.A. (CMAA). A companhia de economia mista ficará responsável pela gestão e pela comercialização de créditos de carbono e de outros ativos ambientais. A comitiva estadual também tem agenda prevista com investidores vinculados à Coalizão LEAF, iniciativa internacional voltada ao financiamento da preservação florestal, da qual participam nações como Reino Unido e Noruega. A ausência do governador provocou alterações temporárias na chefia do Executivo estadual. Desde sexta-feira (6), o presidente da Assembleia Legislativa, Max Russi (Podemos), responde interinamente pelo cargo de governador. O retorno de Pivetta a Mato Grosso está previsto para 18 de novembro e, conforme o Governo do Estado, a viagem está sendo bancada com recursos próprios do governador. O evento em Antália conta ainda com a presença do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), reeleito em outubro, o que abre a possibilidade de um encontro institucional entre os dois governantes, que apoiaram candidaturas presidenciais rivais nas eleições deste ano.

artigo.texto: Southeast Asia's Semiconductor Rise: AI Reshapes Industry Stratification as Singapore Anchors a Regional Innovation and Demand Hub As the global semiconductor industry undergoes a structural revaluation driven by the AI computing boom, Southeast Asia is evolving from a manufacturing hinterland into a dual engine of innovation and demand. AI Reshapes Industry Stratification, with Southeast Asia at the Core The global semiconductor market is expanding faster than expected. According to the World Semiconductor Trade Statistics (WSTS) spring 2026 forecast, the global semiconductor market is projected to grow 90% year-on-year in 2026 to reach US$1.51 trillion, and to grow a further 27% in 2027, approaching US$1.9 trillion. The core driver of this cycle is sustained strong demand for AI infrastructure, high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and accelerated computing platforms. Memory chip sales are expected to rise about 250% year-on-year in 2026, while logic chips grow 37%, as AI redefines capacity priorities from advanced process nodes to advanced packaging. Southeast Asia's position in this cycle is particularly critical. According to the ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office (AMRO) Quarterly Update of the ASEAN+3 Regional Economic Outlook (AREO), the region accounts for nearly half of global AI-related exports, with semiconductor sales accelerating further on the back of strong growth in 2025. As a regional hub, Singapore holds about 10% of global chip capacity and 20% of semiconductor equipment manufacturing share, making it one of the most attractive AI innovation hubs in Asia-Pacific. In 2026, the Singapore government launched the "SG Semiconductor" national brand, focusing on seven technology areas — including advanced packaging, silicon photonics, power electronics, high-frequency gallium nitride, piezoelectric MEMS, planar optics and IC design — to further strengthen its competitive edge across the semiconductor value chain. Singapore's Semiconductor Ecosystem Is Accelerating Its Expansion The decision to hold Asia Semiconductor Expo (ASE) in Singapore reflects the substantive expansion of the city-state's semiconductor supply chain. In September 2026, Advanced Substrate Technologies (AST), a joint venture between Broadcom and Toppan, opened its first high-end FC-BGA substrate manufacturing facility in Singapore, adding more than 330 engineering and technical positions. In the same month, VSMC, a joint venture between Vanguard International Semiconductor and NXP, opened its 12-inch wafer fab, with mass production expected in the first quarter of 2027 and capacity already booked. Dr. Tan See Leng, Minister for Trade and Industry (Energy and Industry), has emphasized on VSMC Grand Opening Ceremony that Singapore plays a trusted role in regional supply chains, and that this influence can extend beyond the semiconductor ecosystem to create opportunities for more local suppliers. From a regional perspective, Southeast Asia's semiconductor landscape is developing across multiple poles: Malaysia accounts for about 13% of global assembly and test capacity and 40% of automotive-grade chip assembly and testing; Thailand ranks among the world's top five in PCB capacity, with its automotive electronics market expected to grow to US$4 billion by 2030; and Vietnam's semiconductor industry output is valued at about US$20 billion, with a compound annual growth rate of around 11%. These dispersed yet complementary capabilities call for a platform at the regional hub that can showcase and connect them—and that is precisely the role Asia Semiconductor Expo is built to play. Take the Lead in the Upward Phase of the AI Chip Cycle WSTS's forecast sends a clear signal: the semiconductor industry has moved from a post-inventory-correction recovery into a phase of structural revaluation driven by AI infrastructure. However, this revaluation is uneven — capacity and customer priorities across AI core chains such as HBM, advanced logic chips, advanced packaging and high-speed interconnects are being redefined. For companies in semiconductor equipment, materials, components and compound semiconductors, whether they can appear in front of key buyers during the 2027 regional procurement decision window will directly affect their position in this cycle. As one of the three themed shows under Asia Photonics Expo 2027 (APE 2027), Asia Semiconductor Expo (ASE) will take place March 3–5, 2027 at the Sands Expo and Convention Centre, Singapore. Anchored in Singapore, reaching across Southeast Asia and connecting to global markets, ASE is dedicated to building an international exhibition and business-matching platform spanning the entire semiconductor value chain. Running alongside it, the newly launched Asia Electronics Expo (AEE) will also debut in Singapore, joining APE 2027 to form a three-show ecosystem spanning semiconductors, photonics, and electronics. Whether you are looking to showcase cutting-edge technologies, innovative products and solutions, or to connect with Southeast Asia's increasingly complete design–manufacturing–packaging and testing–application ecosystem, the show offers an entry point that only a three-show co-location can provide. Secure your booth now to put your innovations in front of key decision-makers — or register to visit and efficiently assess and procure across the entire value chain, all in one place. About the Author Eric Yang Eric Yang is Secretary General of the Asia Photonics Expo. (Source: China International Optoelectronic Exposition)

(File photo) Keystone It is one of the EU's key climate protection tools: the greenhouse gas emissions trading system. For a limited time, relief is to be provided to industry. According to the European Parliament, a temporary change to the EU’s emissions trading system is expected to save the industry several billion euros. Negotiators from the Parliament and the EU member states agreed early Friday morning to allocate approximately 120 million additional free EU emissions trading allowances to industry for the period from 2026 to 2030. Both sides announced the agreement. This means the negotiators are going even further than the European Commission’s proposal from July, which, according to the Commission, would have saved the affected industries approximately 6 billion euros. Since the agreement now provides for even more free allowances, the expected savings are rising, according to Parliament. The so-called Emissions Trading System (ETS) is considered the EU’s key climate protection tool. Emissions caps are intended to serve as an incentive to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, particularly in energy-intensive sectors such as power generation and industry. The affected companies must hold permits for the emission of climate-damaging gases such as carbon dioxide (CO2). They can trade these permits as needed or purchase additional ones at auction. This establishes a price for every metric ton of CO2 emitted. To prevent companies from relocating to countries with less stringent climate regulations, facilities in certain sectors also receive free allowances. Benchmark values are used to calculate the allocation. After these were adjusted in June, some in the industry had feared drastic cuts to their free allowances. The compromise still needs to be formally adopted by the Parliament and the member states. Once that happens, the European Commission can, based on information provided by the member states, issue implementing regulations for calculating the reference values. In July, the European Commission also proposed further adjustments to the emissions trading system, which are currently still under negotiation. The EU has set a goal of reducing its greenhouse gas emissions by 90 percent by 2040 compared to 1990 levels.

artigo.texto: Deutsche Bank and Rabobank are backing an €835 million (about $936 million) financing package to help energy storage company Return expand its battery storage business in Germany. The deal will support new projects as the country works to integrate more wind and solar power into its electricity system. The portfolio facility initially covers three battery energy storage projects with a combined capacity of 117 megawatts (MW). More eligible projects can be added as they reach financial close. The financing combines support for physical battery assets with Return’s Virtual Flexibility Portfolio (VFP). This model connects multiple storage facilities into one virtual system. Energy companies can access flexible electricity capacity through a single platform. The transaction involves several financial and technical advisers. Rabobank acted as financial adviser, while White & Case advised the lenders. Other firms involved included Hogan Lovells Cadwalader, Baker McKenzie, Baringa, DNV, EY, EY-Parthenon, and Marsh. The deal comes as Germany’s battery storage market grows. It also shows how private finance helps build the infrastructure for a power system with more renewable energy. A Financing Framework for Germany’s Battery Expansion The €835 million facility gives Return a way to finance several battery projects under one structure instead of arranging separate financing for every site. This approach could help speed up project development. Eligible facilities can access funding as they progress toward financial close, without having to restart the financing process each time. The initial portfolio includes three projects in Germany with a combined power capacity of 117 MW. Return stated that, with four-hour batteries running two full cycles each day, the facilities could provide enough electricity yearly to power around 100,000 German households. The company plans to add more projects to the financing framework through 2027. Return also has wider growth plans for the German market. It aims to install at least 1 gigawatt (GW) of battery storage capacity each year from 2027. The company estimates that this would require annual investment of €750 million to €1.2 billion, depending on market conditions. The financing is therefore part of a much larger expansion plan. The company has not said that the full €835 million will be used only for the three projects in the initial portfolio. Daniel Witvoet, CFO at Return, remarked: “As demand for energy flexibility grows, we need to scale not just our battery storage capacity, but also the way we finance it. By bringing together physical infrastructure financing and our virtual flexibility model, we can expand more efficiently and respond to our customers’ evolving needs. This is an important step towards our ambition to become a leading independent provider of energy flexibility in Germany.” Why Germany Needs More Battery Storage Germany is adding more wind and solar power to its electricity mix. However, these sources do not produce power at a steady rate. Solar generation changes with daylight and weather, while wind output can rise or fall depending on conditions. Battery storage can help manage these changes. It can store electricity when supply is high and prices are low, then release it when demand rises or renewable generation falls. This can help balance the grid and make better use of clean electricity. Germany’s Federal Network Agency explains that battery systems can respond to electricity market prices, support grid stability, and improve the use of renewable power. The need for this flexibility is becoming clearer as storage projects move through the development pipeline. According to data published by Germany’s Federal Network Agency in August 2026, network operators received 18,158 battery storage connection applications in 2025. These requests represented about 573.5 GW of planned power capacity and 1,583 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of energy capacity. However, these figures do not represent projects that are certain to be built. Developers sometimes submit applications for the same project at several possible locations. The regulator noted that only one location may ultimately be selected. A more advanced measure is the number of grid connection offers. In 2025, network operators issued 1,937 offers covering 54.2 GW of power capacity and 142.4 GWh of energy capacity. These offers provide a clearer picture of project progress because they are binding proposals for connection agreements. Even so, projects still need to secure financing, complete construction, and meet other requirements before they can operate. Germany’s Storage Pipeline Reflects a Growing Market Germany’s battery storage market has expanded as renewable energy has gained a larger role in power generation. Fraunhofer ISE reported that, in 2025, wind and solar power generated more electricity than any other source in Germany’s public electricity mix. The shift increases the need for storage and other flexible resources that can help match supply with demand. The International Energy Agency has also identified utility-scale battery storage as an important part of Germany’s energy transition. Large batteries can provide services such as frequency response and reserves, helping the grid remain stable as the electricity mix changes. Globally, battery storage is growing quickly as well. The IEA’s Global Energy Review 2026 reported that 108 GW of new battery storage capacity was deployed worldwide in 2025, 40% more than in 2024. Global installed capacity was 11 times higher than in 2021. These trends are creating opportunities for developers, utilities, and financial institutions. However, the scale of Germany’s connection requests also shows that grid access and project delivery remain important challenges. artigo.texto: (Photo: Courtesy of More Than Just Parks) As America grapples with the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence data centers, two brothers have set out to map infrastructure project proposals nationwide—including those near public lands and national parks. Will Pattiz is the cofounder of More Than Just Parks, an independent public lands publication that tracks AI data centers. According to his research, at least 14 proposed data center projects are within ten miles of a national park boundary. His data also shows that 38 sites are planned within 25 miles of a national park, and 131 are within 50 miles. “The basic idea is that a lot of these [projects] are being done under the cloak of darkness or secrecy, and we want folks to know where they’re coming in and who’s building them,” Pattiz, a resident of Portland, Oregon, told Outside. “The stance that we take is that we don’t want them on public lands.” “Places like Utah, for example, have a huge amount of data center projects and some of the biggest ones that are being proposed,” Pattiz said. “Just depending on the size and scale, they take up a massive amount of resources and will have impacts on public lands one way or the other, whether it’s taking water or the land itself.” Data centers are rapidly popping up across the United States, fueled by the computing needs of artificial intelligence and cloud-based software. These centers house massive servers, data storage systems, and networking equipment, and they require sizable amounts of electricity and water to run and maintain the hardware. “The question that we want to see asked is: ‘What is the public benefit from this?’” Pattiz said. “So far, the ones that have been proposed on public lands, there’s no public benefit that’s been outlined.” To use Pattiz’s map, a user inputs their zip code, and the site shows the closest data center or proposed facility. The site then suggests how the center will affect utility costs, as well as the groups that support the center. “You can go through that discovery process yourself to decide whether you support [the center] or not, because these are things that are going to impact all of us, and you can decide where you land on that,” Pattiz said. The map auto-populates as more information becomes available. As of this writing, the tool reflects 2,086 data centers, 741 of which are still in the proposal phase. Of those, 77 are located within ten miles of protected land like national parks, wildlife refuges, and wilderness or conservation areas. Roughly half are in the American West. In Virginia, 97 data centers are proposed, and 12 are within 25 miles of Shenandoah National Park. At least 25 data centers are proposed in Indiana, according to the map, and eight are located within 25 miles of Indiana Dunes National Park. The map also includes several construction proposals that are extremely close to iconic National Park Service sites. Arizona alone has 26 active proposals, with three within 25 miles of a national park. In January, the City of Page sold roughly 500 acres to developers planning to build a $10 billion data center next to Horseshoe Bend, an iconic viewpoint along the Colorado River. The 500-acre parcel was previously protected for outdoor recreation. According to the City of Page, the proposal is undergoing public review and has not yet been formally adopted, but a planning and zoning meeting is scheduled for November 17. According to Pattiz’s map, the center is also located about five miles from the northeastern edge of Grand Canyon National Park near Lees Ferry. Just outside of Price, Utah, Pattiz found that a company called Valar Atomics applied for more than 9,000 acres of Bureau of Land Management land for data center buildouts, including permits for hundreds of small nuclear reactors, a fuel plant, and nuclear waste storage. According to a report published by NPR, the so-called Project Beehive would produce about 9.6 gigawatts of power for data centers. Currently, the entire state of Utah produces less than half of that on average, NPR reports. The land is about two hours from both Arches and Canyonlands National Parks. Located about 40 miles from Zion National Park, Antelope Data Center is slated for development as part of a 640-acre, 1.5-gigawatt project that will include an on-site natural gas power plant, according to The Salt Lake Tribune. The Iron County Commission approved a conditional use permit in June 2026. Large-scale data center rollouts represent an inflection point in American history, Pattiz said. As construction crews have erected these centers, they have become political lightning rods in American towns and cities. Pattiz believes that giving Americans transparent, readily available information about where big tech is breaking ground will help them track what developers are building in their backyards. “At the end of the day, data is data,” he added. “Whether or not there’s a need for these things is a totally separate question from where they’re being built and what impact they’re going to have on you and the places that you love.”
