artigo.texto: Marijuana, guns and data centers: What Texas lawmakers are proposing BRYAN, Texas (KBTX) - Texas lawmakers have filed nearly 1,500 bills and resolutions ahead of the 2027 legislative session. Some of them could change how Texans spend money, play and share personal information. The 90th Legislature convenes Jan. 12 with a new political makeup. Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa is expected to take office in January. Democrats are also taking control of the Texas House for the first time in more than 20 years. As of Nov. 12, the House had 1,121 filed measures and the Senate had 336, according to Texas Legislature Online. Lawmakers can keep filing bills and joint resolutions through March 12. Data centers Sixteen bills, 12 in the House and four in the Senate, deal with data centers. House Bill 732 would make certain data centers ineligible for state and local economic development incentives, including the Texas Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation Act program, known as JETI. JETI gives companies a 10-year school tax break if they promise to create jobs and invest in the community. The Grimes County Terafab project has already received one. Marijuana Six bills deal with marijuana. House Bill 369 would legalize recreational marijuana for adults 21 and older. House Bill 330 takes a different approach. It would expand access to medical cannabis by letting doctors prescribe low-THC cannabis to patients with conditions that cause menstrual cramps. Guns Twenty-five bills deal with firearms. They include proposals that could change who can buy a gun, where people can carry one and when authorities can temporarily remove firearms. Gambling House Bill 1031 could classify paid fantasy sports as betting. That would subject those platforms to gambling regulations. License plate readers Flock cameras were a topic on the campaign trail. House Bill 331 would ban government agencies from using license plate readers. It would also let people sue for $1,000 if their rights are violated. Two other bills would allow police to use the cameras in limited situations. Health insurance House Bill 996 would require Medicaid and certain health plans to cover abortion, birth control and voluntary sterilization without charging patients out of pocket. Filing a bill is only the first step. To become law, a bill must pass both the House and the Senate and then get the governor’s approval. Copyright 2026 KBTX. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: The Korea Overseas Infrastructure & Urban Development Corporation (KIND) will jointly develop an energy storage system (ESS) project in Ireland with Shinhan Asset Management, Hyosung Heavy Industries and Irish developer Lumcloon Energy. KIND said on the 11th that it signed a memorandum of understanding with the three companies at the Embassy of Ireland in Seoul on the 10th to jointly develop the ESS project and to pursue overseas infrastructure projects together. The agreement covers an ESS project being developed in the Coolpowra area of County Galway, Ireland. KIND and Shinhan Asset Management agreed to build a strategic cooperation framework with Hyosung Heavy Industries and Lumcloon Energy for the development of and investment in the project. The partners agreed to pursue grid connection for the large-scale ESS and to cooperate across the entire development process, from project permitting and transmission grid connection to deal structuring and financing. If the project moves ahead, it will stabilize output from renewable sources such as wind power and improve both the flexibility of electricity supply and grid stability, the parties to the agreement said. Ireland is expanding its use of renewable energy in response to rising electricity demand and the need to secure grid stability. The country is positioned to tap wind resources along the Atlantic coast, while the need to expand energy storage infrastructure to cope with the intermittency of renewable power is also growing. "Ireland is a market where the importance of grid stability and energy storage infrastructure is growing, driven by the expansion of renewable energy and rising large-scale power demand from facilities such as data centers," a KIND official said. "Using this memorandum of understanding as a starting point, we will work closely with local partners and Korean EPC companies to advance project development, and contribute to expanding Ireland's stable power infrastructure and to broadening Korean companies' entry into the European market."

artigo.texto: da Agência iNFRA Sete associações do setor elétrico enviaram carta ao governo federal solicitando apoio à aprovação do PL 3.716/2026, que propõe alterar as regras de custeio da contratação de sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias no âmbito da reserva de capacidade. O documento pede prioridade na tramitação da proposta para garantir segurança jurídica à realização do primeiro leilão de reserva de capacidade voltado a baterias. A carta é assinada pela ABEEólica (Associação Brasileira de Energia Eólica e Novas Tecnologias), ABIHV (Associação Brasileira da Indústria do Hidrogênio Verde), Abrage (Associação Brasileira das Empresas Geradoras de Energia Elétrica), Abragel (Associação Brasileira de Geração de Energia Limpa), Absae (Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia), Absolar (Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica) e Apine (Associação Brasileira dos Produtores Independentes de Energia Elétrica). O projeto, de autoria do deputado Arnaldo Jardim, prevê a revogação do dispositivo da Lei 10.848/2004 que determina o rateio dos custos da contratação de baterias exclusivamente entre os agentes de geração. As entidades defendem que o custeio siga critérios semelhantes aos aplicados às demais tecnologias contratadas para a reserva de capacidade, considerando que o serviço beneficia todo o sistema elétrico. Segundo as associações, a concentração dos custos nos geradores não impede seu repasse aos consumidores, uma vez que os encargos podem ser incorporados aos preços da energia. “Esse encargo será incorporado aos preços da energia, conforme as condições contratuais e de mercado, e repercutirá nos custos de produção de bens e serviços, possivelmente de forma opaca ou pouco clara”, afirmam as entidades na carta. As associações também alertam que a manutenção das regras atuais pode elevar os riscos dos empreendimentos, encarecer as contratações e provocar questionamentos administrativos e judiciais, com possíveis impactos sobre o cronograma do certame. A carta foi encaminhada a seis ministros, incluindo os titulares de Minas e Energia, Fazenda e Casa Civil, e solicita articulação do Executivo para a aprovação do projeto.

artigo.texto: NYU Researcher: Data Centers Must Offer More to Local Communities Data center developers face growing pressure to deliver local benefits Kate Keith WASHINGTON, Nov. 11, 2026 — Data center developers must do more than minimize environmental and economic harms if they want to gain public support for new construction, according to a researcher at New York University. Scott Brennan, director of NYU’s Center on Technology Policy, said data centers should become more active contributors to the communities where they operate, including by paying property taxes, investing in local infrastructure and supporting workforce development. Brennen's research focuses on technology policy, media and misinformation. He previously held research and policy positions at the University of Oxford, Duke University and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. He holds a doctorate and master's degree in communication from UNC-Chapel Hill and a bachelor's degree in chemistry from Grinnell College. Before pursuing his doctorate, he served in the U.S. Peace Corps as a high school chemistry teacher in northern Mozambique. Speaking during a Fiber Broadband Association Fiber for Breakfast discussion, Brennan said the benefits of data center development, including lower computing costs, technological innovation and U.S. competitiveness in artificial intelligence, are largely shared across society. The costs, however, often fall on the communities hosting the facilities. “The purported benefits of data center buildout are all collective goods, but the harms are localized in specific communities,” Brennan said. “This mismatch between collective goods and local harms is not sustainable.” Public opposition to data centers has grown as residents raise concerns about electricity prices, water consumption, pollution, environmental damage and the effects of large facilities on nearby neighborhoods. Brennan said opposition also reflects broader public distrust of technology companies and concerns about artificial intelligence, including potential job losses and other economic disruptions. He said data center developers have spent years pursuing tax exemptions and other incentives from state and local governments while employing relatively few local workers. As a result, they have not necessarily developed strong constituencies within the communities where they operate. “If data centers are to survive and to gain public support, they need not only ask how to minimize the harms, but ask how to be positive additions to communities,” Brennan said. In a report released over the summer, Brennan's center outlined 10 recommendations for making data centers more beneficial to local communities. The proposals generally focus on improving energy infrastructure, supporting local economies and providing direct community benefits. Brennan said data center operators should help pay for necessary electricity infrastructure upgrades rather than allowing those costs to fall on other utility customers. He also suggested that new demand could create opportunities to modernize aging power grids and expand cleaner energy supplies. Another recommendation is for data centers to pay their fair share of local taxes. “I don't see any reason why data centers shouldn't pay their fair share of taxes,” Brennan said, pointing to the potential for property tax revenue to support local schools and other public services. He also advocated establishing local funds to support workforce development, environmental improvements and other community priorities. Community benefit agreements could provide another way to ensure residents receive something tangible from data center development. Such agreements could support local parks, educational institutions, broadband infrastructure and other projects identified by residents. Brennan said some state governors have begun referencing community benefit agreements in executive orders, but those directives have not necessarily established specific requirements for what the agreements should include. He said communities should have an opportunity to identify their priorities and negotiate agreements that reflect local needs. The growing number of temporary data center moratoriums could give local governments time to develop those expectations, Brennan said. He cautioned, however, that pauses in development should be accompanied by efforts to determine how future projects can benefit residents. Brennan also acknowledged the national competitiveness argument for expanding data center capacity, saying insufficient computing infrastructure could raise costs and limit access to artificial intelligence models. He said the United States needs sufficient computing capacity to remain central to the global AI economy but argued that expanding infrastructure and addressing community concerns should not be mutually exclusive.

artigo.texto: According to a news release, the new system involves a rechargeable technology using zinc-manganese dioxide, which is a non-toxic, readily available material that poses no fire risks, unlike the conventional lithium rechargeable batteries. The system will connect to the grid and may charge from either the utility or campus solar generators and have a power rating of 600 kW and energy capacity of 3,600 kWh. Located near the university’s maintenance building off West Street and occupying an area about the size of one to two tennis courts, the system will reduce utility strain by discharging power during peak demand and providing backup power to residence halls. Lachlan Squair, SUNY Oneonta associate vice president of facilities management, said Wednesday, Nov. 11 the project aligns with the university’s clean energy master plan. “What we’re going to do is demonstrate the technology under real-world conditions,” he said. “For instance, in the summer, a local electricity grid gets really overloaded. You know, at 4 o’clock on a Thursday afternoon in summer when it’s hot, it gets really maxed out. If we charge this energy storage system at night and discharge it during the day, it’s the same as taking 60 houses off the utility.” Students may have opportunities for applied learning and future workforce development training related to clean energy industries. “They can see all this technology in action,” Squair said. If proven beneficial during a three-year trial, the university intends to continue operating the system, and if not, there are funds included in the project budget for system removal. The news release said NYPA is working to select a contractor for engineering and construction services while UEP is finalizing the system design. Engineering in support of installation construction will begin later this year, with construction anticipated to start in 2027. NYPA and UEP will co-fund the $6 million project. In addition, the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority is funding nearly $1 million in project-related costs. The project initially was announced in 2024 as a dual-site demonstration to be partially funded by the U.S. Department of Energy. The DOE later withdrew from the project due to changing priorities. NYPA and UEP re-scoped the effort and advanced it as a single-site project, the release stated. “Advancing next-generation energy storage technology is essential to New York’s all-of-the-above approach to building a cleaner, more resilient electric grid,” NYPA President and CEO Justin E. Driscoll said in the news release. “With this non-lithium energy storage demonstration, we can increase consumer confidence in new storage solutions, expand our use of renewable power and deliver more reliable, affordable electricity to communities across the state.” Improved energy storage technologies can strengthen grid reliability and enable better peak load management, which helps utilities avoid costly transmission upgrades that can drive energy prices up, the release said. “Campuses, hospitals and other critical facilities need energy storage they can place near the buildings they serve,” UEP CEO Gabriel Cowles said in the news release. “Our batteries use the same basic chemistry as everyday alkaline batteries, are made rechargeable, and our systems are manufactured in Pearl River, New York. We’re grateful to NYPA, SUNY Oneonta and NYSERDA for keeping this project moving after the loss of federal funding, and we look forward to showing what safe, New York -made storage can do for SUNY Oneonta’s campus and the grid.” © 2026 The Daily Star (Oneonta, N.Y.). artigo.texto: O avanço do mercado de carbono no Brasil tem alcançado territórios de povos indígenas, quilombolas e outras comunidades tradicionais, onde se localiza parte dos projetos de maior potencial, como os de redução de emissões por desmatamento e degradação florestal (REDD+). Nesse contexto, a advogada socioambiental Ana Carolina de Campos Honora, […] 11 de novembro de 2026, às 12:12 O avanço do mercado de carbono no Brasil tem alcançado territórios de povos indígenas, quilombolas e outras comunidades tradicionais, onde se localiza parte dos projetos de maior potencial, como os de redução de emissões por desmatamento e degradação florestal (REDD+). Nesse contexto, a advogada socioambiental Ana Carolina de Campos Honora, doutoranda em Mudança Social e Participação Política pela Universidade de São Paulo (USP), e a oceanógrafa (UFES) e mestre em Planejamento Energético (COPPE/UFRJ) Larissa Albino, gerente de Operações de Clima e Inteligência Artificial da Future Climate Group, examinam uma pergunta ainda sem resposta simples: quem fica com o valor do carbono. Para elas, o debate vai além do volume financeiro dos créditos. “A discussão não se limita à geração de valor: é preciso saber quanto efetivamente chega às comunidades, segundo quais regras e com que grau de influência sobre o desenho, a negociação e a governança dos projetos”, afirmam. Uma cadeia extensa entre o crédito e o território Segundo as especialistas, não há um número único que indique a fatia destinada às comunidades, e essa ausência integra o problema. A receita se dilui entre desenvolvimento do projeto, estruturação jurídica, auditoria, certificação, intermediação e venda. A parcela da repartição de benefícios costuma ser pactuada caso a caso, em contratos privados entre a comunidade, ou suas entidades representativas, e o desenvolvedor. O retorno também varia de forma. Estudo apresentado em 2023 no encontro da Sociedade Brasileira de Economia Ecológica (EcoEco) apontou que, em projetos REDD+ da Amazônia, os mecanismos vão de pagamentos em dinheiro a regularização fundiária, infraestrutura, apoio produtivo e fortalecimento de organizações locais. Para Ana Carolina e Larissa, essa diversidade dificulta a comparação entre iniciativas e pode ocultar quanto de fato permanece no território. O que a legislação já prevê No campo legal, a Lei nº 15.042/2024 criou o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (SBCE) e trouxe a primeira garantia federal explícita no tema. O artigo 47 assegura a povos indígenas e comunidades tradicionais, via entidades representativas, o direito de vender créditos de carbono e Certificados de Redução ou Remoção Verificada de Emissões (CRVEs) gerados em suas terras, cumpridas as salvaguardas socioambientais. A comercialização depende de consentimento obtido em consulta livre, prévia e informada, nos termos da Convenção nº 169 da Organização Internacional do Trabalho (OIT), custeada pelo desenvolvedor. A lei exige repartição justa e equitativa, gestão participativa dos recursos em conta específica e garante às comunidades ao menos 50% dos créditos de projetos de remoção e 70% nos de REDD+ de abordagem de mercado. A operacionalização desses mecanismos ainda depende de regulamentação, iniciada parcialmente pela Resolução nº 19, de 1º de agosto de 2025, da Comissão Nacional para REDD+ (CONAREDD+). As duas lembram que a norma já foi questionada: em agosto de 2026, o Ministério Público Federal (MPF) recomendou a revisão do artigo 7º, por entender que planos de consulta feitos pelo Estado podem enfraquecer o veto de cada comunidade e ignorar protocolos autônomos. Certificação e integridade Outra camada de regras vem de padrões privados, como Verra, Gold Standard e Cercarbono, que exigem salvaguardas sociais e planos de repartição, mas priorizaram a comprovação de processos em vez de resultados distributivos uniformes. Em novembro de 2024, o Conselho de Integridade do Mercado Voluntário de Carbono (ICVCM) aprovou três metodologias de REDD+ e apontou que versões antigas da Verra, fora da avaliação, respondiam por cerca de um quarto dos créditos aposentados em 2023. Consulta não equivale a poder de decisão Para Ana Carolina e Larissa, a comunidade ser ouvida e poder recusar um projeto é fundamental, mas difere de ter assento real na negociação. “O direito de ser consultada e de recusar a implementação de um projeto não assegura às comunidades, por si só, condições equitativas de negociação sobre aspectos essenciais da relação contratual, como a definição de preços, a duração dos contratos, os critérios de reajuste, a governança dos fundos e a destinação das receitas”, observam. Assimetrias de informação técnica, jurídica e comercial podem desequilibrar essa participação. Por isso, as salvaguardas socioambientais devem ser rigorosas e integralmente observadas e cumpridas em todas as etapas do projeto, garantindo assessoria independente, acesso a informações claras e acessíveis, tempo adequado para a tomada de decisões, representação legítima, governança transparente e mecanismos efetivos de resolução de conflitos. O cumprimento dessas salvaguardas deve ser contínuo, verificável e não pode ser tratado como mera formalidade. A Future Climate Group atua com projetos de carbono baseados na natureza e em transição energética, consultoria e educação climática. Um deles é o Projeto Rio Madeira, de REDD+ agrupado, que, segundo a empresa, protege mais de 52 mil hectares de floresta em Rondônia e no Amazonas e capacita coletores de castanha em parceria com a Empresa Brasileira de Pesquisa Agropecuária (Embrapa). Os próximos passos O principal desafio de curto prazo, na avaliação das especialistas, é a regulamentação do SBCE, que deverá converter a repartição justa e equitativa em procedimentos verificáveis e exigíveis, como financiamento da consulta, gestão financeira participativa, monitoramento, prestação de contas e solução de controvérsias. artigo.texto: Boise City Council approves 6-month moratorium on large data center construction BOISE – A standing-room-only crowd of more than 100 people applauded after the Boise City Council voted unanimously Tuesday night to place a six-month moratorium on the construction of large new data centers. The moratorium went into effect immediately, and applies to all data center projects that are 100,000 square-feet or larger, or use 20 megawatts of power. Passing the moratorium means Boise will not accept or process any applications for large data centers that fall within the moratorium’s parameters. “It’s a six-month moratorium that will put the brakes on hyperscale data centers in Boise, so it gives us the time to better determine and understand the impacts that these will have,” said Boise Mayor Lauren McLean, who proposed the moratorium Friday. McLean said the city does not currently have any large data center applications pending. “I’m doing this now before we have an application so that we can be sure that we get it right,” McLean said. Boise city officials will use the moratorium to review code and policies, study the impact on water, energy use, wastewater, noise and public safety, and gather public feedback. Chief of Staff Hannah Brass Greer said Boise’s existing code does not address data centers. “One of the things we would be doing is looking at our code and where it would fit and what restrictions or guidelines we want to put in place,” Brass Greer said. The Boise City Council approved the emergency moratorium following an approximately one-hour public hearing during its meeting Tuesday at Boise City Hall. ‘Don’t sell off our future to the highest bidder’: Public testimony supported the pause Everyone who spoke during the public hearing either supported the data center moratorium or asked city leaders to go even farther. “Just please don’t sell off our future to the highest bidder,” Sydney Hair told the Boise City Council. “I am very concerned about this. AI has taken so much from my generation and it is taking so much from the planet.” Mia Benson, a junior at Marsing High School and a fellow at the Idaho Climate Justice League, urged council members to approve the moratorium and develop strict permanent regulations around data center construction. “I encourage the city of Boise to collaborate with the local community to develop accountability policies within the next coming months that require future data center projects to cover 100% of their power costs, use 100% clean energy, pay 100% of their taxes and be 100% transparent on anything that impacts the public,” Benson said. “Data centers are not worth the intense pollution and depletion of our water resources.” Officials from several groups including the Golden Eagle Audubon Society, Conservation Voters for Idaho, the Idaho Conservation League, the Wilderness Society and Idaho Data Center Reform, added their support to the moratorium. “Given the potential long-term and irreversible impacts these centers may have on our landscapes and lives, we applaud the foresight this ordinance provides,” Cynthia Wallace of the Golden Eagle Audubon Society said. “Voting to approve this ordinance could also inspire other governments to preemptively evaluate and regulate data center permit requests.” Nobody spoke in favor of data centers or urged the Boise City Council to reconsider the moratorium. Lisa Young, director of the Idaho Chapter of the Sierra Club, applauded McLean and the Boise City Council for taking on data centers. “We commend Mayor McLean for hearing the growing concerns of Boiseans and proposing a moratorium on data centers within Idaho’s largest municipality, and we hope this will encourage other neighboring cities and Ada County to do the same,” Young said in a written statement. Data centers – and their energy use, water use and impact on wildlife – have become hot-button public issues in Idaho. Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, recently turned on a new data center south of Kuna. Meanwhile, Conservation Voters for Idaho Executive Director Ryan McGoldrick told the Idaho Capital Sun he is monitoring multiple data center proposals across Idaho. That includes a proposed 4-million-square-foot Rhea Data data center proposed south of Boise that the Washington Sun broke the news of and another data center proposed outside of Twin Falls. The Boise City Council is not the first local government entity in Idaho to place a moratorium on data center construction. In July, the Bannock County Board of Commissioners in eastern Idaho signed a 180-day moratorium on accepting or processing data center permit applications to give officials time to study and draft a comprehensive data center ordinance. This story originally appeared in the Idaho Capital Sun.

artigo.texto: Data center projects, moratoriums and proposed rules vary by county Construction is underway in Hancock County, while other counties have paused applications or are drafting new rules EVANSVILLE, Ind. (WFIE) - Construction is underway on a data center campus in Hancock County, while other area counties have approved moratoriums, delayed decisions or begun drafting rules for data centers. Watch us when we are live, right here ⬇️ Hancock County Infrastructure company TeraWulf will take over the former Century Aluminum smelter site in Hawesville and turn it into an AI and high-performance computing campus. Construction is underway. The campus will partially open in 2027, and construction will be finished in 2028. Lewisport resident George Holland said he believes the construction is good for the county. “You can never complain about having good jobs coming to your area. And that is a valuable piece of property up there,” Holland said. Some longtime residents said they still have questions about noise, power use and water use. “We’re always looking for industry to come in and create jobs, but I want to know what it is before it starts,” said Carl Elliott, who lives in Hancock County. Evansville and Vanderburgh County The Evansville City Council approved a 180-day moratorium on new data center developments within city limits in October. The pause gives officials time to study resource impacts, infrastructure demands and zoning laws. Evansville resident Connie Whitman spoke at a recent City Council meeting. “From what I’ve heard, they use an awful lot of resources, and a lot of people who are deeply involved in it and experts in it have concerns,” Whitman said. City Council President Ben Trockman said the pause will give the council time to learn about the demands of data centers. “Our hope is that we get more knowledge on data centers, the good and the bad that would be implicated in our community by having them,” Trockman said. In Vanderburgh County, a 13-member county committee is studying how data centers would affect land, water, electricity, noise and emergency services. The work is meant to help shape local zoning and safety rules. County leaders have put new data center applications on hold during the study. Recent committee meetings have focused heavily on fire safety protocols. The committee is expected to deliver final recommendations by Dec. 31. “I think some of the big issues for the community are electric, gas, water, and sewer, and noise. I think those are the things that certainly the community wants to know more about,” Lloyd Lamberton said. Posey County Amazon has confirmed it is in the early stages of evaluating a data center in Posey County. Attorney Mike Schopmeyer, who represents Amazon Web Services, told Posey County leaders the company will develop an industrial site closer to highways. “Amazon is the gold standard for data centers and I’m proud that they are looking at our region,” Schopmeyer said. At a recent Area Plan Commission meeting, members voted to recommend a nearly 40-page ordinance. The ordinance covers height limits, noise limits, setbacks, water and power use, and environmental impacts. “A lot of what we were adding is just protections from industrial to other zone property, especially residential,” said Joseph Marvel, Posey County Area Plan Commission president. Warrick County Warrick County commissioners voted unanimously this month to table a proposal for new data center rules after hearing from residents. Some residents called for another six-month pause on data center development. The Area Plan Commission sent the draft to commissioners last week with an unfavorable recommendation. Meanwhile, a development team is exploring a data center on Alcoa-owned land. The team said it has a letter of intent involving about 700 acres, but only a portion would be developed. Warrick County Commissioner Sarah Seaton said she finds the proposal exciting because the development team is local. “It is here. They are Warrick County. They live and work here. They have a vested interest in the success of the county, not just the success of the data center, but the success of the people that live here,” Seaton said. Daviess and Henderson counties In May, the Daviess County Fiscal Court approved a one-year moratorium on all new data center applications for the county and the city of Owensboro. The moratorium allows time to study potential community and infrastructure impacts. Henderson County does not currently have any active or formally proposed commercial data center projects. Local officials have taken steps to regulate potential future development. Hopkins County and Madisonville Hopkins County Judge-Executive Jack Whitfield said no official projects have been submitted to the Hopkins County Fiscal Court. Whitfield said that if data centers are not allowed in the United States, they will be built elsewhere. He cited China and Russia and said the data would then be controlled by those countries. “So that’s an important question that I think we have to answer, is, ‘How do we control the data centers, so we can have them here?’” Whitfield said. Madisonville officials are drafting an ordinance that would set rules for how data centers can be built. The ordinance would address zoning, buffers, height limits, noise and utility cost. Residents filled the room at a recent meeting, but public comment was limited to about 10 minutes total. Some residents raised concerns about how much input the community can provide. “What is the rush? Can we not get a moratorium in place to expand the time that we can find for sure what are the benefits of a data center?” said Faye Fuller, a Madisonville resident. Copyright 2026 WFIE. artigo.texto: Vanderburgh County data center committee hosts meeting Tuesday EVANSVILLE, Ind. (WFIE) - Residents from across Vanderburgh County spoke out about data centers at a public forum hosted by the Vanderburgh County Data Center Committee Tuesday at Ivy Tech’s auditorium. Most who spoke opposed data centers. Others backed them, saying the facilities would bring jobs and strengthen the community. The committee decided at its last meeting to hold the forum, making a point to hold at least one. Water, noise and security concerns Opponents cited concerns about water usage, noise, data security and environmental impact. Several questioned whether data centers are needed at all. Leann Rippy said she wants answers about the county’s water supply. “A geologist told us that all of our water is going to be dried up within 5 mile radius and within a short period of time. The data center representatives say different. Who’s correct? Who’s going to fix our water well if it’s damaged or drained?” Beverly White-Rowley urged the committee to reject data centers outright. “If you love your family, just say absolutely not to data centers. We don’t need any more data. I can find out about you and you and you and you and everyone in here on the Internet today. I don’t need to know all your dirt.” Many opponents spoke two or even three times, arguing data centers should not be in the county. Supporters point to jobs Supporters said data centers would create work. Ryan McRoberts said construction alone would employ many people. “These data centers will provide hundreds and thousands of jobs for construction over the next couple of years. They will also provide dozens and dozens of maintenance jobs after the facility is up and going.” Money questions Some opponents said data center supporters stand to profit. Kaleb Brown said the people speaking in favor have a financial stake. “The only people who’ve had anything positive to say about this data center all have financial gain to make from the situation. They all have construction businesses. The only people that are for this have a financial incentive. When does the money stop? I guarantee you every single person sitting in this chair makes more money than I do.” What’s next A moratorium on data centers has been in place for the past few months while the committee researches their impacts. The committee is preparing a report and recommendation for the Vanderburgh County commissioners. Committee officials said they will consider all of the public comment as they prepare for their next meeting, scheduled for Nov. 17. Copyright 2026 WFIE. All rights reserved.

A Prefeitura de Campo Grande abriu pregão eletrônico para contratar a locação de uma solução de alta disponibilidade de data center em contêiner, com entrega da estrutura, operação ininterrupta e manutenção integral. artigo.texto: City of Boise approves emergency moratorium on large data centers Boise, Idaho (CBS2) — The city of Boise has approved an emergency moratorium that temporarily pauses the development of large data centers within city limits. The ordinance, passed Tuesday evening during a city Council meeting, halts new applications for data centers for up to six months. It applies to facilities larger than 100,000 square feet or those with a projected power demand of at least 20 megawatts at full buildout. City leaders said concerns about potential impacts on water resources, energy use and land development led to the decision. They also mentioned the rise of moratoriums across 44 other states. Boise residents weighed in on the proposed moratorium with the majority of feedback in support of the moratorium. “These data centers use a tremendous amount of water and as our state goes through this predicted drought through the winter, i feel it's incredibly important to have guidelines in place before more data centers move in and take up what little resources we have,” Boise resident, Kyle Chandler said during Tuesday meeting. Another Boise resident urged leaders to consider long-term impacts. “We must understand that every decision we make, not only the impact it has on us here and now, but on the next seven generations to come,” the resident said. “I don't hear anybody talking about the future, i hear people trying to make a profit quick and dirty," she said. City leaders said they would take the next months to revise Boise's city code as well as restrictions and guidelines they would want to put in place in regard to large data centers, with public feedback from the community. Council members also discussed the importance of county and state level elected officials dong their part to put those guidelines in place. Council members voted unanimously on the moratorium, and the ordinance is set to go into effect immediately.

artigo.texto: Clarksville leaders cite water and power limits for another data center Mayor and neighbor describe life near Google’s 1.4-million-square-foot Montgomery County facility CLARKSVILLE, Tenn. (WFIE) - Clarksville and Montgomery County leaders said limits on water and electricity make them unwilling to bring in another data center. Google has operated a 1.4-million-square-foot data center in the county since late 2019. Clarksville has nearly 200,000 residents and is the fifth-largest city in Tennessee. Watch us when we are live, right here ⬇️ Google’s arrival in Montgomery County Google officially made a home in Montgomery County with a data center in late 2019. Clarksville Mayor Joe Pitts said, “Data centers were not the juggernaut they are now.” Pitts said the community was indifferent about Google’s arrival. “So we didn’t know what to expect. We just knew they were gonna be a heavy water-user, and they were gonna deal directly with the Tennessee Valley Authority as far as electricity. So we really don’t know details,” he said. The data center sits on a site just outside Clarksville city limits that was formerly planned for Hemlock Semiconductor, a manufacturer that makes parts for solar panels. “They didn’t produce the number of jobs that a Hemlock Semiconductor was gonna do. But yet, they were able to rescue the site. It would’ve been an abandoned, brown field site, where it just sat empty, and was really a blight,” Pitts said. The site is part of a large industrial park bordered by berms installed by Hemlock. The data center powers Google features such as search, cloud storage and Gmail. Neighbor reports no noise or light issues Neighbor Greg Farmer said the berms keep light and sound from the site from reaching his home. He said the data center is less than a half-mile away, just over the berm. “If that berm wasn’t there because of the other company that was coming in, we would probably see more lights. But because it’s an industrial park anyways, we were getting lights from them prior to the berm being put up,” Farmer said. Farmer said the data center has not affected his water or electric bills. “I don’t know much about the data center itself. I know they’re expanding. I like the fact that they are. It’s given a lot of people here locally jobs they wouldn’t normally have,” Farmer said. “That’s all I’ve seen, is benefits to the community, benefits to our house, here locally.” Water use under non-disclosure agreement The servers inside the data center generate heat, and the facility uses water for cooling. The exact amount of water the center uses is unclear because Google and the local government signed a non-disclosure agreement when the company first came to town. “Yes, it is confidential, and it’s something I wasn’t curious about, I just know that we’ve hit our limit,” Pitts said. Pitts said the agreement is not a great concern now that it has been signed. He said the issue arises when Google discusses expansion. “We say, ‘We’ve reached our limit in terms of the amount of water that we can provide for that site.’ So that kind of limits what they do. And they’re having to get creative with our gas and water department. To determine how best to meet the needs, the growing needs, of their data center,” Pitts said. Rates and community investment Bills across the county have gone up. Pitts said TVA raised its rates, which caused the city’s electricity department to raise its rates. “So that’s not due to Google necessarily, data centers. That’s just regular inflation. Water rates have also gone up. Prices of gas, you name it. Inflation’s impacted everything,” Pitts said. Google says it has invested more than $6 billion in Tennessee since coming to town. Pitts said Google has sponsored events and supported the nonprofit community. He said that when the company first arrived, the city was able to expand Wi-Fi in three parks and in low- to moderate-income neighborhoods for homes that could not afford internet. Leaders on another data center Asked how he would feel about another data center coming to Clarksville, Pitts said he would say no. “Just because we do not know what the impacts are. Plus we don’t have the water capacity that they would need. And TVA is struggling to keep up with demand, just the residential and commercial growth. So we’ve, we’re really reticent to approve another data center to come into our community,” Pitts said. The future of data centers in Montgomery County is up for debate. County Mayor Wes Golden said the county has no resources left to welcome another data center. County commissioners are putting regulations in place in case one is proposed. Asked whether he would like to see another data center come to the county, Golden said, “Not at this time, to be honest with you. Just because of the amount of resources that they currently use. But no telling what’s going to happen in the future, as far as better resources, better technology that doesn’t need as much resources. So hopefully that’ll be the case in the future.” Perspectives from neighbor and mayor Farmer said he has not seen negative effects from the data center. “The data centers around the United States, everybody’s saying how bad they’re gonna be, how much they’re going to affect the community. I haven’t seen anything negative. I’ve only seen the positive side,” Farmer said. Pitts said not all data centers are the same. “If you’ve seen one data center, you’ve seen one. Not all of the data centers are the same. Not all of them have the resources that Google has to make sure they’re environmentally sound and safe... that’s part of the homework we talk about. Making sure you do your homework. Your local elected officials do their homework, and not just sign off on whatever they put in front,” Pitts said. Copyright 2026 WFIE. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Typically, hybrid cars consist of a petrol engine, a small battery and an electric motor. However, the electric mode is available only for shorter periods, and most of the time, the car runs on its engine. The same principle applies to a plug-in hybrid, but the recipe is different. Here, the battery size and electric motor dominate, meaning you drive more in electric mode. However, you also have to charge the car and fill it with petrol. So, does a plug-in hybrid mean double the work of charging and refuelling, or does it make sense? Our first taste of this technology came in the form of the BYD DM-i powertrain. BYD is known for its EVs, and in India, it will be bringing its first plug-in hybrid. However, its approach here is electric-first. The Blade Battery used here is different and runs on battery power, while the 1.5-litre petrol engine acts as a generator. Hence, the engine powers the battery, which, in turn, powers the wheels. ALSO READ: Tata Motors, Mahindra Most Popular Among Indian EV Buyers: Here's Why BYD says the car has an electric-only range of up to 126 km, which is much higher than that of strong hybrids. It has an 18.3 kWh battery pack, which can be charged from 30 to 80 per cent in 35 minutes using an 18 kW DC charger. The range on offer is 1,080 km, while the claimed efficiency is 4.8 litres per 100 km. There are dual motors, and the car is quick, with a 0–100 km/h acceleration time of 5.5 seconds. Driving Experience: An EV With A Petrol Backup We drove the car in traffic and on the highway, while also testing its acceleration. We realised that this car is an EV, but the petrol engine helps it keep going even when the battery charge is depleted. You drive it like an EV, which means it is fast and smooth. Even when the battery range goes down, the EV power remains, and only under hard acceleration does the engine become somewhat audible, although the sound is faint. We got 5 litres per 100 km. After driving it for two days, the battery range went down slightly, while consumption went up to 6 litres per 100 km. However, that is still very low consumption overall. The car is very fast, and the acceleration is smooth. The appeal of a plug-in hybrid is essentially that of an EV, but without any range anxiety. We ran the car on E20 petrol and did not charge it during the two days we had it. Does A Plug-In Hybrid Make Sense? As a piece of technology, it is impressive, if complex. But for the buyer, it is basically like an EV that will not run out of juice or cause any range anxiety. That said, you will have to charge the car for this powertrain to operate efficiently. Plug-in hybrids make sense for those who want to avoid range anxiety and travel long distances easily. Plus, unlike strong hybrids, the performance feels like that of an EV all the time. That said, the big talking point is the cost, as plug-in hybrid technology is expensive, but it can work in India. Unlike regular hybrids, it also requires external charging in addition to petrol. BYD's DM-i powertrain is electric-first, using a Blade Battery to power the wheels. The 1.5-litre petrol engine primarily acts as a generator to charge the battery. It offers an electric-only range of up to 126 km and a total range of 1,080 km. Claimed efficiency is 4.8 litres per 100 km. Plug-in hybrids offer the smooth, fast performance of an EV without range anxiety. They are suitable for long distances, providing a petrol backup when needed. Yes, you need to charge a plug-in hybrid for its powertrain to operate efficiently and to maximize its electric driving range and benefits.

artigo.texto: Home › Energy Storage ›MHI Receives 22 Bids for 10 GWh ACC Battery Storage Capacity MHI Receives 22 Bids for 10 GWh ACC Battery Storage Capacity The Ministry of Heavy Industries has received 22 bids for 10 GWh of ACC battery manufacturing capacity tendered for grid-scale stationary storage applications under the PLI Scheme for the National Programme on Advanced Chemistry Cell Battery Storage. November 13, 2026. By Mrinmoy Dey The Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI) has announced that it has received 22 bids for 10 GWh of Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) battery manufacturing capacity earmarked for Grid-Scale Stationary Storage (GSSS) applications under the National Programme on Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) Battery Storage. The capacity forms part of the programme's overall target of establishing 50 GWh of domestic ACC manufacturing capacity. The Request for Proposal (RFP) was issued on the Central Public Procurement (CPP) Portal on July 15, 2026, with the pre-bid conference held on July 29, 2026. The deadline for bid submissions was November 10, 2026, and technical bids were opened on November 11, 2026, at MHI in the presence of bidders. The 22 bidders include ACME Solar Holdings, Amara Raja Advanced Cell Technologies, Avaada Electro, Exide Energy Solutions, Fujiyama Power Systems, GK Energy, Godawari New Energy, JPM Energy Solutions (JP Minda Group), JSW Neo Energy (JSW Energy), Lineage Power (Pace Digitek), Mahendra Sponge and Power, Megha Engineering and Infrastructures, Nsure Reliable Power Solutions, Reliance Industries, Renew Photovoltaics, Sai Bioenergy, Shirdi Sai Electricals, Sun Drops Energia (KP Group), Utex New Energy, Vikram Solar, Waaree Energy Storage Solutions and Zetsol Energy. The bidding is being conducted through an online, two-stage Quality and Cost Based Selection (QCBS) mechanism to select beneficiary firms for setting up giga-scale ACC manufacturing facilities in India. In May 2021, the Union Cabinet approved the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme for the National Programme on Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) Battery Storage with a budgetary outlay of INR 18,100 crore to establish 50 GWh of domestic ACC manufacturing capacity. The scheme aims to strengthen domestic battery manufacturing, attract investments and develop a competitive ACC ecosystem. The 10 GWh allocation for grid-scale stationary storage is intended to support India's growing energy storage requirements alongside the expansion of renewable energy capacity. It is also expected to strengthen domestic manufacturing and the supply chain for ACC technologies. artigo.texto: Wynne City Council approves one-year moratorium on new data centers Ordinance 926 applies to new data centers inside city limits WYNNE, Ark. (KAIT) — The Wynne City Council passed an ordinance that places a one-year moratorium on new data centers. City leaders said they want more time to prepare for the possibility of a data center coming to the city. The council passed Ordinance 926 this week. It places a one-year moratorium on new data centers within city limits. Alderman Jason Nichols said the goal is “just so that we have time to prepare anything, our infrastructure, utilities, any usage, zoning.” Nichols said the city also wants to consider how a project could affect residents, including “noise-wise or location-wise.” “We also want to make sure that any large projects that are coming in, that they’re a good fit for our community,” Nichols said. “And what we wouldn’t want to do is expend our utilities or our water supply.” Wynne resident Brittany Hammit said she supports the moratorium. “I don’t think we should have data centers,” Hammit said. Hammit said she is concerned about water use and the environment. “I think that they take up too much water,” she said. “I think that it’s a detriment to the environment, to the animals around, to the wildlife.” The moratorium is temporary. Hammit said she would rather see something else come to Wynne. “I don’t think that data centers are totally the worst thing in the world, but I just don’t think that they should be here,” Hammit said. The moratorium is set to last one year. The council will need to take action if it wants to extend it. To report a typo or correction, please click here. Copyright 2026 KAIT. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: The Washington County Chamber of Commerce will host its next Eggs and Issues program on Wednesday, December 2, featuring a discussion about the growth of the data center industry and lessons learned in Loudoun County, Virginia. The program, titled “Data Centers: The Loudoun County Experience,” will feature Joe Kroboth, deputy county administrator for Loudoun County. Breakfast will begin at 6:45 a.m., with the program starting at 7:30 a.m. at Hagerstown Community College in Rooms 211 and 213 of the Career Programs Building. Kroboth brings experience from both sides of the regional data center discussion. He spent seven years as public works director in Washington County, Maryland, before serving 14 years as deputy county administrator in Loudoun County, which is widely known as the “Data Center Capital of the World.” Loudoun County was among the first communities in the country to embrace the data center industry. Today, the county has more than 230 data center facilities operating or in development. The industry has brought significant economic benefits to Loudoun County. Data centers account for nearly 40% of the county’s tax base and generate approximately $1.3 billion in annual tax revenue. County officials say the revenue has helped lower property tax rates for residents every year since 2016. However, the growth has also brought challenges, including concerns about noise, backup diesel generators, electric transmission lines and the placement of facilities near residential neighborhoods. Loudoun County is now revisiting some of its land-use regulations and development standards based on lessons learned over the past two decades. Kroboth will share his firsthand perspective on the opportunities and challenges associated with data center development, including what has worked, what has not and what communities should consider before making decisions with long-term consequences. The Chamber says the program is intended to provide community leaders and residents with an opportunity to learn from a county with extensive experience in the industry. The Chamber is not advocating for or against data center development but hopes to provide a balanced discussion as interest in the industry grows in Washington County and the surrounding region. A question-and-answer session will follow Kroboth’s presentation. Registration is available at www.hagerstown.org. The event will be held at Hagerstown Community College, 11400 Robinwood Drive in Hagerstown. Attendees should use Parking Lot F.

artigo.texto: The Oakland City Council voted unanimously to extend the city's current data center moratorium for nearly a year, keeping restrictions in place that were originally set to expire next week. The decision was met with a standing ovation inside City Hall, as council members approved a 10-month extension to give municipal staff more time to study data center development, energy use, and environmental impacts while drafting potential new regulations. Watch NBC Bay Area News free wherever you are "We need more research and that’s what the community asked for. They want to know the risk of water going up and PG&E going up, and they deserve that," said Tonisha Scott, an Oakland resident. Public commenters at the meeting voiced strong concerns regarding transparency and resource consumption. "We pay taxes here! … and whatever goes on in Oakland, we are supposed to know about it!" said one public commenter. City officials plan to host community meetings over the coming months to allow residents to weigh in. "The importance of extending the moratorium is to give the city the adequate amount of time for our staff… to come back to the council with some firm guidelines," said District 3 City Councilmember Carroll Fife. Local While the extension provides a temporary pause, some community advocates view it as a stepping stone toward a permanent ban. "This is really a first step for a lot of the communities…," said Zoe Jonick, an organizer with 350 Bay Area, a climate group that has advocated for similar local moratoriums across the region. "You heard that a lot at the meeting tonight in Oakland… where a lot of people said yes we want this extended 10 more months, but really we want it extended forever," Jonick added. Oakland's original 45-day moratorium was slated to expire on Nov. 20. Tuesday's vote extends the restrictions through Oct. 5 of next year.

artigo.texto: Grupos da América Latina defenderam a criação de regulamentações específicas para definirem o escopo da expansão dos centros de dados (data centers) e garantir proteção às regiões que recebem essas infraestruturas. A demanda foi apresentada durante o segundo seminário realizado pelo Laboratório de Políticas Públicas e Internet (Lapin), que ocorre em Fortaleza, no Brasil. O encontro, com duração de três dias, reúne pesquisadores, jornalistas, ativistas e representantes de comunidades de diferentes países da América Latina para discutir os impactos do rápido crescimento da infraestrutura digital. Um dos principais pontos do debate é a diferença entre a velocidade com que esses projetos avançam e a capacidade das regulamentações existentes de avaliar seus impactos. Os participantes defendem procedimentos de autorização mais rigorosos e transparentes, que garantam a participação das populações afetadas. Segundo eles, sem essas medidas, os custos ambientais e sociais podem recair inteiramente sobre as comunidades locais, enquanto os benefícios ficam concentrados em outras regiões. Entre os principais temas discutidos estão o consumo de água e energia, a transição energética, o racismo ambiental e o chamado "extrativismo digital". Os centros de dados são infraestruturas físicas essenciais para o funcionamento de serviços online e sistemas de inteligência artificial, mas exigem recursos naturais e grandes áreas para sua instalação. Por isso, conforme destacado durante o seminário em Fortaleza, o planejamento desses empreendimentos não deve ser tratado apenas como uma questão tecnológica, mas também ambiental e social. artigo.texto: Westlake approves construction on data center near Keller border WESTLAKE, Texas - Westlake has approved construction on a data center near its border with Keller after months of debate and a protracted legal battle. Westlake Data Center construction approved What we know: On Thursday, November 12, Westlake's City Council unanimously approved a measure to allow a 1.1 million-square-foot data center to be built in the city. The data center complex will be built near Westlake's border with Keller, something that has been at the center of a monthslong debate between the two cities. Keller residents said they were not given proper notice about the development, which would be near Keller's Marshall Ridge neighborhood. The City of Keller filed for a temporary injunction to halt any further development. That injunction expired in late September. On November 5, Keller and Westlake announced they had reached an agreement in their legal battle over the data center. Keller says the agreement will allow the city to enforce noise limits, and will create quarterly noise monitoring for the first three years of the data center's operations. The agreement also includes landscaping requirements, emissions controls, and a contribution to Keller Fire-Rescue. What they're saying: At Thursday's Westlake City Council meeting, some speakers accused the city's leaders of not being transparent during the process. Westlake leaders say the data center is part of the cost of growth. "Yes, residents may bear slightly higher electricity costs, but we're going to keep costs in other ways because of the additional revenue." Big picture view: Data centers were a hot political topic during the midterm elections. Gov. Greg Abbott shifted course after initially welcoming data centers to Texas, pushing to slow development by requiring resource audits before new permits are issued. Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic challenger who unseated Abbott, has called for an immediate moratorium on data centers until the Texas Legislature can meet. What's next: Keller says it will work with Hinojosa on statewide discussions surrounding data center regulation. The Source: Information in this story comes from a Westlake City Council meeting and previous FOX 4 reporting.

artigo.texto: O primeiro leilão brasileiro de armazenamento em baterias recebeu 6.091 cadastros, um recorde para contratação de projetos no setor elétrico segundo a Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE). Os certames estão marcados para 2 e 4 de dezembro e somam 296.807 megawatts de potência inscrita. O leilão de 2 de dezembro exige componentes nacionais e terá financiamento de R$ 30 bilhões do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) via Finame. A etapa de 4 de dezembro aceita equipamentos importados, mas ainda não tem linha de crédito público definida. A diferença entre as duas datas transforma o certame em disputa de política industrial, não apenas em compra de reserva de capacidade. O banco público cria demanda para fabricação e montagem de baterias, produção de componentes, engenharia e serviços tecnológicos no país, segundo avaliação de Rosana Santos, diretora-executiva do Instituto E+ Transição Energética. A corrida global ajuda a explicar a pressa brasileira em ter capacidade própria de armazenamento. Em 2025, o mundo instalou 108 gigawatts de baterias, alta de 40% sobre 2024 e volume 11 vezes maior que o de 2021, puxado por China, Estados Unidos e Europa, segundo o relatório Global Energy Review 2026 da Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA). No Brasil, as hidrelétricas não suprem sozinhas a flexibilidade operacional que o sistema elétrico ganha com sistemas químicos de armazenamento. Os conjuntos de baterias entram em operação em um a dois anos e descarregam energia em ciclos de quatro a oito horas, enquanto usinas hidrelétricas reversíveis levam de sete a oito anos para ficar prontas. Esses sistemas ajudam a aproveitar o excesso de geração eólica e solar e a reduzir cortes de geração (curtailment) que hoje não são ressarcidos aos produtores. Rodrigo Sauaia, presidente da Associação Brasileira de Energia Solar Fotovoltaica (Absolar), afirma que os geradores deixam de receber pelo que não injetam na rede e enfrentam prejuízos financeiros. A queda internacional dos custos também viabilizou os sistemas de baterias no mercado brasileiro. Desde 2010, o preço médio global caiu de mais de US$ 1.000 por quilowatt-hora para cerca de US$ 108 por quilowatt-hora em 2025, de acordo com levantamento anual da consultoria BloombergNEF. A Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) aprovou os editais em 27 de outubro e reduziu o investimento de referência de R$ 9,8 milhões por megawatt para R$ 6 milhões por megawatt. As garantias de proposta e de fiel cumprimento também caíram, o que diminui a barreira de entrada e amplia a competição. Os contratos valem por 15 anos, com início de suprimento em 1º de agosto de 2028. A bateria precisa garantir potência por quatro horas a cada ciclo diário, com receita anual ajustada pelo desempenho efetivo. A Associação Brasileira de Soluções de Armazenamento de Energia (ABSAE) calcula que a rede básica possui cerca de 56 gigawatts de margem de conexão para baterias, com base em nota técnica do Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) e da EPE. Esse volume supera em até 12 vezes a necessidade estimada para o período de 2028 a 2030. Nos pontos com bônus locacional, a folga chega a 13,7 gigawatts, concentrada principalmente na Bahia, no Piauí, no Ceará e no norte de Minas Gerais. Para a ABSAE, a infraestrutura de transmissão não deve ser gargalo para os primeiros leilões. Os preços-teto ficaram em R$ 1,76 milhão por megawatt-ano no leilão com exigência de conteúdo nacional e R$ 1,58 milhão no certame aberto a importados. A associação considera os valores alinhados às projeções do mercado e suficientes para atrair investidores qualificados. Os 6.091 projetos cadastrados ainda passarão por análise e habilitação técnica conduzida pela EPE antes da disputa. A proporção final entre equipamentos fabricados no país e sistemas importados nos leilões de dezembro definirá o alcance industrial do financiamento público.

artigo.texto: As ações da AAON Inc (NASDAQ:AAON) subiram aproximadamente 22% nas negociações pré-mercado de terça-feira, após a fabricante de equipamentos de aquecimento, ventilação e ar condicionado (HVAC) divulgar resultados do terceiro trimestre e receita acima das expectativas dos analistas, além de elevar sua projeção financeira para o ano de 2026. A empresa reportou lucro ajustado de US$ 0,83 por ação, superando a estimativa de consenso dos analistas de US$ 0,56 em US$ 0,27. A receita trimestral aumentou 84,1% em relação ao ano anterior, atingindo o recorde de US$ 707,4 milhões, comparada a US$ 384,2 milhões no mesmo período de 2025 e às expectativas dos analistas de US$ 599,7 milhões. O aumento da receita refletiu a demanda pelas linhas de produtos AAON e BASX da empresa, maior produção e maior utilização da capacidade produtiva recentemente ampliada. A receita do terceiro trimestre subiu 84,1%, atingindo o recorde de US$ 707,4 milhões A AAON reportou vendas líquidas de US$ 707,4 milhões no terceiro trimestre, representando um aumento de US$ 323,2 milhões em relação ao mesmo período do ano anterior. O resultado superou a estimativa consensual dos analistas em aproximadamente US$ 107,7 milhões. O lucro ajustado por ação atingiu US$ 0,83, em comparação com as expectativas do mercado de US$ 0,56, refletindo a maior receita e o melhor desempenho operacional da empresa durante o trimestre. O lucro bruto aumentou 76,4%, atingindo US$ 188,5 milhões, enquanto a margem bruta alcançou 26,7%, uma melhoria de 60 pontos base em comparação com o segundo trimestre. O lucro operacional mais que dobrou, aumentando 129,3% para US$ 100 milhões. A empresa atribuiu os resultados ao aumento da produção, às medidas de precificação e à maior utilização de suas instalações fabris. A receita da BASX aumentou 218,3%, impulsionada pela demanda por data centers A AAON registrou crescimento de receita em ambas as suas principais marcas de produtos. As vendas de produtos da marca AAON aumentaram 19,6%, atingindo US$ 310,2 milhões, enquanto a receita da marca BASX subiu 218,3%, para US$ 397,2 milhões. O aumento na receita da BASX refletiu a demanda por equipamentos de refrigeração e controle ambiental utilizados em centros de dados, incluindo instalações operadas por grandes provedores de computação em nuvem. A expansão da capacidade de produção da empresa também contribuiu para sua capacidade de atender a pedidos adicionais de clientes durante o trimestre. Os analistas da William Blair destacaram o desempenho da unidade de negócios BASX, observando que os pedidos aceleraram durante o terceiro trimestre. Os analistas disseram que as encomendas do quarto trimestre deveriam “igualar ou superar” o “resultado excepcionalmente forte de 586 milhões de dólares do ano anterior”. Segundo sua avaliação, a demanda foi sustentada por pedidos repetidos de clientes de computação em hiperescala e pela adição de novos clientes. AAON eleva sua previsão de crescimento de vendas para 2026 para 72% a 75% Após a divulgação dos resultados trimestrais, a AAON aumentou sua previsão de crescimento das vendas líquidas para o ano de 2026 para entre 72% e 75%, em comparação com a previsão anterior de 55% a 60%. O ponto médio da faixa revisada é de 73,5%, representando um aumento de 16 pontos percentuais em relação ao ponto médio da previsão anterior. A empresa também atualizou suas expectativas de rentabilidade e despesas operacionais. A AAON agora prevê uma margem bruta anual de aproximadamente 26%, em comparação com a projeção anterior de 25% a 26%. Prevê-se que as despesas com vendas, gerais e administrativas representem aproximadamente 13% das vendas, em comparação com a previsão anterior de 13% a 14%. A revisão das perspectivas reflete as expectativas da administração em relação à atividade de produção, à demanda por produtos e aos custos operacionais durante o restante do ano. Analistas destacam o crescimento dos pedidos e a melhoria das margens Analistas da William Blair afirmaram que a AAON “superou dois obstáculos importantes” com seu relatório financeiro do terceiro trimestre. O primeiro fator foi uma aceleração nos pedidos da BASX, impulsionada pela demanda de operadores de data centers e por novos relacionamentos com clientes. O segundo fator foi a melhoria na margem bruta, que os analistas atribuíram a ações de precificação e maiores volumes de produção. A empresa indicou que as ações da AAON poderiam atingir US$ 100 sob uma estrutura de avaliação que aplica 18 vezes o EBITDA projetado para 2027 ao negócio da marca AAON e de 10 a 11 vezes o EBITDA estimado para 2027 da BASX. A avaliação representa a análise dos analistas, e não uma previsão da empresa ou um preço futuro garantido das ações. A William Blair também identificou uma melhoria adicional na margem bruta em 2027 como um “fator essencial para a criação de mais valor”. Os comentários refletem as expectativas da empresa em relação ao desempenho operacional futuro da companhia e à contribuição de suas duas principais linhas de produtos. AAON reformula resultados do primeiro semestre após identificação de erros contábeis Juntamente com os resultados do terceiro trimestre, a AAON divulgou que identificou erros em suas demonstrações financeiras referentes ao primeiro e segundo trimestres de 2026. Os erros foram descobertos durante a preparação do relatório financeiro do terceiro trimestre da empresa. Como resultado, a AAON revisou seus resultados financeiros do primeiro semestre, aumentando as vendas líquidas anteriormente divulgadas em US$ 10,7 milhões e o lucro diluído por ação em US$ 0,09. A empresa também identificou uma deficiência material em seu controle interno sobre os relatórios financeiros. A AAON afirmou estar implementando medidas destinadas a corrigir as deficiências de controle identificadas. artigo.texto: The project will help to support Meta's Eagle Mountain data centre operations, as well as supporting grid reliability in Utah. It consists of a standalone, four-hour lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) battery system and delivers 600 MWh of contracted storage capacity to PacifiCorp under a long-term energy storage agreement. It is situated on an approximately eight-acre site adjacent to the 525 MW Faraday solar facility and shares that facility's substation and interconnection, allowing Lydian to add storage using existing infrastructure. Lydian took Faraday BESS from mobilisation to commercial operation in approximately 10 months. “Faraday BESS shows what a mature platform like Lydian's can deliver” said Kim Smith, Chief Operating Officer of Lydian. “Bringing it online on an extremely tight timeline took close coordination across our own team and our supply chain, construction, and financing partners, from acquisition through commissioning. When a wildfire threatened the area in June, our team put safety first while keeping the project on track. Faraday BESS enhances PacifiCorp’s reliable, contracted capacity for Utah customers.” The completion of Faraday BESS draws on Lydian's integrated platform, which spans development, capital markets, and project delivery. Lydian is also developing Faraday BESS 2 at the Utah site, which would add up to 375 MW/1,500 MWh of storage with a targeted in-service date of the fourth quarter of 2028. artigo.texto: BHP World's largest miner by market cap A new report from DLA Piper indicates that price volatility in critical minerals is holding back a significant share of energy storage projects, according to Mining.com. The study, based on interviews with 550 participants across the energy storage, investment and mining sectors, found that 23% said projects that had appeared viable were deferred or cancelled because of unpredictable commodity prices shaped by tariffs, wars and other geopolitical tensions. A further 12% of respondents described price volatility as a dealbreaker for project development. DLA Piper natural resources partner Alex Jones said unpredictable pricing pressures were producing a cascading effect across the sector, weakening investor confidence, limiting financing and structuring, and contributing to delays, repricing and, in some cases, abandoned projects. The report identifies the reluctance to commit capital amid uncertain and volatile future commodity prices as the leading obstacle to investment. More than half of respondents called price volatility a major constraint on mining or processing investment, with consequences felt across the project lifecycle. Among them, 28% reported difficulty securing bankable long-term offtake agreements, 27% had postponed investment decisions and 26% faced a higher cost of capital. The impact varies by region. Participants in the United Kingdom and the United States reported the strongest effects, with 16% and 18% respectively calling volatility a dealbreaker for project development. German participants stood apart, being the only group to say volatility was not a dealbreaker, with just 8% treating it as a major problem. Australian participants viewed volatility as one of several material considerations rather than a major roadblock. DLA Piper partner Oliver Wright suggested that capital is likely to concentrate in regions seen as offering execution credibility and proximity to supply chains and demand, as developers seek locations where they can exercise more control and stay closer to the supply chain through market cycles. Companies are increasingly adopting vertical integration to limit exposure to volatile commodity markets and to pricing benchmarks influenced by China, the report found. At least 37% of surveyed developers and 32% of mining and raw materials producers have taken this route, which lets businesses control more stages of production, from extraction and refining to manufacturing and recycling. Wright said companies had long depended on supply chains they did not control, and that recent volatility had demonstrated how quickly pricing and supply terms can change. He said developers and miners are now working to hold the parts of the chain they rely on most, from mine through refinery to recycling plant, so that an upstream squeeze no longer disrupts operations. Participants are also reconsidering how prices are set. Some 37% believe component-linked pricing would work better than raw material spot prices, while 48% of mining and raw materials producers favor long-term fixed pricing with periodic resets. Rare Earth Americas chief executive and president Donald S. Swartz II said in the report that strategic mineral supply chains carry value beyond the daily spot price. Wright added that the industry is expected to shift what contracts are priced against, whether component-linked pricing, price floors or hybrid structures. artigo.texto: At a consultation workshop held on November 10, the Carbon Market Division under the Department of Climate Change (the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment) provided updates on key proposed regulations. Regarding climate change adaptation, the draft mandates announcing climate change scenarios every five years. These scenarios will serve as the foundation for impact assessments and risk identification across development strategies and plans. Ministries, sectors, and localities will assess losses and damages while developing tailored adaptation solutions. The draft also introduces a monitoring framework linking implementation results with investment resources and management responsibilities, prioritizing water security, food security, ecosystems, and key infrastructure. For greenhouse gas emission management, facilities emitting 3,000 tons of CO2 equivalent or more annually must conduct inventories. Select facilities in energy, transport, industrial, commercial, and waste treatment sectors will also fall under this mandate based on specific technical thresholds. The draft adds a Measurement, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) mechanism based on national standards to ensure accurate and verifiable data, which is essential for allocating quotas and facilitating carbon market transactions. Quota allocation for applicable facilities will continue through the 2027-2028 period under the proposed roadmap. Starting in 2029, an auction mechanism will supplement standard allocation methods. According to the Department of Climate Change, auctions aim to enhance transparency while encouraging businesses to adopt clean technologies and improve energy efficiency. The draft includes market stabilization measures for instances of abnormal price fluctuations or severe supply imbalances. Solutions include adjusting the timing and volume of auctioned quotas, utilizing reserve quotas, and enhancing transaction monitoring. Establishing national carbon credit standards will ensure emission reduction results are verifiable and prevent double-counting. At the workshop, Deputy Minister of Agriculture and Environment Le Trong Yen highlighted Conclusion 75-KL/TW dated July 28, 2026, issued by the 14th Central Party Committee, as a key political basis for perfecting environmental protection laws. The goal is building a modern governance system supporting a green and circular economy targeting net-zero emissions by 2050. On decentralization, the draft proposes that sectoral management ministries monitor Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs). Localities will directly issue and update the list of facilities subject to greenhouse gas inventories, replacing the current role of the Prime Minister. Delegates also discussed the pilot quota allocation for thermal power, steel, and cement plants, where inconsistent input data previously created challenges. A representative from the Ministry of Industry and Trade stressed evaluating pilot outcomes and completing database systems. A representative from the Energy and Environment Consulting Joint Stock Company recommended requiring independent verification only for facilities participating directly in the quota system to reduce compliance costs for businesses. In response, the drafting committee stated it would adjust regulations to exempt non-quota facilities from mandatory independent verification. The Department of Climate Change will coordinate with the Ministry of Industry and Trade to refine calculation methods and review regulations on carbon credit standards to align with international commitments and domestic operating conditions.
