artigo.texto: Riverside will keep data centers off-limits while a city working group studies their potential impacts and develops recommendations on whether — and under what conditions — they should be allowed. The City Council voted 5-2 on Nov. 10 to affirm the city's interpretation that data centers are prohibited under existing zoning rules. Councilmembers Chuck Conder and Sean Mill opposed the resolution. The decision leaves the city unable to issue permits for data centers while the council's artificial intelligence working group completes its review. The approved motion ties that prohibition to the group finishing its work and the council adopting its recommendations. Councilmembers chose this approach over a proposed 45-day moratorium, which would have required subsequent votes to extend. The resolution affirms an existing restriction rather than adopting a new zoning ordinance permanently banning the facilities. Conder called the proposed restrictions “premature and a little bit overreactive,” arguing that facilities vary in size and that cooling technology and development conditions could address concerns. Mill emphasized electrical capacity while urging the city to include organized labor in discussions about future standards, local hiring and apprenticeship opportunities. Data centers house computer servers and related equipment used to store and process information. City officials are weighing concerns about their electricity and water demands, noise and use of limited land against potential economic benefits. City Planner Laurel Reimer said Riverside has received inquiries from people interested in locating data centers in the city, but no formal applications. Under Riverside's zoning code, uses that are not listed are prohibited unless the Community & Economic Development director determines they are similar to, and no more detrimental than, an allowed use. The director has made no such determination for data centers. “Data centers are considered a prohibited use,” Reimer told the council as members clarified the motion before voting. “So we would not be issuing permits for them.” Councilmember Steven Robillard, who made the motion, said the city needs to distinguish among different types of facilities before deciding what might fit Riverside. He pointed to an existing Spectrum facility in Ward 3 and suggested a smaller center serving local research or businesses could warrant consideration. “Not all data centers are these behemoths that are sucking up all of our power and water,” Robillard said. Councilmember Philip Falcone, who initially brought a proposed ban to the Land Use Committee in September, said pausing development would give the city time to establish safeguards. “You need to pause the moving forward of development so you can figure out and do that deep dive and do that research and set those regulations and set those parameters,” Falcone said. The staff report identified potential effects on electrical reliability, long-term water supplies, air quality and nearby neighborhoods. It also questioned whether large facilities would provide enough permanent employment to justify their land and infrastructure demands. Riverside currently has one connection to the statewide electrical grid. Riverside Public Utilities representative David Garcia said the Riverside Transmission Reliability Project, which would provide a second connection, is expected to be completed in late 2029 or early 2030. Whether the city could serve a data center would depend on its size and location, Garcia said. Some areas with older infrastructure would be less suitable, though developers could potentially pay for upgrades. The hearing also drew opposition from building trades representatives who said restrictions could cost local workers construction jobs. “When people hear data centers, they usually think of servers, microchips and giant tech corporations,” said Johnny Escobedo, representing the Ironworkers Union. “But as iron workers, when I see a data center project, I see something very different. I see hundreds of thousands of man hours of good union labor." Escobedo continued, "I see structural steel, reinforced concrete, rebar, and real heavy industrial construction right here in Riverside. A blanket moratorium does not put a hold on tech building. It puts a hold on local paychecks. Right now, working families in Riverside and across the Inland Empire are dealing with rising costs of living. Our members do not want handouts. We want work. High tech infrastructure projects like data centers provide the exact kind of high wage commercial construction jobs that allow our men and women to buy homes here, raise their families here, and put money back into their local businesses." Other speakers urged caution. Ward 4 resident Stephanie Casper raised concerns about electricity costs, heat, noise and outages. Mike McCarthy, representing the Sierra Club Box Springs Group, supported a moratorium to give the city time to define data centers and determine what protections would be needed. The three-member AI working group, established in September with a 13-month assignment, will study data center infrastructure and land use alongside broader AI issues.

artigo.texto: Minneapolis City Council approves data center ordinance, but fails to pass full ban MINNEAPOLIS (FOX 9) - The Minneapolis City Council passed a data center ordinance on Thursday, but wasn't able to fully ban them. Minneapolis data center ordinance What we know: The Minneapolis City Council passed the data center ordinance 7-6. One of the compromises that was made after the full ban failed to pass was the overlay district. Meaning, any new data center would need to be approved by the council, and they are not allowed in new construction, only in existing buildings. Data centers cannot be the primary use of the building, according to the city council. The regulations also include a mandatory disclosure of energy, water and generator use. A sound attenuation plan is also required. The City Council also added a requirement to submit a plan for decommissioning data centers if they no longer function or go out of business. Data centers that go above 50,000 square feet will be required to enter into a program with Xcel Energy, where the owners would be required to pay a premium, "to build out renewable energy in the large grid through the purchase of renewable energy credits," Council member Aurin Chowdhury said. The council's ordinance also doesn't allow data centers to be on the first or second floor of buildings. What's next: The ordinance now goes to Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey for approval. The City of Minneapolis currently has a moratorium on data centers, but it expires on Nov. 21. Data centers in Minneapolis The backstory: The city says downtown has eight data centers serving tech companies right now. Many more data centers serving onsite computing needs of existing businesses exist around the city, according to city staff. Council members said they heard from Xcel Energy that there is interest in up to eight more data center projects downtown. artigo.texto: Impôr limites aos data centers (centros de dados) deixou de ser uma bandeira de poucos. A oposição a essas instalações está hoje no centro da política norte-americana: 78% dos congressistas eleitos nas recentes eleições de meio de mandato apoiam algum tipo de regulamentação ou restrição, e a proporção chega a 94% entre os governadores. É o que revela uma análise preliminar publicada pelo Data Center Watch, um projeto da empresa de segurança em inteligência artificial (IA) 10a Labs que há dois anos acompanha a oposição a essas infraestruturas. O estudo rastreou as posições públicas de candidatos ao Congresso e aos governos estaduais em todo o país. Com os resultados disponíveis em 4 de novembro, ele analisa 393 congressistas e 34 governadores eleitos. “Era um tema que todos tinham em suas plataformas políticas. No fim das contas, a diferença estava na intensidade”, resume Miquel Vila, analista-chefe do Data Center Watch. Vila vem alertando há dois anos que os data centers, os centros de dados, acabariam se tornando um tema eleitoral. Embora isso não tenha ocorrido quando ele esperava, nas eleições presidenciais de 2024, a questão acabou por surgir nas urnas agora. Ainda que o resultado, ele reconhece, o tenha surpreendido pela sua magnitude: “Foi até mais do que eu imaginava”. Dos congressistas eleitos analisados, 246 apoiam a regulamentação do setor ou a imposição de condições ao seu desenvolvimento, enquanto 61 defendem proibições ou moratórias — locais, estaduais ou federais. Outros 68 não têm uma posição mais ampla documentada, mas apoiaram a Ratepayer Protection Act, uma iniciativa que visa fazer com que os grandes consumidores de energia elétrica arquem com os custos das melhorias de infraestrutura necessárias para abastecê-los. A diferença entre os partidos está, sobretudo, no alcance das restrições. Entre os congressistas democratas eleitos, 23% apoiam proibições ou moratórias, contra 3% dos republicanos. Entre os governadores, a proporção é de 50% contra 8%. A republicana Kelly Ayotte, reeleita em New Hampshire, é a única governadora de seu partido que defende uma moratória e pretende incluir uma pausa temporária para novas construções de data centers no orçamento estadual de 2027. “A regulamentação dos centros de dados é um tema que atravessa os dois partidos, mas é mais forte entre os candidatos democratas”, explica Vila. Para o analista, o resultado das eleições para governador tem especial importância. Os governadores supervisionam órgãos reguladores, intervêm na concessão de licenças e decidem sobre incentivos públicos. “Os estados têm mais capacidade do que o Congresso para influenciar o desenvolvimento de centros de dados. Eles têm um canal mais direto”, afirma. Isso não significa que as promessas eleitorais se transformem automaticamente em normas, e sua aplicação dependerá das competências de cada governador e das assembleias legislativas estaduais. Uma mudança importante no Texas Nenhum resultado ilustra melhor essa mudança do que o do Texas. A democrata Gina Hinojosa derrotou o governador republicano Greg Abbott com uma proposta de moratória imediata para novos centros de dados, até que sejam reforçadas as garantias para as comunidades e revisados os incentivos públicos ao setor. Trata-se de uma reviravolta histórica, já que os democratas não governavam o estado desde 1995. Nos últimos anos, o Texas havia se tornado um dos principais destinos da expansão da infraestrutura de IA. A ERCOT, operadora de sua rede elétrica, está analisando entre 250 e 300 projetos de grandes consumidores, em sua maioria centros de dados, que, se vierem a ser construídos, poderiam necessitar, juntos, de até 200 gigawatts de eletricidade. A crescente pressão sobre a rede elétrica e os recursos hídricos já havia levado Abbott a ordenar uma revisão dos procedimentos para conectar grandes consumidores. Agora, Hinojosa promete ir muito além. “É uma mudança radical. O Texas era o ‘estado reserva’. Se as coisas complicassem em outro estado, você sempre podia ir para lá para construir”, diz Vila. “Agora não sei quem vai desempenhar esse papel.” A reação também chegou aos mercados. Na quarta-feira (4), enquanto Wall Street fechava em alta, as ações de várias empresas dedicadas à construção e operação de centros de dados sofreram quedas superiores a 10%. Elon Musk, que havia apoiado financeiramente candidatos republicanos no Texas, reagiu no X com um comentário que resumia a inquietação do setor: “Os centros de dados no espaço começam a parecer bastante atraentes”. A mudança não se limita ao Texas. Na Geórgia, a democrata Keisha Lance Bottoms venceu a eleição para governadora com uma proposta de suspensão estadual de novas construções enquanto se avaliam suas consequências econômicas e para as comunidades. O estado era um dos grandes mercados em expansão para essas infraestruturas tecnológicas. No Meio-Oeste, as restrições aos centros de dados também encontraram apoio entre candidatos de ambos os partidos. Em Ohio, tanto a democrata Amy Acton quanto seu rival, Vivek Ramaswamy, defendiam a limitação de novas construções, embora com propostas distintas. Acton, que acabou vencendo, propunha uma moratória condicionada a garantias sobre os custos de energia elétrica, a transparência e os benefícios para as comunidades. Ramaswamy propunha suspender temporariamente as autorizações até a aprovação de uma lei que impusesse requisitos aos promotores. Em Michigan, Jocelyn Benson, a democrata eleita, defende uma moratória estadual, enquanto o republicano John James, que inicialmente havia apoiado uma pausa temporária, acabou rejeitando uma proibição estadual e defendendo que as decisões fossem de competência das autoridades locais. A pressão também se fez sentir nas votações locais. Das 47 consultas sobre centros de dados cujos resultados já haviam sido decididos após as eleições, 46 deram a vitória a opções favoráveis a maiores restrições. artigo.texto: Drone and missile strikes have inflicted unprecedented damage on data centers in Eastern Europe and the Middle East this year, disrupting cloud services for millions of people and permanently deleting some Amazon Web Services customer data. This trend represents a new concern for Big Tech companies—but also for governments and everyone else who depends on common digital services in modern life. To explore what this all means for modern society’s reliance on cloud resilience, I will be hosting a live conversation titled “Drone attacks and data centers: New Risks for Big Tech” on Tuesday, November 17 at 1 pm ET with Joseph Jarnecki, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK defense and security think tank. He leads RUSI’s work on how cloud services factor into national security and defense, along with tech sovereignty efforts. Jarnecki has done extensive research on how Ukraine strengthened its cloud resilience with Western partners despite facing both cyberattacks and kinetic attacks at the start of the full-scale Russian invasion, and explored what that means for NATO and European governments’ cloud adoption plans. This year, Jarnecki has written about Iran’s drone and missile strikes on Amazon data centers in the Middle East during the US-Israeli war with Iran, and the broader implications for governments and Big Tech. He has also commented on the impacts of Russia and Ukraine exchanging strikes on each other’s data centers.

artigo.texto: Uma falha de partida pode custar à frota mais do que a substituição de uma bateria. O veículo que deixa de sair pode exigir socorro, reprogramação de entregas ou reorganização de viagens. Com mais equipamentos elétricos e eletrônicos a bordo de caminhões e ônibus, escolher a bateria exige considerar não […] 11 de novembro de 2026, às 13:27 Uma falha de partida pode custar à frota mais do que a substituição de uma bateria. O veículo que deixa de sair pode exigir socorro, reprogramação de entregas ou reorganização de viagens. Com mais equipamentos elétricos e eletrônicos a bordo de caminhões e ônibus, escolher a bateria exige considerar não apenas a partida, mas também o consumo ao longo da operação e o tempo disponível para recarga. Na Fenatran 2026, a Moura apresenta suas tecnologias para atender a diferentes perfis de uso no transporte pesado e responder aos novos desafios das frotas cada vez mais eletrônicas. “Um caminhão não deixa de consumir energia quando o motor é desligado. Dependendo dos equipamentos em uso, a bateria continua trabalhando durante o descanso do motorista e precisa manter reserva para a próxima partida. Para o gestor de frota, a pergunta não é apenas qual bateria cabe no veículo, mas qual atende à sua rotina de consumo e recarga”, afirma Felipe Godoy, diretor de Negócios Corporativos e Novos Mercados da Rede Moura. Nos caminhões de longa distância, geladeiras, iluminação e equipamentos eletrônicos podem permanecer ligados durante os períodos de descanso. Nessas condições, o desafio é conciliar o consumo com o motor desligado, a reserva necessária para a partida e a recuperação da carga quando o veículo volta à operação. Nos ônibus, as exigências variam conforme o serviço. Transporte urbano, rodoviário e fretamento têm diferentes rotinas de funcionamento, períodos de espera e equipamentos de bilhetagem, monitoramento e conforto. Por isso, a escolha da bateria precisa considerar quais sistemas ela alimenta, por quanto tempo e em quais condições de recarga. EFB: tecnologia para operações mais exigentes A EFB, sigla de Enhanced Flooded Battery, utiliza uma construção inundada aprimorada para suportar ciclos de descarga e recarga mais exigentes. A tecnologia foi desenvolvida para aplicações que demandam maior robustez energética e desempenho em condições operacionais mais severas. No mercado de reposição, a tecnologia EFB vem ganhando espaço em aplicações que exigem maior disponibilidade operacional e desempenho energético. A Moura EFB 225 é a primeira tecnologia do tipo 100% nacional, desenvolvida para caminhões e veículos comerciais, garantindo maior capacidade e durabilidade para operações que exigem robustez e confiabilidade energética. O impacto da parada vai além da manutenção Quando a falta de energia impede a partida, os efeitos podem alcançar toda a programação do veículo. Além de diagnóstico, atendimento e eventual substituição da bateria, a ocorrência pode exigir remanejamento de veículos, alterar horários e comprometer entregas ou viagens. A indicação depende das especificações do veículo e das condições de trabalho. Além da capacidade nominal, a avaliação deve considerar a frequência e a intensidade das descargas, as oportunidades de recarga, a resistência à vibração e os requisitos de partida. “A bateria precisa ser avaliada pelo que entrega à operação. A especificação correta deve caminhar com a verificação do sistema elétrico e com a manutenção. É esse conjunto que ajuda a enfrentar os riscos, que podem ganhar escala rapidamente, decorrentes de uma parada”, acrescenta Godoy. artigo.texto: Demand for Battery Storage and String Inverters Growing in India: Interview Grid-forming inverter adoption will depend on policy support and planning by grid operators November 12, 2026 Follow Mercom India on WhatsApp for exclusive updates on clean energy news and insights As battery energy storage systems (BESS) become a key focus for India’s solar inverter market, string inverters are seeing wider adoption in utility-scale projects because of their modularity, lower maintenance needs, and potential to reduce generation losses. In an interview with Mercom India at the recently concluded Renewable Energy India (REI) Expo 2026, Aniket Sawant, Country Head at GoodWe India, discussed emerging trends in India’s inverter market, the growing importance of battery storage, technological developments, component supply challenges, and the company’s expansion plans. What is GoodWe’s current inverter portfolio, and what are the company’s plans for the next two to three years? GoodWe has completed 10 years in India. Our business primarily focuses on on-grid inverters, and we serve residential, commercial and industrial (C&I), and utility-scale customers. Our residential portfolio includes single-phase inverters starting at 3 kW and three-phase inverters up to 10 kW. For C&I applications, we offer inverters ranging from 12 kW to 150 kW, while our utility-scale portfolio includes 350 kW inverters. Looking ahead, we anticipate significant growth in energy storage demand, which will be an important part of our future business. What major trends are emerging in India’s solar inverter market? Battery energy storage is one of the most significant trends in the Indian solar market. Initially, the focus was on generating solar electricity and consuming it immediately or injecting it into the grid. However, the market is shifting towards storing electricity generated during the day and using it at night. Government policies are increasingly addressing the need for energy storage across residential, C&I, and utility-scale applications. We see substantial potential for battery storage as the industry transitions from generation-focused installations toward integrated solutions. Are utility-scale solar developers shifting from central inverters to string inverters? What is driving this transition? Utility-scale projects are clearly shifting toward string inverters. Three to four years ago, central inverters dominated approximately 90% of the utility-scale market. However, developers are increasingly recognizing the technical and operational advantages of string inverters. One advantage is installation flexibility. String inverters can be mounted directly on structures, while central inverters generally require dedicated civil foundations, adding to installation costs. String inverters also offer operational and maintenance advantages because of their modular design. For example, if a central inverter serving a 1 MW block fails, the entire block can go offline, resulting in generation losses. In comparison, if a 300 kW string inverter fails, only the capacity connected to that inverter is affected. This reduces the impact of equipment failures on electricity generation and project revenue. String inverters also integrate effectively with solar trackers, supporting improved generation performance. For projects operating over 10 to 20 years, modularity, maintenance flexibility, and reduced downtime can provide long-term operational benefits. How are advancements in solar module technologies influencing inverter design and technical specifications? Solar module technology is evolving rapidly, and inverter manufacturers must continuously upgrade their products to remain compatible. A few years ago, solar modules typically had power ratings of approximately 400 W to 450 W. Today, modules with capacities reaching around 700 W are available. Inverter manufacturers must adapt their technical specifications, particularly maximum power point tracking (MPPT) current capabilities. For example, newer heterojunction modules may require MPPT current ratings of about 40 A. Inverter manufacturers must increase current handling capabilities and ensure their products remain compatible with emerging module technologies. Monitoring technological developments in solar modules and upgrading inverter specifications accordingly will remain critical. What are the major challenges in inverter manufacturing, particularly regarding semiconductor and IGBT availability? The availability of critical electronic components remains an important challenge for inverter manufacturers. India’s annual renewable energy installations have increased substantially, from approximately 9 GW to 10 GW a few years ago to around 25 GW to 30 GW. As installations increase, demand for semiconductors and insulated gate bipolar transistors (IGBTs) also rises. The global market has relatively few major suppliers of these components, including Infineon, Fuji, and established Chinese manufacturers. Large inverter manufacturers with strategic relationships with component suppliers are generally better positioned to manage supply constraints. However, fluctuations in demand and component availability can still affect procurement costs and inverter prices. How do you see grid-forming inverter technology developing in India over the next two to three years? Grid-forming inverter technology has already gained traction in markets such as the U.S. and Europe. India has its own grid requirements and project-specific challenges. Currently, grid-following inverters remain widely used because they align with existing grid requirements. Grid-forming technology can help improve grid stability through active and reactive power management. However, wider adoption will depend on clear policy direction and coordinated planning involving policymakers, the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, grid operators, and distribution companies. artigo.texto: How BYD Is Combining Solar Power, Batteries And 5-Minute Charging Chinese car manufacturer BYD has announced the launch of a new integrated charging system in the Abu Dhabi desert. The installation combines solar power generation, battery energy storage, ultra-fast charging, and robotic charging technology in a single location. While each of those elements already exists independently, BYD says this is the first time it has brought them together in a fully integrated system. BYD Flash Charging Reducing charging times, alongside increasing range, remains one of the most effective ways to convince drivers to switch from internal combustion engines to EVs. BYD's answer is FLASH Charging, technology that's claimed to charge a car from 10% to 70% in around five minutes, or from 10% to 97% in roughly nine minutes. Rather than relying solely on the grid, the site captures solar energy, stores it in batteries and then delivers it to vehicles when required. By integrating generation, storage and charging into a unified system, BYD hopes to reduce dependence on existing power infrastructure while making charging more viable in remote locations. It's a concept that could prove particularly relevant in regions where electricity networks are under strain or where connecting high-power charging stations remains challenging. Why The Desert? The desert environment provides an abundant supply of sunshine while also presenting some of the harshest operating conditions for energy infrastructure. High temperatures, dust, and limited rainfall create a demanding test bed for both solar generation and charging equipment. Although many consumers know the company primarily as an automaker, BYD has built a substantial renewable energy division over the past two decades. The company says its solar business operates in more than 100 countries and regions, supplying everything from photovoltaic cells to complete energy systems. Where Does Robotics Fit In? Rather than requiring a driver to retrieve a charging cable and connect it manually, a robotic arm handles the process automatically. Using cameras and force-feedback technology, it identifies the charging port, opens the flap, and inserts the connector. Likewise, drivers can leave the vehicle, lock it, and walk away, while the car navigates itself to an available charging bay. Once parked, the charging robot takes over. In locations where temperatures regularly climb well above comfort levels, eliminating the need for drivers to stand outside connecting heavy charging cables may be genuinely appealing. Almost 20 Years In The Making BYD frames the project as the latest step in a strategy first outlined by chairman Wang Chuanfu in 2006. At the time, he described what the company calls its "Three Green Dreams": generating clean electricity from solar power, storing that energy in batteries and then using it to power electric vehicles. Nearly two decades later, the Abu Dhabi installation represents perhaps the clearest physical expression of that idea. Solar panels generate energy, batteries store it, and electric vehicles consume it, all within a single integrated system. It is also a sign of how far EV technology has progressed. Concepts that once sounded ambitious, such as ultra-fast charging and large-scale battery storage, are increasingly becoming commercial realities. Global Expansion BYD says it plans to deploy 6,000 FLASH Charging stations worldwide by the end of 2027, significantly expanding access to its ultra-fast charging technology. Whether every site will eventually incorporate solar generation, battery storage, and robotic charging remains unclear. But the Abu Dhabi project offers a strong indication of the direction BYD wants the industry to travel. This article was originally published on Forbes.com

artigo.texto: - UNCTAD will launch a new global network at COP31 to connect fragmented carbon markets and encourage cross-border investment. - The initiative aims to improve transparency, credit integrity and market infrastructure, with developing economies among its main beneficiaries. - Global carbon pricing generated more than $107 billion in government revenue in 2025, highlighting the growing economic significance of the sector. UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) is preparing to launch the Global Carbon Market Network at COP31, seeking to strengthen carbon finance and attract investment into climate projects across developing countries as international carbon trading faces persistent challenges over transparency, standards and credit quality. The initiative, scheduled to debut on November 12 in Antalya, Türkiye, will bring together carbon exchanges, financial institutions and other market participants to improve connections between carbon markets and capital providers. Rather than establishing another trading platform, the network will focus on making existing systems work together more effectively, facilitating international transactions and building confidence among investors. Connecting Fragmented Markets Differences in verification requirements, registries and trading frameworks have complicated the development of international carbon markets. Concerns over unreliable credits and double counting have also discouraged potential buyers and investors. UNCTAD plans to address these obstacles through cooperation between market institutions, technical exchanges and initiatives aimed at improving the measurement and verification of emissions reductions. The network will also explore digital technologies that could improve transparency and reduce transaction costs. Its work is expected to support Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, which provides a framework for international cooperation through carbon credits and emissions reductions transferred between countries. Developing Economies In Focus The initiative comes as carbon pricing continues to expand globally. According to the World Bank’s 2026 State and Trends of Carbon Pricing report, carbon pricing mechanisms covered nearly 30% of global greenhouse gas emissions and generated more than $107 billion in government revenue during 2025. Developing economies could benefit from stronger connections between carbon markets, particularly as many carbon credit projects originate in these countries while buyers are frequently based in wealthier economies. However, access to international finance remains constrained by verification costs, regulatory uncertainty and concerns about project credibility. The network’s initial programme will include capacity-building, market benchmarking and engagement with regulators. Its longer-term success will depend on whether improved cooperation translates into greater investment and demand for credible carbon credits. artigo.texto: Power Entergy Powers Up Texas, Louisiana for Data Centers Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $33 billion of projects from Entergy, with nearly $16 billion attributed to grassroot developments Released Wednesday, November 11, 2026 Reports related to this article: Written by Will Ploch, Assistant Editor-in-Chief for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary Entergy is turning to Texas and Louisiana to build out some of its highest-profile power-generation and transmission projects, including several attached to data centers. Powering Up the Pelican State Entergy Incorporated, a utility that serves parts of Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Arkansas, is taking a bigger role in powering up the data center market, while scrambling to reinforce a regional power grid under growing stress. Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $33 billion worth of active and proposed projects from Entergy, nearly $16 billion of which is attributed to grassroot developments. According to Industrial Info Resources data, more than 50% of the total investment is attributed to projects in Texas and Louisiana. In a quarterly earnings-related conference call last week, Andrew Marsh, the chief executive officer of Entergy, said his company has more than 1,000 miles of transmission lines planned, "primarily in Louisiana and Texas, 85% of which are 500-kilovolt lines. Approximately 70% of the investment is already approved." Last month, the Louisiana Public Service Commission (LPSC) approved Entergy's Babel-to-Webre Transmission Project, a 147-mile line connecting the company's Babel Substation in South Toledo Bend, Texas, which already is under development, to the existing Webre Substation in New Orleans. The project is part of the Midcontinent Independent System Operator's (MISO) 2025 Transmission Expansion Plan (MTEP25), which comprises 432 transmission projects intended to support rapid load growth and improve system reliability. Industrial Info Resources offers more information on the Babel-to-Webre project in its Global Market Intelligence (GMI) Power Project Database, where subscribers can find details--including construction schedules, investment values and necessary equipment--in reports on the transmission line and substation. Marsh also said the U.S. Gulf Coast was a hotspot for its power-generation business: "We also have nine plants in regulatory review in Louisiana, with schedules to support decisions later this year. We have an additional four plants that are in our supply plan, but later in the cycle. That leaves eight units that are available for new growth opportunities." Hyperscalers are among the customers for Entergy's power-generation projects in Louisiana, Marsh said: "We have been innovative in expanding our investment by accessing less-traditional markets. For example, in October, we closed on our second build-to-suit lease" for a unit addition at its Waterford Power Station in Killona, Louisiana, which is being developed partly to service Facebook parent Meta Platforms Incorporated's Hyperion Data Center in Rayville, Louisiana, the first phase of which is under construction. Subscribers can learn more from detailed reports on the Waterford addition and the first phase of Hyperion. Subscribers also can consult a full list of project reports for Meta's nearly $79 billion worth of data center projects in Louisiana. By the Numbers - More than $33 billion: Total investment value of active and proposed projects from Entergy - More than 50%: Share of the total investment attributed to projects in Texas and Louisiana - $940.3 million: Entergy's third-quarter net income, a 35.5% year-over-year increase Shaking Hands with Google Renewable energy also is in Entergy's project mix, including one project intended to serve a data center: the Cypress Solar & Battery Storage Project in Wright, Arkansas, which is designed to generate 600 megawatts (MW) from photovoltaic (PV) panels provided by Canadian Solar Incorporated and store up to 350 MW in a battery energy-storage system (BESS) unit. The Cypress complex will serve Google parent Alphabet Incorporated's West Memphis Data Center, nicknamed "Project Pyramid," a $10 billion investment across five buildings. To ward off public criticism surrounding data center growth, Google agreed to cover all power and infrastructure costs, including $600 million in new grid enhancements. The grid enhancements include a 250-MW BESS unit at the Driver Solar Plant in Osceola, Arkansas, and the 100-MW, standalone Jones Mill BESS unit in Malvern, Arkansas. Both projects are owned by Entergy. Subscribers can learn more from detailed project reports on Cypress, Driver and Jones Mill. Subscribers also can consult a list of reports for projects related to the West Memphis Data Center. Entergy reported consolidated operating revenues of $4.37 billion for third-quarter 2026, a 14.7% increase from the same period last year. Net income stood at $940.3 million, a 35.5% increase. Industrial Info Resources also offers a full list of reports for active and proposed projects from Entergy. artigo.texto: Anthropic proposes IPO price as data center communities ask who benefits Company could be valued at up to $1.4 trillion; residents near projects seek a direct financial stake GREEN BAY, Wis. (WBAY) - Anthropic, the company behind the AI assistant Claude, proposed a share price of $70 to $78 on Tuesday for its initial public offering. Communities that host data centers are questioning whether the economic benefits last beyond construction. At the high end, the offering could raise up to $64 billion. The stock sale could value the company at up to $1.4 trillion. The sale has not happened yet. Data centers need land, power and approvals The industry’s growth depends on more data centers. Those projects require land, electricity, infrastructure and local approvals. Janine Yorio, CEO of Community Digital Technologies, works with residents near data center projects. She said there is a difference between building the facilities and sharing in the wealth they generate. “Part of the reason why people were so upset about data centers is because they see billions of dollars being poured into their local community to build them,” Yorio said. “But then the local prosperity ends there. After construction stops, there are very few jobs for local workers.” Tax revenue does not necessarily reach homeowners Data centers can generate tax revenue. Those benefits do not necessarily reach individual homeowners. Communities are pushing for residents to have a more direct financial stake in projects built near them. They also want more control over what gets built and who pays the price. As communities question the impacts, developers may face more pressure to offer benefits beyond tax revenue. Yorio said approaches used in the past may not be enough. “Developers have already tried lots of different things. They’ve tried giving towns new schools and paying taxes. And even that hasn’t been enough,” Yorio said. “So the next step is to talk to the neighbors like potential partners and offer them a piece of the upside. People want to understand that they are not going to get left behind by the AI economy that’s being built in their neighborhood.” Payments and ownership stakes Possible benefits include direct payments or ownership stakes for homeowners near data centers. There is no guarantee developers would agree. Copyright 2026 WBAY. All rights reserved.

artigo.texto: Em um agronegócio que amplia a área cultivada e depende de janelas climáticas para plantar e colher, manter tratores e colheitadeiras disponíveis é parte da gestão da produtividade. Com esse foco, a Moura apresenta na Fenatran 2026, de 9 a 13 de novembro, em São Paulo, a M100HA, bateria de […] 10 de novembro de 2026, às 17:42 Em um agronegócio que amplia a área cultivada e depende de janelas climáticas para plantar e colher, manter tratores e colheitadeiras disponíveis é parte da gestão da produtividade. Com esse foco, a Moura apresenta na Fenatran 2026, de 9 a 13 de novembro, em São Paulo, a M100HA, bateria de sua linha pesada desenvolvida para atender às exigências elétricas cada vez mais complexas de máquinas agrícolas. Segundo levantamento da Companhia Nacional de Abastecimento (Conab), a safra brasileira de grãos 2026/27 poderá alcançar 367,1 milhões de toneladas, alta de 1,4% sobre o ciclo anterior. A área prevista de plantio chega a 85,4 milhões de hectares, expansão de 2,3%. Ao mesmo tempo, a Anfavea registra queda de 15,8% nas vendas de máquinas agrícolas de janeiro a agosto de 2026. Com a renovação mais lenta, preservar a disponibilidade dos equipamentos ganha peso na gestão da safra. A indisponibilidade de uma máquina pode exigir socorro, reparos e reprogramação de atividades, além de afetar o ritmo de outros equipamentos envolvidos no plantio ou na colheita. Ao apresentar a M100HA, a Moura reforça sua atuação em soluções de energia para o agronegócio, com suporte de sua rede nacional de pós-venda e destinação ambientalmente adequada das baterias ao fim da vida útil. “No campo, a produtividade não depende apenas da capacidade da máquina, mas de ela estar disponível quando o clima permite operar. Uma falha na partida pode interromper uma frente de trabalho inteira. Por isso, a escolha da bateria deve considerar o motor, as condições de uso e a instalação elétrica”, afirma Felipe Godoy, Diretor de Negócios Corporativos e Novos Mercados da Rede Moura. Além do esforço exigido na partida de motores a diesel, tratores e colheitadeiras incorporam atualmente computadores de bordo, GPS, telemetria, sensores e iluminação auxiliar. Esses recursos exigem conexões elétricas confiáveis. Com o motor ligado, o sistema de geração assume o fornecimento de energia. À bateria cabe garantir a corrente de partida e as funções previstas no projeto. A M100HA é uma bateria chumbo-ácido de 12 volts e 100 ampères-hora, com corrente de partida a frio de 930 ampères. Um de seus diferenciais é o posicionamento dos terminais, adequado aos chicotes originais de determinadas máquinas agrícolas. Quando a aplicação é compatível, a configuração dispensa extensões, emendas e esforços indevidos nos cabos, fatores que podem comprometer conexões sob vibração. A estrutura interna também contempla proteção e sustentação das placas, além de ligas de chumbo e separadores de alta retenção, recursos voltados à resistência mecânica e à durabilidade. Esses elementos são relevantes para máquinas submetidas à trepidação e ao uso intensivo no campo. A escolha exige observar as especificações do equipamento e não dispensa manutenção preventiva. artigo.texto: The world’s largest demonstration plant for a new kind of renewable energy storage is up and running in the west of the China. Called liquid-air energy storage (LAES) the plant uses renewable electricity to compress air to extreme densities until it turns to liquid. It can then be rapidly released to power a turbine and discharge that green energy back into the grid. China has received numerous plaudits for its rapid adoption of renewable energy at both scale and speed, and this new facility in Qinghai Province brings in a key missing element to the renewable build-out: grid-scale battery storage for when the Sun isn’t shining and the wind isn’t blowing. Not that either of those happen very often in Qinghai, which encompasses parts of the Tibetan Plateau, and Mongolia-like grasslands and desert, where both sun and wind are famously relentless. Described as “the world’s largest grid-connected liquid-air energy storage facility by both rated power and energy capacity,” the facility is rated at 600 megawatt-hours, and will substantially back up the renewable contribution to the regional power grid by providing 10 hours of continual power supply when necessary. Additionally, it was built with its own solar farm, rated at 250MW. LAES works by turning ordinary air into a liquid, keeping that liquid in insulated tanks, and then converting it back into electricity when needed. When electricity is plentiful, it powers machinery that draws in air, compresses it and cools it to extremely low temperatures of around -190°C. At this point, the air becomes a liquid, taking up far less space than it did as a gas. When power is needed, the liquid air is pumped to high pressure and warmed. As it warms, it rapidly expands back into a gas and can be used to spin a turbine connected to an electricity generator, sending power back to the grid. A cool party trick is how the system utilizes the excess heat and cold: it stores both for heating and cooling the air as needed, reducing energy consumption and environmental disturbance. The development was undertaken by Highview Power and Encore Renewable Energy, and if built will help solar and wind gain a larger purchase in a high-demand energy district known as the Sheffield-Highgate Export Interface. SCALING UP RENEWABLE ENERGY: World’s Largest Battery to Revolutionize Renewable Energy Storage in Maine with ‘Reverse Rusting’ Rated at 400MWh, it could deliver grid-scale renewable electricity for 8 hours straight, helping to reduce the use of fossil fuels when the interface is overloaded, which according to Recharge News happens frequently. Cost comparisons with standard lithium-ion battery storage systems are apparently very appealing, with LAES costing at least 33 cents on the dollar when the two systems are compared, according to financial analyst and asset management firm Lazard. artigo.texto: Residents raise concerns over planned expansion of Montgomery data center MONTGOMERY, Ala. (WSFA) - A handful of Montgomery residents gathered at City Hall Thursday night to raise concerns about a planned expansion of Meta’s data center campus off Hyundai Boulevard, where some urged city leaders to slow down. Phase four calls for four more buildings at the facility off I-65 on Hyundai Boulevard. The plan includes two more data halls, an administration building, a warehouse and other infrastructure, all powered by an existing substation. The public hearing during the planning commission meeting did not end in a vote. Project details Trevor Kropp, a civil engineer with Barge Design Solutions of Memphis, Tennessee, who represents Meta’s project, presented phase four of the data center development at 1055 Hyundai Boulevard during the meeting. Kropp said phase four is located just south of the first three phases. He said the property is zoned M1 light industrial. The phase includes two data halls, an administration building and a warehouse, Kropp said: - The two data halls are pre-engineered metal buildings. Each is about 414,000 square feet and about 41 feet tall. - The administration building is a mass timber structure of approximately 53,000 square feet and 27 feet in height. - The warehouse is a mass timber building of approximately 86,000 square feet and about 35 feet in height. Kropp said all of the buildings are about 6,000 feet south of Hyundai Boulevard. He said the plan also includes four new stormwater management ponds to reduce runoff. He said no new intersections or ingress on Hyundai Boulevard are required for the development. Residents voice concerns A nearby resident said they are already feeling the impact. “I have seen them at 2 o’clock coming in on 18-wheelers,” said Elizabeth Low, a neighbor and volunteer firefighter. “Y’all are appointed to look out for our safety. It’s not going to only affect the water in our community. It’s going to affect the water here in Montgomery City and the whole Montgomery area.” Others want answers before the complex more than doubles in size. “Is the City of Montgomery and the County of Montgomery just going to get screwed over by this massive data center?” said Amanda Thornton, a Montgomery resident. “We just need to seriously consider what currently is here, how it’s affecting the sound, the animals, the water, the land, the people around it.” Some residents pointed to other cities that have put the brakes on data center growth. “I just ask that we not go too far before we can’t turn around,” said James Warren, a Montgomery resident. What happens next The Planning Commission did not vote. It reviewed the plan and took public comment. Kropp declined to comment after the meeting. Neighbors said they will keep pressing for answers on water, power, and health impacts before the campus expands again. City staff will continue reviewing the development plan. Any formal expansion would still have to go before the City Council for final approval. Not reading this story on the WSFA News App? artigo.texto: New Approaches to Data Center Power Procurement As grid limits tighten, data centers may need to diversify power strategies to secure reliable capacity, control costs, and support faster growth. Data centers are consuming more power than ever, and many operators are adopting new strategies to secure the energy they need. Indeed, the era when a data center could simply connect to the public grid and call it a day may be coming to an end. Instead, data center operators are increasingly pursuing more creative strategies, from partnering with utilities to expand grid capacity to building dedicated power plants for their own use or installing generators that can both power a facility and feed electricity back to the grid. Here’s a look at these and other trends shaping data center power procurement. 1. Power Purchase Agreements In a world where public power grids are increasingly struggling to supply enough electricity to data centers, operators are keen to guarantee access to power. One way to do that is through power purchase agreements (PPAs), which are contracts that allow a data center to buy electricity at a fixed price from a utility or power producer. PPAs can help improve price predictability and, in some situations, support faster access to new power capacity. PPAs can also serve a separate purpose. In some cases, they provide data centers with access to electricity from renewable energy generation. This allows operators to reduce reliance on fossil fuels without having to build and operate their own solar, wind, or geothermal plants. That said, most grids cannot guarantee that the electricity delivered to a specific facility comes exclusively from renewable sources. For that reason, renewable energy PPAs are often better understood as a way for data centers to financially support the expansion of clean energy generation on the grid rather than as a direct source of fully renewable energy. 2. Behind-the-Meter Power Rather than relying primarily on utilities, some data center operators are choosing to generate their own electricity through a behind-the-meter approach. This strategy involves installing on-site generators capable of meeting all, or most, of a facility’s energy needs. This approach is expensive, but it gives operators greater control over their energy sources. It can also help them avoid delays associated with grid interconnection. And while fluctuations in fuel prices mean that behind-the-meter power costs aren’t entirely predictable, operators that run their own power generation assets typically have more direct control over energy planning than those that depend solely on utility-supplied power. 3. Microgrids Microgrids are another emerging strategy that some data center operators are using to procure power. A data center supported by a microgrid relies on a network of generators or small-scale power resources to supply electricity. These resources may be located on-site or in a nearby location connected directly to the facility. Microgrids are similar to behind-the-meter power, and in some cases the terms are used interchangeably. However, microgrids usually imply a more distributed system with multiple energy sources, which can improve resilience. They may also include energy storage infrastructure that data centers can use for backup power or load shifting. For example, a microgrid could capture and store solar power during the day, then deliver it to the data center at night. 4. Phased Energization In a growing number of cases, the public energy grid cannot supply enough electricity to meet a data center’s full power requirements on day one. The grid must expand its own capacity first. To address this challenge, some data centers are turning to phased energization. Although the term sounds technical, the idea is simple: instead of waiting until the grid can support a facility’s full electricity demand, a data center begins operations incrementally as power becomes available. The downside is that facilities using phased energization cannot support their full capacity from the moment they open. The upside is that they can begin partial deployment sooner, which is often preferable to waiting years for full grid capacity to come online. 5. Front-of-the-Meter Power Although the primary goal of most data center operators is securing enough electricity for their own needs, some, especially large hyperscalers, are experimenting with supplying power back to the grid. In other words, they are using on-site generation assets not only to support their own facilities but also to supply electricity to the broader grid. This strategy, known as front-of-the-meter power, may prove beneficial to the data center industry as it seeks to address concerns from regulators and the public that data centers are placing excessive strain on the grid and contributing to rising electricity costs. It may also help operators make better use of backup generators, which have traditionally been reserved for emergencies but could serve as supplementary grid resources during peak-demand periods, such as hot summer days when air conditioning places additional pressure on electricity networks. The New Reality of Data Center Power Procurement As power demand continues to rise, operators will need to look beyond traditional grid connections and tap into a wider mix of energy procurement strategies. Whether through PPAs, on-site generation, microgrids, or phased energization, the future of data center growth will depend largely on how effectively data centers secure reliable, flexible power.

artigo.texto: Jensen-Gate isn't just Nvidia's problem anymore. Data center operators across Southeast Asia might be getting caught in the fallout. In case you missed it, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has had a rough week. On Sunday, The New York Times published an exposé that the executive had an affair with Singapore-based Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, believed to be passing sensitive Nvidia information to Beijing. Alice Huang worked at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that is the largest Nvidia customer in Southeast Asia, per Bloomberg. US authorities have investigated the company on suspicion that it helped Chinese customers obtain advanced Nvidia AI chips in violation of US export restrictions. Huang resigned from his role on Thursday. Industry sources in data center financing and operations told Business Insider that Jensen-Gate could increase scrutiny on Southeast Asia's AI infrastructure companies. Jensengate could lead to increased oversight Chris Miller, the author of "Chip War" and a professor at Tufts University, said to Yahoo Finance on Monday that it was widely known that Megaspeed was "primarily building data centers in Southeast Asia to serve Chinese customers, especially Alibaba in their case." He added that Megaspeed isn't alone, and that there are many data centers in Malaysia, Thailand, and Singapore that buy advanced American chips and sell them to customers in China. He expects these relationships to face more oversight from Washington after Huang's scandal. SEA AI infrastructure operations may get slower and more expensive More scrutiny means slower and more expensive processes. Lior Prosor, the managing partner of Deep33, an NYC-headquartered venture fund that invests in AI infrastructure, told Business Insider that the Huang affair would intensify scrutiny of American tech deployments in Southeast Asia, especially which customers' hands they end up in. "That could increase financing costs and create additional hurdles for some operators," Prosor said. He said this could temporarily create a broader risk premium for Southeast Asian operators, even those with no connection to Megaspeed. Chinmoy Baruah, the CEO of Dublin-based semiconductor company ChipX, said he expects approvals for AI infrastructure projects in the region to take longer, as investors and partners will ask more detailed questions on compliance. ChipX has committed to building wafer fabrication plants in Malaysia. "That may slow some projects at the margin, particularly those with less transparent structures," Baruah told Business Insider. Michael Heinrich, the CEO of Singapore-based decentralized AI compute company 0G, said he could see fundraising for AI infrastructure get more selective over the next year. "The next round of capital will go to the operators who can prove where their chips are, who uses them, and who owns the business," Heinrich said. Bitter medicine, but better long-term health The Huang scandal won't have a lasting impact on demand for Southeast Asian AI infrastructure, but rather on the standards for it, said Baruah. He said the region's fundamentals — growing digital economies, supportive governments, improving connectivity, and rising AI adoption — remain strong. This incident, however, will make rules clearer and increase diligence among operators, chip suppliers, and regulators. "That is a positive outcome for Southeast Asia, because it strengthens the region's position as a reliable, long-term destination for global digital infrastructure investment, not a shortcut around the rules," Baruah said. Prosor from Deep33 added that AI compute is in "extraordinarily short supply, and capital will flow to wherever companies can reliably build up compute. "Southeast Asia remains an important part of that equation," he said. Southeast Asia's data center boom The Huang scandal comes as the data center industry in Southeast Asia is booming. Ember Energy, a London-headquartered energy think tank, wrote in a 2025 report that ASEAN — a bloc of 11 member states in Southeast Asia — was emerging as a "global data center hot spot" due to lower construction costs and electricity levies. Malaysia, for instance, had live data center operations totaling about 1.3 gigawatts in June, which was a tenfold increase from 2022, per a report by BloombergNEF, a think tank under Bloomberg. It has another 4.7 gigawatts planned or under construction, the report added. Indonesia had about 450 megawatts of live data-center capacity as of June, with more than four times that amount currently under construction or committed, per the BloombergNEF report. A rough week for Nvidia Huang's resignation comes after a tumultuous few days for Nvidia. Its stock took a hit after the US midterm elections on November 3, which flipped control of Congress to the Democrats, many of whom had made anti-data-center messaging a major part of their campaigns. A few days after reports on Huang's affair, on Wednesday, the Times published another report that said Huang had had a second extramarital relationship, this time with Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, Kimberly Powell. The Wall Street Journal wrote on Wednesday that Nvidia's board was preparing to oust Huang. Early Thursday morning, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned from the role, and CFO Colette Kress would take over as interim CEO.

artigo.texto: Virginia organizations push for pause in new data center construction Groups say they want better safeguards put in place HANOVER, Va. (WWBT) - A coalition of more than a dozen Virginia-based environmental organizations hosted a press conference Wednesday at the Hanover Humane Society to unveil a “Pause to Protect” policy platform, which calls for a pause on data center construction. The event was held at the Hanover Humane Society, where a new data center is under construction just feet away from the walking trails. “Our goals are not that lofty,” said : Blair St. Ledger-Olson with the Virginia League of Conservation Voters. “We simply want data centers to be better neighbors.” The coalition said the event comes as Virginians across the Commonwealth demand a data center moratorium. “There is no more time to waste. Urgency is now,” said Elena Schlossberg with the Coalition to Protect Prince William County. “We don’t have six months, we don’t have a year. The pause needs to happen now.” The groups believe a statewide moratorium would to develop and implement regulations to protect Virginia’s air and waterways. “We need to get those protections and safeguards put in place before any more of these data centers are getting permitted at the local level, so we’re not creating essentially a gold rush and before they’re getting interconnected so we can make sure our grid is protected,” said St. Ledger-Olson. This demand comes on the heels of the upcoming General Assembly session, where state lawmakers have filed bills for a data center moratorium. However, the Data Center Coalition believes a statewide moratorium is the wrong approach. Nicole Riley, director of Virginia government affairs for the Data Center Coalition, sent 12 On Your Side the following statement: “Data centers can play a crucial role in advancing Virginians’ top priorities including affordability, job creation, local tax revenue, and bringing investment and opportunity to communities. Our industry remains committed to being responsible partners, engaging with residents and local leaders to understand community priorities, and ensuring digital infrastructure meets local standards and delivers the clear benefits that communities are seeking. We join the many local governments, economic developers, business leaders, and labor unions who believe a top-down, statewide moratorium is the wrong approach to regulating this economically impactful industry. States and communities that signal that they are closed for business and investment risk relinquishing substantial long-term economic investment, high-wage jobs, and critical tax revenue to neighboring areas or other states. As we approach the 2027 General Assembly session, DCC looks forward to working with Governor Spanberger, legislators, local communities and state leaders to maintain trust, support responsible development, and help build a stronger economic future for every Virginian.” However, the groups pushing for a statewide moratorium believe the time for a pause is now. “That we can build on the foundation of a pause to deliver a future that all Virginians deserve,” said Tim Cywinski, communications director of the Sierra Club Virginia Chapter. artigo.texto: Newport Beach, CA, Nov. 11, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Bimergen Energy Corporation (NYSE American: BESS), a developer, owner, and operator of utility-scale and distributed battery energy storage systems, today announced that members of its management team plan to attend RE+ 2026, taking place November 16–19 at the Las Vegas Convention Center. During RE+ 2026, Bimergen management plans to meet with existing joint venture partners, battery technology manufacturers, project financing providers, and tax equity participants, while actively pursuing additional strategic relationships with technology providers, developers, and institutional capital partners. These discussions will focus on expanding Bimergen's strategic network, advancing existing partnerships, evaluating additional financing opportunities, and supporting the continued development and commercialization of the Company's battery energy storage portfolio. Bimergen reports a development portfolio of 33 battery energy storage projects representing approximately 2.0 gigawatts across U.S. electricity markets. The projects are at varying stages of development and are not all necessarily financed, under construction, or operating. The company expects its participation in RE+ to support its ongoing work with technology and capital partners as it seeks to advance projects toward commercialization. About Bimergen Energy Corporation Bimergen Energy Corporation (NYSE American: BESS) is a U.S.-based energy infrastructure developer, asset owner, and operator focused on utility-scale and distributed battery energy storage systems (BESS). The Company develops projects designed to enhance grid reliability, support renewable energy integration, and provide flexible energy solutions across key U.S. power markets. Bimergen works with technology providers and capital partners to advance projects through development, construction, and long-term operation. For more information about Bimergen Energy, please visit www.bimergen.com. About RE + RE+ is North America's largest clean energy industry event, powered by SEIA (Solar Energy Industries Association) and SEPA (Smart Electric Power Alliance). The 2026 conference will bring together industry participants across energy storage, solar, grid, infrastructure and related technologies. artigo.texto: Mineração e infraestrutura: a era da IA e do data center Para que as vantagens materiais e normativas convertam o país em um polo internacional seguro de processamento de dados, serão indispensáveis a convergência de planejamento energético coordenado, transparência regulatória e rigor socioambiental Atualizado A convergência digital e a demanda mineral-energética são realidades globais na atualidade. Nesse contexto, o avanço exponencial da inteligência artificial (IA) e a transformação digital impulsionam uma expansão sem precedentes no ecossistema de data centers. Por trás da aparente intangibilidade dos algoritmos, reside uma dependência material determinante: o processamento computacional massivo exige cadeias produtivas de minerais críticos e uma infraestrutura energética altamente robusta. O Brasil, detentor de vantagens comparativas singulares, posiciona-se no epicentro dessa transformação, na qual a segurança digital computacional se torna indissociável das suas vastas reservas minerais próprias e da sua singular capacidade de fornecimento de energia contínua e descarbonizada. Em resposta a essa conjuntura, a Lei nº 15.506, de 16 de setembro, instituiu a Política Nacional de Minerais Críticos e Estratégicos (PNMCE) e o Conselho Nacional para Industrialização de Minerais Críticos e Estratégicos (CIMCE). O diploma legal define formalmente os minerais críticos como insumos vitais para setores socioeconômicos prioritários, marcados por vulnerabilidades de abastecimento interno, forte dependência de importações, acentuada concentração geográfica global e riscos geopolíticos crescentes. A nova legislação introduziu mecanismos essenciais para adensar a cadeia produtiva local, entre eles o Certificado Mineral de Baixo Carbono (CMBC), o fomento à mineração urbana voltada à recuperação sustentável de resíduos eletroeletrônicos e baterias, e a estruturação do Fundo Garantidor da Atividade Mineral (FGAM), respaldado por uma participação da União de até R$ 2 bilhões. No campo das finanças minerárias, consolidam-se os contratos de streaming e os royalties associados, além do enquadramento em incentivos fiscais como o Regime Especial de Incentivos para o Desenvolvimento da Infraestrutura (Reidi) e as debêntures incentivadas. Paralelamente, o Programa Federal de Beneficiamento e Transformação de Minerais Críticos e Estratégicos (PFMCE) garante crédito fiscal de até 20% do dispêndio. Com uma previsão de R$ 7 bilhões em incentivos e R$ 5 bilhões em crédito tributário, o país prepara-se para ampliar a exploração de suas reservas de terras-raras - situadas entre as maiores do planeta - e escalar a industrialização dos Elementos de Terras Raras (ETRs), viabilizando os componentes eletroeletrônicos indispensáveis aos grandes complexos tecnológicos. No âmbito da infraestrutura digital computacional, a Lei nº 15.504/2026 instituiu o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata). O programa prevê a suspensão de tributos federais por cinco anos na aquisição de equipamentos de processamento, conferindo uma desoneração estimada em R$ 5,2 bilhões em 2026. Em contrapartida, estabelece rigorosas obrigações institucionais: exigência de contratação de energia renovável ou de baixa emissão de carbono, destinação mínima de 10% da capacidade operacional ao mercado interno, índice estrito de eficiência no consumo de água de até 0,05 L/kWh, reinvestimento compulsório de 2% do valor dos produtos e a apresentação periódica de relatórios auditados de sustentabilidade. A implementação desses parques tecnológicos defronta-se com um desafio físico imediato. Conforme dados da Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE), a demanda energética associada aos data centers pode atingir 20 GW em uma década, ao passo que o Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) já projeta uma carga adicional de 3,5 GW em 2030. Os pedidos formais de acesso à rede somam aproximadamente 26 GW até 2038. O principal “nó” da questão, portanto, migra do equilíbrio da geração estrita para os limites das redes de transmissão e a celeridade indispensável dos processos de licenciamento ambiental. Para resguardar a confiabilidade do Sistema Interligado Nacional diante da intermitência típica dos polos computacionais, o aproveitamento do gás de xisto - hoje, extraído de fonte não convencional e sujeito à regulação da ANP (Agência Nacional do Petróleo, Gás Natural e Biocombustíveis) - emerge como vetor de segurança de suprimento, detendo o potencial de duplicar as reservas provadas do país, atualmente, fixadas em torno de 64 bilhões de metros cúbicos. Simultaneamente, as tecnologias de armazenamento em larga escala, com destaque para os supercapacitores e as macro baterias (Battery Energy Storage System, BESS) formuladas com Óxido de Grafeno (GO), despontam como solução elementar para atenuar as oscilações de carga com o armazenamento; e, assim, proporcionar estabilidade contínua ao sistema elétrico de distribuição e consumo a partir da nanotecnologia aplicada, catalisando uma verdadeira revolução na infraestrutura responsável por abastecer os grandes centros de dados. Enfim, a estruturação normativa inaugurada pelas recentes leis desenha um caminho concreto para alçar o Brasil ao topo da economia do novo conhecimento generativo e dos negócios orientados pela inteligência artificial. Para que as vantagens materiais e normativas convertam o país em um polo internacional seguro de processamento de dados, serão indispensáveis a convergência de planejamento energético coordenado, transparência regulatória e rigor socioambiental, além de investimentos em novos projetos e startups. João Bosco Coelho Pasin é presidente da Comissão de Direito Minerário do Instituto dos Advogados de São Paulo (IASP), doutor em Direito pela Universidade de Salamanca (USAL) Este artigo reflete as opiniões do autor, e não do jornal Valor Econômico. artigo.texto: Maine developer revives plan to turn former Jay paper mill into AI data center JAY (WGME) -- A local developer has revived plans to turn a former paper mill in Jay into an AI data center, teaming up with the same national partner that pulled out of the original project in June. The local developer intends to file permit applications with the Maine Department of Environmental Protection to redevelop a portion of the former Androscoggin Paper Mill in Jay into a data center. Six years ago, a wood pulp digester exploded at the paper mill in Jay, eventually leading to the closing of the mill and a loss of 170 jobs. The $550 million facility Sentinel Data Centers wants to build wouldn't bring back all those jobs, but it could significantly ease some of the tax burden in Jay. "If we have nothing there, we have no tax base, and we have a property just sitting there with really no purpose,” Jay resident Jason Mancine said. “So, I think it's an opportunity." "I think it's a good idea,” Jay resident Elizabeth Bates said. “If not that, something else. They should do something with it." Some people in town say they're concerned about all the electricity and water data centers use. - Also read: After Mills vetoes statewide pause, Maine towns move to halt data center projects locally Town leaders say it would be about the same as what the paper mill used, and they don't expect much of an environmental impact change. "It's a former industrial site, so it's not as though we're putting this in the middle of a forested wetland or something like that," Jay Town Manager Shiloh LaFreniere said. "I understand people's concerns about environmental impacts, but I think it would be miniscule compared to what paper mills were," Mancine said. CBS13 reached out to the developer and was told they are not commenting at this time. Earlier this year, Governor Janet Mills vetoed a moratorium on data centers after lawmakers refused to carve out an exception for the Town of Jay. Governor-Elect Hannah Pingree has said she would sign a bill to ban new data centers in Maine. "I don't know how that will play out," LaFreniere said. "My hope personally is that what they're coming out with at the state level will be met by this developer anyway." Developers plan to hold a public meeting at the Jay mill site in one month to talk about the impact of water and electricity use by the proposed data center.

artigo.texto: Safety remains a concern as the use of batteries spreads throughout the economy but they’re getting safer, Christopher Rahn, a professor of mechanical engineering at the Pennsylvania State University, said in an interview. Lithium-ion batteries pose the greatest fire risk because they have high density and use a flammable solvent. But manufacturers are getting better at shipping packs with fewer bad cells, said Rahn, who serves as co-director of the Battery and Energy Storage Technology Center at Penn State. “If you’re going with a well-known supplier, like LG Chem, they do a lot of testing to weed out the weak cells,” he said. Battery management systems are getting better, too, he said. “They make sure you don’t over-charge, don’t over-discharge,” he said. “They make sure they’re working normally and, if anything’s abnormal, they alert you so you stop using the pack. That can help prevent a thermal runaway event.” Manufacturers are also getting smarter about how they control propagation, whether cell-to-cell, pack-to-pack, module-to-module or container-to-container. “The individual cells have different types of materials between them so they don’t propagate to a module-level event,” said Rahn, who’s worked with research teams to develop algorithms for monitoring battery health. At the module level, manufacturers are improving venting to enable gases to escape more effectively. “If there's anything burning and it needs to vent hot gases, you give them an exit from that module,” he said. And at the container level, battery system suppliers are spacing containers further apart during set-up. “If there’s an issue with one container, it doesn’t affect the other ones,” he said. “So, there are three levels of safety, and all of that is maturing,” Rahn said. “The technology of the cells and the quality of manufacturing, the ability to detect when there are anomalies and the ideas and concepts of how to prevent propagation are all maturing." Manufacturers are also investing more resources into alternatives to lithium-ion, which remains the go-to battery despite its risks because its high density makes it the most efficient rechargeable battery on the market. Rahn said he’s seeing manufacturers release more batteries that have aqueous, water-based chemistries, which are considered safer because they don’t rely on a flammable solvent. That means the market is seeing new approaches to traditional lead-acid batteries but also improvements to nickel-zinc batteries to lengthen their lifespan and to iron-air batteries, which use rust conversion to store and discharge energy. He’s also seeing greater use of lithium iron phosphate batteries, which have a lower density than lithium-ion but are less likely to have a thermal event. “So, there’s a spectrum,” he said, “everything from very high-energy density lithium-ion that would typically be used in vehicles through lithium iron phosphate, which is less energy dense but has a safer chemistry, to aqueous chemistries like lead-acid, nickel-zinc and iron-air.”

artigo.texto: O Ministério das Comunicações aprovou R$ 46,3 milhões do Fundo para o Desenvolvimento Tecnológico das Telecomunicações (Funttel) para o projeto Prisma, plataforma que usa inteligência artificial para distribuir o processamento de dados entre infraestruturas, inclusive mini data centers, segundo o ministério em 9 de novembro de 2026. O Centro Brasileiro de Inovação em Tecnologias da Informação e da Comunicação (CPQD), de Campinas (SP), executa o projeto, e a Financiadora de Estudos e Projetos (Finep) gere os recursos. O prazo é de 36 meses, contados a partir do convênio entre as duas instituições. Leia também - João Pessoa já sedia data center que vai quadruplicar de tamanho; Nordeste tem vantagem de US$ 17,4 bilhões no setor, aponta Redata - Brasil lidera expansão de data centers na América Latina - IA pressiona consumo de energia dos data centers O que o projeto Prisma prevê Segundo o Ministério das Comunicações, a plataforma deve decidir com IA onde e como os dados serão processados, distribuindo recursos computacionais entre diferentes infraestruturas. Os objetivos são reduzir o consumo e os custos de energia, cortar custos operacionais, acelerar o acesso à informação e proteger dados estratégicos. Os mini data centers são instalações menores, que processam dados mais perto de onde são gerados. O projeto prevê estimular a expansão dessas unidades em diversas regiões do país, sem informar quantidade nem localização. - Setores atendidos: saúde, defesa, segurança pública, educação e telecomunicações. - Energia: soluções de armazenamento de eletricidade, para dar mais autonomia e continuidade aos serviços. - Segurança e governança: padrões internacionais de segurança e diretrizes da Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD). De onde vem o dinheiro O Funttel é um fundo de natureza contábil, alimentado por contribuição de 0,5% sobre a receita bruta das prestadoras de serviços de telecomunicações, segundo o Ministério das Comunicações. Nos últimos anos, o fundo destinou mais de R$ 362 milhões a empresas do setor, segundo a pasta. O Prisma já aparecia entre os projetos do pacote de cerca de R$ 104 milhões do Funttel para o CPQD, anunciado em março de 2026 para 6G, nuvem e IA, com execução entre 2026 e 2028. O comunicado de 9 de novembro não informa se os R$ 46,3 milhões fazem parte desse total. O que dizem os envolvidos Frederico de Siqueira Filho, ministro das Comunicações, afirmou que investir em tecnologia nacional garante ao Brasil mais autonomia para proteger informações e reduz a dependência de tecnologias desenvolvidas no exterior. Gustavo Correa Lima, diretor de Tecnologia e Inovação do CPQD, destacou que a arquitetura permite “maior controle sobre o dado que está na borda”, ou seja, nas unidades próximas a quem gera a informação. Joana Meirelles, superintendente da Área de Saúde e Transformação Digital da Finep, citou o objetivo de disponibilizar uma plataforma nacional segura e sustentável. O que falta para o projeto sair do papel O aporte mostra a direção do governo, que é a de levar processamento para perto dos usuários com tecnologia desenvolvida no país. O que falta para isso se concretizar são os detalhes de execução. O comunicado não informa se o convênio entre Finep e CPQD já foi assinado, em quais regiões os mini data centers serão instalados, quantas unidades serão e quantos empregos o projeto gera.
