artigo.texto: RWE has started construction of its first battery energy storage system (BESS) in Italy. The 62.5 MW Ragusa battery will be located in Sicily. It will consist of 42 containers with lithium-ion batteries, being able to deliver its maximum output for four hours. This corresponds to a nominal storage capacity of 262.5 MWh. Commissioning is scheduled for the end of 2027. Sopna Sury, CEO RWE Renewables Europe & Australia, said: “The start of construction of our Ragusa battery storage marks an important milestone. We have been operating in Italy for many years, using the energy from the wind and the sun. In a world of growing renewable energy, battery storage systems are crucial for stabilising the grid and ensuring that electricity is used when it is needed most. Ragusa battery will be capable of covering the evening peak demand of around 21 000 households for four hours. We look forward to establishing further battery storage capacity in Italy soon – in addition to wind and solar power – in order to support Italy in building a resilient energy system.” Ragusa battery will provide balancing energy to stabilise the electricity grid. It also features the technology necessary to provide new grid forming services such as instantaneous reserve (inertia). In addition to the batteries, RWE will build the associated grid infrastructure. This includes a high-voltage transformer to connect to the 150-kV grid. artigo.texto: Since I became a Climate Justice Fellow at ANCA, I’ve learned a lot about energy in New York and the North Country, including the important role that battery storage could play. As we continue to discuss what battery storage looks like in the region, I wanted to share some of what I’ve learned in the last few months. What is BESS? Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) are large battery installations that connect to a home, business, or the larger electrical grid. As shown in the diagram below, BESS consist of cells, modules and racks, which are then controlled with a Battery Management System (BMS). The BMS is the brain of the battery system and monitors the whole system down to individual cells. There are two options for BESS. First, it can be part of a renewable energy installation, like a solar farm, and be charged when more energy is being produced than the grid needs at that time. Then, when energy is needed, the batteries can send that stored energy to the grid. READ MORE: In Northern NY, Battery energy storage system moratoriums and bans stack up The second option is a standalone BESS, meaning it is not “co-located” with clean energy generation. In this case, it charges directly from the grid when energy demand is low and costs are cheaper, before discharging when costs and demand are high. Both of these options can help keep energy costs from spiking and reduce the need to turn on peaker plants, which operate when demand is especially high, are expensive to operate, and burn fossil fuels. New York’s electric grid is facing strain due to increasing electricity demand and aging infrastructure. Adding BESS to the grid will support the grid by responding to energy supply and demand quickly and without burning polluting fossil fuels. Day to day, BESS can help meet peak energy demand and create a balance of electricity supply. This is referred to as “peak shaving” since we’re “shaving” the top of the energy demand spike. Long term, BESS can also reduce or defer the need for expensive grid infrastructure upgrades needed to meet future peak demand. Grid infrastructure upgrades contribute to increased delivery charges on your electric bill, and deferring or eliminating expensive upgrades would help keep costs down. BESS and the North Country In the North Country, we have lots of hydropower, as well as wind and solar, so I wasn’t sure at first why we would need batteries too. But as we shift our reliance from fossil fuels, batteries are needed to enable the transition to renewables and energy independence. By supporting the state-wide grid, batteries can improve energy affordability, as mentioned before, by supporting peak demand and reducing the need for more expensive grid upgrades. Just like your taxes go to paying for upkeep of the roads in your town, but you drive roads of other municipalities too, the energy made and used in the Adirondacks isn’t confined by the Blue Line. We’re part of the larger state-wide grid, and the system needs to be evaluated and supported as a whole. There have been some BESS proposals made by developers in communities all over the state recently, including the North Country, such as part of a solar installation in Elizabethtown and standalone BESS in St. Armand. Developers look for locations based on factors such as size, local zoning and avoiding sensitive environmental areas. Crucially, they also look for locations which have strong grid connections with enough extra energy that can be stored for later to be able to support additional infrastructure like a BESS, and there are some locations in the region that meet those requirements. Fire risks and solutions Historically, the main risk commonly associated with BESS, as with any electrical infrastructure, is fire. Fires can happen when components of the battery overheat, including by “thermal runaway,” where battery temperatures self-accelerate. Battery fires, especially lithium-ion batteries, which are currently the most common type used in BESS, are not like a house fire we may be more familiar with. For lithium-ion battery fires the recommended strategy is to monitor and let the fire burn itself out. Obviously that sounds very scary, but studies have shown no lasting environmental impact on soil, air or water after this type of fire, which I know is a concern for me, personally. Because of the unique nature of BESS fires, there are specific, detailed trainings for first responders that are required to be provided to EMS with BESS nearby. For example, in 2023, in East Hampton on Long Island, the way that a BESS was handled led to PFAS contamination in local wells, but this was due to firefighters using water to suppress the fire and washing the built-in fire suppressant chemicals out of the system which would have been self-contained if not for the water used. This just goes to show how important site-specific training is. Since 2023, there were four cases of BESS facilities catching fire in New York, such as in Warwick. As a result, the state has taken major steps to improve fire safety around BESS, including New York’s Inter-Agency Fire Safety Working Group, which created the new Fire Code of the State of New York. They gave 11 recommendations, including requiring “industry-funded peer review” of BESS projects and increased monitoring and fire detection, which were incorporated into the fire code and made it much more rigorous. For anyone interested, those documents and more can be accessed on their website. There are also site-specific, annual trainings for first responders that are required to be provided to local EMS by the owner of BESS facilities for installations of a certain size. Technological advancements also mean that lithium batteries are safer than they were a few years ago. So fires that have happened at older BESS facilities are much less likely to occur in ones built today, as shown in the orange line on the graph below. artigo.texto: Indonesia Accelerates Energy Transition with Landmark Carbon Market Agreement at COP31 November 11, 2026 Category Norway and Indonesia sign Indonesia’s first Mitigation Outcome Purchase Agreement under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement, marking a significant milestone in the country’s carbon market implementation. ANTALYA, TÜRKIYE, November 11, 2026 – Norway and Indonesia have signed a Mitigation Outcome Purchase Agreement (MOPA) at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye. The agreement is facilitated by GGGI and marks Indonesia’s first MOPA to operationalize Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement, representing a significant milestone in the country’s participation in the international carbon markets. Supported through the Norwegian Article 6 Climate Action (NACA) Fund – a carbon fund hosted under GGGI’s Carbon Transaction Facility (CTF) – the agreement is expected to be among the largest transactions under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement to date. It represents an important step in translating international carbon market cooperation into practical implementation and mobilizing climate finance for Indonesia’s energy transition. The signing took place at the Indonesia Pavilion during COP31. The agreement signing was witnessed by Moh Jumhur Hidayat, Minister of Environment/Head of Environmental Protection Agency of Indonesia, and Sigrun Aasland, Minister of Climate and Environment of Norway, serving as witnesses. Following the signing, GGGI will work closely with the Government of Indonesia, PT PLN (Persero) – Indonesia’s state-owned electricity company, and the Norwegian Ministry of Climate and Environment to finalize implementation and operational arrangements. “This agreement marks a concrete step in implementing the Article 6.2 bilateral agreement between Indonesia’s Ministry of Environment/Environmental Protection Agency and Norway’s Ministry of Climate and Environment. Through this cooperation, we seek to mobilize carbon finance to support Indonesia’s energy transition and contribute to the achievement of our national climate targets. This cooperation will also support efforts to strengthen Indonesia’s SRUK (Carbon Unit Registry System) and ensure transparent recording and tracking of international transfers. Our priority is to ensure that this cooperation delivers credible mitigation outcomes, upholds environmental integrity, and is implemented in line with Indonesia’s national climate commitments,” said Moh Jumhur Hidayat, Minister of Environment/Head of Environmental Protection Agency of Indonesia. The MOPA supports the implementation of Indonesia’s Generation-Based Incentive (GBI) Program, a results-based crediting mechanism designed to accelerate investment in new and additional clean, grid-connected electricity generation. As a sectoral financing mechanism, the GBI can be applied across renewable energy technologies. Its initial technological window in Indonesia focuses on floating solar photovoltaic (PV), in line with national priorities and Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. “Indonesia’s emissions are growing rapidly. Norway’s cooperation with Indonesia is helping ensure that more of the country’s electricity comes from solar power rather than coal. This demonstrates how international cooperation can contribute both to reducing emissions and accelerating the transition to renewable energy,” said Sigrun Aasland, Norway’s Minister of Climate and Environment. The program addresses financial, regulatory, and grid-related constraints that have slowed renewable energy investment in Indonesia. It provides additional incentive payments when the standard power purchase price is insufficient to make an eligible project financially viable. By prioritizing new and additional renewable energy generation paired with battery energy storage systems (BESS), the program enables renewable electricity delivery during peak and evening hours, when grid emissions are highest. This approach aims to reduce intermittency, enhance grid stability, and support the transition to a low-carbon power system. Under the GBI Program, participation is voluntary. Independent Power Producers (IPPs) may apply for inclusion if they meet established financial, technical, and geographic criteria and demonstrate genuine additionality, measurable emission reductions, and positive sustainable development impacts. The program uses a digital Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) system to capture electricity generated and supplied to the grid. The data is reviewed through an independent audit process to ensure accuracy, transparency, and environmental integrity. Following verification, carbon payments are issued to project operators based on actual performance. The resulting emission reductions are aggregated, authorized, and traded as Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs) under a cooperative approach between Indonesia and the Norwegian Ministry of Environment, as part of the Norwegian Global Emissions Reduction (NOGER) Initiative. The program applies dynamic baselines anchored in Indonesia’s unconditional Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), helping safeguard environmental integrity while supporting national climate objectives. “Article 6 is moving from readiness to implementation, and this agreement is a clear example of what that transition requires: strong national drive and dedicated partners. GGGI is proud to have facilitated this agreement between Norway and Indonesia, building on our support to countries as they prepare for and take part in carbon markets. Results-based mechanisms like this can give governments and investors the clarity they need to mobilize finance for climate action at scale.” – Sang-hyup Kim, Executive Director of GGGI. This signing demonstrates Indonesia’s continued efforts to translate climate commitments into bankable projects, commercial agreements, and sustained implementation. artigo.texto: Power PPL Pours Capital into PJM as Data Center Plans Grow Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $7 billion worth of active and proposed projects from PPL, nearly half of which is attributed to grassroot projects Released Wednesday, November 11, 2026 Reports related to this article: Written by Will Ploch, Assistant Editor-in-Chief for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary PPL expects growing energy demand from data centers in the PJM region will necessitate the development of more gas-fired and T&D capacity. Data Dominates the Agenda PPL Corporation, an important energy provider on the PJM Interconnection, is building out its gas-fired power-generation capacity to meet the ever-growing demand from data centers--especially in Kentucky and Pennsylvania, which have emerged as investment hotspots for the company. Industrial Info Resources is tracking more than $7 billion worth of active and proposed projects from PPL, nearly half of which is attributed to grassroot projects. Companywide, PPL plans to raise its base capital expenditures for 2027 through 2030 to $25 billion, which is $2 billion more than the 2026-29 plan. In Kentucky alone, the company's spending is set to increase from $2.3 billion in 2026 to $3.6 billion in 2027. "Through 2032, additional capital investment opportunities could reach a total of $12 billion to $16 billion," in addition to the amount projected through 2030, said Vince Sorgi, the chief executive officer of PPL, in a quarterly earnings-related conference call. "This includes additional regulated generation investment in Kentucky required to meet continued increases in potential demand growth." The increased spending in Kentucky is attributed largely to the proposed construction of a 645-megawatt (MW), natural gas-fired, combined-cycle (NGCC) turbine, subject to regulatory approval. But that approval could be a tough process: The Kentucky Public Service Commission (KPSC) has denied several requests from PPL in recent years to add new gas-fired capacity. However, KPSC did grant a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) in October 2025 for the proposed Unit 6 at Mill Creek Power Station in Louisville, Kentucky, which also is a 645-MW, NGCC unit. Louisville Gas and Electric Company (LG&E), a PPL subsidiary, owns Mill Creek and is developing the project, which is set to follow the ongoing construction of the 621-MW Unit 5. PPL expects Unit 5 will be completed sometime in the second half of 2027. Together, the two new units would nearly double capacity at Mill Creek, which has an operational output of at least 1,361.7 MW. Industrial Info Resources offers more information on the Mill Creek developments in its Global Market Intelligence (GMI) Power Plant and Project databases, where subscribers can find details--including construction schedules, investment values and necessary equipment--in a plant profile and detailed project reports on Unit 5 and Unit 6. Concurrent with the Mill Creek 6 approval, the KPSC granted a CPCN to PPL's proposed, 621-MW unit addition at the E.W. Brown Power Station in Harrodsburg, Kentucky, which currently has an output of at least 1,457.6 MW. Subscribers can learn more from a detailed plant profile and project report. By the Numbers - More than $7 billion: Total investment value of active and proposed projects from PPL - $25 billion: The company's base capital expenditures for 2027 through 2030 - $12 billion to $16 billion: Additional capital investment opportunities from 2031 to 2032 Keystone State Key to Growth Sorgi announced in the earnings call that Invitium Energy, a joint venture between PPL Corporation (with a 51% stake) and Blackstone Infrastructure (49%), "signed a letter of intent (LOI) with Quality Technology Services (QTS) to be their generation solution provider in portions of Pennsylvania. Under that LOI, we have agreed with QTS on all key commercial terms for approximately 2 gigawatts (GW) of generation capacity for its Salem Township Data Center project, with a 20-year initial term allowing for multiple five-year renewals." According to Industrial Info Resources data, the Salem Data Center, which is located in Luzerne County, comprises 12 buildings and more than $10 billion of investment value. Sorgi also noted PPL's large load tariffs "require data centers to cover the cost of serving them, so existing customers don't bear that burden." Subscribers can learn more from a plant profile and a detailed list of project reports. Through Invitium, PPL has proposed the Luzerne County Power Station, which is designed to generate at least 1.5 GW for data centers in the area. The company also is looking into additional transmission and distribution (T&D) capacity to support the load growth. Subscribers can learn more about the Luzerne County Power Station from a detailed project report. PPL's net earnings for the third quarter were reported to be $367 million, a 15.4% increase from third-quarter 2025. Operating revenues stood at $2.5 billion, an 11.5% increase. artigo.texto: SMUD discusses policies for large data centers as two major electricity inquiries advance The Sacramento Municipal Utility District held a public meeting Wednesday night to discuss how it would serve large electricity customers as two potential data center projects enter the feasibility stages and community members raise concerns about energy use, pollution, water consumption and transparency. SMUD confirmed it has received two inquiries from prospective large-load customers, each seeking more than 50 megawatts of electricity capacity. According to a SMUD spokesperson, one megawatt of power is enough to supply approximately 1,000 homes. That means each inquiry represents a potential electricity demand equivalent to more than 50,000 homes. If both projects move forward, they would represent the largest electricity demands among SMUD's 16 data centers, according to the utility. The inquiries come as communities across the country debate the potential costs and benefits of large data centers, including their demands on electricity, water and local infrastructure. SMUD says it has longstanding policies and procedures intended to ensure the costs of serving large electricity customers are not passed on to existing ratepayers. Those principles were the focus of Wednesday night's public meeting. However, SMUD spokesperson Gamaliel Ortiz told CBS News Sacramento the discussion was not centered on any specific projects. One company that has confirmed early conversations with SMUD is Link Logistics, a New York-based real estate company owned by Blackstone Inc. The company said it has owned and operated Depot Park for many years. "We regularly evaluate opportunities to make the best long-term use of the property in ways that support jobs and economic growth in the community, and that includes early conversations with SMUD about the site's potential," a Link Logistics spokesperson said in a statement. The company confirmed it has not submitted an application for a new project. "Any future proposal would go through the City of Sacramento's full public entitlement and environmental review process, with opportunities for community input, and we look forward to sharing more with the community at that time," the spokesperson added. SMUD did not confirm the conversations involving Depot Park. In a separate statement, a spokesperson reiterated the utility's policy on large electricity customers. "It is a longstanding SMUD policy and procedure that costs associated with serving large electrical load customers are paid for by the customer, ensuring these costs are not passed on to existing customers," the spokesperson said. SMUD does not make land-use decisions. Those decisions fall to local jurisdictions. Any data center of this scale proposed within Sacramento city limits would require approval from city leaders. During a Sept. 15 City Council meeting, Sacramento Mayor Kevin McCarty called for a review of the city's policies and additional information about how potential data center projects could affect the community. "I want Sacramento to be prepared if and when a project comes our way. I'm asking our city manager and staff to consider a policy that considers potential impacts on our communities, energy, water, infrastructure, neighborhoods and what safeguards we may need if such a proposal is forwarded to the City of Sacramento for consideration," McCarty said. SMUD leadership is scheduled to vote next week on the large-load customer service principles discussed Wednesday.

artigo.texto: Minneapolis City Council to vote on data center regulations Go Deeper. Create an account or log in to save stories. Like this? Thanks for liking this story! We have added it to a list of your favorite stories. Quick Read The Minneapolis City Council is poised to pass zoning regulations Thursday that limit the size of new data centers and restrict them to the city’s downtown. City leaders agree that, at a minimum, data centers must be regulated. But they disagree on how strict those regulations should be, and some back a full ban. Supporters of data center development argue it can bring in needed jobs and tax revenue to communities. “Look around our city. We do not see cranes. We are not building, and our construction trades need work,” said council member Elizabeth Shaffer, who was one of the lead writers of the regulations. Turn Up Your Support MPR News helps you turn down the noise and build shared understanding. Turn up your support for this public resource and keep trusted journalism accessible to all. “Do data centers drive a lot of permanent jobs? No. Do they drive more jobs than vacant space? Absolutely,” she said. Proponents also argue new centers are required to support cloud storage and the computing needs of artificial intelligence. Data centers emerged as a key issue nationally ahead of the 2026 midterm election as communities protested the massive utility usage, noise pollution and secretive deals that can come with their development. The most controversial centers are supersized facilities located in rural communities and suburbs, but even small projects have prompted public outcry. The Minneapolis regulations on the table Minneapolis leaders are trying to put regulations in place before a six-month moratorium on most new data centers expires Nov. 21. The moratorium exempted downtown projects under 350,000 square feet and went into effect without Mayor Jacob Frey’s signature. The city of Minneapolis received about 1,600 written public comments about potential regulations of data centers. The vast majority opposed data centers and almost half called for an outright ban, according to an MPR News analysis. However, labor organizations including the Minnesota AFL-CIO and the Minneapolis Building and Construction Trades Council wrote in favor of looser rules, including allowing data centers outside of downtown and dropping or raising the size cap. The mayor supports specific regulations for data centers and told WCCO in August he believes data centers should not be the sole use of a building. "It generates tax revenue that helps drive down taxes for everybody else. But, too, it enables the owner to do something awesome that helps the community," Frey said. City staff proposed allowing new data centers only in downtown, with server space capped at 175,000 square feet. The city’s planning commission recommended stricter rules: a rigid 50,000-square-foot cap and a council vote on each new data center. A compromise measure was unanimously passed at a council committee meeting Monday — with council member Jamison Whiting absent — to be taken up for a final council vote Thursday. The ordinance would limit the server space of new centers to 150,000 square feet, which is in between the 175,000 square feet suggested by city staff and the 50,000 square feet recommended by the planning commission. It would also restrict new centers to existing buildings downtown, require mixed-use of buildings with data centers and require any center with server space over 50,000 square feet to buy into a renewable energy program. Regulate or ban? Attempts by progressive members to pass a full ban or require council approval for each new center failed on a 6-6 vote Monday. “We don’t need more computers in our downtown,” said council member Soren Stevenson. “We need people down here, and so I want to fight for a vision where people are thriving in our city, not for a vision where stockholders are thriving in our city.” A potential mayoral veto hung over the committee meeting, which included the full council. Several council members called for Frey to publicly state what proposals he would veto. “If you’re gonna veto, email us. Let us know. Let the public know your stance,” said council member Jason Chavez. Instead, the mayor indicated his position through statements from his office to the press and conversations with city staff and council members. Council member Linnea Palmisano said the mayor authorized her to share his position. “Mayor Frey does not support the planning commission’s amendments. If those are included in the final package, he will veto it,” she said. “The reality we live in is that any action we take today that's not supported by the mayor will get vetoed,” council member Jamal Osman said Monday. Osman said he’d heard from city staff and other council members that Frey would veto both a full ban and creating an overlay district, which would have required any new center to earn council approval. If no new rules pass before the moratorium expires, data centers would fall back under the city’s existing zoning code, which allows them with a permit in 10 of the city’s 15 zoning districts. Frey’s office confirmed to MPR News that he “supports the regulatory framework” of the compromise ordinance approved Monday. Some council members said they’d propose additional amendments at Thursday’s meeting, which starts at 9:30 a.m. The council needs a minimum of seven votes to pass legislation and a minimum of nine votes to override a mayoral veto. MRP News correspondent Matt Sepic contributed to this reporting.

artigo.texto: The Global Carbon Council (GCC), the first independent carbon crediting standard established in the Global South, headquartered in Qatar and internationally recognised under the UN ICAO's CORSIA scheme and ICVCM, has joined a global coalition of leading financial institutions, exchanges and carbon market organisations as a founding member of the Global Carbon Market Network, officially launched at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkiye. The launch ceremony was held at the Arab Climate Pavilion, jointly hosted by the GCC and the League of Arab States, in the COP31 Blue Zone, bringing together hundreds of participants in person and virtually, including climate experts, government representatives, financial institutions, carbon market organisations, standard-setting bodies, and other stakeholders. The launch featured keynote addresses by Pedro Manuel Moreno, acting secretary-general of UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD); Nan Li Collins, chair of the UN Sustainable Stock Exchanges Initiative and lead of the World Investment Forum; Salim bin Nasser al-Aufi, Minister of Energy and Minerals of the Sultanate of Oman; Sammy Sau Kuen Yeung, commissioner for Climate Change of Hong Kong SAR (China); and Dr Yousef Alhorr, founding chairman of the Global Carbon Council (GCC). Their participation highlighted the importance of international co-operation in strengthening carbon markets and advancing climate finance. The Global Carbon Market Network addresses persistent market fragmentation caused by differing regulatory frameworks, standards, registries and trading systems. Rather than establishing another carbon market or competing standard, it seeks to connect existing voluntary and compliance markets, improve interoperability and promote consistent market practices. Its launch comes as emissions trading systems and carbon taxes cover nearly 30% of global greenhouse gas emissions and generated more than $107bn in public revenue in 2025. Yet stronger market connections are needed to translate carbon pricing into greater investment in measurable emissions reductions and sustainable development. Dr Alhorr, said: “The future of carbon markets will not be determined by how many markets we create, but by how effectively we connect them, build trust and translate carbon transactions into measurable climate impact. The Global Carbon Market Network represents an important step towards overcoming fragmentation, strengthening international cooperation and unlocking climate finance, particularly for developing countries.” The network will promote co-operation among carbon market institutions, exchanges and financial stakeholders, focusing on market integrity, emissions measurement and verification, digital technologies and interoperability. Stronger connections between registries, trading platforms and financial institutions could reduce transaction costs and improve market access for project developers. The initiative also recognises the role of non-state actors, including private sector institutions and financial intermediaries, in mobilising climate finance beyond traditional public funding. Ahead of the launch, UNCTAD acting secretary-general Pedro Manuel Moreno expressed hope that the network would make carbon pricing a more effective instrument for reducing emissions and mobilising climate finance for developing countries. "Carbon markets can play a role in putting a price on emissions and mobilising finance for climate action, but their effectiveness depends on trust, integrity and functioning market infrastructure," said Nan Li Collins, UNCTAD's director of Investment and Enterprise and Chair of the UN Sustainable Stock Exchanges Initiative. The Global Carbon Market Network brings together institutions from Africa, Asia, the Middle East, Europe and Latin America, representing a diverse range of carbon market and financial stakeholders.

artigo.texto: Will data centers raise your utility bills? Tri-State utilities respond 14News Investigates asked local utilities whether residents could pay more for electricity and water as data centers move into the region EVANSVILLE, Ind. (WFIE) - Marie Moyer has a question shared by many of her neighbors: If a data center moves in, will residents pick up the tab? “Basic economic law of supply and demand can predict there’s a future problem there,” Moyer said. Data centers can use large amounts of electricity and water, and the substations, power lines and pipes needed to serve them can be costly. 14News Investigates asked utilities across the Tri-State whether residents would see rate increases because of data centers and who would pay for infrastructure upgrades. After weeks of emails and phone calls, the answers varied. Watch us when we are live, right here ⬇️ What utilities told 14News CenterPoint did not answer yes or no. In a statement, the company said adding a large customer could lower bills by more than $250 million over 15 years. It did not say whether an individual customer’s bill would go up or who would pay for upgrades. Other utilities offered more direct responses: - Kentucky Utilities said, “NO, and safeguards are in place to protect the customer.” - Kenergy said it opposes raising electric rates to support data centers. - The city of Madisonville initially provided a response that did not answer the question. When 14News followed up, the city said no. - Indiana Michigan Power said, “If Indiana Michigan Power were to work with a data center in Spencer County, it would not affect customer bills.” - Henderson Municipal said a data center coming to the city would have to pay for upgrades and that customers would not. Owensboro Municipal Utilities did not directly answer the question but said it would make a reasonable effort to protect customers from an increase. Why rates can be difficult to predict 14News shared the utilities’ responses with an energy expert at Penn State Dickinson Law, who said she was not surprised by the range of answers. “There’s an excellent study out of Harvard showing that it’s very difficult to pick apart every aspect of a utility rate,” she said. “These are complex processes.” The expert advised residents to follow decisions by state regulators when data centers are proposed in their communities. “Customers should pay attention to what’s happening at the state regulatory level, because it’s the state utility commission or public service commission that is approving the rates that utilities charge data centers,” she said. What other cities have experienced 14News Investigates also contacted cities across the country that already have data centers. Most said they required the companies to pay for new infrastructure for their projects. Those cities also cautioned that additional demand can put pressure on local water systems, potentially leading to higher rates for residents. A University of Maryland professor told 14News that, hypothetically, if a data center were built near someone’s home, it could take a year or two for any change to show up on that person’s utility bill. artigo.texto: A Rússia submeteu à convenção climática da ONU, antes da COP31 na Turquia, um marco metodológico para transformar pequenos reatores modulares (SMR, na sigla em inglês) em geradores de crédito no mercado internacional de carbono. O documento, proposto ao mecanismo de crédito do Artigo 6.4 do Acordo de Paris, reconhece os benefícios de baixo carbono da tecnologia e inclui o cálculo das emissões de gás de efeito estufa evitadas. Em paralelo, segundo o OneStopESG, o governo russo aprovou resolução que reserva parte das unidades emitidas por projetos com risco de devolver gases à atmosfera no futuro, caso da captura e do armazenamento de carbono, em conta especial onde nada pode ser vendido, onerado ou penhorado. A liberação só ocorre para baixa definitiva, depois de relatório verificado. O mercado interno que sustenta a estratégia já tem dimensão rastreável. O registro nacional de unidades de carbono guarda cerca de 37,66 milhões delas e mais de 535.200 unidades de conformidade em circulação, mostra levantamento do OneStopESG. Cada crédito corresponde a uma tonelada de emissões de gás de efeito estufa evitada. Países do Acordo de Paris e organizações podem usar as unidades para cumprir metas climáticas. O mercado-alvo ainda engatinha. O mecanismo de crédito do Artigo 6.4 do Acordo de Paris tem cinco metodologias de projeto aprovadas até agora, entre elas uma dedicada às renováveis, e outras 20 em revisão. A proposta, noticiada em primeiro lugar pelo World Nuclear News, não se prende a nenhum desenho de reator. A norma alcança unidades de até 300 megawatts, fixas em terra ou flutuantes, e detalha o cálculo dos gases de efeito estufa evitados. Quem conduz o argumento é Polina Lion, executiva-chefe de sustentabilidade da Rosatom. Segundo Lion, nenhum projeto climático baseado em usina nuclear foi registrado em mercado de carbono, e não existe metodologia aprovada para isso. Ela afirmou que o princípio da neutralidade tecnológica é reconhecido na política climática internacional, mas nem sempre seguido na prática. Para Lion, o problema começa na régua dos mercados. Documentos, planos de ação climática e iniciativas verdes raramente saem das fontes renováveis, por intuição ou porque ninguém pensou no nuclear. A energia atômica fica de fora por padrão, o que ela classifica como um erro grave. O custo da exclusão aparece na indústria. Indústrias de países com matriz nuclear precisam demonstrar consumo de eletricidade de baixo carbono, e, sem instrumentos adequados, o aço e o cimento perdem competitividade no mercado internacional. Lion afirma que a energia nuclear fica fora das contas climáticas internacionais, e o marco russo é a tentativa de reverter esse quadro. Se a metodologia for aprovada, os reatores pequenos ganham no mercado de carbono a porta que as renováveis já têm aberta no Artigo 6.4. A proposta ainda precisa passar pelo crivo do mecanismo do Artigo 6.4, que não aprovou nenhuma norma nuclear e não registrou projeto do gênero em mercado algum. Para Lion, a energia nuclear, grande ou pequena, em terra ou flutuante, é essencial para a transição e a segurança energéticas.

A pauta foi a política de Data Centers no Ceará e o Polo Automotivo de Horizonte. Em vídeo publicado nas redes sociais, o chefe do Executivo cearense afirmou que estão em discussão ajustes legislativos com o Ministério da Fazenda e o Ministério da Indústria e Comércio. Siga o canal do CN7 no WhatsApp No Polo Automotivo, a discussão envolve a produção de veículos elétricos no Estado e a necessidade de garantias legais para os investimentos. O polo, em Horizonte, é apresentado pelo governo como o primeiro multimarcas do Brasil. Nos Data Centers, a discussão envolve as regras para a política estadual e para novos investimentos. O governo estadual cita a instalação do primeiro Data Center do TikTok na América Latina no Ceará. Siga o canal do CN7 no Telegram Elmano afirmou que espera definições sobre os dois temas nas próximas semanas. "O ministro foi muito sensível e eu tenho convicção de que nas próximas semanas nós vamos ter novidades muito importantes para garantirmos investimentos de novos Data Center no Ceará, como garantirmos o crescimento do polo automotivo no estado do Ceará", disse. artigo.texto: Every day, Wang Bing drives his big electric lorry to send about five tonnes of goods between the cities of Haikou and Dongfang on Hainan, a tropical island in southern China. A round trip covers about 500 kilometres (310 miles). But refuelling is not something Wang worries about. “When my battery runs low, I just drive my truck into a battery-swapping station to get a fully charged one,” says the 53-year-old, who shares the journey with a colleague in eight-hour shifts. Wang has been a lorry driver for nearly three decades. In the first two of those, he drove conventional lorries fuelled by diesel. About five years ago, he began driving an electric model after the logistics company he worked for upgraded its fleet. In July this year, his old e-truck, which used conventional plug-in charging, was replaced by one with a swappable battery. In the past, Wang had to spend an hour and half charging his battery each time, but with his new truck, it takes just five minutes or so to have a drained battery removed and a fresh one replaced. “I am very happy,” he says. Battery swapping is not new in China, where more than 400,000 e-trucks (or over 90% of the global total) were sold last year. The Chinese carmaker Nio commercialised the technology nearly a decade ago for smaller electric vehicles (EVs). But in 2023, the Chinese battery behemoth CATL launched a battery-swapping system for electric lorries through a subsidiary brand called Qiji Energy. To Wang, the biggest advantage of the technology is the time it saves. “It is much, much faster,” he says. “I don’t even need to leave my truck when the battery is being swapped.” This swiftness builds on the cost advantage e-trucks already have over their fossil-fuelled peers when it comes to refuelling. “Electricity is cheaper than oil,” Wang says. The per-kilometre fuelling cost for an e-truck works out about 1.1 yuan (12p) in Hainan, he says, significantly lower than that for a diesel truck, which exceeds 2 yuan (22p) a kilometre. “That means my e-truck can save more than 20,000 yuan (£2,200) per month,” Wang says. When a truck approaches a battery-swapping station, the station’s cameras automatically identify the type of battery it uses by checking its number plate. “All the driver needs to do is to drive the truck into a designated area, and the battery will be swapped completely automatically,” says Wei Jiuchun, 46, a test driver at a Qiji Energy battery-swapping station in Suzhou, east China. Wei’s job is to help the station test its system for different models of heavy trucks and under different weather conditions. It is not just time and fuel costs the technology saves but, in China, the initial lump sum a buyer has to put down to get an e-truck, says Mao Shiyue, a Beijing-based researcher at the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT). The upfront purchase price for an e-truck is significantly higher than for a comparable diesel model, a major obstacle for those vehicles’ wider adoption in many parts of the world. In China, a customer opting for battery swapping typically buys an e-truck without a battery, and then rents the battery from a service provider. As the cost of a battery is about 40% of an e-truck’s price, the business model can make e-trucks a lot more affordable, Mao says. The technology can also help minimise the pressure EV charging brings to the power grid, according to Mao, because swapping stations have more flexibility to spread out the charging time for the depleted batteries. “If the grid sees a spike in electricity demand during peak hours, those stations can even act as an energy-storage station by returning the electricity stored in their batteries back to the grid to ease the strain,” he says. CATL, the world’s biggest battery manufacturer, is a key player in promoting battery swapping for heavy trucks in China. The company’s support for the technology is critical for its large-scale rollout, says Phate Zhang, the founder of CnEVPost, a Shanghai-based outlet focusing on EVs. CATL plans to put 900 battery-swapping stations into operation across China by the end of this year, expanding its current network twice more. By the end of 2027, it wants the number to reach 2,000. The company has also teamed up with the London-based renewable energy supplier Octopus to bring the technology to Europe. It intends to open its first group of battery-swapping “mega hubs” in the UK next year, and a network of more than 30 hubs in Europe by 2035. In China, battery-swapping is still a minority charging method for its rapidly growing e-truck fleet. In 2024, about one-third of the zero-emission trucks in the country featured this technology, while the rest largely had conventional plug-in charging, according to the latest available figures. One downside is that drivers often need to stick to a particular service provider that caters to the specific type of swappable batteries their e-trucks use. “For example, some batteries are swapped from the chassis, while others are swapped from the top of the truck,” says Xue Lulu, a senior associate at World Resources Institute China. “Even under the same technological route, batteries made by different companies often have different specifications.” This means drivers cannot drop into any random swapping station to get their trucks replenished, which could restrict the journeys they can make, she says. Plus, battery swapping doesn’t necessarily mean drivers will save time, Xue says. During her field research in China, she found some lorry drivers would wait outside battery-swapping stations for one to two hours before going in because they wanted to avoid using the service during peak hours, to save money. “Logistics firms are extremely sensitive to costs,” she says. The most suitable users are probably drivers who, like Wang, work on fixed routes served by battery-swapping stations. Mao says the charging method has been rolled out most successfully among companies that use heavy truck

artigo.texto: The city’s Land Use Commission on Wednesday night recommended two proposals for City Council approval, one for the creation of an urban farm at Elks Park in south Evanston, and another for a one-year moratorium on data centers. In 2023, local nonprofit Evanston Grows won $350,000 in participatory budgeting funds after an urban farm was one of the process’ winning ideas, but finding a suitable location and neighbor opposition to suggestions have delayed the process. During Wednesday’s commission meeting, the group finally received a positive recommendation to locate the farm at Elks Park, 301 Callan Ave., despite some pushback from residents who said it would impact children’s use of the park. The farm would take up about an acre of the park, or 28% of its total land area, according to Evanston Grows’ application. Evanston Grows Executive Director Laurell Sims assured the commission and neighbors that the park would still have plenty of space for other activities. “We’ve had great feedback and had really great experiences with the youth who have been on the site, and we’re excited to be able to offer both educational opportunities and a farm for them to grow up in,” Sims said. The group also teamed up with Ridgeville Park District in 2025, entering a 10-year partnership lease to operate a space there. Ridgeville invited community members to share input on the Elks Park proposal, according to Marlon Rodas, the park district’s executive director. Surveys and in-person meetings all indicated overall support for the urban farm idea, Rodas said. Gregory Hardin said that while he supports Evanston Grows, he objects to the farm because it would make Elks Park no longer an “occupiable space.” “Over the years, there have been soccer, badminton games, people practicing softball and baseball at the diamonds, people running around and across the park for exercise, people just sitting on a blanket and reading in the sun,” Hardin said. “Often, several of these things happen at the same time, and Elks Park is big enough that all those people can have that space without getting in each other’s way.” Alan Goldberg, was also opposed the urban farm, asked commissioners not to remove green space. “Please do not dump this project in the Eighth Ward because no other Evanston neighborhoods will approve it,” he said. “If your ward did not approve this farm, do not allow this special use in Elks Park.” But another park neighbor, Rick Marsh, disagreed. As a 42-year resident, he said the park is “underutilized,” and that there will be plenty of space for kids and adults alike even with the farm. “There’s no baseball out in that park whatsoever,” he said. “I’ve gone out there taking a bat and ball and bases, and had kids come out, but the programming there has been less than.” Marco Carranza-Walter, a dad of three young kids, said the farm would “bring neighbors and new families together.” “I picture my kids out there pulling out their first carrot, asking another neighbor how to tell when a tomato’s ripe, and bringing home something they grew themselves,” he said. “Kids don’t forget that, and neither do the neighbors who teach them.” Ultimately, the commission recommended the proposal for City Council approval in a 5-1 vote, with Luke Harris-Ferree, Darush Mabadi, Loren Berlin, Jeanne Lindwall and Jameika Mangum voting in favor, and Myrna Arevalo voting against. Data center pause The commission also backed a councilmember-initiated zoning text amendment that would place a one-year moratorium on the approval or construction of any data centers in Evanston, while the city conducts studies on their potential impacts. Back in September, Councilmembers Clare Kelly (1st Ward), Krissie Harris (2nd), Bobby Burns (5th), Parielle Davis (7th) and Matt Rodgers (8th) submitted a referral on the matter. Liza Roberson-Young, the city’s chief legislative policy advisor, said the city unofficially has “a de facto data center moratorium” already. “But the ordinance would basically codify that de facto moratorium for a one-year period, starting on the ordinance’s effective date,” Roberson-Young said. After that one-year period, city staff would also have the option to extend the moratorium for an additional 30 days if needed. Staff would then recommend a permanent policy approach toward data centers, “including considering whether the right long-term framework is regulation or a ban,” she said. Councilmembers are aiming to pass the ordinance by the end of the year, according to Roberson-Young. The ordinance referral came after the city received a zoning analysis application for “determination of use for a computer processing center” at a 20,000-square-foot property at 1265 Hartrey Ave. in the Second Ward. The moratorium would not be applied retroactively, however, so that application would not be impacted, although city staff also determined it to be incomplete. “We did not render a decision on it because we deemed it incomplete,” said Jeremiah Bebo, the city’s zoning administrator. “But it looked, felt, smelled like a data center. And we don’t currently have a definition for it, regardless of this moratorium, and so we would not be able to approve it.” The commission unanimously recommended the moratorium for full council approval.

artigo.texto: Efficient storage of renewable energy is key to ensuring a reliable electricity supply and advancing the decarbonization of the economy and transportation. Emerging solutions such as salt caverns, compressed air energy storage (CAES), sand batteries, and gravity-based systems all aim to make the most of natural resources. Pioneering solutions that seek to combine these two qualities, storage and sustainability, are being deployed around the world. From Switzerland to China, and from Finland to Chile, here are some examples. Gravity-based energy storage The company Energy Vault has devised a gravity-based energy storage system. From the outside, it looks like a set of enormous steel-frame towers or cranes holding large blocks made of composite materials such as concrete. The tower, already operating in both Switzerland and China, uses surplus renewable energy to lift these blocks to a higher position. When a nearby power grid needs to supply homes or businesses, the structure itself lowers the blocks in a controlled descent, using the force of gravity to generate kinetic energy that is then converted into electricity. The first of these gravity storage facilities was built in 2019 in Arbedo-Castione, Switzerland, home to the company’s research and development center. In this case, six arms hang from a crane and, driven by electric motors powered by the surplus energy, pick up blocks and stack them around it. When the grid needs electricity, those same arms lower the blocks back to the ground, and the resulting kinetic energy generates electricity for the system. The concept is similar to the well-established technology used in pumped-storage hydroelectric plants, which use surplus electricity to pump water to upper reservoirs and then release it to generate power again when needed. The towers can be modular, so they can be scaled up to store several gigawatt-hours, and are designed to be built with recycled materials. They can also be built alongside renewable energy installations, such as solar panels, to draw power directly from them, or operate as standalone systems that feed the grid when needed. Salt caverns Another notable initiative to improve energy storage takes its cue from the past. A study by German researchers has focused on salt caverns, underground formations created by dissolving salt deposits with water. The result is a cavity with strong walls that provides a large storage space at a constant temperature. Their low permeability reduces the risk of the stored contents coming into contact with outside impurities. The contents can also be drawn off gradually as needed, while the rest remains safely underground. The experts conclude that these caverns are ideal for storing fuels thanks to their operational safety, low cost, and sealing capacity, among other factors. These age-old caves are an option already being developed in the United States. The federal government has funded projects such as the Advanced Clean Energy Storage (ACES) facility in Utah, which already stores renewable hydrogen and other energy sources. The facility uses two salt caverns to store surplus renewable energy, converting it into hydrogen through electrolysis to supply a power plant that aims to gradually increase its share of this renewable fuel to 100% by 2045. Compressed air energy storage Meanwhile, China is working on compressed air energy storage (CAES). In this process, surplus energy is used to compress air and store it underground; when the grid needs electricity, the air is expanded through a turbine to generate it. The city of Changzhou, in the eastern part of the country, is home to one of these facilities and is also part of a project that combines CAES in salt caverns with rooftop solar installations and charging stations, among other elements. Sand batteries Among the materials and environments used to store renewable energy, one stands out for its abundance in nature: sand. Sand batteries consist of containers or silos fitted with heating elements through which electricity flows, reaching high temperatures. The surrounding sand retains the heat, which it can hold for months thanks to its high heat capacity, releasing it when needed for space heating or other industrial processes. These “batteries”, which can also use crushed soapstone (a rock known for its thermal properties), offer low cost and low environmental impact, since the materials are abundant. The resulting batteries have a service life of more than 30 years, are clean, and require little maintenance. The shift toward steel silos One example of this type of battery can be found in Finland, with a twist: the company Polar Night Energy has developed a steel silo, a giant “container” that holds the heat-storing material and works much like other sand batteries. Through a closed circuit, the energy is stored as heat, and the interior can reach 600°C (1,112°F). When needed, the system releases water, steam, and air at output temperatures of up to 400°C (752°F), with an efficiency of 85% to 90% in harnessing the energy generated. The company offers two modular models to match demand: 2 MW for smaller industrial facilities (space heating or district heating networks) and 10 MW for industrial processes. Last year, the company commissioned one of these silos to power the district heating system of the Finnish town of Pornainen. Ultimately, the future of decarbonization depends not only on generating clean energy but also on the capacity and ingenuity to store it. By using natural elements such as salt, sand, and gravity as potential strategic reserves, science could close the sustainability loop, delivering an energy supply that is steady, efficient, and in harmony with the planet.

artigo.texto: AMD Launches Epyc SP7, Helion as AI Rack Demand Rises AMD has begun shipping sixth-gen Epyc servers and is rolling out Helion AI racks, signaling a bigger push into enterprise and agentic AI infrastructure. AMD said Tuesday that its sixth-generation Epyc SP7 server processor is now generally available and that hardware makers have begun shipping servers powered by the new chip. The company also said the first Helion racks for agentic AI, which hardware vendors build from an AMD blueprint, will become available throughout this month. The new SP7 processor, which features up to 256 cores, is the first of four sixth-generation Epyc CPUs to become available. The other three are expected in 2027, AMD said. The broader family of sixth-generation processors, much of which is code-named “Venice,” is designed for enterprise, cloud, high-performance computing, and AI workloads, including agentic AI. AMD said it is seeing strong demand for the new chip. During the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week, AMD Chair and CEO Lisa Su said early demand for Venice is the strongest AMD has seen for any new generation of Epyc processors. Su said AMD began revenue shipments of Venice during the third quarter and that hardware makers have committed to more than 240 Venice platforms, 20% more than the number committed for Turin, AMD’s fifth-generation Epyc chip. AMD is working to capture more market share in CPUs, GPUs, and overall AI infrastructure as it competes with rivals amid surging AI demand. AMD is directly challenging market leader Nvidia in GPUs and rack-scale systems, while Nvidia is taking on AMD with its own CPU. Arm has also introduced its own Arm-based CPU to compete with Intel and AMD’s x86 processors, and cloud providers AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure have built their own custom AI accelerators and Arm-based CPUs. Sixth-Gen Epyc Targets AI Infrastructure as Helion Comes Online During the earnings call, Su said Venice delivers significantly better performance per watt, per core, and per dollar than any other x86 or Arm server CPU. AMD said systems based on the new Epyc SP7 processor deliver up to 3.7 times more performance than an Nvidia Vera CPU-based system and up to 2.2 times the performance of an Intel Xeon 6980P system. Agentic AI is driving demand for server CPUs, which play three distinct roles for the emerging workload: general-purpose services, GPU host nodes, and agent sandboxes. While GPUs handle inference, organizations still need a large number of CPUs to orchestrate the workflow, from invoking tools to retrieving data. AMD introduced Helion in October as an open rack-scale design for agentic AI. Hardware partners include Dell Technologies, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, Lenovo, Supermicro, and Cisco. Helion racks, built for agentic AI, are different from AMD’s Helios racks, which are designed for large-scale inference, frontier model training, and fine-tuning. AMD said Helion will come in three versions: - Helion Liquid, a CPU-only, liquid-cooled rack designed to operate side by side with a Helios rack for large-scale agentic AI deployments; - Helion Air, a CPU-only rack designed to expand agent capacity within existing air-cooled data centers; and - AMD Helion Air Inference, an air-cooled rack that combines CPUs and GPUs for inference. AMD also said Meta is preparing to deploy sixth-generation AMD Epyc CPU-based platforms at scale and that Microsoft Azure’s Azure HDv2 service for AI data processing is now in preview. Why Venice Matters to Enterprise Data Centers Matt Kimball, vice president and principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, said Venice is an important launch for AMD and for enterprises. Enterprise CIOs have fixed power budgets in their data centers and need infrastructure that supports not only traditional workloads today, but also agentic AI in the years ahead, Kimball said. With up to 256 cores, Venice lets companies run traditional workloads on fewer servers, freeing up space for AI infrastructure. Servers running sixth-generation Epyc processors today are also well suited to support agentic workloads in the future because of the CPU’s high core count and large cache and memory, Kimball noted. “It’s huge for those enterprise organizations that are in the beginning stages of the AI-ification of their business,” he said.

artigo.texto: Ouça este conteúdo O Partido Democrata dos Estados Unidos, que conquistou nas eleições de meio de mandato presidencial da semana passada o controle do Congresso e os governos da maioria dos estados americanos, promete promover a partir de janeiro uma ofensiva contra a expansão dos data centers, da Inteligência Artificial (IA) e das big techs, o que vem gerando preocupações a respeito da concorrência tecnológica do país com a China. “Os democratas concorreram e venceram com pautas voltadas à acessibilidade de custos e à responsabilização de data centers; a BAAJA [Lei Bipartidária Americana de Acessibilidade e Empregos, na sigla em inglês] nos permitirá começar a cumprir, de imediato, ambas as promessas de campanha”, disse à agência Reuters o senador democrata Sheldon Whitehouse, integrante da Comissão de Meio Ambiente do Senado, ao comentar o avanço, nesta semana, de um projeto de lei que visa agilizar a aprovação de novas usinas de energia e linhas de transmissão e exigir que os operadores de grandes data centers arquem com uma parcela maior dos custos das melhorias na rede elétrica. “Seríamos tolos se não aproveitássemos essa vitória.” Outros parlamentares da oposição a Donald Trump também sinalizaram um cerco aos data centers, à IA e às big techs, alegando preocupações com o impacto da expansão do setor no meio ambiente e na segurança nacional. No X, o senador Bernie Sanders, independente que já fez parte do Partido Democrata e segue votando com a legenda, disse após as midterms que é necessário impor uma “moratória nacional” para impedir a construção de novos data centers. “Os americanos não querem que os oligarcas das big techs destruam o meio ambiente, eliminem empregos e ameacem o futuro da humanidade”, afirmou Sanders. Também no X, a deputada democrata reeleita Yassamin Ansari escreveu que “a prioridade na agenda democrata, logo no primeiro dia [do novo Congresso], deve ser uma pausa no desenvolvimento de IA avançada, a regulação desse setor que está fora de controle e a proibição da superinteligência artificial”. Elon Musk, dono da SpaceX, que pretende construir um grande data center no Arizona — estado que Ansari representa na Câmara dos Estados Unidos –, trocou farpas com a deputada democrata no X e a parlamentar sugeriu que vai intimar o empresário para audiências no Congresso americano. “Nos vemos em breve”, ameaçou. No Senado, Ed Markey, democrata reeleito para representar o estado de Massachusetts, escreveu nas redes sociais que os executivos das big techs “precisarão plantar novas florestas para [compensar] todas as intimações contra eles que imprimiremos”. Segundo a agência Associated Press, o banco Morgan Stanley afirmou em um relatório que a vitória dos democratas nas midterms traz “maiores expectativas de restrições a data centers” e que novas regulamentações estaduais podem “dividir o país entre áreas abertas a novos data centers e áreas onde eles não seriam permitidos”. VEJA TAMBÉM: O relatório destacou a eleição de Gina Hinojosa para o governo do Texas como o “resultado eleitoral mais importante” para o setor de data centers, já que a democrata prometeu regras mais rígidas para a implantação dessas estruturas no estado. Antes da eleição da semana passada, o Texas estava a caminho de superar o norte da Virgínia como o maior mercado global de data centers até 2030, segundo análise da JLL, gigante do setor imobiliário comercial. O presidente americano, Donald Trump, alega que o freio à IA, aos data centers e às big techs – também defendido por alguns republicanos, mas enfatizado com mais força pelos democratas – pode fazer os EUA perderem a guerra tecnológica contra a China. Na semana passada, depois que a vitória da oposição nas midterms levou a uma forte queda das ações das empresas de tecnologia, o mandatário republicano responsabilizou os eleitores americanos. “A culpa é toda de vocês!”, escreveu na rede Truth Social. Analista alerta para risco de criar vantagem competitiva para a China Em entrevista à Gazeta do Povo, Allan Gallo, professor de economia internacional no curso de comércio exterior da Universidade Mackenzie, disse que a pressão democrata imediata em nível federal sobre esses setores deverá ser mais pela via da fiscalização do que pela aprovação de novas leis. “Os democratas já anunciaram propostas para exigir auditorias independentes dos sistemas de IA, responsabilizar empresas por danos e impedir que os custos energéticos dos data centers sejam transferidos aos consumidores. Com a maioria no Congresso, eles até poderão convocar executivos e aprofundar investigações, mesmo diante de uma provável resistência de Trump”, disse o analista, que afirmou que o impacto mais concreto poderá ocorrer nos estados. “Estados onde os democratas poderão impor restrições concentram mais de 40% da capacidade de data centers planejada nos EUA”, afirmou. Gallo disse que a regulação desses setores pode “garantir responsabilidade e preservar a concorrência”, mas há um risco importante caso ela comece a se tornar uma barreira para a entrada de novas unidades e sinalizar uma restrição de oferta e desestímulo ao investimento. O analista afirmou que o fator decisivo na corrida tecnológica com a China não será somente a qualidade dos algoritmos, mas a disponibilidade de capacidade computacional e energia. “Nesse cenário, impedir ou retardar sistematicamente a construção de infraestrutura pode comprometer a competitividade americana, mas exigir responsabilidade pelos custos energéticos ou por danos causados pela tecnologia não equivale a impedir sua expansão. O risco é o que mencionei: transformar a regulamentação em restrição de oferta, o que criaria uma vantagem competitiva para a China”, alertou.

artigo.texto: RenovaPR amplia incentivo para armazenamento de energia em propriedades Paraná avança no armazenamento de eletricidade dentro da porteira; estado já contabiliza 45.274 unidades rurais de geração distribuída Os produtores rurais do Paraná poderão contar com o apoio do RenovaPR (Programa Paraná Energia Rural Renovável) para investir em sistemas de armazenamento de energia e reduzir os prejuízos provocados por apagões. A medida amplia o alcance do programa, que passa a contemplar também propriedades que já possuem geração própria, por meio de energia solar ou biogás, e desejam reforçar a segurança do abastecimento elétrico. O incentivo será concedido por meio de uma subvenção de três pontos percentuais na taxa de juros, operacionalizada pelo Banco do Agricultor Paranaense. O produtor poderá contratar o financiamento junto ao agente financeiro de sua preferência, enquanto o Governo do Estado ficará responsável por equalizar parte dos juros. O modelo segue a estratégia adotada para impulsionar a expansão da geração distribuída no meio rural. A política conta com R$ 320 milhões em recursos do Governo do Estado, por meio do Fundo de Desenvolvimento Econômico e da Fomento Paraná, e já está presente em 398 municípios. Apesar dos benefícios, o custo dos equipamentos ainda representa um desafio para os produtores. Os sistemas de baterias destinados às atividades rurais custam entre R$ 35 mil e R$ 800 mil, conforme o porte da propriedade e a quantidade de equipamentos que precisam permanecer em funcionamento durante as interrupções no fornecimento. O investimento médio é estimado em R$ 78 mil, com prazo de retorno entre quatro anos e meio e sete anos. Segundo Herlon Almeida, coordenador da Área de Energias Renováveis e Conectividade Rural do IDR-Paraná, a adoção de baterias precisa avançar em conjunto com a melhoria da infraestrutura elétrica no campo. Entre as prioridades estão a ampliação das redes trifásicas e a utilização de sistemas com inversores híbridos, que permitem armazenar o excedente de energia produzido durante o dia. Na prática, a tecnologia possibilita manter equipamentos essenciais em operação mesmo quando há falhas no fornecimento da concessionária. A solução é especialmente importante para atividades como avicultura, suinocultura, produção de leite e piscicultura, que dependem de energia elétrica de forma contínua. Desde agosto de 2021, o Paraná contabiliza 45.274 unidades rurais de geração distribuída, com potência instalada de 1,11 GW e investimentos estimados em R$ 6,4 bilhões. A potência média é de 24,58 kW por unidade, a maior do país. Mesmo com o avanço da geração própria, as falhas no abastecimento continuam sendo um problema para o setor. Levantamento do IDR-Paraná aponta uma média de 4,3 interrupções no fornecimento e 7,17 horas sem energia por consumidor. Em ocorrências mais graves, os prejuízos já alcançaram milhões de reais. Diante da crescente dependência de energia elétrica nas propriedades rurais e do aumento dos eventos climáticos extremos, o armazenamento ganha espaço como uma alternativa para proteger a produção, evitar perdas e ampliar a resiliência do agronegócio paranaense.

artigo.texto: A Smyth County zoning ordinance about requirements for data centers is being challenged in court by a resident concerned it will open up farmland for development. Charles Wassum filed the lawsuit after the county passed a new ordinance establishing a special permit process for data centers across industrial, commercial and agricultural zones. According to court documents obtained by Cardinal News, the suit asks for the Smyth County Circuit Court to void the board of supervisors’ vote on the ordinance, based on a lack of compliance with voting procedures and adherence to the county’s comprehensive plan. The county’s zoning codes used to allow “data processing facilities” in industrial and commercial zones by right — meaning landowners could move forward with no local government approvals required. That changed after a board of supervisors vote in early September, requiring data center developers to apply for a special use permit and move through a public process. But the new ordinance also expanded where data centers could be allowed in Smyth County, adding agricultural zones to the list. Wassum views that as an action to open up the majority of the county to data centers, he said in an interview. That goes against what the board voted on as its comprehensive land use plan in April 2024, he said, which designates much of the county as farmland. “It doesn’t align with the map,” Wassum said. “The map says, this is where farmland is. The ordinance says, we’re going to put data centers there. You can’t go that way.” Filed last month, the lawsuit alleges that the board of supervisors and the planning commission didn’t properly consider whether the ordinance would comply with the county’s comprehensive plan. Virginia law requires “reasonable consideration” for a locality’s plan, which each must have by law, before creating zoning ordinances. “The rural character of the county is extremely important to the quality of life associated with living in Smyth County and the region,” according to Smyth County’s plan, which the lawsuit quotes. “With continued growth, land use and zoning will need to be enforced to ensure orderly growth that does not impact the rural character of the county.” Allowing data centers to exist in agricultural zones goes against the comprehensive plan, in which data centers aren’t mentioned, the lawsuit says. It also alleges that the process of getting to a vote on the ordinance was illegal. The content of the proposed ordinance was amended between a June planning commission public hearing and the September board of supervisors vote, according to the lawsuit, significantly expanding the definition of data centers in the ordinance. The county did not hold an additional hearing to get public input about the changes. Then, during the September meeting, the board moved up the vote on the planning commission amendments to the top of the meeting agenda, before public comment. “This is reflective of the board’s disdain for the rural lifestyles and land uses that local residents wish to preserve,” the lawsuit says. The lawsuit alleges the vote itself was not done properly because some supervisors participated through a speakerphone call. Four out of seven supervisors were physically present during the meeting. Two of the absent supervisors were approved to participate electronically at the beginning of the meeting by the supervisors who were present, but later on in the meeting, Supervisor Rick Billings said he had misgivings about allowing that to happen. “I’m just saying a vote this important, we should all be here, if possible,” Billings said during the meeting. At that point, the vote had already concluded. The four present supervisors approved the ordinance, one of the absent supervisors approved the ordinance by phone and another absent supervisor abstained. Virginia law allows remote participation under specific conditions, like a medical issue that stops someone from attending, but the lawsuit alleges those guidelines were not met during the meeting — stating the absent members were prepping for a football game. It also says the board operated outside of its authority by voting before allowing public comment and voting on an ordinance that had been significantly changed without a public hearing. “The county worked through a thoughtful, engaging process to develop a proposed ordinance related to control of data centers in our community following the requirements set forth by the Code of Virginia,” County Administrator Shawn Utt said by email. The county has no official comment on the lawsuit itself, Utt said. There is no hearing scheduled yet for the case.

artigo.texto: Richard Murphy and Matthew McMurray of Pinsent Masons were commenting on the decision, which authorises EirGrid to run a competitive procurement process for storage projects capable of importing and exporting electricity for at least four hours. The move is an important milestone in Ireland's efforts to build the flexible infrastructure needed to support a renewables-led electricity system. Murphy said: "The decision provides an important indication of how Ireland intends to support investment in large-scale energy storage technologies, which are expected to play a critical role in maintaining grid stability, reducing renewable curtailment and supporting security of supply as the energy transition accelerates." The procurement implements Action 6 of the Irish government's electricity storage policy framework. Under the approved design, up to 500MW of storage capacity will be procured through a technology-neutral competitive process. Supported projects will be required to provide at least four hours of storage duration, achieve a minimum 75% round-trip efficiency and satisfy planning and grid connection requirements. The scheme will operate through a 10-year contract structure and introduce a revenue support mechanism featuring a revenue floor and a 70:30 upside revenue-sharing arrangement. Under that model, investors retain 70% of revenues earned above the contracted floor while 30% is returned to consumers. The approval is likely to be welcomed by developers, investors and energy users who have been seeking greater clarity on the policy framework for long-duration storage in Ireland. Long-duration storage is widely seen as a critical component of a decarbonised electricity system because it can store surplus renewable generation and release it when demand is high or renewable output is low. For project developers and investors, the procurement provides a first route to market for an emerging asset class in Ireland. For businesses and large electricity users, greater storage capacity could help improve system resilience, reduce renewable curtailment and support the delivery of Ireland's clean energy ambitions. However, while the CRU approved the overall design of the support scheme, it stopped short of approving all of the detailed contractual arrangements that will govern the operation of the procurement. As a result, market participants are likely to focus closely on the next phase of the process. McMurray said: "The market will be keen to study the decision alongside the accompanying EirGrid Recommendation Paper and the AFRY Levelized Cost of Storage (LCOS) assessment.” Those documents have now been published by EirGrid and should be read alongside the CRU decision (38 pages/844 KB PDF) as together they provide important context on the assumptions underpinning the procurement design, expected project economics and the role long-duration storage is expected to play within Ireland's future electricity system. McMurray said: "As with any initial procurement of a new asset class, it needs to be viewed as a starting point only. The revenue floor and share model that is proposed is for a ten-year term. This is shorter than what we have seen recently with ESB Networks' Demand Flexibility Product at 15 years and the 25 years offered under cap-and-floor regimes, for example. This will affect debt finance terms and the cost of capital." The relatively short duration is likely to be an important consideration for lenders and developers assessing the bankability of projects, particularly given the capital-intensive nature of long-duration storage technologies. Murphy said: "As a pathfinder, we have observed similar trends with contract terms offered by system operators for new asset classes or services starting shorter in other markets, with subsequent procurements becoming longer dated. This will need to be the case in Ireland for long-duration storage, particularly with an operational trading envelope that the asset owner will need to comply with." The effectiveness of the scheme will ultimately depend on the detailed contractual terms that are yet to be finalised. "There is an important follow-up consultation required on the contractual arrangements, which will ultimately determine how coherent and financeable this first procurement round shall be," said Murphy. He said: "The contract terms, including the operation of the trading envelope and interactions with wider service requirements, will need to provide effective incentives for contracted assets to operate and deliver the system value that is being procured. It will need to work together as a coherent investment package." Looking beyond the immediate procurement, McMurray said policymakers will also need to focus on establishing a longer-term framework capable of delivering the much greater volumes of storage expected to be required in the years ahead. He said: "Ireland will also need to quickly turn attention to progressing an enduring procurement framework needed to deliver the volumes of storage required after 2030."
