artigo.texto: Data centers no Brasil: Como o Redata reforça o papel estratégico da análise imobiliária O regime tributário estabelece incentivos ao setor, mas exige análise prévia dos imóveis para garantir a viabilidade dos empreendimentos. quarta-feira, 11 de novembro de 2026 Atualizado às 14:58 A criação do Redata - Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter, pela lei 15.504, sancionada em setembro de 2026, trouxe importantes benefícios tributários para estimular a instalação e expansão de data centers no Brasil. Além da dimensão tributária, porém, a estruturação desses projetos exige uma análise imobiliária prévia e criteriosa. Essa análise é determinante para a viabilidade dos data centers e para a adequada alocação dos riscos de implantação. Antes de adquirir um terreno, celebrar uma locação ou estruturar um contrato de BTS - Built to Suit, é indispensável avaliar não apenas a segurança jurídica, mas também a capacidade do imóvel de suportar a operação pretendida. No caso de data centers, a due diligence imobiliária assume um escopo significativamente mais amplo. Além da análise tradicional de titularidade e restrições, é preciso avaliar se o imóvel reúne condições operacionais efetivas, como disponibilidade e capacidade de energia, infraestrutura de telecomunicações, recursos hídricos e potencial de expansão. São variáveis que impactam diretamente a viabilidade do projeto e cujo mapeamento exige conhecimento que vai além do registro imobiliário. Os requisitos do Redata ilustram bem esse ponto. Embora os incentivos estejam concentrados na aquisição de equipamentos e infraestrutura tecnológica, o regime impõe condições de energia, sustentabilidade e eficiência operacional que recaem diretamente sobre o imóvel. O atendimento integral da demanda energética por fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão, somado às exigências de eficiência hídrica, pode tornar um terreno aparentemente adequado inviável na prática, seja pela incapacidade da infraestrutura local, por prazos de conexão incompatíveis com o cronograma ou pela impossibilidade de expansão. Na prática, isso significa que a due diligence imobiliária precisa ocorrer antes da decisão de investimento, e não apenas para confirmá-la. Em projetos de grande escala, uma restrição identificada após a aquisição do terreno pode comprometer significativamente o cronograma e o custo do empreendimento. Essa abordagem se reflete diretamente na estruturação das operações imobiliárias relacionadas a data centers, seja na aquisição de terrenos, na celebração de locações, na elaboração de contratos de Built to Suit ou em operações de investimento. Em qualquer dessas modalidades, as condições de infraestrutura são determinantes para a operação e precisam ser tratadas como riscos contratuais. Responsabilidades pela obtenção de licenças, implantação de infraestrutura, conexão de energia, investimentos adicionais, cumprimento de requisitos técnicos e ambientais e consequências de alterações regulatórias devem ser adequadamente distribuídas entre as partes envolvidas. O Brasil já ocupa posição de destaque no mercado global de data centers, com volumes expressivos de investimento sendo direcionados ao país. A rápida expansão do setor, impulsionada pela crescente demanda por infraestrutura capaz de suportar aplicações de inteligência artificial, reforça a urgência dessa análise. A escala e a densidade tecnológica exigidas por operações de IA ampliam significativamente os requisitos de energia, refrigeração e conectividade. Esse movimento já se reflete na expansão geográfica dos empreendimentos, evidenciando que a escolha da localização depende não apenas da disponibilidade de terrenos, mas também da infraestrutura necessária para suportar operações de alta densidade. A escolha do site para um data center, portanto, não é mais uma decisão puramente imobiliária. Localização, capacidade energética, conectividade, disponibilidade hídrica e possibilidade de expansão compõem uma equação de viabilidade que precisa ser resolvida antes, e não depois, da contratação. Embora o Redata tenha natureza predominantemente tributária e tecnológica, seus incentivos tendem a impulsionar a demanda por áreas aptas à instalação de data centers, reforçando a relevância de uma due diligence imobiliária que vá além da verificação registral e abranja regularidade fundiária, urbanística, ambiental e de infraestrutura. Os benefícios do regime não eliminam os desafios de implantação; ao contrário, reforçam a necessidade de uma análise integrada, conduzida antes da aquisição ou contratação do imóvel, capaz de orientar a decisão de investimento, a estruturação dos contratos e a alocação dos riscos do empreendimento. Os benefícios do Redata podem estar nos equipamentos, mas as condições para viabilizá-los começam muito antes: na escolha e na análise do imóvel. Mariana Araujo Ozanan Advogada do Machado Meyer Advogados.

artigo.texto: Patrocinado por: (Google/Divulgação) Repórter de Inteligência Artificial e Tecnologia Publicado em 10 de novembro de 2026 às 15h58. Última atualização em 11 de novembro de 2026 às 10h51. O Google lançou o Gemini 4 Carbon, seu modelo de IA mais avançado, para usuários do Google AI Ultra e desenvolvedores através de uma API paga. O Carbon é destinado a tarefas complexas que exigem análise detalhada, enquanto o Gemini 4 Argon continua como opção para a maioria das atividades cotidianas. A empresa também introduziu o Swarm, um sistema que distribui tarefas entre múltiplos agentes de IA trabalhando em paralelo. O Gemini 4 Carbon, modelo de inteligência artificial mais avançado do Google, começou a chegar nesta terça-feira, 10, ao aplicativo Gemini e ao Modo IA da Busca para assinantes do Google AI Ultra. A empresa também liberou o acesso a desenvolvedores e empresas pela API paga, que permite incorporar o modelo a outros softwares. Apresentado em 28 de outubro, o Carbon estava restrito inicialmente a um grupo de profissionais de segurança digital. Para usar o Carbon no aplicativo Gemini, no Modo IA da Busca ou no Antigravity, é preciso ser assinante do Google AI Ultra. Desenvolvedores e empresas também podem acessar o modelo pela API paga, com cobrança por uso separada da mensalidade. A abertura amplia a família Gemini 4, que já inclui o Argon. O Google mantém o Argon como opção para a maior parte do trabalho cotidiano e reserva o Carbon para problemas que exigem mais tempo de análise, como investigar um erro espalhado por vários componentes de um software ou examinar dados de uma pesquisa. Junto com o Carbon, o Google começou a liberar uma prévia do Swarm no Antigravity, sua plataforma de desenvolvimento com IA. O recurso distribui um mesmo pedido entre agentes que trabalham em paralelo. Em um projeto de software, um deles pode planejar as mudanças, enquanto outros editam partes do código e testam se as alterações funcionam. O usuário pode acompanhar o progresso em tempo real. Em uma demonstração divulgada pelo Google, um grupo de agentes recebeu fotografias históricas e desenhos de engenharia da Torre Eiffel e montou, a partir de um único pedido, uma exposição interativa em 3D sobre a construção do monumento. A plataforma também permite combinar o Carbon, em funções como planejamento e revisão, com modelos mais leves nas demais etapas. No CursorBench 4.0, teste que reúne tarefas de programação envolvendo vários arquivos, o Carbon liderava a tabela consultada nesta terça, com 60,4% na configuração de raciocínio alto. O Claude Fable 5.2 Max registrou 60%, e o Gemini 4 Argon, também com raciocínio alto, marcou 52,9%. O custo médio estimado pelo teste foi de US$ 9,22 por tarefa para o Carbon, ante US$ 4,57 para o Argon. O resultado mostra que, nesse conjunto de tarefas, o Carbon obteve uma pontuação maior, enquanto o Argon custou cerca de metade por execução. Na API do Google, o preço promocional do Carbon é de US$ 2 por milhão de tokens de entrada e US$ 10 por milhão de tokens de saída. Tokens são as unidades em que a IA divide o conteúdo para processá-lo. Com o fim da promoção em 30 de novembro, os preços passam a US$ 4 e US$ 20, respectivamente. Essa cobrança por uso é separada da mensalidade do Google AI Ultra. O Google começou a liberar o Carbon para assinantes do Google AI Ultra no aplicativo Gemini, no Modo IA da Busca e no Antigravity. Desenvolvedores e empresas também podem acessar o modelo pela API paga. O Google posiciona o Argon para a maior parte das tarefas de trabalho e programação. O Carbon foi desenvolvido para problemas mais complexos, que exigem mais etapas de análise, execução e verificação. É um recurso em prévia que divide um projeto entre vários agentes de IA. Eles podem planejar, executar e testar partes da tarefa em paralelo. Sim. Depois de 30 de novembro, o preço por milhão de tokens passa de US$ 2 para US$ 4 na entrada e de US$ 10 para US$ 20 na saída.

artigo.texto: A massive data center development proposed in Sutton could bring nearly $28 million a year in property tax revenue to the Massachusetts town, but the project is already drawing concerns from residents about its potential impact on their community. The proposal calls for a 10-building data center campus off Boston and Providence roads. Each building would be roughly 250,000 square feet, bringing the development to approximately 2.5 million square feet at full build-out — the equivalent of about 43 football fields of floor space. Stream NBC10 Boston news for free, 24/7, wherever you are. The project is associated with the Kraft Group and Unified Global Packaging Group, which owns the property. The development could represent approximately $16.75 billion in investment and require about 900 megawatts of electricity at full build-out, according to the town's preliminary review. That amount of power would put the proposal among the larger data center developments being planned nationwide. For Sutton, the financial implications could be significant. Town projections estimate the first two buildings could generate about $10.4 million in annual property taxes by fiscal year 2031. Once all 10 buildings are assessed, the town estimates annual property tax revenue could reach approximately $27.8 million by fiscal year 2035. The town's financial modeling also predicts that the average single-family homeowner could pay approximately $5,800 less annually by fiscal year 2035 than under the town's projected tax bills without the development. The possibility of financial relief comes as Sutton projects a structural budget deficit that could grow to approximately $9.1 million by fiscal year 2033 without corrective action. But some residents say the potential financial benefits do not outweigh their concerns. Neighbors raised questions Tuesday about noise, water and electricity use, generators, traffic and potential costs for municipal services. The town's review identifies several of those issues as areas requiring further study, including water supply, wastewater, noise, lighting, traffic and emergency response. "This is just the very, very beginning of this," Jonathan Anderson, chair of the Sutton Select Board, told residents. No final approval has been granted. Town officials expect additional technical review and negotiations over zoning regulations and a community benefits agreement. A zoning change would require a Planning Board hearing and approval by a two-thirds vote at Town Meeting. Residents made clear Tuesday that scrutiny of the proposal is just beginning. "I have a 3-year-old grandson," longtime resident Mario Giamie told NBC10 Boston. "And I'm not going to subject him to this if I can fight it, and I will fight it."

artigo.texto: From Nov. 9 to 20, Antalya, Türkiye, is hosting the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31). Its main themes are climate finance, adaptation, the energy transition, reducing the energy intensity of buildings and reporting on commitments made. Since the first days of its independence, Kazakhstan has been an active and responsible participant in global processes on sustainable development and climate change: it signed and ratified the Kyoto Protocol in 2009 and subsequently joined the Paris Agreement in 2016. This was preceded by extensive expert and analytical work by the Ministry of Environmental Protection, renamed the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources in 2021, with support from the World Bank, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), the Asian Development Bank (ADB), the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the United Nations Development Program (UNDP), national experts and the National Chamber of Entrepreneurs of Kazakhstan. Today, Kazakhstan positions itself as a leader in advancing the green energy transition not only in Central Asia but also across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). Kazakhstan was the first country in the region to adopt a Strategy for Achieving Carbon Neutrality by 2060. This year, by Sept. 1 order of the Prime Minister, a Plan of Organizational Measures for implementing the Strategy was approved. The plan will help integrate decarbonization principles into all areas of the national economy, including sectoral planning systems and the monitoring, reporting and accounting of greenhouse gas emissions on an innovative, digital basis. The initiative of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev to harness the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) is especially relevant to resetting the country’s national emissions trading system. Speaking at the BRICS+ summit on Sept. 13, he again underlined the role of AI in global development and noted that “Kazakhstan regards AI as a strategic priority and is ready to use its advanced computing infrastructure, as well as national and UN digital centers, to expand effective cooperation” for the country’s sustainable development. COP31 experts note a revival of global carbon trading, particularly in the submission of projects to the voluntary carbon market, which undergo a multi-stage review by the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM). As regards the regulated greenhouse gas market – existing national emissions trading systems and their participation in global carbon trading – discussions continue on avoiding double counting and on building the necessary carbon infrastructure. Among Asian countries, Kazakhstan was one of the first to launch an emissions trading system (KazETS). It covers 220 installations in the six basic sectors of the economy and is now undergoing a transformation through the development and introduction of auctioning and of production benchmarks drawing on EU and OECD experience. At the same time, full participation of Kazakh enterprises in global carbon trading and access to the carbon markets of other countries require, first and foremost: a gradual phase-out of free allowances; a higher price per tonne of greenhouse gases; the transfer of the existing MRV (monitoring, reporting and verification) system to a digital platform. For Kazakh exporters, the absence of a modern, internationally recognised infrastructure for monitoring, reporting and verifying CO₂ emissions, and of verifiers accredited in line with international requirements, is currently a serious challenge. At the same time, the experience of leading carbon market players and platforms such as Sylvera, BeZero Carbon, Isometric and Calyx Global shows that AI makes it possible to assess the integrity and risks of carbon projects, to evaluate the carbon footprint and the contribution of enterprises and sectors to the Sustainable Development Goals, and to build digital solutions, including under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement. At COP31, the National Pavilion of Kazakhstan will also present a number of digital solutions for resetting the national ETS and creating a regional digital climate hub with the support of the UNFCCC. We hope that this initiative, developed by experts of Astana Hub together with Green Academy, the University of Central Asia and the Kunayev Institute of Mining, with the support of the Swedish company Planboo and SagtaAI, will be supported by the delegations of the Central Asian countries and included in the outcome document of COP31. The author is Professor Dr. Bakhyt Yessekina, a member of the Green Council under the President of Kazakhstan. Yessekina is the head of the Green Academy Scientific Research and Education Center. artigo.texto: Proposed Auburndale data center draws scrutiny over power demand, water use and impact AUBURNDALE, Fla. - Hundreds packed a public workshop Tuesday night as Auburndale residents and local leaders challenged developers over the massive power and water demands of a proposed hyperscale data center. Auburndale technology center proposal The backstory: The proposed data center would sit on 75 acres along Pace Road. The project is part of the Florida High Tech Corridor, an innovation district established about 30 years ago. In December 2023, Auburndale city commissioners approved a new land-use designation and rezoning for the property, allowing for industrial and certain technology uses, including a data center. Construction on the first two of four approved buildings began in early 2024. The property was purchased in December 2025 by Pace Road DC Development LLC, the company behind the current proposal. Some current commissioners acknowledged they were not in office when the original land-use and zoning decisions were made. City Commissioner Sean Levy said, "I will not allow a rubber stamp process to jeopardize our resources, economy or the peace of our schools." Power grid and water concerns By the numbers: One of the biggest questions surrounding the project is how much electricity it could require. TECO would supply the power, with demand expected to start at 350 megawatts and eventually increase to 700 megawatts. That's enough electricity to power an estimated 350,000 to 500,000 homes. Residents also raised questions about water use and noise. Teresa Detweiler said, "People put their whole life savings into their property and homeownership, and you have a data center that's coming in and your property drops by 10 percent." Polk County economic impact The other side: The developer estimates the facility would use more than 4,600 gallons of potable water per day, compared with as much as 10,000 gallons for a warehouse of the same size. The company says it plans to use a closed-loop cooling system and limit noise at the property line to 50 decibels, about the level of a quiet office. They are also projecting 292 permanent jobs and say the project will not receive financial incentives. The first two buildings are expected to be operational by 2029. State utility cost regulations What's next: The developer submitted a building permit application and interior retrofit site plan on November 4. The city still needs to review those plans. There are also questions about who will pay for the electricity and infrastructure needed to serve the data center. Florida Senate Bill 484, signed into law this year, requires data centers to cover their electricity and infrastructure costs rather than pass them on to other ratepayers. However, TECO still needs approval from the Florida Public Service Commission for its new tariff, which will govern how those costs are charged. The Source: FOX 13 attended the public workshop and heard from Auburndale city commissioners, residents, the developer, Pace Road DC Development LLC, and TECO. Project details and estimates were presented during the workshop.

artigo.texto: Chinese battery giant CATL has confirmed that it is currently in the very early process of researching lithium-air battery technology, a battery format which could bring dramatic improvements to energy density – potentially enough to allow an EV fitted with a lithium-air battery pack to travel up to 2,000 kilometres (1,240 miles) between charges. Lithium-air batteries – will they be the next big thing for premium EVs of the future? Right now, the electric car industry is dominated by lithium-ion batteries. Nickel-rich NMC (nickel manganese cobalt) packs are the most common choice, though LFP (lithium iron phosphate) packs are also rapidly growing in popularity. LFP offers lower energy density than NMC, but it is cheaper to produce and avoids the use of critical materials like nickel and cobalt, while technological advances have narrowed the range gap between the two. Solid-state batteries, which replace the liquid electrolyte found in today’s lithium-ion cells with a solid one, are widely seen as the next big development, with major gains in range, charging speed and safety, and fully solid-state batteries are expected to arrive in high-end EVs over the next few years. Looking even further ahead, however, lithium-air technology could offer another leap forward, although CATL’s research remains in its early stages. While conventional lithium-ion batteries work by moving lithium ions between an anode and a cathode through a liquid or gel electrolyte, a lithium-air battery pairs a lithium-metal anode with a lightweight, porous cathode that draws in oxygen from the surrounding air. During discharge, lithium ions react with that oxygen to form lithium peroxide, releasing energy. Because one of the key ingredients is taken from the air rather than carried inside the cell, the chemistry is far lighter than conventional lithium-ion, allowing much more energy to be stored in a battery pack of the same weight. CATL hasn’t placed an official figure on what energy density they expect to see in their lithium-air research, but current data puts that at a best-case scenario of 3,500Wh per kg. In comparison, the average lithium-ion battery has an energy density between just 250-300Wh per kg. CATL have also made clear that it is a ‘long-term’ research project, rather than something coming around the corner. If such battery technology does eventually make it to the EV market however, expect it to be limited to high-end expensive EVs at first.

artigo.texto: China has officially connected the world’s largest liquid air energy storage (LAES) facility to the electricity grid in Golmud, Qinghai Province, marking a major development in long-duration energy storage technology. The 60 MW project is located in the Qaidam Basin, adjacent to a large solar power facility, and is designed to improve renewable energy integration and grid stability. The facility aims to address the challenge of balancing electricity supply and demand as solar and wind generation fluctuate throughout the day. It uses surplus electricity generated during periods of high renewable energy production to store energy for later use when demand increases. The storage process begins with ordinary air, which is purified and compressed using a multi-stage centrifugal compressor. During compression, the system captures and stores the generated heat in insulated tanks. The compressed air is then cooled to approximately minus 194 degrees Celsius, converting it into liquid form. This liquid air is stored in large tanks under near-atmospheric pressure until electricity is required. When power demand rises, the stored liquid air is pumped and heated before being converted back into gas. The expanding gas drives turbines, generating electricity that can be supplied to the grid. This process allows the facility to store surplus renewable energy and release it during periods of higher electricity consumption. The project can absorb approximately 600 MWh of surplus electricity per day and is expected to deliver around 180 GWh of electricity annually. Its capacity could support the electricity requirements of tens of thousands of households while helping reduce the challenges associated with intermittent renewable energy generation. Unlike conventional battery storage systems that depend on minerals such as lithium, liquid air energy storage uses ordinary atmospheric air as its primary storage medium. It also does not require specific underground geological formations, making the technology more flexible in terms of project locations and deployment. Another important feature of the facility is its 100% domestic equipment localization rate. The project uses locally developed intellectual property, equipment and manufacturing supply chains, highlighting China’s efforts to strengthen its domestic energy storage industry. The commissioning of the Golmud facility represents an important milestone for large-scale energy storage. Its operational performance is expected to provide valuable experience for future projects and demonstrate how long-duration storage technologies can support renewable energy expansion, improve grid flexibility and strengthen electricity supply reliability. artigo.texto: TotalEnergies acquires 450MW solar, 150MW BESS NSIP project On 31 October, the special purpose vehicle (SPV) Steeple Solar Farm Limited changed hands, with TotalEnergies taking it over from RES UK & Ireland. French integrated energy and petroleum company TotalEnergies has acquired the Steeple Renewables Project from developer RES. On 31 October, the special purpose vehicle (SPV) Steeple Solar Farm Limited changed hands, with TotalEnergies taking it over from RES UK & Ireland. Steeple Renewables Project will comprise 450MW solar energy generation and a 150MW battery energy storage system (BESS). The Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project (NSIP) was granted a development consent order (DCO) in early October. Due to be constructed in Nottinghamshire, the Steeple Renewables Project is located near the decommissioned West Burton Power Station and will use existing grid capacity and infrastructure in the area. TotalEnergies did at one point have its own projects in the NSIP process: the 98MW Hedgehog Grove and 98MW North Ray Solar Farm projects. However, the capacity boundary that classifies NSIPs, requiring government approval and superseding local council planning authorities, changed to 100MW earlier this year. This saw the projects moved to be approved under the Town and Country Planning Act (TCPA), which TotalEnergies said “allows for a more locally focused consultation”. Read more about:

artigo.texto: Grupo ABL estreia data center de 3,5 MW em Curitiba mirando soberania de dados Por Raphael Giannotti | Em um cenário em que empresas, instituições financeiras e órgãos públicos exigem cada vez mais controle sobre onde suas informações críticas são armazenadas e processadas, a soberania de dados tornou-se um ativo estratégico. Apostando nessa demanda com capital 100% nacional e em processo de credenciamento junto à Defesa Nacional, o Grupo ABL revelou, nesta quarta-feira (11), seu primeiro data center, Astella, no centro de Curitiba (PR), com operações iniciando ainda em novembro. Instalada em um edifício de 8.800 m² e 16 pavimentos que já abrigou grandes operadoras de telecomunicações, a unidade curitibana estreia com capacidade inicial de aproximadamente 3,5 MW, podendo escalar de forma modular até cerca de 5 MW conforme a ocupação e contratação de energia. A estrutura já reúne mais de R$ 150 milhões em investimentos (sendo cerca de R$ 20 milhões apenas na rede elétrica) e receberá outros R$ 30 milhões em modernização tecnológica até o fim de 2026. Expansão já está nos planos da empresa Para expandir essa arquitetura para seis novas localidades pelo Brasil entre 2027 e 2028, a companhia projeta aportes adicionais de R$ 300 milhões. Tecnicamente, o polo nasce preparado para cargas intensivas de inteligência artificial e GPUs, contando com refrigeração líquida, racks de alta densidade e monitoramento inteligente Gestão 360. "Estamos transformando quase três décadas de experiência em tecnologia, conectividade e infraestrutura crítica em uma plataforma preparada para uma nova demanda do mercado. A inteligência artificial está mudando a escala e a localização da capacidade computacional, e nossa estratégia é construir uma infraestrutura nacional capaz de acompanhar essa transformação com segurança, conectividade e eficiência", disse Agnaldo Lopes, Presidente do Grupo ABL. Além da segurança física e digital, a empresa aposta na verticalização energética ao incorporar uma usina solar de aproximadamente 2,7 MWp conectada à rede para avançar rumo à autossuficiência sem abrir mão da redundância. Segundo o presidente da empresa, o foco em Curitiba acontece por conta de uma demanda local, até mesmo da região Sul, nesse tipo de infraestrutura, algo que, em nível nacional, é bastante concentrado em São Paulo.

artigo.texto: Microsoft pressiona Trump contra veto a componentes chineses para data centers | Vero NotíciasMicrosoft pressiona Trump contra veto a componentes chineses para data centers A Microsoft pressiona o governo de Donald Trump a abandonar os planos de proibir a importação de transceptores ópticos chineses, componentes essenciais para data centers de inteligência artificial. A empresa alerta que a medida pode atrasar a expansão da infraestrutura tecnológica dos EUA. A gigante de tecnologia possui 35 data centers em construção e outros 134 planejados no país. A empresa argumenta que a proibição pode comprometer a cadeia de suprimentos e deixar chips de IA sem utilização por falta de componentes para conectá-los. O governo americano avalia o veto por preocupações de segurança nacional, incluindo riscos de espionagem e ataques cibernéticos atribuídos à China. A Comissão Federal de Comunicações (FCC) trabalha na restrição, enquanto empresas do setor alertam para possíveis prejuízos à competitividade. O bitcoin recuava 1,94% nesta terça-feira (10), a US$ 73.570, às 17h15, segundo a Binance. Durante o dia, atingiu o menor nível desde agosto. O ethereum caía 3,93%, cotado a US$ 2.051,06. A queda ocorreu após dados de inflação dos Estados Unidos reforçarem expectativas de aumento dos juros em dezembro. Antes da divulgação, o diretor do Federal Reserve, Christopher Waller, havia defendido considerar uma alta de 0,5 ponto percentual. O dólar comercial subiu 1,48% nesta terça-feira (10) e fechou a R$ 5,58, maior cotação de 2026. A moeda norte-americana também atingiu o patamar mais elevado desde 31 de julho de 2025. A alta ocorreu após a inflação ao consumidor dos Estados Unidos avançar 0,4% em outubro, acima dos 0,3% esperados pelo mercado. O indicador influencia as decisões do Federal Reserve sobre os juros americanos. A Anthropic pretende captar até US$ 62,5 bilhões em sua oferta pública inicial de ações, com preço entre US$ 70 e US$ 78 por papel. A operação pode avaliar a desenvolvedora de IA em aproximadamente US$ 1,03 trilhão. A companhia colocou à venda cerca de 801,4 milhões de ações da Classe A. A avaliação total considera também outras classes de papéis e a possibilidade de compras adicionais pelos bancos responsáveis pela oferta. Deputados afirmaram nesta terça-feira (10), após reunião com o ministro da Fazenda, Dario Durigan, que não há negociação para adiar a reforma tributária. Segundo eles, o governo mantém o início da CBS em janeiro de 2027. O presidente da Frente Parlamentar do Empreendedorismo, deputado Joaquim Passarinho (PL-PA), disse que a prioridade é implementar a mudança. A CBS substituirá PIS e Cofins, enquanto a CNI defende adiar o início para 2028. A Petrobras registrou lucro líquido de R$ 39,75 bilhões no terceiro trimestre de 2026, alta de 21,5% na comparação anual. O balanço foi divulgado nesta terça-feira (10). A receita da estatal somou R$ 169,3 bilhões, crescimento de 32,4% em relação ao mesmo período de 2025. A produção de petróleo também avançou, com aumento de 11,9%.

artigo.texto: TREX Energy, an Indian energy storage solutions company, has inaugurated its lithium battery manufacturing facility at E-City, Raviryal, Maheshwaram, Hyderabad. The facility is equipped with a 12 PPM automatic module assembly line designed to manufacture 52S battery packs for energy storage applications, including 261 kWh configurations and 5 MWh systems. The new facility marks an important step in the company’s efforts to strengthen domestic manufacturing capabilities and address India’s growing demand for Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS). With renewable energy adoption expanding across the country, energy storage solutions are becoming increasingly important for managing fluctuations in power supply, supporting peak-load requirements and providing reliable backup across residential, commercial, industrial and utility-scale applications. The automated assembly line, with a production capability of 12 parts per minute, is designed to improve manufacturing efficiency, consistency and quality control. It will support the production of battery modules and packs for TREX Energy’s portfolio of energy storage solutions, ranging from 5 kWh to 5 MWh. Bharat S Chhittarka, Director, TREX Energy, said, “We’re focused on reducing financing costs to make BESS more affordable and reliable for the Indian market. Energy must be available when it’s needed, and BESS is a key solution.” Roshan Shaik, Technical Director, TREX Energy, said the 12 PPM automatic module assembly line would strengthen the company’s manufacturing capabilities and enable efficient, consistent production. He added that the facility would support scalable energy storage solutions for India’s expanding market requirements. TREX Energy’s product portfolio caters to a wide range of applications. Its Commercial and Industrial (C&I) BESS solutions are designed for factories, offices and commercial establishments seeking to manage energy consumption, improve operational resilience and access backup power. Its utility-scale systems address requirements associated with grid applications and large renewable energy projects. The company also offers residential energy storage systems, home inverter batteries and customised battery packs. As part of its expansion plans, TREX Energy is preparing to establish a second manufacturing facility in Madhya Pradesh. The Madhya Pradesh Government has allotted four acres of land to the company for the proposed Phase 2 facility. Further details on its production capacity, development schedule and commissioning will be announced in due course. The Hyderabad facility reflects TREX Energy’s focus on developing local manufacturing and technology capabilities to serve India’s evolving energy storage ecosystem. Through its expanding product range and planned investments, the company aims to support energy storage adoption across homes, businesses and large infrastructure projects. TREX Energy is a Hyderabad-based energy storage solutions company focused on designing and delivering Battery Energy Storage Systems for commercial, industrial and utility applications. Operating under the tagline “We Store Electrons”, the company aims to support India’s clean energy transition through reliable and intelligent energy storage technologies. It has registered offices in Hyderabad, Telangana, and Pune, Maharashtra.

artigo.texto: Karpowership acquires UK 100MWh BESS site for development The Turkish renewable energy company has bought a fully consented plot near Birmingham in the UK's Midlands for a 100MWh BESS installation. Anglo Renewables has sold a fully consented 50MW/100MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) project near Birmingham to Kinetics Energies for an undisclosed sum. The 2-hour project, dubbed Kitwell, is expected to connect to the grid in 2028. Northamptonshire-based Anglo Renewables is a micro-business (having a turnover of less than £1 million annually) that enters into agreements with landowners and steers appropriate permitting for change of land use and planning permission for battery energy storage system or solar PV installations. In the case of the Kitwell site, it is presumed any agreement between the landowner and Anglo Renewables passes to Kinetics Energies, part of Karpowership, the Turkish energy group. The head of commercial at Karpowership and CEO of Kinetics Energies, Mehmet Katmer, said: "Battery storage has an important role to play in keeping the grid flexible and reliable, and we look forward to delivering an operating BESS project as part of our strategy to deliver 800MW of low and zero carbon assets across Europe." In England and Wales, BESS sites are not considered to be nationally significant infrastructure regardless of their size, and permission for development is subject to approval by the relevant local planning authority. artigo.texto: Ohio Chamber study: Data centers added more than $9B to state economy in 2025 COLUMBUS, Ohio (WSYX) — Ohio’s growing data center industry added more than $9 billion to the state’s economy last year, according to a new study commissioned by the Ohio Chamber of Commerce. The study found that data centers and the construction needed to build them supported nearly 70,000 jobs in Ohio last year. About 14,000 people work directly in the data center industry, with average pay and benefits of about $148,000 a year, the report said. Looking ahead, the study estimated that planned construction and equipment spending through 2030 could support more than 257,000 jobs for a year. The report also examined the fiscal impact of incentives and investment tied to the industry. It said the state gave up more than $1.5 billion in tax revenue, but that the investment has generated a $2.7 billion fiscal surplus.

artigo.texto: Building owners are turning to battery energy storage systems to lower energy costs, add resilience against grid disruptions and support decarbonization. Despite momentum, their adoption faces a number of persistent obstacles, said panelists at the Greenbuild conference last month. Nationwide, nearly 58 gigawatt-hours of on-site battery storage capacity was installed in 2025, the largest single year of new battery capacity on record, according to a report by the Urban Land Institute and UL Standards & Engagement, drawing on data from the American Clean Power Association. Looking ahead, the sector is expected to install 500 GWh of battery storage between 2026 and 2032, the report says. Notwithstanding the success of these models, several barriers are keeping the market from growing more quickly, according Jill Maltby-Abbott, senior environmental and sustainability standards engineer at UL Standards & Engagement, a panelist who contributed to the ULI and UL report. Location-specific challenges. Even when a project makes economic sense, it can be stopped by interconnection and permitting woes, unclear approvals, shifting local requirements and unfamiliarity with the technology, according to Maltby-Abbott. Even where interconnection and permitting processes exist, commercial-scale storage projects can take years to deliver, the report said. Long and unpredictable timelines can cause projects to accumulate soft costs — like time and money spent on community engagement or engineering fees — and be exposed to changing market conditions, incentive structures and regulatory requirements, adding to the financial risk of implementation, per the report. Risk thresholds. Another key consideration is how municipalities view the risk and governance of these assets, Maltby-Abbott said. “How are [municipalities] defining the [risk] thresholds that they’ll accept? It’s very much on a per-project, per-owner basis, and this is a challenge that a lot of people experience with multiple emerging technologies.” Concern over risk can lead to delays as local officials put up hurdles, Dean Apostoleris, practice leader of renewable energy development at Kimley-Horn, said at the conference. “What we see as a really big barrier in terms of penetration into new markets and, even in some situations, mature markets is resistance from the regulatory, zoning, land use and siting perspective of these batteries,” he said. Even in really population-dense markets, where storage development has been a priority for quite some time, there has only been increased adoption of on-site battery energy storage in the past five or so years, according to Apostoleris. “That issue stems from a lack of education and lack of knowledge about what battery energy storage really is,” he said. For example, New York state has established a mandate to procure 6 GW of battery energy storage by 2030, with Illinois and Massachusetts setting targets of 3 GW and 5,000 MW as well, respectively. But with those targets close to just three years away, New York only has 415 MW of battery storage installed, or 7% of its target, as of the presentation, Aposoleris said. State mandates aim to spur battery adoption but development "comes down to the local and community level,” Apostoleris said. “And a lot of these communities have not yet had the bandwidth, the knowledge or the education to implement some of these regulations.” “As a result, when you actually go to permit and construct BESS, ultimately the reviews and approvals are … preventing a lot of that mandate and that goal from being achieved,” he said. Fire risk. Of all the risks, fire is one of the first localities worry about, said Kara Kokernak, senior director of the ULI Lewis Center for Sustainability in Real Estate. “That is something that became very apparent” when conducting research for the report, she said. “That was tagged in most of our conversations, but having fire safety teams part of that education can help ease those concerns.” Because of this pushback, Apostoleris said, it can be much easier to implement these projects in jurisdictions that have already established BESS safety requirements and review processes, which provide more prescriptive guidance on how projects will be evaluated. He points to the Massachusetts Energy Facilities Siting Board as a good example. It “allows a lot of developers to push through their projects in a very prescriptive manner that reduces some of the risk that often comes with uncertainty of reviews and approvals they might have at the state level,” Apostoleris said. Even when requirements are stringent, this predictability can help project teams incorporate safety considerations earlier while supporting fire department preparedness and confidence in how potential incidents will be avoided or managed, the report says. Community engagement, or lack thereof, can often delay, constrain or stop otherwise viable projects, the report says. For that reason, early engagement, before formal filings, is a “consistent recommendation from those who have successfully navigated community opposition,” the report says. “This gives developers the opportunity to understand specific concerns, explain safety and emergency response approaches, and adjust the project so that community input is reflected in project planning from the start.”

artigo.texto: Congresso aprova R$ 34,9 milhões para datacenter do Serpro Da Agência Senado | 12/11/2026, 18h44 O Congresso Nacional aprovou nesta quinta-feira (12) um projeto de lei, de autoria do Executivo, que abre crédito suplementar de R$ 34,9 milhões para o Serviço Federal de Processamento de Dados (Serpro). A verba, proveniente de recursos próprios do Serpro, deve ser destinada ao Datacenter Modular de São Paulo — centro de processamento de dados dessa empresa pública. Na exposição de motivos que acompanhou a proposta (PLN 22/2026), o governo destaca que o crédito "tem a finalidade de atender às necessidades contratuais do Datacenter Modular de São Paulo, do contrato vigente, abrangendo a execução das etapas 6 e 7, bem como atender o aditivo de serviços previsto para o projeto". O projeto foi aprovado sem alterações em relação ao texto original do Executivo e segue para a sanção da Presidência da República. Porto de Salvador Também nesta quinta-feira, o Congresso aprovou um projeto de crédito especial do governo que destina R$ 700 mil para a Companhia das Docas do Estado da Bahia (Codeba). Esses recursos devem ser utilizados na reforma da pavimentação da retroárea do Porto de Salvador. O projeto (PLN 33/2026) prevê, para financiar a ação, o cancelamento parcial de uma dotação destinada à dragagem de aprofundamento do canal de acesso ao Porto de Salvador. De acordo com o governo, a realocação não prejudica a execução da dragagem nem altera o resultado primário projetado para as empresas estatais federais não dependentes do Tesouro Nacional. Esse projeto também foi aprovado sem alterações e segue para a sanção presidencial. Créditos adicionais Tanto o crédito suplementar (como no caso do datacenter do Serpro) quanto o crédito especial (como no caso do Porto de Salvador) são tipos de créditos adicionais. O crédito suplementar é a autorização para o governo aumentar uma dotação orçamentária que já existe na Lei Orçamentária Anual (LOA). Já o crédito especial é uma autorização para o governo incluir no Orçamento uma despesa que não estava prevista. Vitória Clementino, sob supervisão de Dante Accioly Agência Senado (Reprodução autorizada mediante citação da Agência Senado) MAIS NOTÍCIAS SOBRE:

artigo.texto: Northpoint residents worry proposed data center will add to neighborhood's rapid change SALT LAKE CITY (KUTV) — Northpoint residents worry proposed data center will add to neighborhood's rapid change. “I used to be able to see all the way out to the island,” he said. Now, he said, his view is “a building.” Bangerter has lived in Salt Lake City’s Northpoint neighborhood his entire life. He said the area has changed dramatically over the past decade as commercial warehouses have been built around his property. Now, a proposed data center could be built across the street. A city building permit application for the property, submitted May 21, describes Project Bedrock as a one-story data center. A separate application for diesel-fired emergency generators and fuel storage was submitted to the Utah Division of Air Quality in late September. Dungan Adams, an environmental engineer with the division, said the generators would provide backup power if electricity from the grid is interrupted. The application says the facility’s primary power would come from the grid, he said. MORE: AI stock selloff fuels questions about Utah's data center future after midterms The air-quality application is still in an early stage and has not been deemed complete. Adams said the state is evaluating the proposed emissions. The review’s timeline depends on the information submitted, though the process can take about 180 days from start to finish, he said. Residents’ concerns extend beyond the data center. Less than a half-mile away is the proposed site of a homelessness campus, adding to questions some neighbors have about how the area will change. “There’s been a lot more sound pollution, noise pollution, air pollution,” said Chris Souther, who operates a recording studio at his home. He said trucks have been driving by with open loads and leaving dust. Souther said the development has affected his quality of life. He also said he believes commercial growth has hurt his property’s value. “The city’s already pretty much trashed our property value by commercializing everything around us, so our house is worth essentially zero,” he said. Bangerter said he would consider leaving if he received enough money, but the offers he has received would not allow him to replace the homes on his property. Salt Lake City Council member Victoria Petro, who represents the area, did not respond to a request for comment. The city building application still requires approval before construction can begin. The Division of Air Quality said its application is incomplete. _____

artigo.texto: A new battery energy storage system (BESS) being built on the former coal power station at Fiddler’s Ferry has passed a major milestone, with the installation of key electrical equipment. The site is owned by SSE Renewables, with infrastructure specialists OCU Energy and Fluence building the 150 MW BESS. When complete, it will be capable of providing power for approximately 250 000 homes for a two-hour period at a time. An SSE Renewables spokesperson previously said: “Similar to our Ferrybridge project, our grid scale battery at Fiddler’s Ferry will be built on what was a former SSE-owned coal-fired power station and highlights the transition away from fossil fuels towards a net-zero future.” Kiosk buildings, which will house electrical relays, switchgear, control panels, and communication systems, are now in place, fabricated by RSK Group companies AJ Engineering & Construction Services and Northern Engineering & Welding Co. (NEWCo). AJ Engineering & Construction Services Pre-Construction Manager, Lee Binks, said: “When fully operational, the BESS site will store power for release back to the UK national grid when it is needed the most – helping to manage peaks of energy demand and supporting a transition away from fossil fuels. “We have designed, fabricated and cladded two auxiliary transformer buildings and one portable relay room for the site in a modular format, reducing the time spent on site. These buildings provide compact, weatherproof enclosures that house the equipment that ultimately connects the battery system to the national grid. In addition to this, we have fabricated and erected the switch room, which is a structural steel portal frame building with insulated cladding. “Usually, for the aux buildings and portable relay rooms, these types of small buildings are manufactured using glass reinforced plastic or brick and built on site. To speed up delivery and reduce complexity, we built them off-site using fabricated steel modules. They were then transported to the site and lifted into place, already cladded and ready for fit-out.” Binks explained that because they are widely used in both the water and the en-ergy sectors, they are in high demand, and lead times for their procurement can be significant. He concluded: “Having been built with steel and cladding, the kiosks were ready to be installed on site within six weeks. Normally this team of structural designers, detailers, fabricators, steel erectors and site management would have to do this on-site. By building the kiosks off-site, we have avoided adding further complexity to an already busy construction site.” Fellow RSK company, Acies, carried out the connection design on the structural frame for the switch room, working in collaboration with AJ Engineering while it carried out the modelling of the building. With the kiosks in place, OCU Group will begin the fit-out process of the internal equipment that will connect the site to the national grid. It is expected to be operational in 2027. artigo.texto: The Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission recently approved AES Indiana’s plan to serve a Google data center in a contested case that highlights the complex challenges regulators and utilities face in allocating system costs for large computational loads. According to the Oct. 7 order, AES will acquire or build new generation, storage and grid infrastructure for a 390-MW data center planned for Monrovia, a town Southwest of Indianapolis, at an estimated project cost of about $737 million. The new generation, storage and transmission assets included in the Monrovia Project will go into the utility’s rate base. AES says its electric service agreement with Google is designed to ensure the revenues will be sufficient to “reimburse at least 100%” of the project’s incremental direct costs. But the contract itself is heavily redacted, and an estimated $74 million in network upgrades has been explicitly allocated to all customers as a reliability need, prompting criticism from consumer advocates that the arrangement is shifting costs onto other ratepayers. What are ‘reasonably allocable’ costs? Indiana state law requires large load customers to reimburse at least 80% of project costs “reasonably allocable” to them. Claire Wayner, a senior associate at the clean energy nonprofit RMI, said in an interview that while local projects are fairly easy to trace back to a specific data center, broader regional system upgrades raise more complex questions about who benefits and how costs are allocated across jurisdictions. “Maybe they're upgrading a part of the grid that they were going to have to upgrade anyway because it's aging infrastructure,” Wayner said. “If that's the case, they should have to demonstrate that, and then maybe cross socialization makes sense.” But, she continued, “If that upgrade was not going to be built without the data center, without benefits modeling or just a demonstration of the benefits to the rest of the zone, it's difficult to make the claim that all ratepayers in that zone should pay for it.” AES Indiana will serve Google’s data center from its portfolio of shared generation and battery assets. The new generation and storage assets built to meet the additional demand will be owned through a subsidiary by the utility and go into its rate base. In testimony to the commission, a utility representative said the transmission infrastructure included in the Monrovia Project falls into three basic categories: interconnection infrastructure for the generation and storage; “direct connection” infrastructure for connecting the data center to the system; and network upgrades necessary “primarily” to serve Google “but also to meet other customer demand or energy needs.” Google will pay about $32 million upfront for the direct connection, but $73.8 million in network upgrades will be included in AES Indiana’s transmission rate base and recovered through future rates from all customers, including residential ones. Commissioners approved the proposal 5-0, saying in their order that “although the Customer may be the impetus for the network upgrades being made, this does not preclude the upgrades from providing system-wide benefits.” “Network upgrades, as the name implies, are upgrades or additions to the transmission network intended to provide reliability, resiliency, and stability to the system at large,” it said. “Just as the Customer will be allocated a portion of the existing network transmission infrastructure, it is reasonable for existing customers to also be allocated a portion of the network upgrades.” The Midcontinent Independent System Operator approved some of the network upgrades, which include a new substation, citing reliability and load growth. Although the order says the portfolio proposed in AES’ filing is for 390 MW of new load with 460 MW of new 4-hour storage and 130 MW of solar generation, the substation planned for the project is designed for 1,200 MW of load, creating opportunity for future expansion at the site. The generation and storage resources consist of one 200-MW and one 130-MW battery energy storage system, called Foundry Works and Hardy Hills, respectively, as well as a 130-MW solar facility paired with a 130-MW BESS called Crosstrack. Their cost is redacted in the case filings. ‘Cost allocation and cost recovery are two different concepts’ Ben Inskeep, program director at the Citizens Action Coalition, a consumer advocacy group that intervened in the case, sees the deal as running counter to President Donald Trump’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge signed earlier this year by tech companies and utilities, including Google and AES Indiana. “These network upgrades are specifically driven by the Google data center,” Inskeep told Utility Dive in an interview. “Instead of making the cost causer pay, AES Indiana has decided to spread the costs out to other ratepayers, and our commission has unfortunately approved that.” Ben Gavelek, a spokesperson for the commission, declined to comment on the deal. Google did not respond to requests for comment. Claire Rice, a spokesperson for AES Indiana, said in an email that although the transmission assets are being allocated through the normal cost-of-service process, Google’s rate includes a “separate incremental-cost test designed to recover the incremental costs required to serve Google, including the network upgrades.” “Cost allocation and cost recovery are two different concepts,” she added. Many of the exact terms of the service agreement, including monthly energy and demand charges and riders, are redacted in the public record. Parts of other contracts underpinning the deal are also confidential. The assets will be included in future base rate case filings. Until those new rates are established, the utility plans to recover those costs through its Environmental Cost Recovery and netted with contract revenues. artigo.texto: Lea County commissioners may vote next week to approve up to $134 billion in industrial revenue bonds for a 1,890-acre hyperscale Google data center on Hobbs’ outskirts. Google officials, in their first public appearance in Southern New Mexico, held town halls in Lovington, Tatum and Hobbs on Monday and Tuesday to discuss the project, which is similar in size to the 1,400-acre Project Jupiter in Santa Teresa. That development secured $165 billion in industrial revenue bonds from Doña Ana County. Google said ground work will begin in 2027, and construction will continue through 2030. While Google touted its potential to generate over 1,000 construction jobs and “substantial” tax revenue for the county, and proposed an $18 million housing fund, critics said the company had few answers to attendees’ questions, and the town halls didn’t feel like a meaningful attempt for the technology giant to engage with the community. “The meetings were hosted to ensure every member of Lea County had an opportunity to speak directly to members of the Google team and get their questions answered,” Google said in a statement provided by spokesperson Leslie Schuman. Clayburn Griffin, a business owner in Lovington, is pushing for a six-month data center moratorium in Lea County. Project opponents had called for independent experts to respond to their concerns about water and energy use, said Griffin, who attended all three events, but commissioners instead set up the Google town halls. “We knew it was going to be a Google PR event, which was not what we were asking for,” Griffin said in an interview Wednesday. “… The commission said that they would be transparent, but they obviously have not been fair in this process.” Lea County commissioners did not immediately respond to The New Mexican‘s requests for comment Wednesday. The Hobbs meeting at the Lea County Event Center — set up like a science fair, with multiple information booths for various topics — prevented any kind of public conversation, Griffin added. Notably, deputies from the Lea County Sheriff’s Office attended the town halls, including a sizable group at the Lovington event. Members of Protect Lea County, an organization that opposes the data center project, were told they could not bring clipboards, petitions or pamphlets inside the building, attendee Pam Keller said, adding people also were not permitted to film Google representatives’ responses to questions. A Google spokesperson denied attendees were prohibited from recording the events. In its flyer distributed at the meetings, Google said: “We will continue to listen, learn and support our local communities wherever we operate.” Google representatives at the town hall framed the newly dubbed “Project Rancho” as a “potential” data center, which would “power the essential technology that America relies on daily, from emergency 911 systems and electronic health records, to local small business operations and digital classrooms.” The project would be developed on county land under an option-to-purchase agreement with Excelsior Hobbs Power LLC, a company created for the project with ties to private equity firm Excelsior Energy Capital. Excelsior Energy would be responsible for constructing a 2-gigawatt solar field three miles away to help power the data center, a fueling decision few data center developers in New Mexico have turned to so far. For the 125 to 130 full-time positions that eventually would be offered at the site, one Google representative said the salaries would be between $85,000 and $100,000. And Google pledged to cover 100% of its energy costs, replenish more water to the community than the data center will consume, and “utilize high-tech, low-noise equipment and sound walls to meet or exceed all noise ordinances.” Like Project Jupiter, Google said it will use a closed-loop cooling system to recirculate its water, which requires a one-time initial fill of up to 9.7 million gallons. The site will then use roughly 40,000 gallons a day for activities like bathroom and kitchen use — or about 14.6 million gallons a year. However, asked for specific details on the expected energy consumption, the company’s promises when it comes to water use and timeline for the project, Google representatives were hesitant to provide official statements. Lorraine Villegas, a member of Protect Lea County, spoke about the county’s consideration of up to $134 billion in industrial revenue bonds for the project: “They want us to pay for it, but we don’t even know what they’re doing or how they’re going to do it,” she said in a statement. “… If they can’t find the decency to properly inform us, then I think the $3 trillion company is fully capable of funding itself.” “Just having Google sales pitches for the community is not a democratic way to go about this. And I think people deserve to have their voices heard,” Griffin said. “For that to happen, we need to have, first of all, a moratorium to give us more time on this … and then actual proper town halls set up so that the community can come out and discuss this issue.” Clayburn has collected almost 900 signatures in favor of a six-month data center moratorium, which he plans to bring to commissioners at a special meeting scheduled Thursday. The only items on the agenda were certification of the canvass for the Nov. 3 election and an executive session to discuss potential real estate transactions. The commission’s next regular meeting is scheduled Nov. 19. An agenda for the meeting is not yet available. Data center moratoriums have been proliferating nationwide as controversy grows over the facilities. artigo.texto: BYD is testing a system in the Abu Dhabi desert that handles every step of charging an electric vehicle using solar power. The automaker launched a new setup that combines solar panels, battery storage, ultra-fast “FLASH” chargers, and a robotic arm into one single solution. It is designed to work in extreme heat, hence the desert location, and places where the local power grid is weak or nonexistent. “For the first time, BYD is bringing its integrated Solar-Storage-FLASH Charging technology to the global stage,” said Stella Li, BYD Executive Vice President. “We are providing clean energy generation, energy storage and ultra-fast charging together, and we are making the charging experience smarter, simpler and more seamless for drivers around the world.” Fast Power Straight From the Sun Speed is far and away the main focus. For example, BYD’s FLASH Charging tech takes a battery from 10% to 70% in five minutes, and up to 97% in nine minutes. If you’re an owner of an electric vehicle then you probably know the process of waiting around for the car to charge. With this charging technology, juicing up a battery takes about as much time as it does to fill a tank of gas. Advertisement The setup relies on BYD’s Solar-Storage-Charging system rather than pulling energy from utility lines. BYD Solar has spent over 16 years building solar technology across more than 100 countries and regions and will handle the energy capture. The panels soak up the intense desert sunlight, and giant batteries store that energy so it is ready whenever a car pulls up. Because it can run off the grid, BYD can set these stations up in remote areas. Hands-Free Parking and Plugging In BYD also addresses dealing with a charging cable in the scorching desert using the Automated Valet Parking with a charging robot. When a car pulls up, step out of the car, lock the doors, and walk away. The car drives itself into an open charging spot. Once parked, a robotic arm uses cameras and force sensors to find the car’s charging port, pop open the cover, and plug in the fast charger. This desert site is the result of a goal Chairman and President Wang Chuanfu introduced in 2006. He called it the “Three Green Dreams,” which includes generating clean solar power, storing it in batteries, and using it to run electric cars.

artigo.texto: A Botetourt County resident’s lawsuit alleging that the county’s board of supervisors violated the state’s open meetings and open records law when it greenlit a Google data center campus is legally sufficient to move forward, a circuit judge ruled Tuesday. But after nearly three hours, which featured some testimony and a lot of arguments about the case’s merits, substitute Judge Michael Doucette said court schedule issues forced him to postpone a further hearing on the matter until next week. Robert Dallas, who lives near the Botetourt Center at Greenfield site, filed suit Nov. 2, seeking to invalidate the county’s economic development performance agreement with the limited liability company behind the project. His case alleges that the county violated the Virginia Freedom of Information Act when it approved documentation advancing the Google project. Dallas’s suit also asks the court to “rescind all actions” carried out in connection with the June 2025 document. Respondents in the case are the county, its board of supervisors, its economic development authority and Google-owned Helio Capital LLC. Julian Harf, representing the county, elicited testimony showing that Google has transferred $2.5 million of a promised $4 million to the county, helping pay for ambulances, fire trucks, heart monitors, body cameras and more. Further testimony showed ground clearing work has already started. Harf used the testimony to help support a plea filed in response to the suit. He asked the court to find that even if Dallas’ allegations are true, his case is legally insufficient. “Remedies” for a FOIA violation “do not include rescission” of the agreement and its effects, Hart said. An invalidated agreement would not be the court’s problem, said John Fishwick, who leads Dallas’ legal team. Google, the county and Helio could work out those ramifications among themselves, Fishwick said. FOIA law calls for a hearing within seven days of a suit’s filing, but it took eight before Doucette could be available. By the time the recently retired Nelson County judge decided in the plaintiff’s favor, the hearing time had bumped up against an already scheduled criminal court docket that included several cases in which jail sentences could be ended. “I won’t force an inmate to spend one more day in jail,” he said as he told those gathered in the courtroom that the trial would be set for 9 a.m. Monday. It was unclear why Botetourt County Circuit Judge Joel Branscom was unavailable to hear the case. According to the suit, the county’s board of supervisors did not disclose on its published agenda that it would be discussing the agreement or a resolution to enact it in a closed meeting on June 24, 2025. After the board returned to public session, it voted 5-0, with no discussion, to approve the resolution and the agreement, after they were added to the agenda during the meeting as so-called “walk-on” items, the case alleges. After a recess, the board returned to address another walk-on item — announcing the data center project. Yet another item that hadn’t appeared on the agenda was a board resolution approving Google’s agreement with the Western Virginia Water Authority, Dallas alleges. Harf and Helio’s lawyer, Graham Bryant, told the court that information on the agenda denoted an economic development project in the industrial park, which they argued was the most the board needed to disclose, to protect the negotiations. Harf said that county officials discussed the matter in detail after the vote, and any violation committed was “technical.” Fishwick said the board sneaked the matter into its meeting that day, part of an atmosphere of secrecy it had developed. “They treat FOIA like it’s a little technical thing, and they can run roughshod,” Fishwick said, adding that the supervisors’ later announcement of the project was more of a “cheerleading session” than an information share.

artigo.texto: The German Chancellor has warned against weakening the EU's carbon market, insisting that businesses need predictable carbon prices despite mounting pressure from member states and his own economy minister. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has urged Brussels to stand firm on the EU's carbon market reforms and reject further changes to its second phase, signalling Berlin's opposition to reopening a hard-fought political compromise on carbon pricing, according to a letter seen by Euronews. "It is extraordinarily important that the EU ensures investment certainty in emissions trading," reads the letter. The intervention comes as the European Parliament and EU governments negotiate the European Commission's July 17 proposal to align the Emissions Trading System (ETS) with the bloc's 2040 climate target. The reform has become increasingly contentious, with several EU countries seeking to weaken or even scrap parts of the system, blaming carbon pricing for high electricity costs. Merz warned that businesses need predictable carbon prices to make long-term investment decisions, and that uncertainty risks undermining investment in Europe's energy and industrial sectors. His stance contrasts with that of his own Economy and Energy Minister, Katherina Reiche, who has pushed to relax carbon rules and extend free emissions allowances for industry. The ETS, the EU's carbon market, requires power generators and energy-intensive industries to pay for their greenhouse gas emissions. However, some heavy industries receive free allowances to help them cope with the costs of decarbonisation and international competition. Merz called on Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to conclude the ongoing reform swiftly, citing competitiveness concerns without weakening the carbon market. "European companies in the energy and industrial sectors have built their business models on the expectation of reliable CO2 price signals," the letter says. He argued that the impact of carbon pricing on electricity bills should be addressed through existing compensation mechanisms rather than changes to the ETS itself. These mechanisms allow governments to offset indirect carbon costs faced by electricity-intensive industries, helping to protect European manufacturing. Merz rejects further changes to ETS2 Merz took an even firmer line on ETS2, the EU's second carbon market, which is due to take effect in 2028 and will extend carbon pricing to fuels used in road transport and heating buildings. He argued that the compromise reached in early 2026 to delay its introduction until 2028, alongside measures to stabilise prices, should be sufficient to keep costs under control. The German Chancellor rejected any further adjustments and insisted that negotiations on ETS1 and ETS2 must remain separate. His position could put Berlin at odds with governments seeking further concessions on ETS2, particularly those concerned about the political and social impact of higher fuel and heating costs on households. Several member states have called for additional delays or changes to ETS2's price-stabilisation mechanism, which allows more emissions allowances to enter the market if carbon prices rise too sharply. Berlin draws a red line on carbon pricing Merz's intervention comes amid mounting pressure on the EU to soften its climate policies in response to concerns over industrial competitiveness and household energy bills. While acknowledging that industry needs protection from high electricity costs, the Chancellor wants that support delivered through compensation mechanisms rather than by weakening the carbon price signal that underpins the ETS. His letter amounts to a warning against allowing political pressure over energy costs to trigger a broader retreat from the EU's carbon market. Reacting to the letter, Linda Kalcher, executive director of the think tank Strategic Partnerships, said Merz's direct intervention "carries real weight". “His letter sends an unmistakable signal: a robust ETS is vital for industrial competitiveness and future investment. So I expect Germany — and him — to step up and lead to help broker an agreement in December,” Kalcher said. After the European Parliament votes in plenary in mid-December, political talks among the EU co-legislators will start.

artigo.texto: Edward Burgess is a partner at Current Energy Group. The debate over the impacts of new data centers on customers' electricity bills is only intensifying. On the one hand, many people blame data center companies for triggering new grid costs that others will pay. On the other, data centers hold great promise to lower customer bills. For the latter, the theory is that, as high-utilization infrastructure users, data centers can absorb a large share of fixed costs that would otherwise be charged to existing customers. To their credit, nearly 200 data center companies have signed the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, committing to pay their fair share of costs. However, achieving this commitment depends on cooperative action by local utilities to update their rates accordingly. This raises an important question: Are investor-owned utilities willing to share the benefits of large-load growth with existing customers? Recent evidence suggests otherwise in some cases. To fully understand this problem, let’s revisit the fundamentals of electricity ratemaking. New rates are typically proposed by utilities but ultimately approved by state utility regulators. When utilities propose new rates, the core calculation is based on two key inputs: 1) utility costs in the numerator, and 2) utility sales in the denominator. If the denominator increases more than the numerator (i.e., sales increase more than costs), then customer rates should decline on average. But in the era of hyperscale load growth, the specifics of these inputs — how they are defined and when relative changes occur — matter a great deal. In several recent cases, utilities have simply neglected to increase kWh sales from new data center load in their rate proposals, while still including related cost increases. For example, in North Carolina, Duke Energy recently proposed increasing customer rates by over 15% over the next two years. However, this increase was based on a rate calculation that kept the denominator essentially frozen at 2024 levels — even though Duke had already contracted to add hundreds of MWs of new data centers in the coming years, and included costs triggered by this in its proposal. Current Energy Group analyzed Duke’s proposal and presented expert testimony to the North Carolina Utilities Commission on behalf of the state’s Attorney General’s office. We found that 54% of the requested rate increase — approximately $1 billion annually — could be erased if kWh sales in the rate formula were simply corrected to reflect Duke’s own planning assumptions. In fact, correcting just the kWh sales figure and one other key variable — return on equity — was enough to turn the proposed 15% rate increase into a 4% decrease, even with significant new grid investments. A similar pattern emerged in Missouri, where Evergy Missouri Metro included costs for new gas generation to serve new data centers but did not account for the increased sales to those data centers in its rate calculation. As data center sales ramp up, the utility would see a windfall over the four years the new rates are in effect. In Louisiana, increased sales from a new Meta data center could trigger an immediate customer refund over the next three years. Instead, Entergy proposed accounting methods to defer that benefit over a 20-year period. This “one simple trick” of immediately updating kWh sales in the rate formula could save customers billions in the coming years. So why do utility rate proposals keep failing to account for data center load growth? Some utility analysts might point to arcane explanations, such as the traditional practice of using a “historic test year.” There may be a grain of truth to that, but it is not a convincing argument given widespread concerns about affordability. Duke, for instance, had the legal ability to propose a forward-looking Multi-Year Rate Plan but chose not to include any load growth in its rate proposal. A more cynical view is that utilities are seeking to “lock in” higher rates before new data center load fully materializes and the denominator rises. This creates a major windfall for utilities, at least temporarily, as data center load ramps up before rates can catch up. Traditionally, utilities have complained about “regulatory lag,” which arises when rates are not increased quickly enough to capture rising costs. Now, in the era of hyperscale load growth, we have the opposite problem — a “reverse regulatory lag.” Instead, rates are not being reduced quickly enough to capture rising revenue from large loads. This problem is exacerbated by another challenge: As utilities slow-walk updates to the denominator (kWh sales), they speed-run updates to the numerator (costs recovered). Many utilities, including Duke, use accelerated cost recovery mechanisms, such as Construction Work in Progress, to fund new infrastructure for load growth. This further strains affordability. Infrastructure costs are front-loaded through near-term rate increases, while any rate relief from load growth won’t materialize for years. Under Duke’s original proposal, customers would pay for the construction of new gas-fired power plants four years before they start operating, and six years before data center load appears in the denominator. As affordability concerns persist, what solutions should regulators consider? - Regulators should insist on up-to-date sales forecasts for any rate proposal and apply them immediately. If utilities rely on forecasts to plan and build generation, they should rely on those same forecasts to reduce rates by updating the billing determinants. - When revenue grows rapidly, regulators should ensure that utilities absorb more of the initial cost and risk involved rather than passing this on to consumers. For example, regulators should consider halting accelerated cost-recovery mechanisms. The regulatory lag problems those mechanisms sought to address are much less salient now. - For certain states, full revenue decoupling mechani
