artigo.texto: Insights > Client Alert Client Alert Ministério da Fazenda estabelece as etapas de implementação das obrigações de MRV no SBCE 12 de novembro de 2026 O Ministério da Fazenda publicou a Portaria SEMC/MF nº 3.199/2026, que estabelece as etapas de implementação das obrigações de mensuração, relato e verificação (MRV) de emissões e remoções de gases de efeito estufa (GEE) no âmbito do Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (SBCE). A portaria sucede a proposta submetida à consulta pública em julho e incorpora alterações relevantes no cronograma de implementação, na distribuição dos setores entre as etapas e na identificação das atividades econômicas abrangidas. Cronograma de implementação das obrigações MRV A Portaria SEMC/MF nº 3.199/2026 prevê uma sequência de ações anuais: A implementação será escalonada em três etapas e abrange os seguintes setores: O órgão gestor deverá publicar um ato específico, ao menos 150 dias antes do início das respectivas obrigações, para disciplinar o conteúdo mínimo e o formato de apresentação das informações, bem como os prazos e os procedimentos para a submissão do plano de monitoramento e do relatório de emissões e remoções verificado. Da proposta à portaria: principais mudanças Em comparação com a proposta submetida à consulta pública, a versão final da Portaria SEMC/MF nº 3.199/2026 alterou significativamente a distribuição dos setores entre as etapas de implementação: Os anexos também foram reorganizados e passaram a apresentar Classificações Nacionais de Atividades Econômicas (CNAE) mais específicas, refletindo, inclusive, a divisão das atividades químicas e minerais entre as duas primeiras etapas. A análise de enquadramento deverá, portanto, considerar os códigos e as atividades listados em cada anexo, não apenas a denominação geral do setor econômico Todavia, embora os códigos da CNAE identifiquem os setores abrangidos, tal referência não sujeita automaticamente todas as atividades neles compreendidas às obrigações de MRV. Caberá ao órgão gestor definir, em regulamentação específica, as fontes, instalações e atividades reguladas, observando as especificidades dos procedimentos de MRV aplicáveis a cada setor. Além disso, os anexos da portaria estabelecem que a atividade regulada será considerada mesmo quando corresponder à CNAE secundária do estabelecimento. Etapas subsequentes Ainda em 2026, está prevista a estruturação da Câmara de Assuntos Regulatórios (Careg), com a participação dos setores incluídos na primeira etapa, e a abertura de consultas públicas sobre dois decretos centrais à regulamentação do SBCE, para instituir: - Programa Brasileiro de Mensuração, Relato e Verificação (PB-MRV) - Programa Brasileiro de Compensação de Emissões (PBCE) Essas iniciativas deverão detalhar elementos relevantes para a operacionalização do SBCE, incluindo diretrizes e metodologias aplicáveis ao MRV, bem como critérios para o credenciamento de metodologias de geração de Certificados de Redução ou Remoção Verificada de Emissões (CRVEs). As equipes de Ambiental e ESG do Demarest estão à disposição para prestar esclarecimentos adicionais. Sócios Relacionados Advogados Relacionados Maria Luisa Paes Priscilla Horn Áreas Relacionadas Ambiental ESG – Ambiental, Social e Governança

artigo.texto: Fort Worth leaders receive data center recommendations that could lead to moratorium on development FORT WORTH, Texas - Fort Worth leaders could put a temporary moratorium on data center developments as the city learns how to manage the industry's growing impact. Fort Worth data center moratorium Local perspective: On Tuesday, November 10, the Fort Worth Data Center & Infrastructure Commission, a commission appointed by the Fort Worth City Council in August, delivered recommendations on data center development in the city. The commission gave 19 recommendations in total after studying four areas of data center development: electricity, water use, land use and neighborhood impacts, and economic impacts. Some of the commission's recommendations include: - Requiring closed-loop cooling systems to recirculate water rather than draw in new water - Increase the distance from homes to data centers from 50 feet to 350 feet - Enforce noise regulations on data centers The recommendations could lead to a 90-day moratorium on data center development in the city, something that has been in the works since the committee was created in August. Such a moratorium would allow the city to review the commission's recommendations and decide whether changes are needed to the city's zoning rules and development codes. You can find the commission's full report below. No action was taken on the commission's findings at Tuesday's meeting. What they're saying: Michael Slattery, the chair of the commission, tells FOX 4's Vania Castillo these recommendations would give the city a "roadmap" on how to move forward with data centers. "It would give data center developers much more certainty. It's certainly not going to please everybody, and I think ever does. And I think that I think it starts to put some certainty around how to move this forward," Slattery said. Some residents at Tuesday's city council meeting said the recommendations don't go far enough. "Two months is not enough time to consider all of the issues involved with a data center," resident Julie Waters said. "Today, you have an opportunity to save your seat in the next election. Listen to the cries of your people who have come before you, meeting after meeting, asking for a moratorium. If not for your people, then for then at least to wipe away the stain of corruption on your reputation and legacy." The backstory: Fort Worth leaders have been considering their position on data center development since this past summer. In early July, Fort Worth's zoning commission voted against new restrictions on future data center projects in the city, citing the need for more information on the rapidly-changing industry. Several days later, five Fort Worth City Council members called for a moratorium on data center construction. They say the pause would allow the city to discuss and refine regulations on data centers. That call led to the creation of the committee that gave today's findings. Fort Worth currently has four operating data centers, with at least four more in development. What's next: Fort Worth city staff say the next public hearing is planned for January 12, 2027. The earliest a data center moratorium could be enacted is February 2027. Officials noted that existing sites and projects already moving through the application pipeline would be exempt from the moratorium if the policy is formally adopted next year. The Source: Information in this story comes from a Fort Worth City Council meeting and previous FOX 4 reporting.

artigo.texto: Founding Chairman of Global Carbon Council Dr. Yousef Alhorr speaking at the event. DOHA: The Global Carbon Council (GCC), the first independent carbon crediting standard established in the Global South, headquartered in Qatar and internationally recognised under UN ICAO’s CORSIA scheme and ICVCM, has joined a global coalition of leading financial institutions, exchanges and carbon market organisations as a founding member of the Global Carbon Market Network, officially launched at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye. The launch ceremony was held at the Arab Climate Pavilion, jointly hosted by GCC and the League of Arab States in the COP31 Blue Zone, bringing together hundreds of participants in person and virtually, including climate experts, government representatives, financial institutions, carbon market organizations, standard-setting bodies and other stakeholders. The launch featured keynote addresses by Acting Secretary-General of UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) Pedro Manuel Moreno, Chair of the UN Sustainable Stock Exchanges Initiative and Lead of the World Investment Forum Nan Li Collins, Minister of Energy and Minerals of the Sultanate of Oman H E Eng Salim bin Nasser Al Aufi, Commissioner for Climate Change of Hong Kong SAR (China) Sammy Sau Kuen Yeung, and Founding Chairman of the Global Carbon Council (GCC) Dr. Yousef Alhorr. Their participation highlighted the importance of international cooperation in strengthening carbon markets and advancing climate finance. Convened by UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD), the network aims to strengthen connections between carbon markets, improve transparency and investor confidence, and facilitate climate finance for mitigation projects, particularly in developing countries. The Global Carbon Market Network addresses persistent market fragmentation caused by differing regulatory frameworks, standards, registries and trading systems. Rather than establishing another carbon market or competing standard, it seeks to connect existing voluntary and compliance markets, improve interoperability and promote consistent market practices. Its launch comes as emissions trading systems and carbon taxes cover nearly 30% of global greenhouse gas emissions and generated more than $107bn in public revenue in 2025. Yet stronger market connections are needed to translate carbon pricing into greater investment in measurable emissions reductions and sustainable development. Speaking at the launch, Founding Chairman of the Global Carbon Council (GCC) Dr. Yousef Alhorr, emphasised the importance of cooperation, market integrity and equitable access to climate finance. “The future of carbon markets will not be determined by how many markets we create, but by how effectively we connect them, build trust and translate carbon transactions into measurable climate impact. The Global Carbon Market Network represents an important step towards overcoming fragmentation, strengthening international cooperation and unlocking climate finance, particularly for developing countries.

artigo.texto: Ecobiz.asia – Indonesia has joined the Forest and Climate Leaders’ Partnership (FCLP), a voluntary international coalition seeking to strengthen the role of forests in global climate action, opening opportunities for cooperation on forest carbon markets, land tenure and tropical peatland and mangrove management. Indonesia’s membership was announced at the Indonesia Pavilion during the UN climate conference COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, on Thursday (Nov. 13, 2026). Deputy Forestry Minister Rohmat Marzuki represented the government at the announcement, which was attended by Guyana Vice President Bharrat Jagdeo, the FCLP Secretariat director and representatives of member countries. A video message from Forestry Minister Raja Juli Antoni was also shown. Rohmat outlined three priority areas for Indonesia’s engagement with the partnership. The first is strengthening high-integrity forest carbon markets by connecting credible demand for carbon credits with verified emissions reductions. He said such cooperation would require national authorization, transparency and safeguards against double counting to ensure the integrity of carbon transactions. The second priority is strengthening tenure security over forests and land, including recognition of customary forests. Rohmat said international support for this agenda should be aligned with Indonesia’s legal framework and accountable national financing mechanisms. The third area involves knowledge exchange and technical cooperation through the International Tropical Peatland Center (ITPC) and the World Mangrove Center. Indonesia also plans to hold technical sessions in 2027 to advance cooperation in these areas. Indonesia manages around 13 million hectares of tropical peatland and 3.4 million hectares of mangroves, Rohmat said, highlighting the country’s experience in managing these ecosystems as a basis for international cooperation. Indonesia also seeks greater international recognition of its timber legality and sustainability verification system, known as the Timber Legality and Sustainability Verification System (SVLK), as part of efforts to promote sustainable timber trade. “Practical cooperation, grounded in national ownership, can deliver long-term benefits for forests, communities and the climate,” Rohmat said. He added that relevant Indonesian officials would follow up with the FCLP Secretariat to discuss cooperation on peatland and mangrove management, land tenure and forestry financing. Launched at COP27 in Egypt in November 2022, the FCLP is a voluntary partnership established to accelerate implementation of the Glasgow Leaders’ Declaration on Forests and Land Use, which aims to halt and reverse forest loss and land degradation by 2030. The partnership currently comprises 42 countries and the European Union. Its agenda includes mobilising forest finance, strengthening forest carbon markets, recognising the land rights of Indigenous Peoples and local communities, and promoting sustainable timber use. Guyana and the United Kingdom serve as its co-chairs. Jagdeo welcomed Indonesia’s participation, saying forests were increasingly important to global priorities beyond climate mitigation, including biodiversity protection, rainfall regulation and agricultural sustainability. “I would like to thank Indonesia for becoming part of the FCLP,” Jagdeo said, also acknowledging Indonesia’s contributions to international forestry initiatives. ***

artigo.texto: Property tax breaks for Nebraska data centers exceed $300 million By Fred Knapp , Senior Reporter/Producer Nebraska Public Media and Maddie Ames , Reporter Nov. 11, 2026, 3:34 p.m. · In the last four years, data centers in Nebraska received personal property tax breaks worth more than $300 million, according to a Nebraska Public Media News analysis of data from the Nebraska Department of Revenue. A tax incentives report released by the agency last month shows that data centers were exempt from property tax on nearly $22 billion worth of equipment from fiscal year 2023 through 2026. Over 99% of last year’s exempted property is located in Nebraska’s three largest counties – Douglas, Sarpy, and Lancaster. Data centers in those three counties received tax exemptions on more than $10 billion worth of equipment last year, according to the Nebraska Department of Revenue (NDOR). Using the average tax rates NDOR listed for those three counties, Nebraska Public Media News calculates data centers saved $196 million last fiscal year. Those exemptions are expected to continue. The report said “significant capital investment in data centers is anticipated to yield substantial tax credits.” In July, Gov. Jim Pillen issued an executive order aimed at denying further state tax incentives for data centers. “We just simply believe that we do not need to bring people together by incredible tax incentives,” Pillen said at the time. “We need to make sure that we attract givers, not takers.” But Pillen’s order does not change the law that allows data centers to exempt “computer systems and peripherals’’ – the guts of data centers – from property taxes, which pay for everything from local schools and police departments to county roads. Taxes that data centers don’t pay may shift to the other taxpayers in the counties where those data centers are located. But the department said the credits will be limited going forward. “Due to tax liability constraints, the utilization of these credits will be restricted,” the NDOR report said. The future impact of data centers and tax exemptions for them is expected to be a major consideration for policymakers when the Legislature reconvenes in January.

artigo.texto: The Bihar Electricity Regulatory Commission (BERC) has approved a proposal by Bihar State Power Holding Company Limited (BSPHCL) to procure 300 MW of solar power integrated with a four-hour Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), marking an important step towards strengthening the state’s renewable energy supply and improving electricity availability during peak demand periods. The approval will enable Bihar’s distribution companies, North Bihar Power Distribution Company Limited and South Bihar Power Distribution Company Limited, to secure renewable electricity through a long-term power procurement agreement for 25 years. The electricity will be procured through NHPC Limited, which will act as the intermediary procurer. SAEL Industries India Limited has been selected as the project developer to supply 300 MW of power from a larger 1,200 MW interstate transmission system-connected renewable energy project. Under the approved arrangement, the discovered tariff is ₹3.13 per kilowatt-hour, while NHPC will receive an additional trading margin of ₹0.07 per kilowatt-hour. The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission had previously adopted the competitively discovered tariff in April 2026. The project includes a four-hour battery storage facility designed to provide 150 MW of firm electricity during evening peak demand hours, between 6:00 PM and midnight. This arrangement is expected to help Bihar manage its rising electricity demand and improve the reliability of power supply when solar generation is unavailable or reduced. The storage component will play an important role in shifting renewable electricity to periods when consumption is higher. The commission has also established strict performance requirements to ensure reliable electricity delivery. The developer must maintain at least 70 percent of the contracted peak capacity on a monthly basis and 85 percent annually. Failure to meet these requirements will attract financial penalties calculated at 1.5 times the applicable tariff rate for the shortfall. These provisions are intended to ensure that the project delivers the required electricity consistently. The regulatory approval was granted by a commission comprising Chairman Amir Subhani, Member Legal P. S. Yadav and Member Technical Manoj Kumar. While examining the petition, the commission considered the national Resource Adequacy framework and Bihar’s growing electricity requirements. It observed that the procurement would help the state address its Renewable Purchase Obligation requirements through FY 2029-30. The project is also expected to reduce Bihar’s dependence on expensive short-term electricity purchases, particularly during evening peak hours. By securing long-term renewable power supported by battery storage, distribution companies will have an additional source of reliable electricity, potentially reducing the need for load shedding and improving consumer supply conditions. SAEL Industries India Limited is expected to operationalise the project on or before June 30, 2028. Achieving this deadline will allow the state to benefit from transmission charge waivers, including a 25 percent waiver on interstate transmission charges for the solar component and a 100 percent waiver for electricity supplied from the co-located battery storage system. Additionally, BERC has approved a modified Power Sale Agreement incorporating consumer protection provisions. These provisions will account for potential tariff reductions arising from future changes in Goods and Services Tax rates. The decision is expected to support Bihar’s renewable energy transition while balancing electricity supply reliability, procurement costs and consumer interests.

artigo.texto: Lydian Energy has brought its 150 MW/600 MWh Faraday battery energy storage system (BESS) into commercial operation in Utah County, adding four hours of contracted electricity storage capacity to the power infrastructure supporting Meta’s Eagle Mountain data center. The facility began operating on September 18, 2026, under a long-term energy storage agreement with PacifiCorp, according to Lydian’s November 10 announcement. The project adds battery storage alongside Lydian’s existing 525 MW Faraday solar facility, using the solar plant’s substation and grid interconnection rather than requiring a separate connection. The arrangement allows the developer to expand the site’s energy infrastructure while making use of existing grid facilities. Faraday BESS occupies approximately eight acres and uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery technology. Its 150 MW power rating and 600 MWh storage capacity provide a four-hour duration at full rated output. Lydian said it completed the project in approximately 10 months from mobilization to commercial operation. The project also establishes the first operating phase of a larger battery storage development at the site. Lydian is developing Faraday BESS 2, which could add another 375 MW/1,500 MWh by the fourth quarter of 2028. Battery storage supports Meta’s Eagle Mountain operations Faraday BESS operates under a Schedule 34 arrangement supporting Meta’s Eagle Mountain data center. PacifiCorp receives the project’s contracted storage capacity under a long-term agreement, placing the battery within a utility-contracted arrangement rather than making it an exclusively dedicated power supply physically connected to Meta’s campus. The project has a longer development history than its commercial operation announcement suggests. In January 2023, PacifiCorp executed a power purchase agreement for 525 MW of solar generation from Faraday Solar and a separate battery storage agreement for a 150 MW, four-hour system. A March 2023 filing before the Utah Public Service Commission identified the two agreements as serving a single Schedule 34 customer. At that time, PacifiCorp expected the solar facility to enter commercial operation on September 30, 2025, and the battery system on June 1, 2026. The battery ultimately began operating on September 18, 2026, approximately three and a half months after the original target recorded in that filing. Lydian’s reported 10-month construction and commissioning period refers to the period from mobilization, not the entire development history dating back to 2023. Meta subsequently identified its involvement directly. In a September 14, 2026, update, the company named Lydian’s 150 MW Faraday battery as part of its investments in energy resources supporting the Eagle Mountain data center. Meta said its Utah energy investments had added more than 1.7 GW of clean and renewable energy and 600 MWh of battery storage across 13 sites. It also said it pays the full costs of its data centers’ electricity use and funds new and upgraded infrastructure needed to support its operations. This arrangement connects three distinct participants. Lydian develops, owns and operates the battery, PacifiCorp contracts for its storage capacity, and Meta supports the energy arrangement as part of its strategy for the Eagle Mountain data center. Shared solar infrastructure supports the battery installation One of Faraday BESS’s most important infrastructure features is its integration with the existing Faraday solar facility. The battery occupies approximately eight acres adjacent to the solar development and shares its substation and grid interconnection. This allows Lydian to add a substantial storage installation without developing an entirely separate grid connection. The solar facility began commercial operation on September 30, 2025, under the associated PacifiCorp agreement. The battery’s September 2026 commissioning therefore adds storage to an existing generation site rather than establishing an entirely new energy development. The technical arrangement also requires an important distinction when assessing the site’s combined capacity. Faraday Solar has a stated capacity of 525 MW, while the battery can discharge at up to 150 MW. These ratings should not automatically be combined to suggest that the shared interconnection can export 675 MW simultaneously. The actual combined export capability depends on the approved interconnection limits and operating arrangements. Lydian has not disclosed the site’s detailed export constraints or how PacifiCorp coordinates solar generation and battery dispatch. Nevertheless, reusing the existing substation and interconnection provides a clear infrastructure advantage. It allows the developer to expand the site’s energy capabilities using facilities already established for the solar project. Faraday BESS 2 could add another 1.5 GWh Lydian is developing a second battery installation, Faraday BESS 2, at the Utah site. The proposed expansion would add up to 375 MW of power capacity and 1,500 MWh of storage, with commercial operation targeted for the fourth quarter of 2028. If completed at its announced maximum capacity, the second phase would increase the site’s combined battery storage to 525 MW and 2,100 MWh. That would establish a substantially larger storage development alongside the existing 525 MW Faraday solar facility. The expansion would also increase the amount of electricity that can be shifted across different periods, subject to charging availability, grid conditions and contractual dispatch requirements. However, Lydian has not disclosed Faraday BESS 2’s battery supplier, engineering and construction contractor, construction financing or detailed procurement schedule in its November 10 announcement. The second phase therefore remains a development target rather than an operational expansion. Its progress will depend on the remaining development, financing, procurement and construction requirements. C

artigo.texto: Starpointe data center hearings to continue into December The Hanover Township Board of Supervisors scheduled two additional hearings in the ongoing review process for a proposed 350-megawatt data center in Starpointe Business Park after the developer announced that they have two additional witnesses to present. The board has been reviewing the conditional use permit submitted in May by Dallas, Texas-based developer Prime Data Centers LLC since August 2026, with over 20 hours of total testimony across a dozen hearings hampering the pace of proceedings. Prime has called acoustic, civil, electrical, mechanical and natural gas engineers that have worked on the project to testify regarding numerous aspects of the preliminary design, plus the Project Lead Kate Nolan Bryden. Bryden provided an overview of the project during direct testimony at the start of the hearing process, and has been called back for cross-examination several times by a group of attorneys representing concerned residents who live near the proposed site. Thomas Steele, a local attorney representing Prime, said that while the developer has called several witnesses to the stand, their direct testimony only took up less than five hours so far, and that the residents’ attorneys cross-examination has occupied more than 15 hours of hearing time. In addition to the attorneys, several other residents who were granted party status to the hearing have cross-examined Prime’s witnesses, often using the platform to voice their concerns with the potentially harmful environmental impact of the proposed 350-megawatt, seven-building data center campus and attached natural gas power plant. Prime representatives have repeatedly highlighted that the project will create hundreds of jobs to build and maintain the data center campus, and emphasized that Prime will fully comply with all applicable environmental regulations and the commonwealth’s Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development (GRID) standards, which were signed into law earlier this year. The board was to continue its review of the conditional use application on Wednesday, and again on Nov. 18, plus Dec. 9, all at 6 p.m. at the Hanover Volunteer Fire Department at 9 Starck Drive in Burgettstown.

artigo.texto: Foto: Divulgação A prefeita de Uberaba, Elisa Araújo, reuniu-se nesta quarta-feira, 11, em São Paulo (SP), com representantes da Atlas Renewable Energy para avançar nas conversas sobre as condições para a instalação de infraestrutura para data centers na Zona de Processamento de Exportação (ZPE) de Uberaba. Na ocasião, foi assinado o documento que formaliza o interesse da companhia na instalação do empreendimento na ZPE de Uberaba. A agenda integra a estratégia da Prefeitura de posicionar o Município como destino de investimentos em infraestrutura digital e energia, setores estratégicos para o desenvolvimento econômico de Uberaba e de toda a região do Triângulo Mineiro. De acordo com os estudos preliminares, a iniciativa tem potencial de investimento inicial superior a R$ 10 bilhões em edificações, instalações de conexão e infraestrutura. Com o avanço do projeto, poderão ser acrescentados cerca de R$ 30 bilhões em equipamentos de tecnologia da informação, o que poderia elevar o investimento total estimado a aproximadamente R$ 40 bilhões. Se concretizado, o empreendimento estará entre os maiores da história do Município. O projeto encontra-se em fase de avaliação e depende ainda de etapas técnicas, regulatórias e de aprovação, entre elas a análise pelo Conselho Nacional das Zonas de Processamento de Exportação (CZPE), órgão do Governo Federal responsável por autorizar a instalação de empresas nessas áreas. “Uberaba reúne condições muito favoráveis para receber investimentos dessa natureza: localização estratégica, infraestrutura energética e logística, e uma ZPE alfandegada e pronta para operar. O nosso papel é criar o ambiente para que projetos como este possam se concretizar, com planejamento, segurança jurídica e responsabilidade ambiental. E queremos fazer isso de mãos dadas com empresas que tenham trajetória sólida em infraestrutura energética e compromisso real com o meio ambiente e com as comunidades. Nosso compromisso é transformar o potencial de Uberaba em empregos e oportunidades para a nossa gente”, destacou a prefeita Elisa Araújo. A demanda por capacidade de processamento de dados e inteligência artificial cresce de forma acelerada no Brasil e no mundo, e a combinação de energia renovável, disponibilidade de área e incentivos à exportação coloca a região em posição de destaque para atrair esse tipo de empreendimento. Caso se concretize, a iniciativa poderá gerar empregos diretos e indiretos durante as obras e a operação, estimular a participação de fornecedores locais, promover a capacitação profissional da população e fortalecer a infraestrutura energética regional. Além disso, a concretização da iniciativa abriria caminho para a chegada de novos investimentos ao Município e posicionaria Uberaba como um polo competitivo, em nível internacional, para o desenvolvimento de infraestrutura de data centers. As ZPEs, enquanto áreas de livre comércio com o exterior, oferecem benefícios tributários, administrativos e cambiais à exportação de bens e serviços. A Zona de Processamento de Exportação de Uberaba é uma das quatro do Brasil alfandegadas pela Receita Federal e prontas para receber investimentos. A Atlas Renewable Energy, empresa que avalia a iniciativa, possui trajetória consolidada no desenvolvimento, financiamento, construção e operação de projetos de infraestrutura de energia renovável de grande escala na América Latina e atua com elevados padrões de responsabilidade ambiental e social em seus projetos. Na frente social, a companhia desenvolve iniciativas voltadas à capacitação profissional, à inclusão de mulheres no mercado de trabalho, à educação e ao apoio à infraestrutura comunitária, com o objetivo de deixar um legado positivo e duradouro nos territórios onde atua. “Uberaba tem características que a tornam uma região de grande potencial para o desenvolvimento de infraestrutura digital sustentável no país. Seguimos avaliando a iniciativa em diálogo com o Município e com os órgãos competentes”, afirmou Fábio Bortoluzo, presidente da Atlas Renewable Energy no Brasil. Também participaram da reunião, na capital paulista, o secretário de Governo, Caio Presotto, o secretário adjunto de Desenvolvimento Econômico, Turismo e Inovação, Alexandre Cury, a diretora Comercial e de Assuntos Aduaneiros da ZPE Uberaba, Maria Letícia Mesquita, e do sócio da Cassu Participações, Mário Renato Palmério. A Atlas Renewable Energy é uma empresa internacional de infraestrutura de energia limpa, fundada em 2017, com mais de 10,8 GW em sua base de ativos renováveis. Líder no segmento na América Latina, a empresa é controlada pela Global Infrastructure Partners (GIP), da BlackRock.

artigo.texto: Tsunami democrata tira de Donald Trump o controle da Câmara e do Senado Oposição terá, no mínimo, 54 senadores, caminha para maioria robusta na Câmara e elege governadores em estados importantes e simbólicos. Crédito: Estadão O mercado financeiro focado em tecnologia não tem vivido seus melhores dias recentemente e o índice Nasdaq chegou a registrar sua maior queda diária desde abril de 2025 na última quinta-feira (5). A queda foi de 5,5% e resultou na redução de US$ 2,5 trilhões (R$ 13,4 trilhões em conversão direta) do valor de mercado das principais empresas do setor, influenciadas pelas midterms dos Estados Unidos. O motivo para esse derretimento abrupto tem relação com as recentes eleições de meio de mandato, as midterms norte-americanas. Na última rodada, a expressiva vitória do Partido Democrata contra o Partido Republicano no pleito acendeu o temor de que a expansão da inteligência artificial sofra mais regulações nas mãos dos democratas. A Nvidia, empresa mais poderosa do planeta e absoluta na venda de chips para servidores, viu suas ações caírem 9%. Com a rival direta, a AMD, a queda foi ainda mais chamativa e bateu nos 17%. O índice de semicondutores da Filadélfia (SOX) também registrou uma queda notória de 12%, o nível mais baixo dos últimos seis meses. O clima pesado não está restrito somente aos Estados Unidos e chega a outros países em um efeito cascata. Bolsas asiáticas, como a japonesa Nikkei e a sul-coreana Kospi, operaram em forte queda. O índice VIX, chamado de “termômetro do medo” em Wall Street, registrou seu maior salto desde 2024 e aumentou a apreensão dos acionistas. - 🪧Índice VIX (Termômetro do medo): essa é uma métrica de Wall Street que mede a expectativa de volatilidade do mercado para os próximos 30 dias. Quando o índice dispara, significa que há insegurança por parte de investidores e possibilidade de quedas na bolsa. IA pode esbarrar em decisões políticas Analistas do mercado financeiro mostram que o receio de acionistas e investidores é que os democratas façam força contra a construção de novos data centers em solo americano. Um dos motivos é o fato desses centros de dados exigirem grandes volumes de água para resfriar os servidores, além dos gastos em energia e o barulho. Uma estimativa do UBS aponta que quase 30% da capacidade adicional de data centers esperada para 2028 nos Estados Unidos tem risco de sofrer paralisações. Como o mercado de IA se expandiu rapidamente nos últimos anos, isso se tornou um empecilho para investidores da categoria, que demandam novas instalações para o treinamento dos modelos de IA. Gigantes responsáveis por essas tecnologias, como a Amazon e Alphabet (dona do Google) viram quedas de 2,2%. No caso da Microsoft, o recuo foi de 3,6%. Aliás, a companhia de Redmond já teria começado a apertar a supervisão de projetos terceirizados de data centers. Por falar em IA e problemas financeiros, o caso de infidelidade do CEO da Nvidia pode trazer grandes consequências à empresa e ao mercado global. Não esqueça de continuar ligado no TecMundo para acompanhar outros artigos como esse e não perder as principais informações da indústria de tecnologia. Com informações de Reuters.

artigo.texto: Plataforma de IA – O Ministério das Comunicações vai aplicar R$ 46,3 milhões no desenvolvimento de uma plataforma nacional de gerenciamento de data centers. Batizado de Prisma, o projeto utilizará inteligência artificial (IA) para distribuir recursos computacionais entre diferentes estruturas, buscando melhorar a eficiência e a segurança do processamento de dados no país. A iniciativa, aprovada pelo Conselho Gestor do Fundo para o Desenvolvimento Tecnológico das Telecomunicações (Funttel), pretende reduzir gastos operacionais, consumo de energia e riscos relacionados à proteção de informações estratégicas. A execução ficará sob responsabilidade do Centro Brasileiro de Inovação em Tecnologias da Informação e da Comunicação (CPQD), em Campinas (SP), com recursos administrados pela Finep. LEIA: Suposto ataque à Polícia Civil de SP envolve venda de dados por US$ 40 mil Funcionamento do Prisma A plataforma identificará automaticamente os locais mais adequados para processar cada conjunto de dados, incluindo estruturas menores distribuídas pelo território nacional. Com isso, as informações poderão ser tratadas mais perto de sua origem, diminuindo o tempo de resposta dos serviços digitais. Segundo a superintendente da Área de Saúde e Transformação Digital da Finep, Joana Meirelles, a proposta é oferecer uma infraestrutura segura e sustentável para áreas como saúde, defesa, segurança pública, educação e telecomunicações. O diretor de Tecnologia e Inovação do CPQD, Gustavo Correa Lima, destaca que a descentralização também amplia o controle sobre as informações: “Além de tornar mais rápidos o processamento e o acesso às informações, essa arquitetura permite maior controle sobre o dado que está na borda”. Eficiência energética e autonomia tecnológica Entre os benefícios previstos estão a redução da pegada de carbono dos data centers, maior resistência a falhas no fornecimento de energia e proteção contra ataques cibernéticos. O projeto também contempla soluções de armazenamento elétrico para manter os serviços em funcionamento durante instabilidades no abastecimento. A plataforma deverá seguir padrões internacionais de segurança e as diretrizes da Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD). Para o ministro das Comunicações, Frederico de Siqueira Filho, o investimento também representa um avanço na autonomia tecnológica brasileira e na redução da dependência de soluções estrangeiras. O desenvolvimento do Prisma terá duração de 36 meses, a partir da assinatura do convênio de pesquisa, desenvolvimento e inovação entre Finep e CPQD. artigo.texto: ENERGY Governor’s energy council recommends data centers, large users cover grid costs Report offers 22 recommendations, including zero-carbon standard shift A council appointed by Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham is urging lawmakers to make data centers and other large power users pay for the grid costs they create, according to a report released this month. In April, Lujan Grisham established the 13-member Energy Affordability and Grid Reliability Council through an executive order to develop recommendations addressing energy affordability, grid reliability, infrastructure investment and economic development. State Economic Development Secretary Rob Black, acting Energy, Minerals and Natural Resources Secretary Erin Taylor and Rep. Meredith Dixon, D-Albuquerque, were among the public officials appointed to the council. El Paso Electric President and CEO Kelly Tomblin and TXNM Energy President and CEO Don Tarry also serve on the council. The council’s report includes 22 recommendations to inform future legislative, regulatory and administrative actions. Among them: Large industrial customers should “bear costs attributable to serving them and existing customers should be held harmless from costs and financial risks caused by new large loads,” the report said. The report said the state Energy, Minerals and Natural Resources Department should develop a database of large electricity users, noting that industrial customers accounted for about 47% of New Mexico’s 2025 electricity sales, followed by commercial users at 30% and residential at 23%. “Meeting growing demand requires careful planning and prudent investment,” Tarry said in a statement announcing the report. The report notes that future energy demand is expected to grow, though the “scale, timing and location of that growth remain uncertain.” “New Mexico’s three major (investor-owned utilities) are all evaluating significant load growth scenarios, including growth from data centers, manufacturing, electrification of oil and gas operations and in other industrial processes, transportation electrification, and broader economic development,” the report said. Already, most New Mexicans have seen increases on their monthly electricity bills — under a staggered rate increase approved last year — to help cover the cost of system expansions for the Public Service Company of New Mexico. Lujan Grisham in 2019 signed into law the Energy Transition Act requiring utilities to go carbon-free by midcentury. The New Mexico Public Regulation Commission in May 2025 approved PNM’s phased-in rate increase request to help cover the costs of renewable energy buildout. That PRC approval hiked average monthly residential bills by roughly $12. The report also recommends that lawmakers shift the state’s renewable-energy standard to a “zero-carbon” standard, giving utilities more flexibility to meet clean energy targets with non-emitting resources such as nuclear power. The council’s report also suggests other measures, such as broadening the availability of energy infrastructure securitization for utilities, which would allow utilities to recover infrastructure costs via bonds backed by ratepayer revenue, thereby reducing financing costs and passing on savings to ratepayers. In a statement, Lujan Grisham said the recommendations “give us a path to protect ratepayers, bring more power onto the grid and keep our energy clean, all at the same time.” Added Dixon, “These recommendations give legislators a practical starting point for protecting customers while supporting responsible growth.” Justin Horwath covers tech and energy for the Journal. You can reach him at jhorwath@abqjournal.com.

artigo.texto: The Telangana Electricity Regulatory Commission (TGERC) has granted in-principle approval to state distribution companies, Telangana State Southern Power Distribution Company Limited (TGSPDCL) and Telangana State Northern Power Distribution Company Limited (TGNPDCL), to procure 7,300 MW of renewable energy along with advanced energy storage systems. The proposed procurement will involve long-term power supply agreements ranging from 15 to 25 years and aims to meet the state’s growing electricity demand while supporting national renewable energy targets. The approval follows a petition submitted by the distribution companies highlighting the need to strengthen Telangana’s future power supply. According to the Central Electricity Authority’s (CEA) Resource Adequacy Plan, the state’s annual energy requirement is expected to increase from 1,08,125 million units (MU) in FY 2026-27 to 1,77,219 MU by FY 2035-36. Peak electricity demand is also projected to rise by nearly 49.4% during this period. The distribution companies are also preparing for the expiry of several existing power purchase agreements, which could create gaps in energy availability and peak power supply. At the same time, meeting the Ministry of Power’s increasing Renewable Consumption Obligation (RCO) targets has become important to avoid regulatory and financial penalties. The approved procurement plan includes four major renewable energy components. The first involves 800 MW of standalone wind power under a 25-year agreement. This capacity is expected to complement solar generation and improve the overall renewable energy supply profile. The second component covers 3,000 MW of solar power integrated with a 6,000 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), configured at 1,000 MW for six hours. The project will operate under a 25-year agreement, allowing electricity generated during periods of high solar availability to be stored and supplied during evening peak demand. The third component includes 2,000 MW of Renewable Energy Round-the-Clock (RE-RTC) power for 25 years. This arrangement is intended to provide a more consistent renewable electricity supply and support the state’s base-load requirements. Additionally, the plan includes 2,000 MWh of Firm and Dispatchable Renewable Energy (FDRE), configured at 500 MW for four hours, under a 15-year agreement to address peak demand periods. During the public consultation process, consumer groups and industry stakeholders raised concerns about the procurement process, demand projections and the possible impact on electricity tariffs. Some participants questioned the initiation of tendering activities before obtaining formal regulatory approval. They also highlighted the importance of promoting distributed renewable energy projects and creating opportunities for local micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs). In response, TGERC directed the distribution companies to obtain prior approval from the Commission before initiating bidding for future long-term or medium-term power procurement. The Commission also clarified that DISCOMs can participate in competitive procurement processes conducted through the Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI) or use state-level tendering mechanisms. The selection between these routes should be based on the most cost-effective landed tariff at the Telangana periphery. The approved renewable procurement is expected to strengthen the state’s energy security, reduce dependence on conventional power sources and limit consumer exposure to rising fuel-linked electricity costs.

artigo.texto: Google’s Utah Deal Puts Geothermal Power on the Data Center Map Key Highlights - Fervo expects the first of eight generating units dedicated to Google’s 396 MW contract to deliver power in mid-2028. A separate expansion option could bring geothermal electricity directly to a proposed Utah campus. - Indonesia’s Pertamina Geothermal Energy is studying a 5 MW data center pilot at an existing field, where it must account for electricity already committed to the national utility. - Google’s first geothermal agreements in Asia target 10 MW for Taiwan’s grid. In Kenya, available power and disagreements over capacity payments have delayed Microsoft and G42’s proposed cloud campus. - New Zealand and Iceland offer two operating examples. Microsoft buys renewable attributes from a 51.4 MW plant supplying New Zealand’s grid, while Verne operates an Icelandic campus served by geothermal and hydroelectric power. In its November 9 project update, Fervo Energy identified the eight geothermal generating units it is building in southwestern Utah to supply Google with 396 megawatts of grid-connected power. As Fervo explained on its third-quarter earnings call, Google has agreed to pay for the power over 15 years even if it never builds the proposed Beaver County data center. The expansion option ties geography more closely to the deal. If Google elects to buy roughly 600 MW more, the companies are pursuing a direct connection that could carry that power from Cape Station to the proposed campus. Years before the AI boom, data centers gave other industries a working example of how a large electricity customer could bring renewable generation to market. In October 2014, Rich Miller reported for Data Center Knowledge on a field of more than 57,000 solar panels serving the QTS Princeton campus in New Jersey. The array could produce up to 14.1 MW. That same year, Facebook, Hewlett-Packard, and Intel joined General Motors, Walmart, Mars, and six other companies in asking utilities for competitive renewable power, access to new projects, and contracts long enough to support investment. By January 2017, 65 companies had signed those buyers’ principles. When Miller revisited the subject in DCF in March 2017, he found that data center providers had contracted for more than 1.2 GW of renewable power in the preceding year. In 2025, Google alone signed agreements for more than 12 GW of new clean energy. Corporate buyers have learned how to help finance power plants at a scale few would have imagined a decade ago. What a data center developer still needs to know is how much electricity will be available on its local grid at two in the morning, through a lull in the wind, and on the day the next hall opens. That question runs through the new DCF Global franchise, most recently in our examination of Britain’s bargain with the AI data center industry, where access to power comes with obligations to host communities and electricity customers. DCF’s geothermal reporting traces one route toward meeting those obligations. In 2023, Google and Fervo’s Nevada pilot began delivering electricity to the local grid. We subsequently examined the case for locating geothermal generation behind the meter. In Utah, Fervo and Google are now pursuing both approaches at the same field. Utah’s First 33 MW Is Operating. Google’s Eight Units Come Next. The clearest measure of progress at Cape Station comes from three generating blocks in different stages of commissioning. The first, rated at 33 MW, entered commercial operation on September 30. By November 9, the second had synchronized with the grid and was delivering test electricity. The third was mechanically complete, with crews checking equipment and systems ahead of live operation. Fervo expects the latter two units to reach commercial operation by January 1, 2027, completing the first phase. Google’s contracted supply will come from blocks four through 11, a group Fervo calls Cape Google 400. Fervo expects first power from those units in mid-2028 and is targeting full contracted capacity by the end of that year. Under the take-or-pay agreement, Fervo has a committed customer as it drills wells and builds generating equipment. Google can secure a substantial block of new supply before settling the scope and location of its Utah data center. The additional 600 MW involves a different decision. Under the agreement announced in September, Fervo committed to offering Google an option to increase its purchases to nearly 1 GW by June 2030. The companies are pursuing behind-the-meter delivery for that expansion under Utah’s SB132 framework. If the arrangement proceeds, proximity to the field would become a condition of receiving that power directly. The nearly 1 GW figure describes potential electricity purchases. The campus remains subject to engineering, approvals, and a commercial decision by Google. In Indonesia, Who Has a Claim on the Next 5 MW? At Kamojang in West Java, Pertamina Geothermal Energy is approaching site selection from the opposite direction. PGE already operates a producing geothermal field and wants to allocate 5 MW to a data center pilot there. Before the company can offer those megawatts to a new customer, it must account for its existing deliveries to Indonesia’s national utility, PLN. At a November 4 briefing covered by Indonesian news agency ANTARA, PGE executives said they had completed an initial technology study for a pilot designed to run entirely on power from the field. The company was examining commercial terms, prospective data center partners, and revisions to the project’s environmental assessment. According to ThinkGeoEnergy’s account of the proposal, PGE expected the reviews to run through late 2026 or early 2027 and envisaged a pilot lasting one to two years. The proposed 5 MW is an allocation at the plant. The share available to servers would depend on cooling and other facility loads. A campus operator would also need to know what carries those loads when

artigo.texto: PRESS RELEASE: Utility-scale solar developers are increasingly co-locating battery storage with new solar photovoltaic capacity. As of September 2026, over 16% of new utility-scale solar capacity added this year is co-located with operable battery storage, compared with 2% in 2017, according to data reported to EIA by operators. Reported plans for solar additions scheduled to come online in the last three months of this year show that the share with co-located battery storage could increase to 19% this year. Longer-term plans indicate that this trend will continue, with the portion increasing to more than 30% in plans submitted for 2027 and 2028. When operators co-locate battery storage with solar, they can direct solar electricity output to the grid or to the battery, depending on the wholesale prices. Wholesale prices in regions with large solar participation tend to fall when solar contributions are high and rise as they decrease. Plants with both solar and battery storage can manage the combined output of their generating resources to maximize their value in a changing wholesale price environment. Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, EIA-860M, Monthly Update to the Annual Electric Generator Report We publish unit-level generator inventory data based on our annual and monthly data collections, including information on design attributes for all utility-scale plants. Although battery storage and solar units at the same plant often enter commercial service at different times, the EIA-860 and EIA-860M data collection program tracks these developments and provides a monthly summary that can be used to identify co-located technologies. Southwest states have higher-than-average solar capacity shares relative to their total generating capacity and also have higher levels of co-located utility-scale solar and battery capacity. As of September, 13% of the total U.S. utility-scale generating capacity is solar photovoltaic, and 18% of that is co-located with battery storage. The share of solar generation co-located with battery capacity in California, Arizona, New Mexico, and Nevada is more than double the national average. Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, EIA-860M, Monthly Update to the Annual Electric Generator Report Principal contributors: Glenn McGrath, Alex Mey

artigo.texto: Less than a month before leaving office, Gov. Mike Dunleavy announced that his administration had formed a public corporation intended to attract data centers to Alaska, along with a new platform to allow individuals to invest in the projects. The initiative is led by the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority, an embattled state-owned corporation whose board members were appointed by Dunleavy. AIDEA partnered with Plural, a California-based startup whose chief executive, Adam Silver, met with Dunleavy several times last year. The Monday announcement about the partnership is part of a flurry of activity as Dunleavy seeks to cement his policy priorities before he leaves office. His administration also announced this week that it transferred thousands of acres in state land to AIDEA to develop an industrial park that could include data centers, and separately approved a 50-year lease for a data center in the Arctic. AIDEA is the sole owner of Alaska Data Corp. LLC, a corporation that formed in March. The company’s president is listed as Brandon Brefczynski, who is AIDEA’s deputy director. The company’s vice president is listed as Dave Stieren, a former talk radio host. Both Brefczynski and Stieren have worked for Dunleavy or AIDEA since 2019. AIDEA board members voted earlier this year to send $20 million to the newly formed Alaska Data Corp., as first reported by the Anchorage Press. Data centers and their construction were a topic of debate in Alaska leading up to this month’s elections. Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, who is poised to succeed Dunleavy as governor, said he would support a moratorium on data center construction in Alaska until the state adopts a comprehensive regulatory package. Kreiss-Tomkins has also said he would support additional oversight of AIDEA, which has been used in recent years to promote Dunleavy’s policy priorities with little public input or oversight. Dunleavy, who has not spoken publicly about what he intends to do after he leaves office next month, released a statement Monday calling for data centers to be built in the state. “As the country debates data centers, in Alaska, we have an opportunity to learn from what has occurred in other states and do it better here in our great state,” Dunleavy said. “If there is an opportunity for data centers here in Alaska, let’s do it right. Let’s build them the right way, let’s locate them in the right places, and let’s explore how individual Alaskans can have an ownership stake so that they clearly and directly benefit all Alaskans. Here in Alaska, we can demonstrate to the world how to do data centers well, so they are a positive, not a negative.” Dunleavy’s spokespeople did not respond to questions about the state’s partnership with Plural, the California startup backing the initiatives, which launched in 2024. Neither did Stieren. Dunleavy first met Plural’s chief executive, Adam Silver, in San Francisco in June 2025, according to his public calendar. In the ensuing months, Dunleavy met with Silver at least seven times, including four times in Washington, D.C. Two of those meetings also included Alaska’s Republican U.S. Rep. Nick Begich. The meetings also included leaders of AIDEA and Dunleavy’s former acting attorney general, Stephen Cox. The fate of the project — and AIDEA itself — remains up in the air with Dunleavy’s impending departure from office. Aubrey Wieber, founder of a progressive advocacy group called the 907 Initiative, said Dunleavy is “using AIDEA to move hundreds of millions of public dollars to Lower 48 corporations he and his closest political allies are tied to,” as he prepares to leave office. “Dunleavy is shelling out our cash to some company named Plural to build multiple data centers as quickly as they can, when he has less than a month in office,” Wieber said. “If Plural had any real interest in doing this, they would hit pause and start building a relationship with the incoming governor’s administration.” A representative of Plural did not respond to an email seeking comment.

artigo.texto: Phillips 66 stock adds SAF portal to carbon-market strategy Published on 11/10/2026 at 14:40 | Editorial responsibility: Rafael Müller, Editor-in-Chief AD HOC NEWS SAF Portal Broadens Phillips 66 Offering - The new platform lets companies buy sustainable aviation fuel environmental attributes through a book-and-claim model. - Customers receive documentation covering the emissions reductions linked to their purchases. - The initiative expands Phillips 66's sustainable aviation fuel sales and distribution strategy. Phillips 66 launched an Environmental Attributes Portal on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, giving companies a direct way to purchase environmental attributes linked to sustainable aviation fuel. Biofuels International Magazine reported that the platform is designed for businesses seeking to address emissions from business travel and upstream transportation. The portal uses a book-and-claim model. Companies can purchase the environmental attributes even when the physical sustainable aviation fuel is not available at their location, allowing the environmental benefit to be separated from the fuel's physical delivery. New Channel For SAF Customers Phillips 66 said the platform lets customers select the environmental attributes they want and complete purchases through flexible payment methods, including credit cards. There is no minimum purchase requirement, which broadens access beyond large-volume fuel buyers. After a purchase, customers receive an Environmental Attribute Document summarizing the associated carbon dioxide emissions reduction. That documentation can support internal emissions analysis and corporate reporting, making the portal a commercial tool as well as a transaction platform. Sunny Lopez, senior director of aviation and sustainable fuel sales at Phillips 66, said the company built the portal around its experience across feedstock sourcing, production, fuel delivery and distribution. The comments underline the company's effort to simplify access to SAF-related claims as corporate buyers face pressure to reduce transport emissions. Building A Broader SAF Platform The portal adds to Phillips 66's recent SAF initiatives. The company announced an agreement with Chooose in 2026 to integrate the technology provider's platform into existing SAF processes, with the aim of streamlining fuel delivery, distribution and documentation. For investors, the portal offers a route to serve sustainability demand without requiring every customer to take physical SAF at its operating locations. Its financial contribution will depend on transaction volumes, customer adoption and the availability of qualifying SAF attributes. The launch therefore supports Phillips 66's commercial positioning in renewable fuels, while the article does not provide revenue or earnings guidance for the portal. Phillips 66 stock traded at 220.80 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 14:33 CET on Tuesday, November 10. artigo.texto: The Nefer Benban Solar and BESS (Battery Energy Storage System) project in Egypt, developed by Infinity Power, secures US$127 million in financing to advance construction. The project is being developed by Nefer Benban for Renewable Energy, a special-purpose company owned by Infinity Power and HAU Energy and is designed to strengthen Egypt’s renewable electricity capacity and grid reliability. Meanwhile, Egypt’s Obelisk solar and battery project has begun operations, marking further progress in the country’s renewable energy expansion. The financing package includes a US$65 million construction bridge loan from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD). Meanwhile, Germany’s development finance institution, DEG, will provide an equal amount. Together, the funding will support a 200MW solar plant and a 120MWh battery energy storage system (BESS) at Benban Solar Park near Aswan. Additionally, the EBRD identifies HAU Energy as the borrower, while Nefer Benban is the project company. The solar-storage development will combine daytime solar generation with battery storage that can release electricity during evening peak-demand periods. Therefore, the project is intended to help manage fluctuations in renewable generation and improve the reliability of electricity supplied to the national grid. The electricity will be sold to the Egyptian Electricity Transmission Company (EETC) under a 25-year power purchase agreement. Project Scope and Technical Specifications The project will use solar PV panels to generate electricity. Meanwhile, the 120MWh battery system will store excess daytime output. It will then release the stored electricity when demand rises or solar generation declines. Project disclosures list the solar plant’s installed capacity at approximately 200MW. However, the EBRD’s November 2026 announcement specifies a 258.5MWp photovoltaic (PV) array. Additionally, the project is among Egypt’s early utility-scale developments combining solar generation with battery storage. The facility will store surplus daytime electricity and release it after sunset. Consequently, it will extend the availability of solar power beyond daylight hours. It is also expected to reduce fluctuations in renewable electricity supply. The project is located within the wider Benban Solar Park, one of Egypt’s major renewable energy hubs. Furthermore, the established site provides an opportunity to expand solar generation and integrate additional flexibility into the electricity grid. Financing Structure and Project Partners The US$127 million financing package comprises a US$65 million construction bridge loan from the EBRD and an equal contribution from DEG. Additionally, the funding will cover eligible development and construction costs. These include engineering, procurement, installation, testing and commissioning. However, the package represents construction debt financing, not the project’s total capital cost. The project has also secured a separate EBRD financing commitment of up to US$63.5 million for Nefer Benban for Renewable Energy. This comprises up to US$56 million from the bank’s own resources and US$7.5 million from the Clean Technology Fund. Additionally, the package supports the combined solar and storage development. However, the two financing arrangements represent separate facilities and should be reported separately when outlining the project’s total funding. Infinity Power is a joint venture between Infinity and Masdar. It focuses on developing renewable energy projects across Africa. Meanwhile, HAU Energy is an investment platform established to develop renewable energy projects in Egypt. It is associated with Hassan Allam Utilities, Meridiam and the EBRD. Additionally, Nefer Benban for Renewable Energy serves as the project-specific company for the Benban development. Construction Status and Expected Impact The financing is intended to support construction and commissioning activities of the Nefer Benban Solar Project. However, the financing announcement alone does not establish that the facility has completed construction or entered commercial operation. The EBRD’s project information describes the development as an implementation-stage investment, while its latest announcement confirms the planned solar and battery configuration. Once operational, the facility will supply electricity under a long-term power purchase agreement with EETC. Additionally, the battery system will release stored solar power during peak demand after sunset. Consequently, it will help the grid accommodate a greater share of variable renewable energy. The Nefer Benban Solar Project also supports Egypt’s energy transition goals. These include expanding private-sector renewable energy capacity and reducing reliance on fossil-fuel generation. However, its long-term contribution will depend on timely construction, successful commissioning and grid integration. Furthermore, its impact will depend on the facility’s operational performance. artigo.texto: Florida Power & Light commissions largest-capacity battery energy storage project Florida Power & Light Company (FPL) announced it had commissioned the Lansing Smith Battery Energy Storage System, the largest battery energy storage system by capacity for the company. The battery storage system in Bay County marks a milestone in the company’s ongoing investments in cost-effective, innovative technologies, the company said, and will increase grid resiliency while helping to deliver reliable electricity and keep customer bills low. The new facility is FPL’s largest battery energy storage system by energy storage capacity, and can supply 400 MW of electricity for up to four hours. The system will store up to 1,600 MW of energy, enough to power 300,000 homes over that four-hour period. Developed on land that previously served as a coal storage area, the site will play a role in supporting the state’s growing energy needs while enhancing reliability across Northwest Florida, officials said. “The commissioning of the Lansing Smith Battery Energy Storage System represents smart investments in the future of our electric grid,” Tim Oliver, vice president of FPL development, said. “By incorporating cutting-edge battery storage technology into our diverse energy mix, we’re strengthening reliability, increasing resiliency and continuing our commitment to provide reliable service while helping keep bills as low as possible for our customers.” Officials said the system will use lithium-ion batteries to store electricity when costs are low and discharged to the electric grid when demand is high. “As Florida continues to grow, projects like Lansing Smith Battery Energy Storage System help ensure we’re prepared to meet our customers’ energy needs today and well into the future,” J.T. Young, vice president and general manager of FPL Northwest Florida, said. “This facility provides additional flexibility to support a reliable electric grid while helping us continue delivering the value and service our customers depend on every day.”

artigo.texto: UK and EU officials are on the brink of an agreement that would link their carbon emissions markets, a move that would save companies millions of euros in carbon border taxes, as the diplomatic push for deeper EU-UK integration accelerates ahead of a key post-Brexit summit next week. The deal would enable carbon permits to be traded across the two emissions systems. The UK’s post-Brexit emissions trading scheme was modelled on the EU’s. The UK’s carbon border adjustment mechanism, which is set to come into force early next year, is also based on the EU’s carbon border levy, a tax on imported industrial goods which are linked to high carbon emissions. Once the UK and EU emissions trading systems are linked, that would pave the way for them to be exempted from their respective CBAM laws. On Tuesday (10 November), UK trade minister Jonathan Reynolds and Europe minister Hamish Falconer held talks with EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič to push for a UK inclusion in the EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ initiative, that would allow UK firms to retain access to the EU’s industrial supply chain. Meetings with vice-president Stéphane Séjourne and defence commissioner Andrius Kubilius were also on the agenda.

artigo.texto: U.S. battery startup Solid Power is moving to restore the competitiveness of the U.S. battery industry with all-solid-state batteries. Rather than directly producing finished batteries, it is focusing on supplying solid electrolytes, a key material, and using existing manufacturers' production equipment. The company is seeking a turnaround with next-generation technology in a battery market led by Asian companies. InsideEVs, an electric-vehicle outlet, reported on Wednesday that Solid Power is concentrating its capabilities on developing and producing sulfide-based solid electrolytes, a key material for commercialising all-solid-state batteries. It aims to speed up commercialisation by having existing battery makers adopt its technology in their production processes. Solid Power, a Colorado-based solid electrolyte specialist, is competing with U.S. all-solid-state battery startups such as QuantumScape and Factorial. The company expects all-solid-state batteries to increase driving range and reduce charging time compared with existing lithium-ion batteries, while also lowering fire risk. Securing stable quality and yields in mass production remains a challenge. Solid Power Chief Executive John Van Scoter (존 밴 스코터) stressed that all-solid-state batteries could lead a rebound in the U.S. battery industry. "All-solid-state batteries could be a way for the United States to re-enter the battery industry and secure competitiveness," he said. Solid Power's differentiating strategy is to focus on electrolytes rather than finished cells. Electrolytes are a key material that helps lithium ions move inside a battery. Unlike existing lithium-ion batteries that use liquid electrolytes, Solid Power is developing sulfide-based solid electrolytes. The company highlights that the technology is easy to integrate into existing battery manufacturers' production systems. Van Scoter said all-solid-state cells can be produced using roll-to-roll equipment used in existing lithium-ion battery production. He said this can reduce the burden of building new plants or replacing production equipment on a large scale. It is also expanding its production base. Last month, Solid Power set up a 'Mobius' pilot production line at its Thornton plant in Colorado. The facility is targeting start-up by year-end and is expected to add annual production capacity of 45 tonnes of solid electrolyte. Including existing facilities, the company's pilot production capacity will rise to 75 tonnes a year. It plans to supply the produced electrolytes to automakers and battery companies. Cooperation with automakers and battery makers is also continuing. Solid Power has worked with Ford, BMW, Samsung SDI and SK On. Joint development agreements with Ford and BMW have been concluded, and it has shifted its focus to discussing ways to expand production with major battery manufacturers. In particular, a three-way agreement with BMW and Samsung SDI is a cooperation model that divides roles among the companies. Solid Power supplies solid electrolytes, Samsung SDI produces battery cells, and BMW is responsible for developing battery modules and packs. The approach is to push commercialisation by linking materials technology with existing manufacturers' production capabilities. The company also presented high figures on performance. Solid Power said using its sulfide electrolyte with a silicon anode and a nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) cathode can raise energy density to 390 Wh per kg and enable more than 1,000 charge-discharge cycles. It said applying a lithium-metal anode could raise energy density to 440 Wh per kg. It said the figures are not the performance of the electrolyte itself, but what can be expected when combined with electrode materials and cell design. Actual battery performance varies depending on the technology of the company that designs and manufactures the cell. Van Scoter also said, "We make the core that makes the cell work," but explained that key indicators such as energy density and lifespan depend on the final cell design. Technical hurdles remain. A representative issue is dendrites. If needle-shaped lithium structures grow inside a battery, they can cause internal short circuits or reduce capacity. Solid Power said it is putting substantial engineering capabilities into solving the problem. Testing for actual vehicle application has also proceeded. BMW last year released images of an i7 prototype fitted with Solid Power's silicon-anode-based solid-state battery. The timing of application in mass-produced vehicles has not yet been set in detail. Solid Power is also focusing on defence, drones and humanoid robots, in addition to electric vehicles, as early markets. It views these areas as having shorter product certification processes and faster replacement cycles than automobiles. Van Scoter said of drones and robots that "the certification cycle is shorter and the platform life cycle is much faster." Solid Power expects all-solid-state batteries to be applied first to some premium electric vehicles in the late 2020s and then spread to a broader market in the early 2030s. Attention is on whether the United States, which ceded leadership in the lithium-ion battery market to Asian companies including those in South Korea and China, can reshape the competitive landscape through next-generation battery technology.
